pages.title: Introduction
pages.description: Loomplane is a self-hosted deployment platform that takes the monorepos you already have from source to running services across your own clouds.
pages.text:
Loomplane takes a Go, Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript, Python or JVM monorepo, or an application split across several repositories, and deploys it to the clouds you already pay for. You give it the repositories, on GitHub or GitLab. It reads the code (and never runs it) to find your services and the databases they need, drafts a `loomplane.yaml`, and plans what a deployment would do. Once someone approves that exact plan, it builds each service on its cloud's own builder and deploys it.

A Next.js app goes to Vercel. A Go API goes to Cloud Run. A worker goes to ECS on Fargate. Postgres lands on Cloud SQL or RDS, and every service gets its connection string through the cloud's own secret store. After that, Loomplane keeps checking that what runs is what it deployed.

Your applications don't need Forge, or Go. Everything runs in your own clouds, on your own accounts, and your traffic never passes through Loomplane.

Clouds aren't the only place it reaches. A machine you run yourself, even one behind a router, can join as a node with `loomctl node join`. It dials out to Loomplane, so there's no port to open. Nodes join, report what the machine has and take signed updates today, and deploying to them comes next.

## Who it's for

If you run a monorepo and you're tired of maintaining a pile of per-cloud deploy scripts, this is for you. It also suits teams that want a person to look at the exact set of changes before any cloud account is touched, and teams that just want one place to see what runs where.

You run Loomplane yourself, and it's small: one API and dashboard process, one analysis worker and one PostgreSQL database. It's free software under the AGPL-3.0. If you run a changed version as a service for other people, you have to offer them the source of your changes too.

## Where to start

- Quick start (/docs/quick-start)
- How it works (/docs/how-it-works)
- Concepts (/docs/concepts/projects-and-environments)
- Clouds (/docs/clouds)
- Nodes (/docs/clouds/nodes)
- Database services (/docs/services/database-services)
- Guides (/docs/guides/deploy-a-monorepo)
- AI agents (/docs/agents/mcp-server)
- Reference (/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml)
- Operations (/docs/operations/production-on-docker)
- Extending (/docs/extending/provider-plugins)

## What's solid and what isn't

Every milestone on the roadmap, through operational maturity, is built. Most cloud paths are tested against fakes that answer the way each real API does. We've also run the Vercel static-site path against a real account, and the acceptance runs on real Google Cloud and AWS accounts are what we do next. Check a target against your own account before you rely on it. Nodes are the first of five phases: they join, report, update and can be revoked, but nothing deploys to them yet.

  Federation (one application spanning clusters and clouds) is still being built and isn't ready for production. Several managed database and recovery paths are qualified against controlled endpoints only, and live cloud qualification is pending. Each page says so where it applies.

pages.title: Talking to the agent
pages.description: Ask the workspace's agent questions from the panel on any page, or from the terminal with loomctl agent.
pages.text:
Once the agent is on for your workspace, you can talk to it from any page. Press ⌘J (Ctrl+J elsewhere), click **Ask the agent** in the top bar, or click **Assistant** in the sidebar. In a terminal, run `loomctl agent`. You need `agent:use`, which every member has, and the agent works with your permissions, not its own. If it isn't on yet, start with [the built-in agent](/docs/agents/built-in-agent).

Ask it things like "why did the last deployment of api fail?" or "what's the latest commit and release of shop?". It reads live state with its tools, links what it mentions, and asks before anything risky.

## The panel

The agent lives in a panel beside your work, so you never leave the page you're on. ⌘J opens it and closes it again, and the command menu has it as **Ask the agent**. The panel can sit in three places, picked from the layout button in its header:

| Place | What you get |
|---|---|
| Docked | On the right, beside the page. Drag its left edge to make it wider or narrower (the arrow keys work too, once the edge has focus), and double-click the edge to put it back. The page scrolls in its own column. |
| Floating | Over the page, in the bottom right corner. |
| Full width | Takes the page's place, with your conversations in a column beside the chat. The expand button in the header gets you here and back. |

On a phone the panel covers the screen. Whatever you pick, Loomplane remembers it in your browser, along with the width, whether the panel was open, and the conversation you had open, so a reload puts you back where you were. If you close the panel while the agent is still answering, the answer keeps coming in, and it's there when you open the panel again.

Old links to `/assistant` still work. They open the panel at full width, on the conversation the link names.

The orb in the panel's header changes with what the agent is doing. It turns slowly when the agent is idle, faster while you type and faster again while the agent works out an answer. A ring goes round it while a tool runs, it pulses while the answer streams in, it turns amber when the agent is waiting on you, and it goes red and stops when a turn failed.

## What a message is about

Above the box, two chips say what you're asking about.

The first is the conversation's scope: a project, or the whole workspace. A new conversation starts on the project of the page you're on, and you can pick another one, or the whole workspace, before you send. After the first message the scope is fixed, and the chip shows it. To change it, start a new conversation.

The second is the page you're looking at, such as "Service web in api, production" or "Deployment plan_42". It goes with your message, so "why is this slow?" on a service's page is about that service, and the agent reads that service before it answers. Click the × to leave the page out of a message; it stays out until you move to another page, and the dashed chip puts it back. The page only goes along when it fits the scope: a page from another project doesn't. Each message you sent shows the page it came from, as a small link above it.

The suggestions on a new conversation follow the page too. On a service you get questions about that service, on a deployment questions about that deployment.

Enter sends and Shift+Enter starts a new line. Up in an empty box brings back the last message you sent. One message is answered at a time: while the agent is on one, the box is off and its button is **Stop**, which cancels the task. If a message goes in anyway (from another tab, say), the server says no with "The agent is still on your last message. Wait for it to finish, answer what it asked, or stop it." The same message comes back from the API as a 409.

## Your conversations

The clock button in the panel's header opens your conversations. You can search them by title or project, filter by **Needs you**, **Working** or **Failed** and by project, and group them by project or by date (the button beside the search switches between the two). Each group folds away.

Hover a conversation to pin it, or open its menu to rename or delete it. Pinned conversations sit at the top, in every browser you sign in from. Deleting one takes it out of your list for good, and stops the agent if it's still working on it. Only the person who started a conversation can pin, rename or delete it.

## What answers look like

The agent writes Markdown, and the panel renders a few things beyond plain text:

- Code comes in blocks with the language named, colours for the common ones (shell, YAML, JSON, Go, HCL, Dockerfile, SQL and a few more) and a copy button.
- Tables put a status word such as **Failed** or **Live** beside a coloured dot, line numbers up on the right, and copy as CSV.
- Links to Loomplane pages stay in the workspace and show what kind of page they open. Links to commits, releases and repositories open in a new tab.
- Figures can come as headline tiles, as a chart (bar, horizontal bar, stacked, line or area), or as a timeline of releases. Every chart opens as a table too, and copies as CSV.
- A note, tip or warning comes as a coloured callout.

The agent only charts numbers its tools gave it. If a chart it wrote can't be drawn, the panel shows what it wrote instead, and says so.

## Steps and how risky they are

Each tool the agent uses shows as one quiet line between the words, such as "Listed deployments" or "Checked the repositories". Steps taken back to back fold into one line that says what they did and how many there were, and it stays open while the agent is on it. Click a line to see the tool, its arguments and what it returned.

A step that's more than a read carries a label for how risky it is. There are six, one for each class on [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#the-risk-table).

| Label | Class | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Read | `read` | It looked at something (no label on the line) |
| Change | `change` | It changed something within your permissions |
| Deploy, not production | `deploy_nonproduction` | It approved a staging, preview or development plan |
| Production release | `promote_production` | A production release, which a person approves |
| Removes production data | `destroy_production` | Deleting or replacing something in production that holds data, always a person |
| Needs a person | `secret_or_external` | A secret or an outside connection, always a person |

A step that failed says so, a step that was refused says "refused", and a step that never got a result says "no result". A turn you stopped says "Stopped."

## Commits and releases

Ask the agent what a repository is on and it reads the repository's host: the head of the branch the project tracks (or the default branch), the latest release (or the newest tag, on Bitbucket, which has no releases), and the commit each environment runs, with links to all three. It works for GitHub, GitLab (self-managed too) and Bitbucket, through the same connections your deployments use. A repository the host won't show is reported as such, and the others still answer.

## When the agent asks you something

If the agent needs an answer, a question appears in the conversation with its options, and you answer it there. The same request shows on **Deployments, Agent** with everything else the agent is waiting on, and answering in either place settles both. Plan approvals, secrets and connections still go through their own cards, with the same rules as before.

## What a safety stop looks like

Loomplane scans every answer before it counts as an answer. If one holds a credential, such as an API key or a token, the agent stops that answer and the conversation shows "Loomplane's safety checks stopped this answer." Tool calls in that answer don't run. Other personal data, an email address for instance, is redacted in place and the answer goes on.

This assumes shield's stock output profile. If you've changed shield's profiles, the line between a stop and a redaction is yours.

## Who can read and add to a conversation

A conversation is private to the person who started it, with one exception.

Someone with `ai:manage`, which admins have, can read everyone's conversations in the workspace, for support and for audit. The API lists them with `GET /api/v1/agent/conversations?everyone=true`. Anyone else asking for a conversation that isn't theirs is told it doesn't exist.

Only the person who started a conversation can add to it, rename it, pin it or delete it. An admin can read it and stop its running task, and can't post in it. If you want to carry on from someone else's thread, start your own.

A message is up to 16,000 characters.

## Report an answer

If an answer is offensive, harmful or wrong, report it. Under every finished answer there's a flag button, **Report answer**. Pick a reason (Offensive, Harmful, Inaccurate or Something else), add a note of up to 1,000 characters if you want to, and send it. The panel says "Thanks. The report went to whoever runs this Loomplane."

Anyone who can read the conversation can report one of its answers: the person who started it, or someone with `ai:manage`. Report the same answer again and you update your report instead of adding a second one. Over the API, it's `POST /api/v1/agent/conversations/{id}/turns/{task}/flag`.

A report keeps the question, the answer (its first 8,000 characters), the reason and your note, plus the ids that say where they came from. If you have `ai:manage` and report an answer in someone else's conversation, their question goes with it. The workspace's audit trail records that a report was made, with those ids and the reason. It never holds the question, the answer or your note.

The report goes to the platform owner, not to your workspace's admins. On your own server that's whoever set it up, and on `app.loomplane.com` it's us. The owner reads reports under **Platform, Flagged answers**, filters them by Open, Dismissed or All, and dismisses one once it's dealt with. Other platform admins don't see the page. A dismissal lands in the audit trail of the workspace that reported, under the owner's name.

A report doesn't expire. It stays after the conversation is deleted, so the owner can still review it, until the owner removes it. To have one removed, ask the owner. On `app.loomplane.com` that's us, at the address under Your rights in the [privacy policy](/privacy#your-rights).

## From the terminal

`loomctl` reads `LOOMPLANE_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY`, as it does for every command. The agent acts as the person who made the key.

```bash
loomctl agent                       # a conversation at a prompt
loomctl agent --project shop        # about one project (slug, name or ID)
loomctl agent --conversation <id>   # pick one up again
```

At the `you>` prompt, type a message and press Enter. Text streams back, and each tool shows on stderr with its risk, such as `· list_deployments (read)`. A few slash commands:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `/stop` | Stops the agent's task |
| `/follow` | Watches a task again, after you left a question pending |
| `/new` | Your next message begins a new conversation |
| `/quit` | Leaves (so does Ctrl-D) |

A question from the agent shows at an `answer>` prompt with numbered options. Type a number or your own words. An empty line leaves it pending, and you can answer later with `loomctl agent requests answer <id> <text>`. Ctrl-C stops the task.

`loomctl agent conversations [--project <ref>] [--json]` lists yours. `loomctl agent conversations rename <id> <title>` renames one and `loomctl agent conversations delete <id>` deletes it, stopping the agent if it's still on it.

### One question, in a script

`loomctl agent ask` sends one message, prints the answer on stdout and exits.

```bash
loomctl agent ask "what changed in the last deployment of shop?" --project shop
```

Anything that isn't the answer, the steps and the reasons it failed, goes to stderr, so you can capture the answer cleanly. `--json` prints every event as one JSON line instead. `--conversation <id>` adds to a conversation you started.

| Exit | Means |
|---|---|
| 0 | The agent answered |
| 1 | It didn't: the task failed, was stopped by a safety check, or the server refused the message (the agent is off, the workspace is out of budget, or the conversation is busy) |
| 3 | The agent is waiting for a person, with `--no-wait` |
| 130 | You pressed Ctrl-C and the task was stopped |

Without `--no-wait`, `ask` waits with the agent, so a question it puts blocks a pipeline until someone answers. In CI you almost always want the flag:

```yaml
- name: Summarise the deployment
  env:
    LOOMPLANE_URL: ${{ vars.LOOMPLANE_URL }}
    LOOMPLANE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LOOMPLANE_API_KEY }}
  run: |
    status=0
    loomctl agent ask "why is the latest production deployment of shop slow to start?" \
      --project shop --no-wait > summary.md || status=$?
    if [ "$status" -eq 3 ]; then
      echo "The agent needs a person. See: loomctl agent requests" >&2
    fi
    exit 0
```

The final `exit 0` is a choice: a summary is rarely worth failing a build for.

pages.title: The built-in agent
pages.description: Turn on Loomplane's own AI agent, choose what it runs on, and see what changes when it's off.
pages.text:
Loomplane can run an infrastructure agent inside the server. It reads your projects, plans and deploys the way a teammate would, and stops to ask a person whenever a change needs one. It's off until you turn it on, and with it off nothing about Loomplane changes: no model call, no agent route, no agent page, no worker.

## Turn it on

Two switches, one for the server and one for each workspace. An operator sets the server's, then a workspace admin sets the workspace's.

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_AI_ENABLED=true
```

Restart Loomplane. The same setting in `config.local.yaml`:

```yaml
ai:
  enabled: true
  provider: anthropic          # anthropic, openai or openai-compatible
  api_key: ""                  # optional, see below
  model: claude-sonnet-5-5
```

Then open **Settings, AI** as a workspace admin (`ai:manage`), pick a provider, give the agent a monthly budget and switch it on. [Workspace settings](/docs/agents/workspace-settings) walks through the page, including the order: the workspace's AI budget comes first, then the agent's share of it, then the switch. Once it's on, [talk to it](/docs/agents/assistant).

## The server's key is optional

`ai.api_key` is the key the agent uses when a workspace doesn't bring its own. Leave it empty and every workspace has to add a key of its own before it can turn the agent on. Set it and a workspace can choose **Server default** and spend your key, within the budget its admin sets.

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ai.enabled` | Turns the agent's routes, pages and workers on for the whole server. Default `false` |
| `ai.provider` | The server's provider: `anthropic`, `openai` or `openai-compatible` |
| `ai.api_key` | The server's key. Optional |
| `ai.base_url` | Required for `openai-compatible`, an optional override otherwise |
| `ai.model` | The server's default model. Defaults to `claude-sonnet-5-5` |
| `ai.prices` | Prices for models the built-in catalog doesn't know, per million tokens in USD |
| `ai.knowledge.*` | One embedding model for the whole server, see below |

The agent only runs on models Loomplane can price, so a model that isn't in the catalog needs an entry in `ai.prices` first. Prices come from the server's config, never from a workspace.

## What it's built on

Four libraries from the same family do the work, and Loomplane carries no AI plumbing of its own on top of them. Cortex runs the agent: its steps, its tool calls and the pauses where it waits for a person. Nexus talks to the model provider and counts what each workspace spends. Shield scans what goes into the model (build logs, commit messages, anything from outside Loomplane) and what comes out, so a secret doesn't leave in a notification. Weave stores and searches the documents the agent can read.

Their tables migrate with the rest of Loomplane even when the agent is off, so turning it on never needs a migration step.

## Knowledge

Knowledge lets the agent search Loomplane's own documentation and your workspace's documents before it answers. It needs two things on the server: the pgvector extension in your Postgres, and an embedding model set under `ai.knowledge` (`embedding_provider`, `embedding_model` and usually `embedding_api_key`). If either is missing, the knowledge switch on the settings page stays off and says which. The agent works fine without it. [Knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge) has every reason and its fix.

## When it's off

With `ai.enabled` false, the sidebar has no AI group and no Agent item, `/agent/...` and `/api/v1/ai/...` answer 404, and `loomctl agent` tells you the server doesn't run the agent, and the Assistant page answers as an unknown address would. Turning a workspace's agent off while the server stays on cancels its running work and its pending requests, stops billing against the workspace and takes the agent's role away.

## How it relates to the MCP server

[`loomctl mcp`](/docs/agents/mcp-server) and the built-in agent do different jobs. The MCP server hands your own key's tools to an agent that lives outside Loomplane, such as Claude Code. The built-in agent runs inside Loomplane as the workspace's agent. Both are built from one definition of every operation, so a tool means the same thing whichever one calls it.

What the agent may do alone, and what always waits for you, is on [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person).

pages.title: Knowledge
pages.description: Let the agent search Loomplane's documentation and your workspace's own documents before it answers, and fix it when the settings page says it can't.
pages.text:
Knowledge is how the agent looks things up before it answers. It searches two places: Loomplane's own documentation, and the documents your workspace keeps. It's optional. The agent works without it, it just answers from the live state of your projects and what the model already knows.

It only ever searches. It doesn't write documents, it can't see another workspace's, and the search is a read, so it never needs a person's approval. If a search fails, the agent gets a short fixed message and carries on, and the real error goes to the server's log.

## What the server needs

Two things: the pgvector extension in Loomplane's Postgres, and one embedding model.

For the embedding model, set `ai.knowledge` on the server. These are also environment variables, listed with the rest in [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration#ai).

```yaml
ai:
  enabled: true
  knowledge:
    embedding_provider: openai         # openai or openai-compatible
    embedding_model: text-embedding-3-small
    embedding_api_key: ""
    dimensions: 1536                   # 1 to 2000
    docs_budget_usd: "5.00"            # 0 to 1000
```

An `openai-compatible` provider also needs `embedding_base_url`. Anthropic has no embeddings API, so it can't be the provider. Leave `embedding_provider` empty and knowledge stays off, with nothing else changing.

**pgvector.** Use a Postgres image that ships it, such as `pgvector/pgvector:pg17`, or run `CREATE EXTENSION vector` on a managed Postgres that offers it. Loomplane checks for it at start and only then creates its vector table. Nothing changes without it, and Loomplane starts either way. For the Compose stack and the chart, see [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker#knowledge-needs-pgvector) and [Production on Kubernetes](/docs/operations/production-on-kubernetes#knowledge-needs-pgvector). To try it on your laptop from a source checkout, `make up-knowledge` starts a Postgres with pgvector.

### Dimensions

`dimensions` is the size of every vector, and it has to match your embedding model. The cap is 2000, so pick a model whose native size is at most that. `text-embedding-3-small` at 1536 is the default. Every workspace shares the one size, because the column in the database has a single fixed width.

Once there are vectors, editing the config won't change it. Loomplane sees the table was made for another size and turns knowledge off, and the settings page tells you both sizes. The quick way back is to put the old `embedding_model` and `dimensions` back and restart. Knowledge comes on again with everything it had indexed.

### Changing the size

If you really do want a new size, you reset knowledge by hand. Dropping the vector table on its own won't do it: Loomplane has recorded that it made the table, so it won't make it again, and the documents it indexed still look current, so it won't embed them again either. The reset below clears the table, the record and the documents.

1. Stop every Loomplane server that uses the database.
2. Set the new `embedding_model` and `dimensions` under `ai.knowledge`.
3. Run this against Loomplane's database, as the role Loomplane connects with:

   ```sql
   BEGIN;
   DROP TABLE weave_vectors;
   DELETE FROM grove_migrations WHERE "group" = 'weave_pgvector';
   DELETE FROM weave_collections WHERE name IN ('loomplane-docs', 'workspace');
   COMMIT;
   ```

4. Start Loomplane.

The first statement drops the vectors. The second deletes the record of the migration that made the table, so the next start makes it again at the new size. The third deletes the docs collection and every workspace's collection, and their documents and chunks go with them. When Loomplane starts, it makes the table, turns knowledge back on and indexes the docs again, which costs one full pass of embeddings billed to `loomplane-system`.

The documents your workspaces had indexed are deleted too. Take a [backup](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) first if you might want them back.

## When the switch is off

On **Settings, AI** the **Knowledge** switch is disabled when the server can't support it, with the reason next to it. Each reason has a fix.

| The page says | Do this |
|---|---|
| No embedding model is set on this server | Set `ai.knowledge` as above and restart |
| `ai.knowledge.embedding_model` has no price, so every embedding would be refused | Use an OpenAI model nexus lists, or add the model to `ai.prices` (see below) |
| Loomplane couldn't check its database for pgvector | The database refused the check. Read the error after the colon, fix the connection or the permission, and restart |
| Knowledge needs the pgvector extension in Loomplane's Postgres | Use a pgvector image or run `CREATE EXTENSION vector`, then restart |
| The knowledge table was made for a different embedding size | Put back the embedding model and the `dimensions` it names, and restart. To move to the new size, follow [Changing the size](#changing-the-size) |
| Setting up the knowledge table failed | Read the error after the colon. It names what the database said |
| The embedding model returned vectors of a different size | Your model's real size isn't what `dimensions` says. Fix `dimensions` to match |

The last one turns knowledge off while the server is running, not at start, the first time an embedding comes back at the wrong size.

### Pricing the embedding model

Every embedding is billed through nexus like any model call, and the agent only runs on models Loomplane can price. An OpenAI model nexus knows about is priced already. For an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, add an entry to `ai.prices` with the provider `openai-compatible`:

```yaml
ai:
  prices:
    - provider: openai-compatible
      model: my-embedder
      input_per_million: "0.02"
      output_per_million: "0"
```

## The documentation

Loomplane's docs and the manifest's JSON schema are built into the binary. When the server starts with knowledge available, it indexes them once for the release. A page that hasn't changed isn't embedded again, so restarting the same release costs nothing, and a new release re-embeds only the pages that moved. Pages the release no longer has are removed.

Every workspace can search this collection and none can change it. Its embeddings are billed to a system tenant of their own, `loomplane-system`, never to a workspace, and capped by `ai.knowledge.docs_budget_usd` (5.00 USD unless you say otherwise). A release's docs embed in a few minutes.

If a run dies partway, a check every five minutes fails any page that went quiet for fifteen minutes and indexes the docs again.

## Your workspace's documents

Each workspace gets a collection of its own, made the first time it's needed, for its own documents, such as reports and runbooks. Only that workspace's agent can search it. A report turns up only when the person the agent works for has `deployment:read` on the report's project, so a search never hands you a report you couldn't open yourself. Embeddings for them are billed to the workspace's AI budget, so they count against the same limit as the agent's other model calls.

## Turning it on for a workspace

The server makes knowledge possible. A workspace admin (`ai:manage`) decides whether this workspace uses it, with the **Knowledge** switch on **Settings, AI**. It's the same call as every other agent setting, `PATCH /api/v1/ai/settings/agent` with `"knowledge": true`. With the server unable to support it, the switch stays off and shows why.

Turning it off stops the agent searching your workspace's documents and the docs.

pages.title: MCP server
pages.description: Let an AI agent analyze projects, write manifests, plan deployments and, if you allow it, approve them, over the Model Context Protocol.
pages.text:
`loomctl mcp` serves Loomplane's tools over the Model Context Protocol on standard input and output. An agent such as Claude Code can analyze a project, write its `loomplane.yaml`, plan a deployment, read what the plan would do and, if you let it, approve it.

This is not the [built-in agent](/docs/agents/built-in-agent). That one runs inside Loomplane as your workspace's agent. `loomctl mcp` serves your own key's tools to an agent outside it. Both are built from one definition of every operation, so a tool means the same thing in either.

## Set it up

Make an API key under **Settings, API keys**, then add `loomctl` to your agent's MCP configuration:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "loomplane": {
      "command": "loomctl",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {
        "LOOMPLANE_URL": "https://loomplane.example.com",
        "LOOMPLANE_API_KEY": "lp_live_..."
      }
    }
  }
}
```

For Claude Code, the same thing in one command:

```bash
claude mcp add loomplane --env LOOMPLANE_URL=... --env LOOMPLANE_API_KEY=... -- loomctl mcp
```

Start with a read-only key if you only want an agent to look around.

## The tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `whoami` | Who the key acts as, and its permissions |
| `list_projects` | The organization's projects |
| `analyze` | Reads a project's repositories, or the ones named in `sources`, and waits until each is done |
| `get_manifest`, `draft_manifest`, `save_manifest` | Reads, drafts and saves `loomplane.yaml` |
| `create_plan`, `list_plans`, `get_plan`, `reject_plan` | Plans an environment and reads the result. `scope` names the repositories a plan moves, and the rest stay as deployed. `from` promotes what another environment runs instead of planning the manifest |
| `get_release_watch` | How a deployment is judged after it finishes: its status and verdict, each service's verdict, the services it can't watch and any rollback plan. Read-only. A deployment with no watch answers not found, and `unverified` means missing evidence, so an agent should ask a person |
| `list_deployments`, `get_deployment`, `deployment_for_plan` | Follows deployments step by step |
| `status` | What runs where, with addresses and drift |
| `list_variables`, `set_variable` | Variables. A secret's value is never shown |
| `approve_plan`, `retry_deployment`, `create_rollback` | Only with `--allow-deploy`. `create_rollback` plans an environment back to its previous successful release and takes a `reason`. Data-bearing resources stay as they are, and nothing changes until the plan is approved |

The manifest's JSON schema is available as the resource `loomplane://schema/loomplane.yaml`, so an agent writing one knows every field. A manifest that doesn't parse comes back as an error listing each problem with its line, which the agent can fix and save again.

## What an agent can't do

Three things decide what an agent may do, and all three have to agree.

The key comes first. An agent acts as the person who made its key, with their role, in one organization. A read-only key can list, read and follow, and the API refuses anything else whatever the agent asks.

Deploying is off by default. Without `--allow-deploy` an agent can analyze, edit the manifest and plan, and approving stays with a person in the dashboard or with `loomctl approve`. `approve_plan` and `retry_deployment` change your clouds, and `create_rollback` starts a rollback, so they're only offered when you start the server like this:

```json
"args": ["mcp", "--allow-deploy"]
```

They're also marked destructive, for clients that ask before running such tools.

An approval names the plan's revision. `approve_plan` takes the revision the agent read with `get_plan`. If what's deployed changed since, the plan comes back stale and nothing happens, so an agent can't approve a plan it hasn't seen.

Everything an agent changes is in the audit trail under the person who made its key.

  `--allow-deploy` with an admin's write key lets an agent change your clouds. Give agents a developer-role key and keep approval with a person unless you've decided otherwise.

pages.title: Release preparation
pages.description: Ask the agent to get a release to production ready, read the report it produces, and learn the seven gates that decide whether it may promote alone.
pages.text:
A release report tells you whether staging is ready to go to production, and whether the agent may take it there itself. You ask for one, Loomplane works it out, and you read the answer. Nothing ships unless someone asks.

## Ask for a release

Pick whichever is closest to hand.

On the project's page, choose **Prepare release**. Choose the staging and production environments, untick any source you want to hold back, and submit. You land on the report.

From a terminal:

```bash
loomctl release prepare checkout-api --wait
loomctl release report rrep_abc123
```

Or ask the agent in a chat, as in "release checkout-api to production". It starts the same preparation on your behalf.

You need `deployment:create` on the project and `agent:use`. The agent has to be on for the workspace. The project needs a staging environment and a production one.

Only one preparation can run per production environment at a time. If a plan is already waiting for a decision there, the request fails and names it. You can replace that plan by ticking **Replace that plan** in the dashboard or passing `--replace` to `loomctl release prepare`. The agent never replaces someone's open plan for you. A plan the agent left waiting after a review stopped is different: the next preparation for that environment replaces it, unless it can reuse it.

## What the report holds

Loomplane plans a promotion from staging to production, collects the evidence, and the agent reviews it. The report shows:

- The state: planning, reviewing, waiting for a person, promoted by the agent, approved, and so on, with the reason.
- The seven gates, each passing or failing, with a sentence saying why.
- For every source, whether staging is ahead of production, the commits between them, and any database migrations, with their patches.
- Which images the plan reuses and which it builds again.
- How long staging has run these commits, and whether it was healthy.
- The production canaries of each changed service, and what a post-deploy watch would cover. A service no canary ran for says so.
- Agent reports still open on staging, the agent's budget, and any evidence Loomplane couldn't read.
- A section called "From the agent", with the concerns it noted.

Commit titles, authors, patches and the agent's concerns come from outside Loomplane. The dashboard shows them as plain text, and the concerns as quotes. `loomctl release report` prints them in quotation marks on one line, so you can tell them from Loomplane's own words.

## The seven gates

Loomplane computes every gate from its own records. The agent can add a reason to ask a person. It can never clear a gate or edit the evidence. A gate that needs evidence Loomplane can't read fails, so missing evidence always means a person decides.

| Gate | It fails when |
|---|---|
| 1. autonomous promotion | The project's autonomous promotion switch is off. The person who asked can't approve production releases in the project. The release was asked for in chat. The release reuses a plan someone else made. |
| 2. promotes what staging runs | The plan isn't the one this preparation built, it changed since it was read, it isn't a promotion from staging to production, or staging no longer runs the commits the plan pins. |
| 3. clean plan | The plan isn't ready, has problems or warnings, deletes or replaces anything in production that holds data, sets a default backup schedule, moves production back to older code, promotes an older manifest than the latest, brings a source production has never run, or has a diff Loomplane couldn't read in full. |
| 4. staging soak | Staging hasn't run the plan's commits long enough, isn't healthy, can't be judged, or its own last release failed or went unverified. The minimum is the project's setting, or one hour if you haven't set one. |
| 5. safety net | A changed service has nothing guarding it once live, a data-bearing resource is updated, production's last release is unverified, or a service's last canary failed and no later one promoted. |
| 6. nothing open on staging | An agent report is still open on staging. |
| 7. budget | The agent's budget is spent, or what's left is under the reserve for the post-deploy watch: $1, or 10% of the limit if that's more. |

## What always goes to a person

Some releases never pass, whatever the gates say about the rest.

- Anything that destroys production data. This one doesn't depend on a gate: [it always goes to a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#what-counts-as-destroying-production).
- Services on Kubernetes, a server, Vercel, DigitalOcean, Firecracker or Cloudflare Workers. Loomplane has no canary or watch it can judge there.
- Updates to anything that holds data, and a production environment moving back to older code.
- Releases from GitLab or Bitbucket. Loomplane can only compare commits on GitHub for now, so it can't read those diffs.
- A source's first production release, on any host. Production has never run it, so there's nothing to compare its changes to. Gate 3 names it: "worker has never run in production, so its changes can't be compared".
- A first production release. Nothing in production has been watched yet, so the evidence isn't there.
- A failed canary, until a later canary of that service promotes.
- A plan that promotes an older manifest than the latest.

Who asked also matters. A release prepared from chat never promotes on its own, because the agent chose to start it and not you. A release that reuses someone else's open plan needs a person too. And if the person who asked can't approve deployments, the review still runs and the plan waits for someone who can.

When [autonomous promotion](/docs/agents/workspace-settings#autonomy-per-project) is off for the project, the agent still asks before production. It starts off for every project.

## When a person decides

A release that fails a gate, or that always asks, ends up in **Needs a person** on its report, with the failed gates listed. The approval request goes to the project's team, or the workspace admins if the project has no [responsible team](/docs/concepts/teams). If you asked for the release and you're not on that team, the request doesn't reach you, so keep the report open to follow it. Approve it as you would any plan, in the dashboard or with the line the report prints:

```bash
loomctl approve plan_abc123 --revision rev_7
```

Approving a production release starts its canary, as one decision. If the plan changed after it was reviewed, say because staging deployed again, the approval is refused as stale and the report says so. Prepare the release again.

## When every gate holds

When you asked from the dashboard or `loomctl`, you can approve production releases in the project, and every gate passes, the agent approves the plan with the revision it read. The report shows the decision as made by the Loomplane agent, and the canary takes over from there. It's the same approval a person would make, in the audit log under the agent's name.

## Who hears about it

When a release is promoted, goes stale, stops, is blocked or fails, Loomplane sends a notice to the person who asked and the project's team. If the project has no team, it goes to the workspace admins. Open it to land on the report.

You can stop a preparation that's still going with **Cancel** or `loomctl release cancel`. The person who asked can do it while they hold `agent:use`, and so can anyone who can approve deployments. The plan, if there is one, waits for a person.

Once every gate has held and the agent is promoting, you can't cancel. Its approval may already be landing, and a cancel then would leave a report saying cancelled while production ramps. Read the report again in a moment: it settles as promoted, or as stopped with the plan waiting for a person if the approval didn't go through.

pages.title: Watching and reports
pages.description: What the agent's watcher looks for, how one problem becomes one report, who hears about it, and when Loomplane opens a GitHub issue.
pages.text:
While the agent is on, it watches your workspace. When a deployment fails, a canary rolls back, a production service drifts or its error rate jumps, Loomplane opens a report, the agent investigates it, and you and the people who answer for the project hear about it. If the project's code lives on GitHub, the report also gets an issue on that repository.

You don't turn anything else on. The watcher starts when a workspace admin switches the agent on in **Settings, AI** and stops when it's switched off.

## What the watcher looks at

Every 30 seconds Loomplane queues a pass for each workspace whose agent is on. A pass reads up to 500 of the workspace's events since the last one, checks the production services that are due a check, rechecks the open reports, starts investigations and sends what's ready.

| What happened | Where | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| A deployment failed | Production | High |
| A deployment failed | Staging | Medium |
| A canary rolled back | Any environment that runs one | High |
| A canary couldn't be rolled back, so traffic may still be split | Any | Critical |
| A release watch rolled a release back | Any | High |
| A release breached its thresholds and its rollback is waiting for a person | Any | High |
| A release breached its thresholds and its rollback failed | Any | Critical |
| A service or resource drifted: changed or deleted outside Loomplane | Production | Medium |
| A service's error rate jumped | Production | High |
| A source's analysis failed three times in a row | The project | Low |

A failed deployment on a preview or development environment doesn't open a report. Whoever started it already gets the deployment's own notice. Drift anywhere but production is someone's experiment, so it doesn't open one either. A canary that rolled back opens its canary report and not a second one for the failed deployment.

Analyses pinned to one commit, the kind a promotion runs, don't count toward the three in a row.

### Error rates

Every 5 minutes the watcher checks production bindings, up to 50 per pass, the ones checked longest ago first. For each service it compares the last 10 minutes of errors with the hour before. The window ends 3 minutes before now, so the cloud has reported all of it.

It only does this where your cloud reports errors: Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Azure Container Apps and Render (the 5xx column in [Where canaries run](/docs/concepts/canary-releases#where-canaries-run)). It judges against the error thresholds of the plan that last deployed the service, or the defaults: an error rate above 1%, or more than 0.5 percentage points above the hour before. Latency isn't judged, because a whole service's latency moves with its traffic. With fewer than the threshold's minimum requests in the window (200 by default) there's nothing to go on, and the check passes over it.

While a canary ramps or a [release watch](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback#watch-a-release-after-it-deploys) judges an environment, the sweep leaves that environment alone. They report what they find themselves.

The same sweep reads each binding's drift, as the [drift check](/docs/concepts/drift) last recorded it, so a drift event the watcher missed still opens a report.

## What costs tokens

Nothing the watcher does calls a model until a report needs investigating. Reading events, the sweep, the rechecks and delivery are all Loomplane's own code, so a workspace where nothing goes wrong costs you no tokens at all.

An investigation is one agent run. It starts with up to 150,000 tokens and 25 steps, and what it spends comes out of the agent's monthly budget, like any other run. See [Workspace settings](/docs/agents/workspace-settings#budget).

## Investigations

Each new report gets one investigation, newest reports first. The agent runs as itself with nobody behind it, and it can only read: deployments and their logs, plans, metrics, drift, canary and release watch verdicts, variables (never secret values), repositories and other reports. The one thing it writes is its findings on the report it's investigating: a summary, the likely cause, up to five things to try, and how sure it is (low, medium or high). It can't deploy, change anything or ask anyone a question. See [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#the-agents-identity).

Error output, verdict reasons and drift messages come from outside Loomplane, so they reach the model quoted as untrusted text, after shield has scanned them.

Three limits apply:

- At most three run at once in a workspace. A report that arrives while three are running is marked "Three investigations were already running." and isn't investigated later.
- An investigation that hasn't finished an hour after it started is marked failed, with "The investigation didn't finish within an hour."
- Reports the agent opened in a chat, because a person asked it to, aren't investigated. The chat that opened one can write its findings itself.

### When the budget runs out

When the agent's budget for the month is spent, the watcher stops investigating. It keeps opening reports from what it sees and sends them as usual, and you'll see a line on each saying the agent didn't investigate it. Owners and admins with `ai:manage` get one notice, "The agent stopped investigating: this workspace has used its AI budget for the month", linking to **Settings, AI**.

Once the budget has room again, because a new month started or an admin raised it, they get "The agent is investigating again" and new reports are investigated. Reports skipped while it was paused stay skipped.

## One report per problem

Loomplane keeps one report per problem. Two signals are the same problem when they share a project, an environment, a kind (from the table above) and a component. The component is the service or resource, such as `service:api` or a binding's name, the source for an analysis, or `deployment` for a deployment that failed before any step. So the same failing step on staging and on production is two reports, and the same step failing again in production before anything fixes it is one.

### Repeats

A deployment that fails again, a retry included, counts as a repeat on the open report. So does another canary or release watch rollback, or another failed analysis. The report's count goes up, and its facts become the latest ones.

You hear about repeats at most once an hour. The notice starts with "Again:" and says how many times it has happened since it was first seen. The GitHub issue gets a "This happened again" comment on the same hourly limit, and its body always carries the current count.

Drift and error rates don't count repeats. While the service is still drifted or failing, it's the same problem still there, and only the time it was last seen moves.

### Resolving and reopening

A report resolves on its own when the problem goes away:

- A later deployment that runs the same component in that environment succeeds. That clears a failed deployment and a canary that couldn't roll back. A deployment that isn't a rollback also clears canary and release watch rollbacks. A rollback's success restores the release before, so it leaves the report that says why the newer one went back.
- The binding matches what Loomplane deployed again, for drift.
- The error rate is back within its thresholds for two checks in a row.
- A later analysis of the source succeeds.

Every 10 minutes the watcher also rechecks each open report against current state, and resolves one whose problem no longer holds, or whose deployment, binding or analysis is gone. Reports opened in a chat never resolve on their own. Only a person closes them.

When the same problem comes back within 24 hours of a report resolving or being closed, Loomplane reopens that report and keeps counting on it. The notice starts with "Back again:", the issue reopens with a comment, and the agent investigates it afresh. After 24 hours it's a new report.

### Closing a report yourself

You can close an open report with an optional reason, up to 500 characters. That needs `deployment:create` on the report's project. If the report has a GitHub issue, Loomplane comments there with who closed it and why, then closes the issue as not planned. A report that resolves on its own closes its issue as completed.

Closing doesn't stop the problem coming back. If it does within 24 hours, the report reopens.

## Notices

Each report's notice goes through Loomplane's notifications: the inbox, email and your workspace's signed webhooks. It goes to:

- the members of the project's [responsible team](/docs/concepts/teams), when the project names a team that has people in it
- the workspace's owners and admins otherwise: when the project has no team, its team is empty, or the report isn't about one project
- the person who started the deployment the report is about, when that was a person and not the agent or Loomplane's own automation

Owners and admins who aren't on the team don't get a notice for that project's reports, but they can still read every report on the **Reports** page.

Each person needs `deployment:read` on the project when the notice is delivered, or they don't get it. Email follows your `agent_email` preference, separate from deployment mail. See [Notifications and webhooks](/docs/guides/notifications-and-webhooks#the-agents-notices).

The title is the project, the environment and what happened: `shop · production: Deployment to production failed at api`. The body is the agent's summary when it has one, and otherwise the facts.

### When notices and issues go out

A new report waits for its investigation, so the first thing you read already says what the agent found. It goes out as soon as the investigation finishes, or 10 minutes after it started, whichever comes first. A report that isn't investigated goes out on the next pass. If findings arrive after the notice went, the issue gets them as a comment and nobody's paged twice.

While the workspace's agent is off, nothing is delivered. Reports that were waiting go out once the agent is back on.

Before anything leaves Loomplane, every title, body and comment has the project's known secret values and any password in a URL redacted, then goes through shield's outbound scan. A text the scan blocks is replaced with a fixed one, such as "Open it in Loomplane to read it." When Loomplane can't read the project's secrets to redact them, it doesn't send anything. It retries the delivery, so if your secrets store is down you get the report late, once the secrets can be read again, and never with that step skipped.

## GitHub issues

Loomplane opens one issue per report on the repository the report is about, through your workspace's GitHub App installation. It picks the repository from the service's source. For a deployment that failed before any step, it's the one repository the deployment moved. A project with a single source always uses that one. When it can't tell, or the installation can't reach the repository, the report goes to Herald only and says why.

Issues are opened on GitHub repositories only. Reports about code on GitLab or Bitbucket go to Herald only.

Every issue carries the `loomplane` label, which Loomplane creates if the repository doesn't have it. The body says how severe it is, where and how often it was seen, what happened, what Loomplane already did and what the agent thinks, with a link back to the report. Error output sits in a code block it can't break out of. Every `@` that could page someone is broken with an invisible character, so a commit message or error can't mention a person or a team. As the report changes, Loomplane edits the issue to match. If someone deletes the issue while the report is open, the next delivery opens a new one.

Loomplane never reads anything people write on the issue. Comments there stay on GitHub, and the agent doesn't see them.

### The Issues permission

The App needs the Issues permission (read and write), and an owner of each account it's installed on has to accept it on GitHub. [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories#issues-for-agent-reports) has the setup.

Until an installation accepts, its reports go to Herald only. The dashboard shows "Herald only: GitHub hasn't accepted the Issues permission yet", and `loomctl` and the API call that state `waiting_for_permission`. The **Watcher** card on **Settings, AI** lists each installation as Accepted, or says it hasn't accepted the Issues permission yet, with a **Review on GitHub** link. `loomctl agent watcher` prints the same. Once an owner accepts, open reports for that installation's repositories get their issues. Loomplane trusts what it last read of an installation's permissions for 5 minutes, so the first report after an owner accepts can still go to Herald only for up to 5 minutes.

## Where you read them

In the dashboard, **Deployments, Reports** lists the open reports, with a count beside it. Filter by status (open, resolved, closed or all) and by project. A report's page has its facts, what Loomplane already did, what the agent thinks, where it went (the issue, or why there's none) and the records it's about. **Close** is there when you can close it. When the watcher has stopped for the budget, a banner says so.

You see a report when you have `agent:use` and `deployment:read` on its project. A team's grant on a project counts there. The agent keeps to the same rule when it searches past reports for you: it only finds reports of projects you can read deployments on.

From the command line:

```bash
loomctl agent reports                       # open reports
loomctl agent reports --all --project shop  # every report of one project
loomctl agent reports show arep_01jd...     # facts, findings, issue link
loomctl agent reports close arep_01jd... --reason "Fixed in the config"
loomctl agent watcher                       # watching or paused, and the Issues permission
```

[loomctl](/docs/reference/loomctl#the-built-in-agent) lists every flag. Over the API it's `GET /api/v1/agent/reports`, `GET /api/v1/agent/reports/{id}`, `POST /api/v1/agent/reports/{id}/close` and `GET /api/v1/agent/watcher`, described in [HTTP API](/docs/reference/http-api#agent-reports). Each report change also arrives on the realtime stream as an `agent_report.updated` event.

## Gaps

When a workspace's watcher hasn't run for more than an hour (the agent was off, say, or the server was down), it doesn't replay what happened meanwhile. It starts from the newest event and rechecks every open report against current state. A deployment that failed while nobody watched doesn't open a report after the fact, even if it's still broken. It opens one the next time it fails. Drift and error rates don't wait like that: the next sweep finds them.

pages.title: What needs a person
pages.description: What the agent does alone, what it always asks for, who it asks, and how a secret reaches Loomplane without reaching the model.
pages.text:
The agent can read anything its role lets it read and change things within its permissions. A short list of changes always goes to a person, and Loomplane enforces it in code, not in the agent's instructions. A model that has been talked into something can at worst make a bad suggestion or a request you see. It can't push through an unapproved production change.

## The risk table

Every operation the agent has belongs to one of six classes. The class decides what the call needs.

| Class | Examples | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `read` | list projects, read a plan, logs, metrics, status | Allowed |
| `change` | create a project or environment, save a manifest, add a source, set a variable that isn't secret, plan staging | Allowed within the permissions of the person it acts for |
| `deploy_nonproduction` | approve a staging, preview or development plan | Allowed within those permissions |
| `promote_production` | approve a production plan that deletes nothing | Asks a person, unless the project allows autonomous promotion and all seven gates hold. See [Release preparation](/docs/agents/release-preparation) |
| `destroy_production` | a production plan with a delete, a delete or replace of anything that holds data, deleting a production environment, connection or project, removing a production variable | Always a person |
| `secret_or_external` | set a secret, connect GitHub, create a cloud connection | Always a person, through a request |

Anything that isn't a staging, preview or development environment counts as production, an unknown kind included.

### What counts as destroying production

Replacing a stateless service isn't destruction. Every routed blue/green release plans as a replace, and so does moving a service to another provider, region or connection, and in each case the old instance is kept and drained. Without that rule a routed service could never be promoted without a person.

Replacing anything that holds data is destruction: a database, a volume, a bucket, a cache. The data doesn't move with the replacement. The same rule binds Loomplane's own automation, automatic rollback included.

A plan that sets a default backup schedule also goes to a person, one who can manage backups, because the agent's role doesn't hold that permission.

## The agent's identity

The agent acts as `agent:<org>`, shown as "Loomplane agent" in plans, deployments, approvals and the audit log. It's not a member of the workspace and has no password or key. Its role is narrower than an admin's.

Who it acts for depends on how the work started.

When a person talks to the agent, in the [Assistant](/docs/agents/assistant) or with `loomctl agent`, it acts on that person's behalf, and a call is allowed only if both the agent's role and that person's role allow it. If the person is a developer, the agent can't do what an admin could. If the person leaves the workspace or loses their key while the agent waits, the next step fails and the run's pending requests are cancelled. Nothing runs as them afterwards.

Background work, such as an investigation the agent starts because something broke, runs as the agent alone, with no person behind it. It can read and report. It can't approve a production change on anyone's authority, because nobody gave it any.

A team's role counts for the person it's given to, so an agent acting for someone who has `deployment:approve` through a team on project P can approve there, and is refused on project Q.

## Audit

Every tool call the agent makes is recorded with `actor` set to `agent` and `actor_name` "Loomplane agent". The entry also carries `on_behalf_of` (the person, when there is one), `task_id`, `run_id` and `tool`. An approval records the person who decided it. The audit log never holds a secret value, a request's text or an answer to a question.

## Requests

When the agent needs a person it creates a request instead of guessing. There are five kinds.

| Kind | What you do |
|---|---|
| Approve a plan | Approve or reject it, with the usual approval card, or decline |
| Provide a secret | Type the value into Loomplane |
| Answer a question | Choose one of its options or write an answer |
| Connect GitHub | Install the GitHub app, then say you did |
| Connect a cloud | Add the account under Clouds, then say you did |

Every kind can be declined, with a reason the agent sees. A request that nobody answers expires: plan approvals follow `planning.approval_window` and questions last 24 hours. Loomplane checks that a connection exists before it believes you said so.

### Who is asked

A request goes to the project's [responsible team](/docs/concepts/teams) by default. If the project has none, or its team is empty, it goes to the workspace admins, and the request says why it fell through. The agent can name a different team for a question, a secret or a connection, but only with a reason, and the request shows both: "Sent to Payments", then why. A team that doesn't exist or has no members is passed over with a note. A request to approve a plan always goes to the project's team, never to one the agent picked.

Every member of the team gets the notice under their own notification preferences, and any one of them can answer. The first answer settles it. A question you asked in a conversation is sent to you alone. It isn't private, though: anyone with `project:read` on its project can see it, and an `ai:manage` holder can answer it.

### Who can see and answer

On the **Agent** page, **For you** shows what was asked of you, what went to a team you're in and, if you're an admin, what went to the admins. **Everyone** shows the rest you're allowed to see. The same filter on the command line is `loomctl agent requests --mine`.

- A request about a project needs `agent:use` and `project:read` on that project.
- A request with no project (a question in a workspace-wide chat, say) is seen by the person who asked, the team it was routed to, and anyone with `ai:manage`. A viewer who isn't any of those doesn't see it.
- Answering a question is for the asker, a current member of the routed team, or an `ai:manage` holder.
- Every other kind needs its own permission and nothing more: `deployment:approve` on the project to approve or decline a plan, `variable:manage` on the project to provide a secret, `repository:connect` to connect GitHub, `cloud_account:manage` to connect a cloud. The page shows the controls only to people who hold it.

### Secrets

The agent never sees a secret's value, and you never type one into a chat. When it needs one it asks with a request that names the key, the environment and, when it has one, the service. You type the value into the field on the request, or pipe it to `loomctl agent requests provide <id>`. The value is sent once, stored as a secret variable by you, and cleared from the page. No response, audit entry, notice or model prompt carries it. If saving fails the request stays open, and your next try replaces the value.

The command line refuses a value given as an argument, so it stays out of your shell history. It reads standard input, and hides what you type when that's a terminal.

## Prompt injection

Anything from outside Loomplane's own state is untrusted: logs, commit messages, README files, issue bodies, error output, and what people wrote elsewhere. Shield scans it before the model sees it, and what survives is wrapped as quoted data with its source. The agent is told never to follow instructions inside it.

A scan can miss something, which is why the table above doesn't rest on the model behaving. The risk class, the permission check and the approval check run in Loomplane's code on every call, and shield's checks on a tool call can only add restrictions. A hostile commit message can make the agent ask you a strange question. It can't make the agent delete a production database.

pages.title: Workspace settings
pages.description: Choose the agent's provider and key, set its monthly budget, decide about knowledge, and set per-project autonomy.
pages.text:
A workspace admin runs the agent from **Settings, AI**. Anyone with `ai:read` can open that page and see the workspace's AI budget. You need `ai:manage` to change anything there, and to see the agent's panel at all. Everyone with `agent:use` can see the agent's requests and [talk to it](/docs/agents/assistant).

## Provider and key

Pick one of four.

| Choice | Runs on |
|---|---|
| Server default | The provider, model and key the operator set under `ai`. The page shows which |
| Anthropic | Your own Anthropic key |
| OpenAI | Your own OpenAI key |
| OpenAI-compatible | Any endpoint that speaks the OpenAI API. You add a base URL too |

Paste the key into **API key** and choose **Save provider**. After that the page shows only `Key set, ends in wxyz`. Nobody can read it back, including you. **Replace** swaps it for a new one, and **Remove** deletes it and sends the agent back to the server default.

Keys live in Vault, never in the database. A key the agent uses has to be available to every project, because the agent works across the workspace, so you can't narrow it to some. You can't delete it while the agent runs on it either.

The base URL for an OpenAI-compatible endpoint is checked when you save. It has to be an absolute URL with no credentials in it, and in production it has to be https. Loomplane refuses addresses on private networks and loopback outside development, link-local and cloud metadata addresses everywhere, and anything in `planning.endpoint_denied_cidrs`, because the agent sends its key there. The refusal names the rule.

The **Model** field starts from the model the agent runs on now. Type another to change it. Loomplane refuses a model it has no price for and says so under the field.

## Budget

There are two budgets, and the order matters. The workspace has a monthly AI budget that everything AI shares: models, embeddings and the agent. The agent gets a share of it. Neither is set when a workspace is new, and the agent can't be turned on until both are.

1. **The workspace's budget.** It's the **AI budget** section at the top of this page. You'll see the budget, how much of it is shared out, what's left and who holds each share. Type an amount into **Workspace budget (USD)** and choose **Save**. It can't go below what's already shared out. The API is `PUT /api/v1/ai/settings/budget` with `monthly_budget_usd` and the `revision` you read from `GET /api/v1/ai/settings`. A stale `revision` is refused, so read again and retry.

2. **The agent's budget.** Further down, in the agent's panel, give the agent a monthly budget in USD and choose **Save budget**. It comes out of what's left of the workspace's budget, and the field tells you how much that is. Ask for more and the page stops you before saving and tells you to raise the workspace's budget first. The page shows what the agent has spent this month beside the limit. The API is `PUT /api/v1/ai/settings/agent/budget` with `monthly_budget_usd` and `revision`.

3. **The switch**, below.

You need both budgets before you can turn the agent on. When the month's spend reaches the limit, the agent's model calls are refused with a message that says the workspace has used its AI budget, and they stay refused until next month or until an admin raises the limit. Work that's already waiting on a person isn't lost. Setting the budget to `0` releases it, which you can only do while the agent is off.

## Knowledge

The **Knowledge** switch lets the agent search documents before it answers. When the server can't support it, the switch is disabled and the reason sits beside it. [Knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge#when-the-switch-is-off) lists each reason and what fixes it.

## Turning it on and off

The switch at the top of the panel turns the agent on for this workspace. If something stops it, the message appears under the field it's about: a missing budget under the budget, an unpriced model under the model. Turning it off cancels running work and pending requests, so don't do it in the middle of a release you care about.

## Autonomy, per project

Open a project's **Settings** tab. When the agent is on, an **Autonomy** card sits beside **Responsible team**.

**Autonomous promotion** says whether the agent may promote a release to production without asking first, once someone has asked it to release and every gate is green. It starts off for every project, so new projects ask first. The **minimum staging soak** (none, 30 minutes, 1, 2, 6, 12 or 24 hours) is how long staging has to have run the same commits, healthy, before the agent may promote them.

With the switch on, the agent promotes only a release someone asked it to prepare, and only when all seven gates hold. [Release preparation](/docs/agents/release-preparation) lists the gates and what always goes to a person. With the switch off, the agent still asks before production.

Both need `deployment:approve` on the project. Without it you see the card with the controls disabled. The agent can't change either setting, whatever it's asked. The same call is `PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/autonomy` with `autonomous_promotion` and `min_staging_soak_seconds`, which must be a multiple of 60 up to a week.

Deleting or replacing anything in production that holds data always waits for a person, and the switch never changes that.

## Requests

Anything the agent asks of a person lands on **Deployments, Agent**. Who sees what is on [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#requests).

pages.title: AI overview
pages.description: What the AI section does today, who can see it, and how to turn it on for your Loomplane server.
pages.text:
The AI section runs open models on your own servers and clusters. You pick a model from Loomplane's registry, or paste any Hugging Face repo, choose a GPU or a server, and Loomplane adds the model to your project's manifest and plans it like any other workload. Services in the same environment link to it and get two variables, `MODEL_URL` and `MODEL_API_KEY`, which they use to call it.

Everything runs on infrastructure you connected. Loomplane's control plane never hosts a model, and your services' requests to one never pass through Loomplane.

## Turn it on

The section is off until an operator turns it on for the server. Set this and restart Loomplane:

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_AI_ENABLED=true
```

An **AI** group then shows in the sidebar for everyone with `ai:read`, which is every role from Viewer up. It holds two pages:

- **Models**, where you browse the registry, deploy a model and see what each deployed model costs. See [Models](/docs/ai/models) and [What models cost](/docs/ai/model-costs).
- **Settings**, which holds the workspace's Hugging Face token for gated models. See [AI settings](/docs/ai/settings).

[AI settings](/docs/ai/settings#turning-ai-off) also covers what happens to running models if you turn the section off again.

## Who can do what

| Permission | Held by | What it allows here |
|---|---|---|
| `ai:read` | Viewer and up | See the AI pages, the registry, deployed models and their costs |
| `ai:edit` | Developer and up | Deploy, move, retry and remove models in environments that aren't production, and set their budget and price |
| `ai:manage` | Admin and up | All of that in production too, and the Hugging Face token |

Creating a DigitalOcean GPU server for a model is a separate thing. It needs `organization_cloud:manage`, which admins hold, because the server bills from the moment it exists. And a model deploy makes a plan, so someone with `deployment:approve` still approves it before anything runs.

## What isn't here yet

A gateway that serves several models behind one address, and agents that use them, are planned for later. Until the gateway exists, a model runs in the one environment you deploy it to, and only services in that environment link to it. If staging and production both need a model, deploy it to each, and each copy holds its own GPU.

The [MCP server](/docs/agents/mcp-server) under AI agents is a different thing: it lets a coding agent such as Claude Code drive Loomplane. It works whether or not the AI section is on.

pages.title: What models cost
pages.description: How Loomplane prices a deployed model by the hour and the month, why an unknown price stays unknown, and how budget alerts reach admins without ever stopping a model.
pages.text:
A GPU costs money every hour it's on, whether the model on it gets traffic or not. So every model shows what it costs: on the **Deployed** tab (**Per hour** and **This month** for each row, and the GPU models' hourly total above them) and in the **Cost** section of its page, which adds a projection for the month.

## Cost per hour

Loomplane prices the GPUs a model holds, by where it runs:

| Where it runs | Price | Shown as |
|---|---|---|
| A DigitalOcean GPU server Loomplane created for the model | The whole server's price from DigitalOcean, while nothing else holds a GPU there | "$12.56/hr", "The server's price for 8 of 8 GPUs." |
| A GPU server Loomplane created that other workloads share | The server's price for the share of its GPUs the model holds | "$1.57/hr", "The server's price for 1 of 8 GPUs." |
| A Kubernetes cluster | The node's list price, for the model's share of its GPUs | "~$0.82/hr", marked estimate |
| A server you connected yourself | Unknown, until you set one | "Price unknown" |
| CPU, on any server or cluster | Part of that server's own cost | "Runs on CPU. Its cost is part of gpu-1." |

List prices are reference prices, not your bill. Anything from them says "estimate".

A server Loomplane created for a model was bought for that model, so the model pays for all of it, even when it needs one GPU of eight. The deploy dialog, the model's page, the month and the budget alerts all use that price. Once another model or service holds a GPU on the same server, each one shows its share instead, and the server's other GPUs aren't charged to anyone.

A model on CPU never shows $0.00. It has no GPU of its own to price, so its cost is the server's, and its page says which server. It has no projection and no budget alert.

### Setting a price

When Loomplane can't price a GPU, or you pay something else for it, open the model's page and type the hourly figure into **It costs me per hour**, then **Save price**. Your price wins from then on, in the hourly figure, the month, the projection and the budget alert. Clear it to go back to the list price.

### Unknown stays unknown

An unknown price is never shown as $0.00, and it's never added in as zero. The model's row says "unknown", the Deployed tab counts it apart ("GPU models cost about $3.40/hr together, plus 1 with an unknown price."), it adds nothing to the month, and it sends no budget alert. When a price becomes known later, Loomplane counts from then on and doesn't charge the time before.

## This month and the projection

Every five minutes, Loomplane adds what each model cost since the last count to its month. A model counts while it's **Deploying** or **Ready**, at the price of the GPUs its engine actually holds, or of the whole server when Loomplane created that server for it and nothing else holds a GPU there. Months are calendar months in UTC. A count that runs past midnight UTC on the first gives the minutes before midnight to the month that's ending, then starts the new month from zero. Those last minutes don't send a budget alert, and once the new month starts, the page shows only the new month.

**Projected** is this month so far plus the hourly price for every hour left in the month. The deploy dialog quotes a simpler figure before anything runs: the hourly price times 730, as "about $1,146/mo while it runs".

A model you added to `loomplane.yaml` by hand shows its hourly price, but Loomplane keeps no month, price or budget for it. Deploy it from the Models page if you want those.

## Budget alerts

Give a model a monthly budget in the deploy dialog under **Budget alert**, or later on its page under **Budget alert per month**, then **Save budget**. It's a dollar amount above 0, up to 100,000.

Two notices can go out each month:

- "qwen2-5-7b-instruct is on track to cost $1180.00 this month", once the projection reaches the budget.
- "qwen2-5-7b-instruct passed its $1000.00 budget", once what it cost this month passes it.

Each goes out once a month. Change the budget and the new amount gets notices of its own.

They go to workspace admins (everyone with `ai:manage`) in their Loomplane inbox and by email, whatever their email preference, and to your [webhook endpoints](/docs/guides/notifications-and-webhooks#signed-webhooks) as `model.budget_projected` and `model.budget_crossed`. Developers and viewers don't get them.

A budget is an alert, never a cutoff. Loomplane never stops a model, scales it down or moves it because of its budget, since that would take every service that uses it offline. The notice says so, and links to the model, where you can move it somewhere cheaper or remove it.

Anyone who can change the model can set its budget and its price: `ai:edit`, or `ai:manage` in production.

## What the model's cost leaves out

The figures are the model's share of its GPUs, or its whole server when the model has that server to itself. They aren't your cloud bill. A GPU server Loomplane created for a model bills for all of it, even once other workloads share it, from the moment it's created until you delete it in **Infrastructure**. Removing or moving the model doesn't delete that server, and the model page tells you when one is left behind. While a model moves to a new GPU server, both places bill once the new one is up, and the page shows the new server's price beside the old.

[Spend and traffic](/docs/clouds/spend-and-traffic) covers what your Clouds cost as a whole.

pages.title: Models
pages.description: Browse the model registry, deploy a model in one click on a GPU or a server you have, run it in more than one environment, link services to it, and move or remove it later.
pages.text:
Open **AI**, then **Models**. The **Registry** tab lists the open models Loomplane knows how to serve, and the **Deployed** tab lists the ones running in your projects, with what each costs per hour and this month.

A model you deploy belongs to one project and runs in the environments you deploy it to, each environment running its own copy on a server or cluster you connected, or on a DigitalOcean GPU server Loomplane creates for it. Services in an environment link to that environment's copy and call it with `MODEL_URL` and `MODEL_API_KEY`.

## The registry

Each card shows the model's publisher, its size in parameters, its context window, its license, what it does (chat, reasoning, code, vision, embeddings, reranking or speech to text) and what it needs to run, such as "Needs 22 GB GPU, or runs on CPU". A badge says how sure Loomplane is that it runs, which the next section explains.

Search by name, or narrow the list:

- **Task**, **Size** (under 4B up to over 100B parameters) and **License**.
- **Commercial use only** keeps models whose license Loomplane knows and that allow commercial use. A license it doesn't know never counts.
- **Fits my GPUs** keeps models that fit a GPU or a server your workspace has, or a GPU server it can create. If Loomplane can't read your targets, it says "Couldn't check your GPUs." and shows everything.
