- **Tested only** keeps models a qualification run served.

Open a card for the model's page. It lists each quantization (the weights Loomplane can serve, each pinned to a Hugging Face commit), where each one fits, the license, and the model card from Hugging Face. **Deploy** is there and on the card.

Every entry and every quantization is pinned to a 40-character commit SHA, never to `main`, so the weights you deploy today are the weights you deploy next month.

## Tested, estimated, failed and untested

Every model, and every GPU it might run on, carries one of these:

| Badge | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Tested on** a GPU | Loomplane's qualification job deployed this quantization on that GPU kind, with the engine version Loomplane ships, and served real requests from it |
| **Estimated** | The memory math says it fits. Nobody has run it there |
| **Failed on** a GPU | A qualification run on that GPU failed. Loomplane won't offer it there, whatever the math says |
| **Untested** | You pasted it from Hugging Face. No qualification run will ever check it |
| **Doesn't fit** | The memory math says it won't fit, with the reason |

An estimate never reads as tested. A test counts only for the GPU kind it ran on, the engine version Loomplane ships today and the weights revision the registry pins. When Loomplane moves to a new engine release, or the registry re-pins a model's weights, its fits go back to **Estimated** until a run proves them again. A passed run at a shorter context than Loomplane would serve proves nothing about the longer one, so that doesn't count either.

### How models get tested

The qualification job runs in Loomplane's own CI, in a DigitalOcean account kept for it alone, never in your workspace or with your credentials. Once a week it creates one GPU Droplet (the GPU kind rotates through the RTX 4000 Ada, the L40S and the H100), starts a sample of registry models on it with the engines Loomplane ships, and calls each one the way your service would: a streamed chat completion, an embedding of the right length, a rerank, a transcription. Then it deletes the Droplet. Each result records the GPU, the GPU count, the context, the engine version and what it measured, or why it failed, and the results ship in the next Loomplane release. Results older than 30 days are run again.

Until a run covers a model, it reads **Estimated**, which is what the memory math alone can promise.

### How fit is estimated

For vLLM, the memory one GPU needs is:

- the weights, divided by the number of GPUs,
- plus the KV cache for the context, at 2 bytes a value, split across GPUs only as far as the model's KV heads allow,
- plus overhead: 1.5 GiB (1 GiB for embedding and rerank models), 8% of that GPU's share of the weights, and another 1 GiB for vision and speech models' encoders.

That has to fit in 90% of the GPU's memory, since vLLM gets `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90`. Loomplane tries 1, 2, 4 and then 8 GPUs and takes the smallest count that fits. It serves the longest context that fits, rounded down to a multiple of 1024, at least 4096 tokens (or the model's own limit if that's shorter) and at most 32,768. Embedding and rerank models keep no KV cache and serve up to 8,192 tokens.

Here's an 8B model with 16 GiB of bf16 weights, 32 layers, 8 KV heads and a head size of 128. Each token of context takes 128 KiB of KV cache. On an NVIDIA L4 (24 GiB, so 21.6 GiB usable) the overhead is 2.78 GiB, and at 4,096 tokens the model needs 16 + 0.5 + 2.78 = 19.28 GiB. It fits. The room left over holds 23,101 tokens, so Loomplane serves 22,528. On an RTX 4000 Ada (20 GiB, 18 GiB usable) it doesn't fit on one GPU. Its card says "Needs 22 GB GPU", which is 19.28 divided by 0.9, rounded up.

The GPU also has to be new enough. vLLM needs CUDA compute capability 7.5, which rules out the V100, and `fp8` and `mxfp4` weights need 8.0, which rules out the T4 as well. llama.cpp runs on 6.1 and up. A GPU kind Loomplane has no compute capability for never fits.

On CPU, a model needs 1.1 times its weights, plus its KV cache, plus 0.5 GiB. That has to fit in 3.5 GiB for Text Embeddings Inference and 7 GiB for llama.cpp, which leaves the operating system room in the 4,096 MB and 8,192 MB those containers reserve. llama.cpp on CPU serves 8,192 tokens.

## The engines

Loomplane runs each model with one of three inference servers, picked by the quantization:

| Engine | Runs on | Serves | Manifest kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| vLLM 0.31 | NVIDIA GPU | Chat, reasoning, code, vision, embeddings and speech to text, from safetensors | `model-vllm` |
| Text Embeddings Inference 1.9 | CPU | Embedding and rerank models | `model-tei` |
| llama.cpp b11580 | CPU or NVIDIA GPU | Models as a single GGUF file (`Q8_0`, `MXFP4` or `Q4_K_M`) | `model-llamacpp`, `model-llamacpp-gpu` |

A model that has both kinds of quantization gives you a **GPU** and **CPU** switch in the deploy dialog. Images are pinned by digest. The GPU images are amd64 only, so a GPU model can't run on an Arm server.

## Deploy a model


Choose **Deploy** on a card or a model's page.


Under **Where**, pick the project and the environment. The dialog says "Runs in staging. Services in staging can link to it." The project needs a saved manifest first.

To add an environment to a model that's already deployed, open its page and choose **Deploy to another environment**. You get the same dialog for the same model, and the environments it runs in already read "(runs there)" and can't be picked.


Pick where it runs. For a GPU model the list shows your connected servers and clusters with GPUs, how many are free (or how many a cluster has per node) and what they cost, and, when the environment's Cloud has a DigitalOcean account, GPU server sizes Loomplane can create, marked **New server**. A target the model doesn't fit says why and can't be picked. For a CPU model, pick a ready server or cluster.


Pick a quantization, or leave it and Loomplane takes the first that fits. Set **Context in tokens**, or leave it for the most that fits, up to 32,768. **Budget alert** is optional; see [What models cost](/docs/ai/model-costs).


Read the summary at the bottom: what it costs per hour and roughly per month, and anything that stops the deploy. Then choose **Plan it**.


Nothing runs before that. **Plan it** adds the model to the project's `loomplane.yaml` and plans the environment, and the plan waits for approval like any other. Once it's approved, the engine downloads the weights and loads them, which for a big model takes a while. Loomplane waits up to two hours for vLLM, an hour for llama.cpp and 30 minutes for Text Embeddings Inference before it calls a start failed.

You need `ai:edit` to deploy to an environment that isn't production, and `ai:manage` for production. The dialog tells you when you can't.

A model already running in that environment is refused ("llm already runs Qwen2.5 7B Instruct in staging."). Deploying a model the project already runs to another environment adds that environment to the same resource: the dialog says "Adds production to llm.", and production gets its own copy on the server you pick, with its own key, cost and budget. The copy has to run on the same engine as the others. Pick a CPU server for a model that runs on vLLM in staging and the dialog refuses it, and tells you to pick a target the model runs on as it is, or deploy it as a separately named model.

### On a new GPU server

When you pick a **New server**, Loomplane creates a DigitalOcean GPU Droplet for the model first. The Droplet bills from the moment it exists, so creating it is a step of its own:

1. **Review server** asks DigitalOcean for the size's price and shows the server Loomplane would create, named after the project, the model and the environment, such as `shop-qwen2-5-7b-instruct-staging-gpu`, in its region and at its hourly price. Nothing is created yet.
2. **Create the server and plan it** approves that server. The review is good for five minutes, so a stale one asks you to review again.

Only admins can review and create GPU servers (`organization_cloud:manage`). Anyone else sees "An admin creates GPU servers. Ask one to deploy this, or pick a server you have." The DigitalOcean account has to be in the environment's Cloud, too.

The model then shows **Waiting for a server**. Once the server is up and has passed its GPU checks, Loomplane adds the model to the manifest and makes the plan. The server bills from the moment it's created until you delete it in **Infrastructure**, whether the model gets traffic or not, and whether the model is still there or not.

The Cloud's capacity policy applies to these servers like any other. When it holds a server back for now (an approval still to come, capacity still to grow, a count that's out of date) the model keeps waiting and says why, with a link to the Cloud's **Capacity** tab for admins. When it refuses (no ceiling for that GPU kind, a ceiling that would be passed, a provider quota with no room) the deploy is refused with the reason. **Cancel** on a waiting model stops the wait. If the server was already approved, it says so, and you delete the server in **Infrastructure**.

## What a deploy writes

A deploy is one edit to `loomplane.yaml`. You can read it, and you could have written it yourself:

```yaml
resources:
  qwen2-5-7b-instruct:
    kind: model-vllm
    version: "0.31"
    provider: server
    target: conn_01jabc...
    gpu: { kind: nvidia-l4, count: 1 }
    settings:
      entry: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      revision: a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28
      quantization: bf16
      served_name: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      max_model_len: "32768"
      cache_mb: "20480"
    environments:
      staging:
        enabled: true
```

Model kinds run only in the environments where they're enabled, and each of those environments runs its own copy. The settings must match the registry's pin for the entry: a `model`, `revision` or GGUF `file` that differs from it is refused. `cache_mb` sizes a GPU model's weight cache on Kubernetes, 20,480 MB by default.

A model you add to the manifest by hand shows on the Models page too, with its state and its hourly price. Loomplane keeps no budget or price override for it, and it isn't counted in the month's spend.

## Run it in more than one environment

Here's the model above running in staging and production. Production has its own block, which says only what's different there:

```yaml
resources:
  qwen2-5-7b-instruct:
    kind: model-vllm
    version: "0.31"
    provider: server
    target: conn_01jabc...
    gpu: { kind: nvidia-l4, count: 1 }
    settings:
      entry: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      revision: a09a35458c702b33eeacc393d103063234e8bc28
      quantization: bf16
      served_name: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
      max_model_len: "32768"
      cache_mb: "20480"
    environments:
      staging:
        enabled: true
      production:
        enabled: true
        target: <production GPU server connection ID>
        gpu: { kind: nvidia-h100, count: 1 }
        settings:
          max_model_len: "16384"
```

Staging reads everything from the top level. Production reads the top level too, except where its block says otherwise, so its copy runs on the production GPU server, on an H100, with a 16,384 token context. Each copy has its own `MODEL_API_KEY`, its own cost and budget alert, and its own row on the **Deployed** tab. Copies usually run on different servers, but nothing stops you picking the server another environment's copy already uses, and then the two share it. A service that needs `qwen2-5-7b-instruct` lists that one name, and in each environment it gets that environment's `MODEL_URL`.

A few rules for the blocks:

- `target` is optional at the top level. Each environment needs one, from its own block or from the top level, and when neither has one, only that environment's plan stops and asks for it. A block that runs the model on another provider doesn't take the top-level target with it.
- One model runs on one engine everywhere. If production needs another engine, say llama.cpp on a CPU server while staging runs vLLM on a GPU, deploy it to production as a separately named model.
- When Loomplane adds an environment, the block's `settings` get only what differs from the top level: `quantization`, `model`, `revision`, `file`, `max_model_len` or `cache_mb`. It never writes `entry` or `served_name` there, so your code asks for the same model name in every environment.
- A block can't say "no file". If the top level names a GGUF `file` that another environment reads, you can't add an environment with weights that have no file: the preview refuses it before anything is written, and tells you to deploy it there as a separately named model or remove it from the other environments first.

The model page shows one environment's copy at a time. When the model runs in more than one, the header links each of them.

## Link a service

On the model's page, under **Linked services**, choose **Link a service** and pick one. That adds the model to the service's `needs`, which you can also write yourself:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    needs: [qwen2-5-7b-instruct]
```

On its next release in that environment the service gets two variables:

- `MODEL_URL`, the model's address on the environment's private network.
- `MODEL_API_KEY`, the key the model's guard checks. Loomplane generates it and never shows it.

The service has to run on the same server or cluster as the model. **Linked services** says **Reachable** when it does, and when it doesn't, why: "api runs on edge-1, and qwen2-5-7b-instruct runs on gpu-1. Run them on the same server or cluster."

Chat models speak the OpenAI API, so the `openai` package works with `MODEL_URL` plus `/v1`:

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["MODEL_URL"] + "/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"],
)

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello."}],
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

The `model` field is the name the model is served as, its Hugging Face repo unless `served_name` says otherwise. The model page's **Example** tab has curl, Python and JavaScript for the model's own tasks: embeddings at `/v1/embeddings` (with the query prefix the model wants, such as `"query: "`, when the registry knows it), reranking at `POST $MODEL_URL/rerank`, and transcription at `POST $MODEL_URL/v1/audio/transcriptions`.

A service that needs the model in an environment where it doesn't run gets a `need-off` warning on that environment's plans, saying it gets no `MODEL_URL` there because the model doesn't run there. The warning doesn't block those deploys. It says how to fix it: "Deploy qwen2-5-7b-instruct to production from its model page."

## Any Hugging Face model

Above the registry, **Any Hugging Face model** takes a repo (`owner/name`) or its page's address. **Check** reads the repo at its current commit, works out what it needs from its `config.json` and its weights, and shows it as a card marked **Untested**, which you deploy like any other. It's kept for your workspace for an hour, and stored once you deploy it. You need `ai:edit` to use it.

Loomplane reads the repo anonymously, and uses the workspace's Hugging Face token only for a gated or private one. Paste a token in this box by mistake and it's caught before it's sent anywhere.

What it can serve:

- single-file GGUF weights ending in `Q8_0`, `MXFP4` or `Q4_K_M`, with llama.cpp,
- safetensors (or `pytorch_model` `.bin`) weights of an architecture the pinned vLLM knows,
- embedding and rerank models Text Embeddings Inference knows, with weights under 1.5 GiB, on CPU.

What it refuses, with the reason:

- a model whose `config.json` points at Python in its own repo (`auto_map`). Loomplane never runs repository code for a pasted model ("needs code from its repository to run, and Loomplane doesn't run repository code for pasted models"). A registry entry can, but only after that code was reviewed at the commit the entry pins.
- a task Loomplane doesn't serve, or a repo that doesn't say on Hugging Face what it does.
- an architecture no shipped engine knows, or a `config.json` that doesn't give the layer count, heads or context length the memory math needs.
- a GGUF split into parts, which llama.cpp can't download.

On Kubernetes, a llama.cpp model on CPU also needs its weights to fit the 20,480 MB volume the CPU kinds get there.

## Gated models

A gated model needs the workspace's Hugging Face token, from an account that has accepted the model's license. Without one, the deploy dialog says the model is gated and links to [AI settings](/docs/ai/settings#the-hugging-face-token). With one, it says "Gated on Hugging Face. The workspace's token can download it." If the account never accepted the license, the engine's download fails, and the model page tells you which license to accept, then **Retry**.

## The model page

Open a row on the **Deployed** tab. The header says the model's state:

| State | What's happening |
|---|---|
| **Planned** | The plan that deploys it waits for approval |
| **Waiting for a server** | Its GPU server is being created, or held back by the capacity policy, with the reason |
| **Deploying** | Downloading and loading weights |
| **Ready** | Serving. The page shows the address linked services reach it at |
| **Failed** | It didn't start. The page says why and what to try |
| **Update failed** | A change didn't start, and the version deployed before is still running, so linked services keep working |
| **Needs attention** | Its GPU server failed or took too long. Fix or retry the server in **Infrastructure**, then **Retry** here |

**Retry** plans the environment again for a model that failed to start, from the manifest as it is. For a model whose server needs attention, it waits for the same server again: Loomplane never creates a second one.

When the engine runs out of GPU memory, the page says so ("The model didn't fit in GPU memory at 22528 tokens. Try a shorter context or a smaller quantization.") and offers **Move it with a shorter context**.

The **Overview** tab also shows where it runs, its engine and version, its quantization, its context, its badge on the GPU it runs on, its [cost](/docs/ai/model-costs) and its linked services.

### Update available

When a Loomplane release pins new weights for a model's registry entry, its page shows **Update available** with what changed. **Move to** the new pin plans the change. The model keeps serving the weights it has until you approve the plan and the new ones are loaded. Planning the model's environment without moving it fails with a sentence that says to do this first, so the change never happens silently.

A pin move changes only the environment you move it from. When the model runs in staging and production and you move production, the page says "Moves production only. staging keeps its weights until you move it from its own page." Staging keeps its weights and keeps showing **Update available** until you move it from staging's page.

### Move it

**Settings**, then **Move**, runs this environment's copy on another GPU, server or cluster, or with another quantization or context. The other environments keep their copies as they are. It's the deploy dialog again, new GPU server and review included. The model keeps its name, so linked services keep their `MODEL_URL`, and it keeps running where it is until the move is deployed. While a move waits for a new GPU server, the page shows what that server costs, since both bill once it's up. A server Loomplane created for the model's old place keeps billing after the move until you delete it in **Infrastructure**, and the page says so.

### Remove it

**Settings**, then **Remove**, takes out the environment you're looking at and plans it. When the model runs in other environments too, that's all it removes: the dialog says "Removes llm from production. It keeps running in staging." A service in production that links to the model goes on linking to it, gets no `MODEL_URL` there once the plan is approved, and the plan warns `need-off` for it. The remove dialog lists those services before you confirm.

Removing the last environment removes the model from the manifest. That one is refused while a service links to it ("checkout in staging links to it. Unlink it first."). The downloaded weights stay on the server as retained storage, so deploying the model there again doesn't download them again. Delete them from the server's storage when you no longer need them. If Loomplane created the GPU server for this model, the server isn't removed with it, and keeps costing money until you delete it in **Infrastructure**.

Move, remove, retry and cancel need the same permission as deploying: `ai:edit`, or `ai:manage` in production. Linking a service is a manifest edit, so it needs `project:update`.

## On a Docker server

`docker ps` shows a llama.cpp engine as `unhealthy`. Its image's own health check looks at a port the engine doesn't listen on. Loomplane checks the engine's `/health` itself, so ignore it.

Each model is two containers: the engine and a guard in front of it. Only the guard's port is ever routed, and it refuses any request without `Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY`, except `/health`. See [GPUs](/docs/clouds/gpus) for what a server or cluster needs before it can run GPU work at all.

pages.title: AI settings
pages.description: Turn the AI section on, add the Hugging Face token gated models download with, and point Loomplane at a Hugging Face mirror.
pages.text:
The AI section has two kinds of settings. The server's live in `config.yaml` and the environment, and an operator sets them. The workspace's live on the **AI settings** page, and a workspace admin sets them.

The same page holds the built-in agent's panel for admins. See [Workspace settings](/docs/agents/workspace-settings).

## Turning AI on

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_AI_ENABLED=true
```

or, in `config.local.yaml`:

```yaml
ai:
  enabled: true
```

Restart Loomplane afterwards. It's off by default. With it off, the sidebar has no AI group, the `/api/v1/ai/...` routes don't exist, and the model kinds can't be planned.

### Turning AI off

Turning it off stops nothing. Models you deployed keep running on their servers and keep costing what they cost, since nothing in Loomplane stops a workload on its own. What changes is planning: any plan of an environment whose manifest still has a model resource gets a `catalog-feature-off` problem, which blocks it, until you turn AI back on or take the model out of `loomplane.yaml`. Remove your models from the Models page first if you mean to switch the section off for good.

## The Hugging Face token

Some models are gated on Hugging Face: you accept their license there before you can download them. Loomplane downloads gated weights with one token per workspace, which you add under **AI**, then **Settings**.

1. On Hugging Face, accept the model's license with the account you'll use.
2. Create a token with read access at `huggingface.co/settings/tokens`.
3. Paste it into **Token** and choose **Save**.

Loomplane checks the token with Hugging Face before it saves it, so a token Hugging Face refuses is refused here too ("Hugging Face didn't accept this token."). A token has to start with `hf_`.

Once saved, the token is write-only. The page shows its last four characters, the Hugging Face account it belongs to and when it was set, and never the token itself, not even to the admin who saved it. Saving a new one replaces it.

Public models deploy without a token. A gated model without one can't be deployed: the deploy dialog says so and links here, or tells you to ask an admin.

Only workspace admins (`ai:manage`) can change the token. Everyone else with `ai:read` sees the same summary and a note saying who can.

### Removing it

**Remove token** deletes it. Loomplane refuses while a deployed gated model still downloads with it, and names each one, such as "llama-8b in shop/production". Remove those models first, or add a new token instead, which replaces the old one in place.

A new token changes what a gated model's engine starts with, so the next plan of its environment shows an update for it. Approve that plan to restart the engine with the new token.

### Where it goes

The token is kept in Vault, never in the database. Loomplane itself sends it only to the Hugging Face host in `ai.models.huggingface_url`, to check whose it is and to read gated or private repos. When a gated model deploys, the token goes into a file only that model's engine can read, and the engine sends it to the same host to download the weights. It never appears in a plan, a log, an error or the audit log. [The security model](/docs/operations/security-model#models) has the details.

## A Hugging Face mirror

`ai.models.huggingface_url` (`LOOMPLANE_AI_MODELS_HUGGINGFACE_URL`) is where Loomplane and your model engines read Hugging Face: a pasted repo's metadata and `config.json`, model cards, the gated checks and the weights themselves. It defaults to `https://huggingface.co`.

```yaml
ai:
  models:
    huggingface_url: https://hf-mirror.example.com
```

It has to be https, because the workspace's token is sent there. Plain http works only for `localhost` or a loopback address. A URL with a user, a query or a fragment stops Loomplane at startup.

The mirror covers engine downloads too. vLLM and Text Embeddings Inference get it as `HF_ENDPOINT`, and llama.cpp fetches its GGUF file from it, so the servers that run your models need to reach the mirror, not `huggingface.co`. Change the URL and the next plan of each environment shows an update for its models; approve it to restart their engines against the new host.

pages.title: Clouds overview
pages.description: Every deployment target Loomplane ships with, what it runs and provisions, and how connections and Clouds fit together.
pages.text:
A target is somewhere Loomplane can run a service or provision a resource. You connect an account for each cloud under **Integrations**, name targets in your manifest, and Loomplane builds and deploys with your credentials in your accounts.

## Targets

Use the provider name in the left column in `provider:` fields in your manifest.

| Provider | Cloud | Runs | Provisions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vercel` | Vercel | Web apps, static sites | |
| `cloud-run` | Google Cloud | HTTP services, web apps | |
| `cloud-sql` | Google Cloud | | Postgres 17, 16, 15 and MySQL 8.4, 8.0 |
| `memorystore` | Google Cloud | | Redis |
| `cloud-storage` | Google Cloud | | Object storage |
| `ecs-fargate` | AWS | HTTP services, web apps, workers | |
| `rds` | AWS | | Postgres 17, 16, 15 and MySQL 8.4, 8.0 |
| `elasticache` | AWS | | Redis |
| `s3` | AWS | | Object storage |
| `cross-cloud-vpn` | Google Cloud and AWS | | [Links](/docs/concepts/gateways-and-networking#links) between them |
| `render` | Render | HTTP services, web apps, workers, static sites | Postgres 17, 16, 15 and Key Value (Redis) |
| `digitalocean` | DigitalOcean | HTTP services, web apps, workers, static sites | Managed PostgreSQL 17, 16, 15, MySQL 8 and Valkey |
| `azure-container-apps` | Azure | HTTP services, web apps, workers, static sites | |
| `azure-database` | Azure | | Postgres 17, 16, 15 and MySQL 8.4, 8.0.21 |
| `azure-managed-redis` | Azure | | Redis |
| `server` | Your SSH/Docker server | HTTP services, web apps, workers, static sites | Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Redis and Valkey containers |
| `kubernetes` | Your cluster | HTTP services, web apps, workers, static sites | Postgres on a StatefulSet |

Where a build runs depends on the target: Vercel builds on Vercel, Cloud Run on Cloud Build, ECS on CodeBuild, Render and DigitalOcean on their own platforms, Azure on ACR Tasks, and servers and clusters on the SSH builder you choose.

  Managed cloud paths (Cloud SQL, RDS and the rest) are checked against controlled provider endpoints. Live cloud creation and recovery are not yet qualified, and the pages that depend on them say so. Run one against a disposable project in your own account before you rely on it.

## Connections

A connection holds the credential for one account. When you add one, Loomplane checks it with the cloud before it keeps it. A credential the cloud refuses is never stored. One that works but lacks permissions is marked incomplete, with every missing permission listed, until you fix it and check again.

Credentials live in Vault, encrypted with a key derived from your secret key. A connection stays usable for as long as a plan, build, binding or deployment references it, so don't delete one that's still in use. You can rotate a credential and keep the same destination.

| Cloud | You provide |
|---|---|
| [Google Cloud](/docs/clouds/google-cloud) | A service account key (JSON) |
| [AWS](/docs/clouds/aws) | An access key ID and secret, plus a region |
| [Vercel](/docs/clouds/vercel) | An access token, and a team ID if you deploy to a team |
| [Render](/docs/clouds/render) | An API key, and a workspace ID if it reaches several |
| [DigitalOcean](/docs/clouds/digitalocean) | A personal access token |
| [Azure](/docs/clouds/azure) | A service principal's client secret, with tenant, client and subscription IDs |
| [Your own servers](/docs/clouds/your-own-servers) | An SSH key and host key, or a Kubernetes kubeconfig |

DigitalOcean, Vercel, Google Cloud and Azure can also [connect by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in), once a platform owner or admin has registered an app for the cloud. AWS, Google Cloud and Azure can [connect keylessly](/docs/clouds/keyless) as well, trusting tokens Loomplane signs itself, and then Vault holds nothing for the connection at all.

The same credential reads what the account costs and how its services are doing, when the cloud reports it. [Spend, latency and traffic](/docs/clouds/spend-and-traffic) lists what each cloud gives you and the permission it needs.

## Clouds and targets

A Cloud (the organization-level object, with a capital C) groups named targets so your manifest can say `cloud_target: frontend` without carrying an account ID. You can also pick targets by tag. [Cloud targets](/docs/clouds/cloud-targets) covers that, and [Adopting and moving services](/docs/clouds/adopting-and-moving) covers changing accounts later.

## Pausing a target

During an incident on a cloud you can pause its target. Plans that use it are still made and can be approved, but they're for review only and deploy nothing. See [Monitoring](/docs/operations/monitoring#pausing-a-target).

## Adding your own

If your target isn't here, write a [provider plugin](/docs/extending/provider-plugins).

pages.title: Adopting and moving services
pages.description: Bring running services under a Cloud target, then move them to another account or provider with a reviewed, recoverable sync.
pages.text:
## Adopt an existing service

Keep your existing manifest until you choose to adopt a Cloud. Create a target with the service's current provider, connection and region, assign that Cloud to its environment, and save a manifest revision that sets `cloud_target` while removing any effective direct `provider` and `target` settings. Check inherited defaults and environment overrides too, because a service can't resolve both forms of placement.

Review the ordinary deployment plan before you approve it. When the resolved placement and configuration match what already serves, the plan records Cloud metadata without a provider deployment. If it proposes a replacement, check the account, region and effective settings first.

Cloud targets currently place services. Resources and gateways keep their direct placement. A Cloud switch doesn't move database or storage contents.

## Replace an account or provider

Connect the destination account under Integrations first. Renewing a token for the same verified account keeps its connection ID and doesn't move services. Replacing the account takes a new connection. Stable provider identities, such as a Vercel user or team ID, tell renewal from replacement. If an older connection lacks its immutable identity, reconnect it before you switch.

```bash
loomctl cloud-targets show my-project cloud_... target_...
loomctl cloud-targets switch my-project cloud_... target_... \
  --provider vercel --connection conn_new --revision 1
```

Read the preview. It lists the old and proposed placement, affected environments and services, action counts, external routing requirements and blockers. A Cloud shared by production and staging can affect both, so use separate Clouds when their destinations should change independently.

To accept a review you already saved, use its ID and digest:

```bash
loomctl cloud-syncs apply my-project \
  --preview cpv_... --revision REVIEW_DIGEST \
  --request-id switch-frontend-2026-10-20 --yes --wait --timeout 30m
```

The command fetches and shows that exact preview before it applies it. Or repeat `cloud-targets switch` with `--yes`, which creates and shows a fresh review before accepting it. Previews expire after 24 hours, and a revision change or altered serving inputs need another review.

The idempotency key belongs to acceptance. After a lost response, reuse the same preview, digest and `--request-id` to recover the original sync ID. A new preview is a separate request, even if the destination looks identical.

A switch migrates the release that currently serves, using each binding's saved source artifact and encrypted variable snapshot. It doesn't deploy an unapproved draft, and missing historical inputs block it. Future ordinary releases use the new account.

A service region set in the manifest, in its environment override or in defaults stays pinned when you change a target's default region. Services that inherit the target or provider default follow the new one. Older bindings without recorded region provenance keep their applied region during a sync. Deploy an ordinary release to record that before you rely on a default change to move them.

### Switch a default

```bash
loomctl clouds switch-default my-project cloud_... \
  --provider vercel --connection conn_new --revision 3
loomctl clouds switch-default my-project cloud_... \
  --provider vercel --connection conn_new --revision 3 \
  --yes --request-id move-default --wait --timeout 30m
```

The review covers every environment that uses the Cloud, across projects, and moves only the services the old default placed. Services on a target, or with their own `provider`, keep theirs, though one that depends on a moved service is redeployed to pick up the new address. Leave out the provider and connection (or pass `--clear`) to remove the default. Clearing is blocked while serving services still use it. One default switch runs per Cloud at a time, and no environment can be assigned to or from the Cloud until it settles.

A Cloud reassignment works the same way for default-placed services: they move to the new Cloud's default, and the review blocks if the new Cloud has none your project can use.

## Follow and recover a sync

```bash
loomctl cloud-syncs my-project
loomctl cloud-syncs show my-project csync_...
loomctl cloud-syncs wait my-project csync_... --timeout 30m
loomctl cloud-syncs retry my-project csync_... --wait --timeout 30m
```

Use `--json` for scripts. Finish or revert unfinished syncs before renaming a Cloud or target in the same project.

| State | Meaning and next action |
|---|---|
| `pending` | Accepted and saved. Dispatch will schedule or recover it |
| `running` | Services are being reconciled from recorded inputs |
| `routing_pending` | The managed deployment finished, but you must verify external routing |
| `cleanup_pending` | Old resources are being removed. An error means cleanup needs recovery or a retry |
| `failed` | Inspect per-environment errors, restore access or dependencies, then retry |
| `succeeded` | Every affected environment and its cleanup finished |
| `reverting` | A compensating operation owns the remaining work. Follow its sync ID |
| `reverted` | Compensation finished and original ownership was released |

Waits stop at success, failure, external routing or a cleanup error, and keep going through active cleanup. A timeout returns the latest record so you can resume. Restarting Loomplane recovers committed work. Partial completion is kept: a successful environment stays deployed when another fails. Old resources stay until managed consumers and required external routing have finished, and failed operations keep their guards so an ordinary release can't race unfinished cleanup.

## Complete external routing, or revert

If you control DNS or another entry point, update it and check that traffic reaches the new service. Then record that for each affected environment:

```bash
loomctl cloud-syncs routing my-project csync_... \
  --environment env_... --evidence 'Production DNS and HTTPS verified' \
  --wait --timeout 10m
```

This records your evidence and schedules the remaining cleanup. It doesn't change DNS. Without that evidence, Loomplane keeps the old resources.

```bash
loomctl cloud-syncs revert my-project csync_...
loomctl cloud-syncs revert my-project csync_... \
  --yes --request-id restore-frontend --wait --timeout 30m
```

Revert reviews compensation from the actual serving state. Read each environment's `compensation_mode` and `compensation_message`. `restore_retained` restores the exact retained original server runtime, `recreate` deploys saved inputs again, and `mixed` does both. A managed platform always recreates from saved inputs. Compensation refuses work that changed outside the original operation, and original credentials must stay available until all cleanup finishes.

  Fixture-backed checks verify persisted switching, historical input recovery and next-release account selection. They don't establish access, quotas, DNS propagation or service behavior in your real provider account. Qualify those yourself before a production migration, and move database or storage contents separately.

pages.title: AWS
pages.description: Connect an AWS account and run services on ECS on Fargate with RDS, ElastiCache and S3.
pages.text:
Loomplane builds a service with CodeBuild, stores the image in ECR and runs it on ECS on Fargate, behind a load balancer when it serves HTTP. It provisions RDS (Postgres and MySQL), ElastiCache (Redis OSS) and S3 buckets alongside it.

## Connect an account

Under **Integrations**, choose AWS and enter an access key ID and secret, then a region. The region is required, because everything Loomplane makes with this connection lives in it. Key IDs start with `AKIA` or `ASIA`.

Loomplane asks STS who the key is, then runs IAM's policy simulator against the actions a deployment needs and lists any the principal can't take. If the key isn't allowed to run the simulator, the connection is ready with its permissions marked unchecked, so a failed step is where you'll find out.

You can add an ACM certificate ARN for the same region as an optional setting. Public ECS services then serve HTTPS. Without one they serve HTTP.

| Used for | Actions Loomplane checks |
|---|---|
| Builds | `codebuild:BatchGetBuilds`, `CreateProject`, `StartBuild`, `UpdateProject`; `ecr:CreateRepository`, `DescribeRepositories`. Recommended, not checked: `ecr:DescribeImages` |
| ECS | `ecs:CreateCluster`, `CreateService`, `DeleteService`, `DescribeClusters`, `DescribeServices`, `RegisterTaskDefinition`, `UpdateService` |
| Load balancing | `elasticloadbalancing:CreateListener`, `CreateLoadBalancer`, `CreateRule`, `CreateTargetGroup`, `DescribeListeners`, `DescribeLoadBalancers`, `DescribeRules`, `DescribeTargetGroups` |
| Canary releases only | `elasticloadbalancing:DeleteTargetGroup`, `DescribeTargetHealth`, `ModifyListener` |
| Networking | `ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress`, `CreateSecurityGroup`, `DescribeSecurityGroups`, `DescribeSubnets`, `DescribeVpcs`; `servicediscovery:CreateHttpNamespace`, `CreateService`, `GetNamespace`, `GetOperation`, `ListNamespaces` |
| IAM and logs | `iam:AttachRolePolicy`, `CreateRole`, `GetRole`, `PassRole`, `PutRolePolicy`; `logs:CreateLogGroup` |
| Secrets | `secretsmanager:CreateSecret`, `PutSecretValue` |
| RDS | `rds:CreateDBInstance`, `CreateDBSubnetGroup`, `DeleteDBInstance`, `DescribeDBInstances`, `DescribeDBSnapshots`, `AddTagsToResource` |
| ElastiCache | `elasticache:CreateCacheSubnetGroup`, `CreateReplicationGroup`, `DeleteReplicationGroup`, `DescribeReplicationGroups` |
| S3 | `s3:CreateBucket`, `DeleteBucket`, `DeleteObject`, `ListBucket`, `PutBucketPublicAccessBlock`, `PutObject` |

With `ecr:DescribeImages`, Loomplane reads the digest of each image a build pushes, deploys the image by that digest and records it with the release. A promotion can then deploy the exact image staging ran, and a rollback the image the previous release ran. Without it you can still deploy: the service runs its image by tag, the step warns you, and promoting or rolling back that service builds it again.

Reading build logs also needs CloudWatch `GetLogEvents`. A cross-cloud link needs the VPN actions listed in the [manifest reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml#links).

## Connect keylessly

You can skip the access key altogether. When Loomplane's public URL is HTTPS and reachable from the internet, the connect dialog offers **Connect keylessly** first. It gives you three things to do in the account: add Loomplane's issuer as an IAM OpenID Connect provider with `sts.amazonaws.com` as its client ID, create a role whose trust policy names this one connection, and attach a policy with the actions in the table above. Each comes with a command or policy to copy.

Then paste the role's ARN and the region and choose **Check and connect**. Loomplane assumes the role with `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` each time it needs AWS, with a token it signs itself that lasts 10 minutes, so you have no access key to store or rotate. Sessions are named `loomplane-` and the connection's ID, which is what you'll see in CloudTrail.

Loomplane asks AWS once a day whether the role still trusts it. If someone deleted the role or the provider, the connection shows as failed and you get a notice. [Connect a cloud keylessly](/docs/clouds/keyless) has the full trust policy, how the signing keys turn over, and how to move a key connection to keyless.

## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
services:
  api:
    source: go:services/api
    provider: ecs-fargate
    needs: [db, cache, uploads]
  worker:
    source: services/worker
    provider: ecs-fargate
    needs: [db]
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    provider: rds
    version: "17"
  cache:
    kind: redis
    provider: elasticache
  uploads:
    kind: object-storage
    provider: s3
```

## How things behave

The region is the connection's. Leave `region` out and you get it. Name a different one and the plan stops, because the deployment would land in the connection's region anyway. To move an environment to another AWS region, choose a connection in that region for it.

Two ECS services in the same environment reach each other inside the VPC at `http://name:port`, whether or not the one they need is public. A worker is an ECS service with no load balancer. RDS and ElastiCache are reachable from the environment's ECS tasks only.

Buckets are private, and services reach them with their task's environment role, so `STORAGE_URL` carries no credentials (`s3://bucket?region=...`). Redis gets an auth token in `REDIS_URL` (`rediss://...`), and ElastiCache encrypts it in transit and at rest.

Secret variables go to Secrets Manager and never into a task definition.

A canary runs the new release as a second ECS service, named after the first with `-canary` on the end, in a target group of its own. Its listener splits traffic between the two target groups by weight. Only traffic through the load balancer is split. Your other services still call the baseline over Service Connect until the canary is promoted.

The canary releases only actions aren't needed for anything else, so a key without them still deploys. The connection lists what's missing, and a canary on ECS refuses to start, when you plan it and again when it runs, naming the actions. Grant them, or release that environment `direct` or `blue_green`.

The candidate reads its secret variables from a Secrets Manager path of its own, the service's path with `-canary` added, so a baseline task that restarts mid-canary keeps its own values. Those secrets and the `-canary` task definition family stay in the account after the canary finishes. The next canary overwrites them.

Supported regions Loomplane lists: `us-east-1`, `us-east-2`, `us-west-2`, `ca-central-1`, `sa-east-1`, `eu-west-1`, `eu-west-2`, `eu-central-1`, `eu-north-1`, `ap-south-1`, `ap-southeast-1`, `ap-southeast-2` and `ap-northeast-1`.

  RDS creation, removal and snapshot handling are checked against controlled AWS endpoints. Live AWS creation, SQL persistence and snapshot restore aren't qualified yet. RDS removal keeps a final snapshot and the automated backups, which can incur storage charges. See [Database services](/docs/services/database-services).

pages.title: Azure
pages.description: Connect an Azure service principal and run services on Container Apps with Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL and Azure Managed Redis.
pages.text:
Loomplane uploads the approved commit to a container registry in your subscription, ACR Tasks builds the service there, and a container app runs the image. Nothing from your repository runs on a Loomplane machine.

## Connect Azure

You connect a service principal: an application registered in Microsoft Entra ID, with a client secret.


In the Azure portal, open **Microsoft Entra ID**, then **App registrations**, and register an application. Note its Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID.


Under **Certificates & secrets**, add a client secret and copy its value. Azure shows it once.


On the subscription you'll deploy to (or on the resource group, if you'd rather keep Loomplane inside one), open **Access control (IAM)** and give the application the Contributor role.


In Loomplane, open **Integrations**, choose **Microsoft Azure**, paste the secret, and fill in the tenant ID, client ID and subscription ID. The resource group is optional and defaults to `loomplane`.


If you prefer the CLI, `az ad sp create-for-rbac --role Contributor --scopes /subscriptions/<id>` does the first three steps at once. Its `appId` is the client ID, `password` the secret and `tenant` the tenant ID.

Loomplane signs in as the principal before it keeps the secret. A wrong or expired secret is refused with Entra ID's own AADSTS code, so you can tell a mistyped secret from an expired one. Then it asks Azure what the principal's role assignments allow in the resource group (or in the subscription while the group isn't there yet), and lists every action a deployment needs that they leave out. Contributor has them all.

### How apps pull images

Contributor can't assign roles, and that decides how your apps pull their images. Give the principal Owner on the resource group, or Role Based Access Control Administrator there as well as Contributor, and each app pulls from the registry as a managed identity called `loomplane-pull`, which holds the AcrPull role on that registry and nothing else. With Contributor alone, apps pull with the registry's admin user, and its password goes into each app as a secret. The connection shows which you get under `registry_pull`, either `identity` or `admin`. Every deployment asks Azure again, so a role you add later counts from the next one. Check the connection again to update what it shows.

Azure takes a while to let a new identity pull. The first deployment after you grant the role can sit at "Waiting for the pull identity's role to reach the container registry" for a few minutes. Loomplane waits up to ten. If that runs out, retry the deployment.

### Resource providers

The subscription needs `Microsoft.App` and `Microsoft.ContainerRegistry`. Loomplane registers them on the first deployment if you haven't, which Contributor on the subscription may do. With Contributor on only a resource group, register them yourself under the subscription's **Resource providers**. Apps that pull with the identity also need `Microsoft.ManagedIdentity`, which Loomplane registers when it first makes `loomplane-pull`.

The subscription and resource group are the connection's account. You can replace the secret, or switch to another principal with access to the same group, and nothing that uses the connection has to change.

## Sign in instead of a secret

If a platform owner or admin has registered an Azure app for sign-in, the connect dialog offers **Sign in with Microsoft Azure** first and **Use a token instead** underneath. Type the tenant ID and subscription ID, and a resource group if you don't want `loomplane`, then sign in to Microsoft and approve. The app needs the delegated `user_impersonation` permission for Azure Service Management, and the callback as a Web redirect URI.

The connection acts as you, so you need a role on the resource group that covers what a deployment does, such as Contributor. Loomplane checks your role assignments the same way it checks a service principal's, and what [How apps pull images](#how-apps-pull-images) says about Owner and Role Based Access Control Administrator applies to you too. The connection shows which Microsoft account it acts as, and which Loomplane member signed in. When that member leaves the organization, the next background run (they're 6 hours apart) asks for a new sign-in, and anyone who manages cloud accounts can do it with their own account.

Microsoft's refresh token lasts 90 days from its last use, and Loomplane renews it every 6 hours. [Connect a cloud by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in) covers registering the app and what happens if Azure stops accepting the sign-in.

## Connect keylessly

An app registration can trust Loomplane with a federated credential, so there's no client secret to expire. When Loomplane's public URL is HTTPS and reachable from the internet, the connect dialog offers **Connect keylessly** (or **Connect keylessly instead**, under the sign-in button). It gives you an `az ad app federated-credential create` command for your app, with Loomplane's issuer, this connection's subject and the audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange`, then a role assignment that makes the app a Contributor on the resource group. If you don't have an app for Loomplane yet, `az ad app create --display-name loomplane` and `az ad sp create --id <client-id>` make one.

The federated credential is named `loomplane-` and the connection's ID, so one app can serve several connections, each with a credential of its own. Fill in the tenant ID, the app's client ID, the subscription ID and the resource group, then choose **Check and connect**. Loomplane signs a 10-minute token for every sign-in to Entra and uses it as the app's client assertion, then checks the app's role assignments as it would a service principal's.

Loomplane asks Entra once a day whether the app still trusts the connection. If the federated credential is gone, the connection shows as failed and you get a notice. [Connect a cloud keylessly](/docs/clouds/keyless) has the whole setup and what happens when Azure refuses the trust.

## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
defaults:
  provider: azure-container-apps
  region: westeurope
services:
  api:
    source: services/api
```

Or make the subscription a target in one of your Clouds and name it with `cloud_target`. See [Cloud targets](/docs/clouds/cloud-targets).

The regions are `eastus`, `eastus2`, `centralus`, `westus2`, `westus3`, `canadacentral`, `brazilsouth`, `northeurope`, `westeurope`, `uksouth`, `francecentral`, `germanywestcentral`, `swedencentral`, `japaneast`, `koreacentral`, `southeastasia`, `centralindia` and `australiaeast`. Leave `region` out and you get `eastus`.

## What gets made

Everything lives in the connection's resource group, which Loomplane creates in the first region you deploy to if it isn't there.

- One Basic container registry, named from a hash of the subscription and resource group, since registry names are global across Azure. Its admin user stays on even when your apps pull with the identity.
- The `loomplane-pull` managed identity, when the principal may assign roles.
- One Container Apps environment per region, called `loomplane-<region>`. It's consumption only, with no Log Analytics workspace.
- A container app for each service in each environment, named after the service, the environment and the project.

A service with a Dockerfile builds from it. Anything else goes through Google's buildpacks, run by `pack` in the same ACR Tasks run. Each deployment builds the approved commit, tagged with its first twelve characters, and the app runs that image in a single active revision, except while a canary ramps (see below).

A public service takes HTTPS traffic from anywhere. A private one only takes traffic from apps in its own Container Apps environment, which means the same connection and the same region. The plan stops with a finding if a service that needs one sits in another region or account, and a service on another cloud can't reach it at all.

`size` picks the smallest consumption size that fits, a quarter CPU at a time with twice as many GiB of memory, up to 4 CPUs and 8 GiB. `scale` sets the minimum and maximum replicas. Without it Container Apps scales with traffic, down to zero.

A worker runs as a container app with no ingress. Nothing calls a worker to wake it, so it never scales to zero: the minimum is one replica even if you set `scale.min` to 0. A static site also runs as a container app, so it needs a Dockerfile that builds the site and serves it with nginx or any other web server. Without a Dockerfile the plan stops with a finding. The app takes traffic on the `port` you set, or the one your Dockerfile exposes, otherwise 8080 (the plan warns when it has to guess). A server that listens on 80, like nginx, needs `EXPOSE 80` in the Dockerfile or `port: 80` in the manifest.

Secret variables go in as app secrets, which Azure never shows again. Removing a service from the manifest deletes its container app. The registry and the environment stay for the group's other apps.

### Canary releases

A canary runs the new release as a second revision of the same container app, beside the one that served before. Loomplane switches the app to multiple revisions mode and moves the traffic between the two revisions by weight, step by step. Promoting puts the app back in single revision mode with all of the traffic on the latest revision, which is the new one, and Container Apps deactivates the old revision. A rollback gives the old revision all of the traffic, puts its template back on the app and deactivates the new one. Putting the template back makes one more revision with the old configuration, which takes no traffic, and Loomplane deactivates it too. The app stays in multiple revisions mode, pinned to the old revision, until your next deploy switches it back.

Container Apps keeps secrets on the app, not on each revision, and a replica reads them when it starts. So the new revision reads its own copies, named after its revision suffix, and the old revision's secrets keep their values the whole time. A replica the old revision starts in the middle of a canary still gets the old values. A rollback removes the new revision's copies once it's deactivated. After a promote, the next deploy keeps them until its own revision has taken over, then removes them.

Ingress is app-wide too: the port, whether the app is public, and its transport apply to every revision at once, and so do the registry it pulls from and the identity it pulls as. A release that changes any of them can't canary, because the old revision would take the change while it still serves. The plan says so, and the canary refuses again before it touches the app. Release that change `direct` or `blue_green` once, and canary the next one.

A canary needs three actions every other deploy can do without:

| Needed for | Actions |
|---|---|
| Canary releases only | `Microsoft.App/containerApps/revisions/read`, `Microsoft.App/containerApps/revisions/deactivate/action`, `Microsoft.App/containerApps/listSecrets/action` |

Contributor has them. The last one is there because Azure never shows a secret's value on a read, and the new revision's update has to send the old revision's secrets back as they are. A principal without them still deploys any app that never ran a canary. Once a canary has left revisions or secrets of its own on an app, the next deploy there needs the first and the last too, since it has to read what the old revisions use before it replaces the app's secrets, and it stops with the missing action named if it can't. The connection lists what's missing, and a canary on Container Apps refuses to start, when you plan it and again when it runs. Grant them, or release that environment `direct` or `blue_green`.

If an earlier canary couldn't roll back and left the traffic split, or left all of it on its new revision, a new canary on that app won't start, since it can't tell which revision is the real one to compare against. Retry or roll back that deployment, or release once with `direct`, which gives the latest revision all of the traffic.

## Databases

| Manifest kind | Made on Azure | Provider | Versions |
|---|---|---|---|
| `postgres` | Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server | `azure-database` | 17, 16, 15 |
| `mysql` | Azure Database for MySQL flexible server | `azure-database` | 8.4, 8.0.21 |
| `redis` | Azure Managed Redis | `azure-managed-redis` | Azure's current one |

```yaml
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    version: "16"
    provider: azure-database
    region: westeurope
  cache:
    kind: redis
    provider: azure-managed-redis
    region: westeurope
```

Leave `version` out and you get Postgres 17 or MySQL 8.4. Each database goes in the connection's resource group. A service that needs one has to run on Azure in the same account, or the plan stops with a finding. It gets the address as an app secret.

Postgres and MySQL run on one `Standard_B1ms` Burstable server, with 32 GiB of storage for Postgres and 20 GiB for MySQL. The admin user is `loomplane`, and its password is 32 random characters Loomplane makes the first time it applies the database and keeps in Vault. Each server has public network access and one firewall rule, `AllowAllAzureServicesAndResourcesWithinAzureIps`. That rule is how your container apps get in, and it also lets in traffic from every other Azure customer's resources, in any subscription. Only the password and TLS stand between them and your data. Addresses ask for TLS (`sslmode=require` for Postgres, `tls=true` for MySQL).

Redis is an Azure Managed Redis cluster on the `Balanced_B0` size with one database called `default`. It only takes TLS connections on port 10000 and authenticates with an access key, so the address looks like `rediss://:<key>@<host>:10000`. It uses Azure's enterprise clustering policy, which gives you a single endpoint, so a client that doesn't speak Redis Cluster works fine. Loomplane reads the key when it applies the cache and keeps the address as a secret. If you regenerate the key in Azure your apps keep the old one and can't connect until the cache is applied again, so don't rotate the key there. Loomplane sets no network rule on the cluster, so its endpoint takes connections from anywhere that has the key. Managed Redis isn't offered in every region. If yours lacks it, the deployment fails with a message that names the region and suggests another.

Server and cluster names are global DNS names across Azure. Each is built from the resource, the environment and the project, and ends in a hyphen and six hex characters of a hash of your subscription ID.

The databases need `Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL`, `Microsoft.DBforMySQL` and `Microsoft.Cache`. Loomplane registers each on the first deployment that makes that kind of database. With Contributor on only a resource group, register them yourself.

Removing a database from the manifest deletes it with its data, so take a backup first.

## What it can't do yet

Databases only have public endpoints for now, and VNet integration and private endpoints aren't there. Every database gets the smallest size, with no way to pick another. Build logs are under **Services**, **Tasks**, **Runs** in the container registry, and Loomplane shows the deployment's progress.

pages.title: Connect a cloud by signing in
pages.description: Register an OAuth app once for the whole instance, then connect DigitalOcean, Vercel, Google Cloud, Azure or Cloudflare by signing in.
pages.text:
A pasted token works, but it's yours to copy, store and rotate. Signing in swaps that for a grant the cloud hands to Loomplane after you approve it, and Loomplane renews the grant on its own. DigitalOcean, Vercel, Google Cloud, Azure and Cloudflare all connect this way. On AWS, Google Cloud and Azure you can also [connect keylessly](/docs/clouds/keyless), where Loomplane holds no grant at all.

## Register the OAuth app

You do this once per cloud for the whole instance, and you need to be the platform owner or a platform admin. Everyone else in every organization only signs in. Until a cloud has an app, its connect dialog can't offer to sign in. You paste a token there, or connect keylessly where the cloud supports it.

The first time you run Loomplane, setup ends with an optional **Cloud sign-in** step. Skip that step and you can register the apps later on the Cloud sign-in page.


In Loomplane, open **Settings**, then **Cloud sign-in** (it's at `/platform/cloud-sign-in`, and only platform owners and admins see it). The page shows a callback URL, which is your public URL followed by `/integrations/oauth/callback`. Copy it. Every cloud uses the same one.


Make the app with the cloud, using the steps for it below, and paste the callback URL wherever it asks for a redirect or callback.


Back on the Cloud sign-in page, choose **Set up** on the cloud's row, paste the app's client ID and client secret, and save. The secret is kept encrypted and never shown again, so replace it there if you lose track of it.


The callback has to match exactly, down to `https` and the host. If you change `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL` later, update the app with each cloud too.

### DigitalOcean

Open **API**, then **OAuth Applications**, and make a new application. Paste the callback URL as the callback. Loomplane asks for the `read write` scope, so the application needs to allow it.

### Vercel

On Vercel you make an Integration, not a plain OAuth app. Open the Integrations Console from your team's settings and create one. Set its redirect URL to the callback URL. Under its permissions, give it read and write on projects, project environment variables, deployments and domains, and read on the team and the user. Loomplane calls all of those when it deploys, the same as it does with a token.

The Integration's settings show its client ID and client secret. The Cloud sign-in page also asks for the **Integration slug**: the last part of the Integration's address on Vercel, so for `https://vercel.com/integrations/loomplane-acme` you'd type `loomplane-acme`. Loomplane sends people to that page to install it.

### Google Cloud

In the Google Cloud console, open **APIs & Services**. Set up the OAuth consent screen first if the project doesn't have one (newer consoles call it **Google Auth Platform**), and add the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform` scope under its data access. Loomplane also asks for `openid` and `email`, which need nothing extra. Then open **Credentials**, create an OAuth client ID of type **Web application**, and add the callback URL under **Authorized redirect URIs**.

Publish the app when you're done. While it's in testing, Google ends every sign-in after 7 days and the connection asks to be signed in again, which the Cloud sign-in page reminds you of.

If you make it an **External** app, Google also has to verify it, because `cloud-platform` is one of its sensitive scopes. Until it does, everyone who signs in sees a warning that Google hasn't verified the app and has to open **Advanced** to carry on, and no more than 100 people can sign in with it. You ask for verification from the consent screen. Google wants a homepage, a privacy policy and a reason for each scope, so expect it to take a while. If everyone who'll sign in is in your Google Workspace, make the app **Internal** instead, which needs neither publishing nor verification and has no 100-person limit.

The person who signs in needs `serviceusage.services.use` on the project they deploy to. Owner, Editor and Service Usage Consumer all include it. Loomplane bills their API calls to that project, not to the one the OAuth client lives in, so the client's project doesn't need any of the APIs turned on. Without the permission the connection lists it as missing.

### Azure

In the Azure portal, open **Microsoft Entra ID**, then **App registrations**, and register an application. Single tenant is fine when everyone signs in from your own directory; pick multitenant if people sign in from other tenants. Under **Authentication**, add a **Web** platform with the callback URL as its redirect URI.

Under **Certificates & secrets**, add a client secret and copy its value, since Azure shows it once. Then under **API permissions**, add **Azure Service Management** with the delegated `user_impersonation` permission. Loomplane also asks for `openid`, `profile` and `offline_access`. If your tenant only lets admins consent to apps, an admin grants consent there once.

The Application (client) ID on the app's overview is the client ID you paste into Loomplane.

### Cloudflare

In Cloudflare, open **Manage Account**, then **OAuth clients**, and create a client. Register the callback shown in Loomplane. Choose **Authorization Code** and **Refresh Token**, response type **code**, and token authentication **client_secret_basic**. Loomplane also sends S256 PKCE.

Enable `account-settings.read` and `offline_access` on the client. For DNS, also enable `zone.read` and `dns.write`. For R2 storage, enable `workers-r2.write`. If you offer both, register all five scopes. Loomplane requests the scopes for the services you choose when connecting. Account Settings Read lets Loomplane verify the selected account. Enable `offline_access` on the client itself, since a grant without a refresh token cannot keep your connection working. Check the current scope IDs in Cloudflare's scope picker or its authenticated `GET /client/v4/oauth/scopes` API.

Copy the client ID and secret into Loomplane's **Cloud sign-in** settings. A private client works only for members of the Cloudflare account that owns it. To serve other accounts, complete Cloudflare's domain verification and public-client requirements. Making a client public is permanent. See [Cloudflare's registration guide](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/oauth/create-an-oauth-client/).

When connecting, enter the **Account ID**, then choose **DNS**, **R2 storage** or **DNS and R2**. Loomplane verifies account access and checks only the selected services. A storage-only connection does not need DNS permissions. Existing connections default to DNS. Replace the credential to add R2 access to one; its account stays fixed. Existing API-token connections continue to work. Extra registrar or cache permissions are needed only for the operations that use them.

R2 API-token connections also need Account Settings Read so resource sync can verify the account. R2 permission checks only list bucket metadata. A successful check does not prove bucket creation permission, and OAuth credentials are never passed to an application's S3 client. A Worker in the same verified Cloudflare account can use a native binding. For other application targets, supply bucket-scoped R2 S3 credentials in Resources and complete its access check. See [R2 authentication](https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/tokens/).

To create a bucket, add an `object-storage` resource to your manifest with `cloudflare-workers` as its provider and your Cloudflare connection ID as its target:

```yaml
version: 1
resources:
  assets:
    kind: object-storage
    provider: cloudflare-workers
    target: conn_your_cloudflare_connection
    settings:
      jurisdiction: default
```

Review and approve the plan before Loomplane creates the bucket. Sync your account in Resources to discover existing buckets. After setting up the selected bucket's application access, you can attach it with its inventory ID:

```yaml
version: 1
resources:
  assets:
    kind: object-storage
    existing_resource: providerresource_your_bucket
```

Add `assets` to your application's `needs` to use it. Native bindings require a Worker in the bucket's account, with Workers deployment permissions on its connection. The R2 OAuth selection grants bucket management access only. Removing an existing-resource attachment disconnects it from the project and keeps the provider bucket.

## Sign in to your cloud

Open **Integrations**, choose the cloud and pick **Sign in with** followed by the cloud's name, or **Use a token instead** underneath if you'd rather paste a token or key. You finish on the cloud's page and land back in Loomplane with the connection ready. Be quick. The sign-in Loomplane starts expires after ten minutes.

What happens on the cloud's page depends on the cloud.

- DigitalOcean asks you to approve Loomplane and pick the team. The connection belongs to that team, the same as a token's.
- Vercel shows the Integration's install page, where you pick the team or your own account to install it on. Install it in the same browser you started from. Vercel doesn't always pass Loomplane's state back, and the dashboard keeps its own copy in that browser for the ten minutes.
- Google Cloud needs the **Project ID** typed in the dialog before you sign in. You sign in to your Google account and approve, and the connection deploys to that project as you.
- Azure needs the **Directory (tenant) ID** and **Subscription ID** before you sign in, and takes an optional resource group, which defaults to `loomplane`. You sign in to Microsoft in that tenant, and the connection deploys into the resource group as you.

Google and Azure act as the person who signed in, so the connection can only do what their own roles let them. Loomplane checks that the same way it checks a key. For Google it asks which of the permissions a deployment needs you hold on the project, and lists any you don't. For Azure it asks what your role assignments allow in the resource group (or in the subscription while the group isn't there yet), so you need a role such as Contributor there. [Google Cloud](/docs/clouds/google-cloud) and [Azure](/docs/clouds/azure) have the full lists.

## Who signed in

A Google or Azure connection shows who it acts as: **Signed in as** the Google or Microsoft account, then the Loomplane member who signed in. A DigitalOcean or Vercel sign-in belongs to the team it was approved for, so there's no person to show.

If that member leaves the connection's organization, the connection shouldn't go on acting as them, so Loomplane notices on its next background run (they're 6 hours apart), marks the connection as needing a new sign-in and sends the usual notice. Anyone who can manage cloud accounts can then choose **Sign in again** with their own account. The connection keeps its ID, and the project, or the tenant, subscription and resource group, have to stay the same.

## Set the app in config instead

If you'd rather keep the app out of the dashboard, put it in `config.yaml` or the environment. It applies to every organization, the same as an app from the page:

```yaml
clouds:
  oauth:
    digitalocean:
      client_id: your-client-id
      client_secret: your-client-secret
    vercel:
      client_id: your-client-id
      client_secret: your-client-secret
      slug: loomplane-acme
    gcp:
      client_id: your-client-id.apps.googleusercontent.com
      client_secret: your-client-secret
    azure:
      client_id: your-application-client-id
      client_secret: your-client-secret
    cloudflare:
      client_id: your-client-id
      client_secret: your-client-secret
```

You only need the clouds you use. Each value also reads from the environment:

| Cloud | Variables |
|---|---|
| DigitalOcean | `LOOMPLANE_DIGITALOCEAN_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `LOOMPLANE_DIGITALOCEAN_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` |
| Vercel | `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_SLUG` |
| Google Cloud | `LOOMPLANE_GCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `LOOMPLANE_GCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` |
| Azure | `LOOMPLANE_AZURE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `LOOMPLANE_AZURE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` |
| Cloudflare | `LOOMPLANE_CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `LOOMPLANE_CLOUDFLARE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` |

Set a cloud's ID and secret together or not at all, because one without the other stops startup. Vercel's slug is required once its ID and secret are set.

Config wins. Once a cloud's app is set there, the Cloud sign-in page shows that cloud as **Set by the deployment** and locks it, so nobody can point it at something else. Clouds you left out of config stay editable on the page.

## When a sign-in lapses

How long a grant lasts depends on the cloud.

- DigitalOcean access tokens last 30 days. Loomplane refreshes the grant when it uses it, and again every 6 hours in the background, so a connection in regular use never gets near the end.
- Vercel's token doesn't expire. It works until someone uninstalls the Integration, so Loomplane asks Vercel once a day whether it still does.
- Google's access tokens last an hour, and deployments renew them as they go. The grant itself lasts until it's revoked, or for 7 days while the OAuth app is in testing.
- Azure's refresh token lasts 90 days from its last use. The background job renews it every 6 hours, which keeps that window moving.

A cloud can still refuse the grant. Someone revoked Loomplane's access, uninstalled the Vercel Integration, or deleted the app. Loomplane finds out the next time it renews the grant, on the daily check, or when you choose **Check again** on the connection, so a deployment that runs in between fails with the cloud's own error.

Once Loomplane knows, the connection shows **Sign-in needed** and nothing deploys through it. Choose **Sign in again**, either on the connection's page or on its row in the **Clouds** list under **Integrations**, and approve once more. The button shows on any signed-in connection that isn't ready. The connection keeps its ID, so your projects and environments carry on without changes.

The person who made the connection and the owners and admins of the connection's organization hear about it in the inbox, and by email if mail is set up. Every webhook endpoint gets a `connection.sign_in_needed` event too, including endpoints you made before sign-in existed. You get one notice per lapse, not one per refresh attempt.

A Google or Azure person can also lose a role without losing the sign-in. The grant still works then, but deployments fail on the permission. **Check again** lists what's missing.

## Replace or remove an app

Choose **Edit** on the cloud's row to change the app. The **Remove** button is in the same dialog. If connections have signed in with the current app, the page tells you how many before you change its client ID or remove it.

Give a cloud a different client ID, or remove its app, and every one of those connections asks to be signed in again, because the old grants belong to the old app. Changing only the client secret keeps them all working. Vercel connections are the exception: Vercel's tokens don't depend on the app once they're issued, so they carry on either way.

## When the cloud refuses the app

If the cloud refuses the app itself, say after someone rotated its client secret, every sign-in through it stops working. A platform owner or admin sees the problem on that cloud's row of the Cloud sign-in page. Save the app again with the new values and it clears. Each connection that tried the app asks to be signed in again as well.

An app set in config isn't recorded on the page, so a refusal there shows only on the connections, with the cloud's message. It clears with the first sign-in that works after you fix config.

## Switch between a token and a sign-in

A token or key connection can move to a sign-in. Open the connection and choose **Replace credential**. The dialog offers the cloud's sign-in first, and once you approve on the cloud you land back on the connection, signed in. The reverse works too: pick **Use a token instead** in the same dialog and paste one. Either way the ID stays, and the account has to be the one the connection already uses (the team on DigitalOcean and Vercel, the project on Google Cloud, the tenant, subscription and resource group on Azure), so nothing that refers to the connection breaks.

pages.title: Cloud targets
pages.description: Group accounts into an organization Cloud, name targets, grant them to projects, and place services by name or tag.
pages.text:
Create an organization Cloud before you create a project. Add named targets, grant a project access, then assign the Cloud to an environment. A Cloud belongs to one organization. A target selects either a managed provider account or a server pool. Your manifest can then say `frontend` without carrying an account ID.

```yaml
version: 1
services:
  web:
    source: node:apps/web
    cloud_target: frontend
```

## Create and grant

Use the IDs these commands return:

```bash
loomctl clouds create --organization --name Production
loomctl cloud-targets create cloud_... --organization \
  --name frontend --provider vercel --connection conn_...
# Once your project exists, grant all targets or select them with --targets.
loomctl cloud-grants grant cloud_... project_... --targets target_...
loomctl clouds assignment my-project env_...
loomctl clouds assign my-project env_... --cloud cloud_... --revision 0
loomctl clouds assign my-project env_... --cloud cloud_... --revision 0 \
  --yes --request-id assign-production --wait --timeout 10m
```

You can list, create, rename and delete organization Clouds with `--organization` and no project argument. The same flag works on `cloud-targets` and `cloud-syncs`. The project forms still work too, such as `clouds create my-project --name Production`. Assignment always needs a project.

```bash
loomctl clouds --organization
loomctl clouds show cloud_... --organization
loomctl cloud-grants cloud_...
loomctl cloud-grants revoke cloud_... project_...
loomctl cloud-syncs --organization
```

An empty `--targets` grants the whole Cloud, including its default placement. A target list grants only those. Revoking prevents fresh placement but keeps the authority needed to clean up work you already accepted. Sharing capacity doesn't grant another project's releases, variables, logs or routes.

The first assignment uses revision `0`. Read `clouds assignment` before later changes, because unassigning keeps the generation. An unassigned environment can have a nonzero revision, and you need it to assign again. An environment from another project returns a scoped error, never an empty assignment.
