## Pick a target by tags

You don't have to name a target. Give your targets tags, then ask for the tags you need:

```bash
loomctl cloud-targets create my-project cloud_... \
  --name eu-gpu --provider cloud-run --connection conn_... --tags eu,gpu
loomctl cloud-targets update my-project cloud_... target_... \
  --display-name "EU GPU" --tags eu,gpu,large --revision 1
```

```yaml
version: 1
defaults:
  cloud_tags: [eu]
services:
  web:
    source: node:apps/web
    cloud_tags: [frontend, eu]
  trainer:
    source: python:trainer
    cloud_tags: [gpu]
    environments:
      staging: { cloud_target: shared-gpu }
```

A tag is a lowercase slug of up to 32 characters, and a target carries at most 16. A service resolves to the one target that carries every tag it lists, looking only at the targets your project's grant allows. If none match, the plan fails with `cloud-tag-unmatched`. If several do, it fails with `cloud-tag-ambiguous` and names each, so you can add a tag only one carries or name the target with `cloud_target`.

`cloud_target` and `cloud_tags` can't sit together at the same level. An environment override that sets one replaces whichever the service set, so staging above uses `shared-gpu` by name. `defaults.cloud_tags` applies to every service that sets no `cloud_target`, `cloud_tags`, `provider` or `target` of its own, and it can't be combined with `defaults.provider`. Like `cloud_target`, tags conflict with an effective direct `provider` or `target`, including an inherited one.

Over HTTP, send `tags` when you create or update a target. Leave `tags` out of an update and they stay. Send `[]` and they're removed (`--clear-tags` in `loomctl`). Changing a target's tags advances its revision, so a plan approved against the old ones has to be planned again.

## A default placement without targets

A Cloud can have a default placement: one provider, one connection and an optional region. While a Cloud has no targets, that default is the only place its services go. Its connection has to be ready and belong to that provider's cloud.

```bash
curl -X PUT .../api/v1/clouds/cloud_.../default-placement \
  -d '{"default_placement":{"provider":"vercel","connection_id":"conn_...","region":"iad1"},"revision":1}'
```

You can also pass `default_placement` when you create the Cloud, and send `"default_placement": null` to clear it. A service uses the default when it has no placement of its own. That keeps working after you add targets: adding a target only places the services that name or tag it. A service with its own `provider` keeps its direct placement.

The default reaches a project only when its grant covers the whole Cloud. If an admin granted a chosen set of targets, your services can use those targets but not the default.

You can set a first default at any time. Once an environment uses the Cloud, `default-placement` refuses to replace or clear it (HTTP 409). Change it with a reviewed switch, described in [Adopting and moving services](/docs/clouds/adopting-and-moving#switch-a-default).

pages.title: DigitalOcean
pages.description: Connect a DigitalOcean team and run services on App Platform with Managed PostgreSQL, MySQL and Valkey.
pages.text:
Loomplane runs your services on DigitalOcean App Platform and gives them Managed PostgreSQL, MySQL and Valkey databases. App Platform builds each service from your repository, so you don't need a registry or a builder of your own.

## Connect DigitalOcean


In DigitalOcean, open **API**, then **Tokens**, and create a personal access token with read and write access. A custom-scoped token needs `app`, `database` and `account:read`.


Under **Settings**, then **GitHub**, give DigitalOcean access to the repositories you'll deploy. App Platform clones them through that connection. Loomplane never hands it your code.


In Loomplane, open **Integrations**, choose **DigitalOcean** and paste the token.


Loomplane asks DigitalOcean whose token it is before it keeps it. A token belongs to one team, and that team is where every app and database is made. A token from a locked account is refused.

## Sign in instead of a token

If a platform owner or admin has registered a DigitalOcean OAuth app, the connect dialog offers **Sign in with DigitalOcean** first and **Use a token instead** underneath. You approve Loomplane on DigitalOcean, and Loomplane renews the grant itself. The app asks for the `read write` scope, which covers what the token steps above grant. [Connect a cloud by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in) covers registering the app and what happens if DigitalOcean stops accepting the sign-in.

## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
defaults:
  provider: digitalocean
  region: ams
services:
  web:
    source: apps/web
    needs: [api]
  api:
    source: services/api
    needs: [db]
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    version: "16"
```

The regions are App Platform's: `nyc`, `sfo`, `tor`, `atl`, `ams`, `fra`, `lon`, `blr`, `sgp` and `syd`. Leave `region` out and you get `nyc`.

Each service in each environment becomes an App Platform app of its own, named after the service, the environment and the project, with deploy on push turned off. A service with a Dockerfile builds from it. Anything else goes through App Platform's buildpacks. Workers run as App Platform workers and static sites as static sites. `size` picks the smallest instance that fits, from `apps-s-1vcpu-0.5gb` up to `apps-d-8vcpu-32gb`, and `scale.min` sets how many instances run. Secret variables go in as App Platform secrets.

## Which commit runs

Every other target here deploys the exact commit a plan approved. App Platform can't, because it always builds the newest commit of a branch and gives you no way to ask for a particular one. So Loomplane checks instead.

It points the app at the branch your project reads, starts the deployment itself, and watches the commit App Platform reports for every component. If that's the approved commit, the deployment goes ahead. If someone pushed to the branch after you approved the plan, Loomplane cancels the deployment before it goes live and the step fails with both commits in the message. In the rare case a wrong build gets live before the check sees it, Loomplane rolls the app back to what ran before, or deletes the app if nothing approved ever ran there.

So don't push to a branch while a plan for it waits for approval. If your repository's default branch isn't `main`, set the branch on the project's repository in Loomplane, because a repository left on its default branch is built from `main`. To deploy another branch for a while, analyze it with **Another branch**: a plan builds the branch its analysis read.

A brand-new app's `ondigitalocean.app` address takes a few minutes to appear in DNS after App Platform says it's live. Loomplane waits for it in public DNS for up to ten minutes before it checks that the service answers. If it still isn't there, the step says the app is deployed, and retrying checks again.

## Databases

| Manifest kind | Made on DigitalOcean | Versions |
|---|---|---|
| `postgres` | Managed PostgreSQL | 17, 16, 15 |
| `mysql` | Managed MySQL | 8 |
| `redis` | Managed Valkey, which speaks the Redis protocol | DigitalOcean's current one |

Each is a single `db-s-1vcpu-1gb` node in the datacenter that matches the region: `nyc` gets `nyc3`, `ams` gets `ams3`, `fra` gets `fra1`, and so on. You can name a datacenter outright, such as `nyc1`, as a resource's region. Services that need a database get its connection string as a secret, with TLS required. Loomplane doesn't set trusted sources, so add them in DigitalOcean if you want only your apps to reach it.

Removing a database from the manifest deletes it with its data, so take a backup first if you need one.

## Hostnames

Open the service's page and use **Add hostname**, the same dialog you use anywhere else. The hostname reaches the service's public HTTP port and nothing else. A private service can't take one, so make it public in the manifest and deploy it first. A public service with no port set can't either, and neither can a static site yet.

What happens next depends on who runs the domain's DNS. If Loomplane manages it, Loomplane writes the records, and the preview refuses before anything is written if the name already has A, AAAA or CNAME records. A subdomain gets a CNAME to the app's `ondigitalocean.app` address. The domain itself (the apex) gets App Platform's static addresses, which are A records for `162.159.140.98` and `172.66.0.96`, and AAAA records for `2606:4700:7::60` and `2a06:98c1:58::60`. If you run the DNS somewhere else, the dialog lists the records and you add them yourself. Loomplane can't see that zone, so remove any A, AAAA or CNAME record already at the name before you add its records.

Loomplane adds the hostname to the app as an alias domain, which leaves the app's own address alone, and DigitalOcean issues the certificate. The hostname shows **Issuing** until DigitalOcean reports the certificate active.

If the app is mid-deployment when you add the hostname, Loomplane waits for that deployment to finish first. Adding a hostname can make App Platform start a deployment of its own. Loomplane checks that it built the commit you reviewed. If it didn't, Loomplane cancels it, or rolls back if it already went live, and asks you to deploy the service and then retry the hostname. If the app runs a different commit from the one you reviewed, the hostname waits until the service's deploy finishes.

Deploys keep the app's hostnames, including any you added in DigitalOcean's control panel.

Wildcard hostnames and blocked paths aren't supported yet. Neither is moving a hostname to another app: remove it and add it again.

## Limits

A private service is only reachable from inside its own App Platform app, and each service here gets its own app, so nothing can call one. The planner says so and asks you to make it public. Build logs stay on the app's **Activity** tab, and Loomplane shows the deployment's progress.

## Droplets and DNS

You can also provision managed Droplets in an organization Cloud, adopt a pinned SSH/Docker host, and place services through server pools. That uses the server runtime, and your App Platform manifests keep using the managed runtime. [Your own servers](/docs/clouds/your-own-servers) has the commands.

GPU Droplets work too, with a GPU-ready image and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit set up for you at first boot. The hourly price shows before you approve. See [GPUs](/docs/clouds/gpus) for pools, ceilings and what happens if the setup fails.

DigitalOcean's compute and DNS capabilities are checked independently. Your App Platform token scopes don't establish Droplet or DNS permissions, so an operation without the permission it needs fails before any new effects. For a managed DNS zone you can use a different account than the one for compute.

  Fixture-backed provider and ACME checks don't qualify your DigitalOcean account, DNS propagation or public certificate issuance. Verify those with your own authorized live scope before a production move.

pages.title: Google Cloud
pages.description: Connect a Google Cloud project and run services on Cloud Run with Cloud SQL, Memorystore and Cloud Storage.
pages.text:
Loomplane builds a service with Cloud Build, stores its image in Artifact Registry and runs it on Cloud Run. It also provisions Cloud SQL (Postgres and MySQL), Memorystore (Redis) and Cloud Storage buckets. Everything happens in your project.

## Connect a project

You connect a service account key.


In the Google Cloud console, create a service account in the project you'll deploy to.


Grant it roles that cover the permissions in the table below.


Create a JSON key for it and download it.


In Loomplane, open **Integrations**, choose Google Cloud, and paste the key.


Loomplane parses the key, then asks Google which permissions the account holds on the project (`testIamPermissions`). A key that isn't a service account key, or that Google has deleted, disabled or revoked, is refused. A key that's missing permissions makes the connection incomplete, and Loomplane lists each one.

The project ID comes from the key. Only the project and the service account's email are ever shown back to you.

| Used for | Permissions Loomplane checks |
|---|---|
| Builds | `cloudbuild.builds.create`, `cloudbuild.builds.get`, `artifactregistry.repositories.create`, `artifactregistry.repositories.get`. Recommended, not checked: `artifactregistry.tags.get` |
| Cloud Run | `run.services.create`, `run.services.get`, `run.services.update`, `run.services.setIamPolicy`, `run.operations.get`, `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` |
| Canary releases only | `run.revisions.get`, `run.revisions.delete` |
| Secrets | `secretmanager.secrets.create`, `secretmanager.secrets.setIamPolicy`, `secretmanager.versions.add` |
| Cloud SQL | `cloudsql.instances.create`, `cloudsql.instances.delete`, `cloudsql.instances.get`, `cloudsql.databases.create`, `cloudsql.users.create`, `cloudsql.users.update` |
| Memorystore | `redis.instances.create`, `redis.instances.delete`, `redis.instances.get`, `redis.instances.getAuthString` |
| Cloud Storage | `storage.buckets.create`, `storage.buckets.delete`, `storage.buckets.get`, `storage.buckets.getIamPolicy`, `storage.buckets.setIamPolicy`, `storage.objects.create`, `storage.objects.delete`, `storage.objects.list` |
| Project | `resourcemanager.projects.get` |

Loomplane deploys each image by the digest its build pushed and records it with the release, so a promotion can deploy the exact image staging ran and a rollback the image the previous release ran. Cloud Build reports the digest of an image built from a Dockerfile. A service without one is built with buildpacks, which push the image themselves, and Loomplane reads its digest from Artifact Registry with `artifactregistry.tags.get`. Without that permission you can still deploy: the service runs its image by tag, the step warns you, and promoting or rolling back that service builds it again.

Build logs come from Cloud Logging, so the account also needs permission to read there. Without it the deployment still works and the logs show as unavailable.

Joining a Cloud Run service to AWS through a link needs Compute Network Admin (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`) as well. See [Gateways and networking](/docs/concepts/gateways-and-networking#links).

## Sign in instead of a key

If a platform owner or admin has registered a Google OAuth client, the connect dialog offers **Sign in with Google Cloud** first and **Use a token instead** underneath. Type the project ID, then sign in to Google and approve. Loomplane asks for `openid`, `email` and `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform`.

The connection acts as you, so your own IAM roles in the project are what it can do. Loomplane checks them against the table above, the same as it checks a key, and lists anything you're missing. You also need `serviceusage.services.use` on the project (Owner, Editor and Service Usage Consumer have it), because your API calls are billed to the project you deploy to, not the one the OAuth client is in. The connection shows the Google account it signed in as and who in Loomplane did it. If that person leaves the organization, the connection asks for a new sign-in within 6 hours and anyone who manages cloud accounts can sign in again as themselves.

Publish the OAuth app. While it's in testing, Google ends every sign-in after 7 days. Once it's published as an **External** app, people see Google's unverified-app warning and no more than 100 of them can sign in until Google verifies it, because `cloud-platform` is a sensitive scope. An **Internal** app, for a Google Workspace, needs neither. [Connect a cloud by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in) covers registering the client and what happens if Google stops accepting the sign-in.

## Connect keylessly

With workload identity federation you don't need a key or a sign-in. When Loomplane's public URL is HTTPS and reachable from the internet, the connect dialog offers **Connect keylessly** (or **Connect keylessly instead**, under the sign-in button). Its four steps make a workload identity pool called `loomplane`, add Loomplane's issuer as an OIDC provider in it, named after the connection's ID, with a condition that lets in this connection's subject alone, let that subject act as a service account through `roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser`, and grant the account a custom role with the permissions in the table above. You copy each `gcloud` command from the dialog.

Paste the project ID, the provider's full name and the service account's email, then choose **Check and connect**. Loomplane trades a 10-minute token it signs itself at Google's security token service, impersonates the service account with what comes back, and checks the account's permissions on the project like a key's. The audience is `//iam.googleapis.com/` followed by the provider's full name, which is the provider's default.

A second keyless connection in the same project skips the pool and the role, which are there already, and its commands make a provider of its own. Loomplane asks Google once a day whether it still trusts each connection, and a refusal marks the connection failed and sends a notice. [Connect a cloud keylessly](/docs/clouds/keyless) has every command and what to do when the trust breaks.

## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
defaults:
  provider: cloud-run
  region: us-central1
services:
  api:
    source: go:services/api
    needs: [db, cache, uploads]
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    provider: cloud-sql
    version: "17"
  cache:
    kind: redis
    provider: memorystore
  uploads:
    kind: object-storage
    provider: cloud-storage
```

Regions Loomplane lists are `us-central1`, `us-east1`, `us-east4`, `us-west1`, `northamerica-northeast1`, `southamerica-east1`, `europe-west1`, `europe-west2`, `europe-west3`, `europe-west4`, `asia-east1`, `asia-northeast1`, `asia-south1`, `asia-southeast1` and `australia-southeast1`. You can name any region, but the planner warns about one it doesn't know, since a typo would otherwise only show up as a failed deployment.

## How things behave

A private Cloud Run service only takes calls from the project's own services, which must send a Google ID token. Services that need a private one get its address in a variable.

Cloud SQL is reached through the Cloud SQL connector. Memorystore only has an address on the project's default network, so Cloud Run services that need it send their private traffic there with direct VPC egress. Buckets are private, and services reach them as the Cloud Run runtime account, so `STORAGE_URL` carries no credentials (`gs://bucket`).

A canary runs the new release as a second revision of the same Cloud Run service, named after the service and the deployment, and splits the service's traffic between that revision and the one that served before. Promoting it sends all of the traffic to the latest revision, so your next deploy takes everything again. A rollback gives the old revision all of the traffic, puts its template back and deletes the new one. Putting the template back makes one more revision with the old configuration, which takes no traffic.

If an earlier canary couldn't roll back and left the traffic split, a new canary on that service won't start, since it can't tell which revision is the real baseline. Retry or roll back that deployment, or release once with `direct`, which gives the latest revision all of the traffic.

The canary releases only permissions aren't needed for anything else, so a service account without them still deploys. The connection lists what's missing, and a canary on Cloud Run refuses to start, when you plan it and again when it runs. Grant them, or release that environment `direct` or `blue_green`.

Each revision reads its secrets at the Secret Manager version it was started with, never `latest`. The candidate stores new versions, so an instance the old revision starts mid-canary still reads its own values.

On Google Cloud you pick the region per service or resource. Moving one starts the new copy first. Cloud SQL instances and Cloud Storage buckets carry their region in their names, so the new one never collides with the one it replaces.

  Managed Cloud SQL creation and recovery are checked against controlled Google endpoints. Live Google Cloud creation, SQL persistence and restore aren't qualified yet. [Database services](/docs/services/database-services) has the details.

pages.title: GPUs
pages.description: What a Kubernetes cluster, your own server or a DigitalOcean GPU Droplet needs before Loomplane can run GPU work on it, and how to ask for GPUs in a manifest.
pages.text:
Loomplane finds GPUs, schedules work onto them and shows what they cost. It never installs a GPU driver, and it never installs the NVIDIA device plugin on your cluster. Whatever the target is, the driver side is yours to set up (DigitalOcean GPU Droplets are the one exception, covered below). Everything on this page is about getting that side right so Loomplane can see the GPUs.

Prices are estimates. When Loomplane doesn't know a price it says "price unknown" and never shows $0. And GPU workloads on your own servers and clusters are never stopped or scaled down for you, since nothing here can tell an idle GPU from a busy one.

## Kubernetes

Install the NVIDIA device plugin or the NVIDIA GPU Operator first. Without one, the nodes have GPUs but nothing advertises `nvidia.com/gpu`, and the connection says so and asks you to install one.

Then let the connection list nodes. Loomplane reads the cluster's nodes to find GPUs, and a namespace-scoped credential can't do that. Without the permission, the connection reads "Loomplane can't list this cluster's nodes, so it can't see GPUs". Fix it with a ClusterRole and a binding to the service account behind your kubeconfig token (swap in your own names):

```yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: loomplane-nodes
rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["nodes"]
    verbs: ["get", "list"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: loomplane-nodes
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: loomplane-nodes
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: loomplane
    namespace: loomplane
```

Check the connection again afterwards.

Each GPU node also needs a label that says what kind of GPU it has. Loomplane tries these in order and uses the first one a node carries:

1. `cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator`
2. `nvidia.com/gpu.product` (GPU feature discovery adds this one)
3. `k8s.amazonaws.com/accelerator`
4. `doks.digitalocean.com/gpu-model`

If none is there, it falls back to the cloud's `node.kubernetes.io/instance-type` label, which only works when Loomplane knows that instance size. A cluster with GPUs but no label that names the kind shows a message asking you to add `nvidia.com/gpu.product`. A cluster with no GPU nodes shows **No GPU nodes**.

You don't have to touch taints. Loomplane turns the taints that every matching GPU node carries into tolerations on the pod. A taint on only some of those nodes isn't tolerated, and neither are the ones Kubernetes sets for a node's state (cordoned, not ready, unreachable), so a GPU pod never lands on a cordoned node or stays on a dead one. A GPU pod gets an `nvidia.com/gpu` limit and a node selector built from the label above, so it only lands on the kind you asked for. Wherever Loomplane lists GPU targets, a cluster's count reads as GPUs per node, not GPUs free, because Loomplane doesn't count what the cluster's other pods are using.

Anything persistent that Loomplane runs on the cluster needs a storage class with a `Retain` reclaim policy and a declared binding mode, and that covers catalog databases and any other volume, not only a model weight cache. Pick the class on the connection and Loomplane checks it. If the cluster has no such class, the plan is refused until you add one.

## Your own servers

A server needs the NVIDIA driver and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. Once both are in, tell Docker to use the toolkit and restart it:

```bash
sudo nvidia-ctk runtime configure --runtime=docker
sudo systemctl restart docker
```

Loomplane runs `nvidia-smi` over SSH when you connect the server and again on every check, so it learns what GPUs the server has and whether Docker can use them. Open the server and choose **Check again** after any change.

When a server has GPUs it can't use yet, it shows **Can't take GPU work** with the reason. There are two common ones. If `nvidia-smi` doesn't answer on a machine with an NVIDIA card, you need the driver. If it answers but Docker can't reach the GPUs, you need the toolkit steps above.

Each container gets its own GPUs, picked when the service is deployed. Two workloads never share a device, so a server with two GPUs runs at most two single-GPU services.

## DigitalOcean GPU Droplets

DigitalOcean is the only cloud where Loomplane creates GPU servers today. Open your Cloud, go to **Servers** and choose **Create server** with a DigitalOcean account that can provision. The size list has a **GPU** group, and each GPU size shows its GPUs, the memory on each one and the hourly price. Pick one and the image list narrows to GPU-ready images, which ship the driver. **Review server** shows the estimated hourly and monthly cost before you approve anything, and the price stays on the server afterwards.

At first boot Loomplane installs Docker only if the image doesn't have it, then installs the NVIDIA Container Toolkit and points Docker at it.

If the toolkit setup fails, the server says so, takes no GPU work and keeps costing money. Nothing retries by itself. The message gives you the commands to run (the `nvidia-ctk` steps above) and then **Check again**, or you can delete the server.

You can put a GPU server in a pool from **Pools and reservations**. Give the pool a GPU kind and each server a GPU budget, which is how many of its GPUs the pool may hand out. A GPU pool refuses CPU work, and a CPU pool can't hold GPU budgets.

Pools can also grow by creating GPU Droplets themselves, inside a GPU ceiling for each kind. You configure that growth and those ceilings through the Cloud's capacity policy, which has no screen in the dashboard yet. None of it happens until the operator sets `LOOMPLANE_AUTOMATIC_CAPACITY_ENABLED=true` (see [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration#cloud-capacity)), which is off by default while it's being qualified. When they are set, a few rules apply:

- A kind with no Cloud ceiling allows no GPUs at all.
- Each GPU pool has its own ceiling for its kind, and it can't go above the Cloud's.
- If one server's GPUs can't be read, growth of GPU capacity pauses until a check on that server succeeds. Nothing buys another GPU on a guess.

## Models

With the [AI section](/docs/ai) on, you don't have to write a GPU request yourself to run an open model. The Models page lists models with where each one fits, and deploying one picks the GPU kind and count, writes the resource into your manifest and plans it. It can run on any server or cluster above that Loomplane can see GPUs on, or on a DigitalOcean GPU Droplet it creates for the model after an admin reviews the price. See [Models](/docs/ai/models) and [What models cost](/docs/ai/model-costs).

## AWS, GCP and Azure

GPU nodes on EKS, GKE and AKS clusters are recognized by their instance type and priced from reference prices, which are estimates. Loomplane doesn't create GPU virtual machines on these clouds yet. You bring the cluster and Loomplane places work on it, using the Kubernetes rules above.

## In a manifest

Ask for GPUs on a service with `size.gpu`. Add `size.shm` (in MiB) if your framework wants a bigger `/dev/shm`, which PyTorch data loaders often do. Shared memory counts toward `memory`, so it has to be smaller.

```yaml
services:
  inference:
    source: services/inference
    provider: kubernetes
    target: conn_cluster
    size:
      cpu: 4
      memory: 32768
      shm: 8192
      gpu: { kind: nvidia-l4, count: 1 }
```

Catalog resources take the same `gpu` field under `resources.<name>`, with `kind` and `count`, and only NVIDIA kinds. The model kinds (`model-vllm` and `model-llamacpp-gpu`) are the ones that use it today. [Models](/docs/ai/models#what-a-deploy-writes) shows what a model resource looks like.

`count` runs from 1 to 8. `kind` is one of these IDs:

| Kind | GPU |
| --- | --- |
| `nvidia-t4` | NVIDIA T4 |
| `nvidia-l4` | NVIDIA L4 |
| `nvidia-a10`, `nvidia-a10g` | NVIDIA A10, A10G |
| `nvidia-l40s` | NVIDIA L40S |
| `nvidia-rtx-4000-ada`, `nvidia-rtx-6000-ada` | NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada, RTX 6000 Ada |
| `nvidia-v100-16gb`, `nvidia-v100-32gb` | NVIDIA V100 |
| `nvidia-a100-40gb`, `nvidia-a100-80gb` | NVIDIA A100 |
| `nvidia-h100-80gb`, `nvidia-h100-nvl-94gb` | NVIDIA H100, H100 NVL |
| `nvidia-h200-141gb` | NVIDIA H200 |
| `amd-mi300x` | AMD Instinct MI300X (listed and priced, but Loomplane can't schedule it yet) |

Planning checks the kind against the target, so a request the target can't meet shows up as a problem on the plan before anything runs. Arm64 targets can't run GPU work, and a gateway can't ask for GPUs.

pages.title: Connect a cloud keylessly
pages.description: Let AWS, Google Cloud or Azure trust tokens Loomplane signs itself, so a connection holds no key, secret or sign-in.
pages.text:
A keyless connection stores nothing you have to rotate. You tell AWS, Google Cloud or Azure to trust Loomplane as an OpenID Connect issuer, much as you'd trust GitHub Actions, and from then on, whenever Loomplane needs the cloud for a check or a deployment, it signs a token that lasts 10 minutes and trades it with the cloud for the cloud's own short-lived credentials. Vault holds no key for the connection. Nobody's sign-in can lapse either.

## Before you start

The clouds fetch Loomplane's keys themselves, over the internet, so your `public_url` has to be HTTPS on a host they can reach. A private address, a `.local` or `.internal` name, or plain `http` won't work. Nor will a path such as `https://example.com/loomplane`: the two documents the clouds read are served at the root, so keyless stays off and says `public_url must not have a path for keyless`. The issuer is your public URL with any trailing slash taken off, and the documents sit under it:

| What | Where |
|---|---|
| Issuer | `https://loomplane.example.com` (your `public_url`) |
| Discovery | `https://loomplane.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| Signing keys (JWKS) | `https://loomplane.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json` |

As a platform owner or admin, open **Settings**, then **Cloud sign-in**, and you'll see **Keyless: on** with the issuer, or **Keyless: off** with what's wrong, such as `public_url isn't HTTPS`. Check from a machine outside your network too:

```bash
curl https://loomplane.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration
curl https://loomplane.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
```

Both answer without a session. If you run Loomplane behind a proxy of your own, it has to pass `/.well-known/` through to the API, which the [Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker) and [Kubernetes](/docs/operations/production-on-kubernetes) setups already do.

In the development environment you can also use a loopback issuer such as `http://localhost:8780`. The settings page warns that it's for development only, and it means it: no real cloud can reach your laptop, so a loopback issuer is good for trying keyless against fakes and nothing else.

## Connect


Open **Integrations**, choose AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure, and type a name. Choose **Connect keylessly**. When the platform has a sign-in app for that cloud, the sign-in button comes first and **Connect keylessly instead** sits under it.


The dialog shows the issuer, the subject and the audience, each with a copy button, then the steps for that cloud with a command to copy for each. Run them in the cloud. The sections below go through them.


Fill in what the dialog asks for (a role ARN on AWS, for instance) and choose **Check and connect**. Loomplane signs a token, the cloud has to accept it, and then Loomplane checks permissions the same way it checks a key and lists anything missing.


The subject names the new connection's ID, so Loomplane reserves that ID for 24 hours when the dialog opens, which gives you time in the cloud's console. Keep the dialog open while you work. If you close it, you get a new ID next time, and the trust you already set up names the old one, so you'd have to set it up again. A check the cloud refuses doesn't use up the reservation, so you can fix the trust and choose **Check and connect** again.

## Subject and audience

Every token Loomplane signs for a connection has the same subject:

```
org:{organization ID}:connection:{connection ID}
```

For example `org:aorg_01m5x1qk7yehs9cjqg0xr6ncny:connection:conn_01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs`. The trust you set up matches it exactly, so a token for any other connection, even one in your own organization, gets nothing. Copy it from the dialog. It's long and easy to mistype.

The audience is what each cloud expects to find in the token's `aud`:

| Cloud | Audience |
|---|---|
| AWS | `sts.amazonaws.com` |
| Google Cloud | `//iam.googleapis.com/` followed by the workload identity provider's full name |
| Azure | `api://AzureADTokenExchange` |

Tokens are signed with RS256. Besides `iss`, `sub` and `aud` they carry `iat`, `nbf`, `exp` and a random `jti`. A token works until 10 minutes after Loomplane signs it. Its `iat` and `nbf` are a minute before that moment, so a cloud whose clock runs a little behind still takes it, which makes `exp` 11 minutes after `iat`.

## AWS

You add Loomplane as an IAM identity provider and make a role that only this connection can assume. The dialog fills in your issuer and subject in each command. With an issuer of `https://loomplane.example.com` the provider is:

```bash
aws iam create-open-id-connect-provider \
  --url https://loomplane.example.com \
  --client-id-list sts.amazonaws.com
```

You can add the provider in the IAM console under **Identity providers** instead. Then create a role with this trust policy, putting your account number in place of `<account-id>`:

```json
{
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "loomplane.example.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "loomplane.example.com:sub": "org:aorg_...:connection:conn_..."
        }
      },
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:oidc-provider/loomplane.example.com"
      }
    }
  ],
  "Version": "2012-10-17"
}
```

The third step's policy allows every action in [the AWS page's table](/docs/clouds/aws#connect-an-account) on `*`. Attach it to the role. If you saved the two policies as `trust.json` and `permissions.json`, the CLI does both in two commands:

```bash
aws iam create-role --role-name loomplane --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name loomplane --policy-name loomplane --policy-document file://permissions.json
```

Back in the dialog, paste the role's ARN (`arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/loomplane`) and the region, and an ACM certificate's ARN if you want public services on ECS to answer over HTTPS, as with a key. Loomplane assumes the role with `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and names each session `loomplane-` followed by the connection ID, so CloudTrail shows which connection acted. The account number in the role's ARN and the region are the connection's account, the same as a key's.

## Google Cloud

You make a workload identity pool, add Loomplane as its provider, and let this connection act as a service account. Run these in Cloud Shell, or anywhere `gcloud` is set to the project. If the project has never used workload identity federation, you'll need its APIs on first:

```bash
gcloud services enable iam.googleapis.com iamcredentials.googleapis.com sts.googleapis.com cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com
```

Then the pool and the provider. Every keyless connection to the project shares the pool, so if you've connected this project keylessly before, it's there already and you skip creating it. The provider is the connection's own, named after its ID: `conn_01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs` gets `conn-01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs`, in lower case with the underscore as a hyphen, the way Google wants a provider ID (4 to 32 letters, digits and hyphens). The dialog fills it in.

```bash
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools create loomplane --location=global

gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers create-oidc conn-01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=loomplane \
  --issuer-uri=https://loomplane.example.com \
  --attribute-mapping=google.subject=assertion.sub \
  --attribute-condition="assertion.sub=='org:aorg_...:connection:conn_...'"
```

The condition lets in this one connection. The provider's default audience is its own full name with `//iam.googleapis.com/` in front, which is what Loomplane sends, so you don't need `--allowed-audiences`. To print the full name you'll paste later:

```bash
gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers describe conn-01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs --location=global \
  --workload-identity-pool=loomplane --format='value(name)'
```

Create a service account if you don't have one for Loomplane (`gcloud iam service-accounts create loomplane`), and let the connection act as it. `<project-number>` is the project's number, not its ID. `gcloud projects describe <project-id> --format='value(projectNumber)'` prints it.

```bash
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding <service-account> \
  --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member=principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<project-number>/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/loomplane/subject/org:aorg_...:connection:conn_...
```

The last step makes a custom role called `loomplane` with every permission in [the Google Cloud page's table](/docs/clouds/google-cloud#connect-a-project) and grants it to the service account. The dialog's command lists them all. If another connection already made the role in this project, skip the first command:

```bash
gcloud iam roles create loomplane --project=<project-id> --title=Loomplane --permissions=...
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <project-id> --member=serviceAccount:<service-account> --role=projects/<project-id>/roles/loomplane
```

Then paste the project ID, the provider's full name (`projects/123456789012/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/loomplane/providers/conn-01m5x2a4bwfx8r0d1k3m7q9tzs`) and the service account's email. You can also name a billing export table, as you would for a key, so Loomplane reads the project's spend. Loomplane trades its token at Google's security token service, then asks IAM Credentials for the service account's access token, and checks the account's permissions on the project.

A second keyless connection to the same project gets a provider of its own, because a provider's condition names one connection. Its commands already carry its own provider name and subject, so you skip the pool and the role and run the rest.

## Azure

You add a federated credential to an app registration, which lets this connection sign in as the app, and give the app Contributor on the resource group. Run these in Cloud Shell, or anywhere `az` is signed in to the tenant. If you don't have an app for Loomplane yet, make one and its service principal, so it can hold roles:

```bash
az ad app create --display-name loomplane
az ad sp create --id <client-id>
```

`<client-id>` is the app's Application (client) ID, which `az ad app create` prints as `appId`. The federated credential the dialog gives you looks like this:

```bash
az ad app federated-credential create --id <client-id> --parameters '{"name":"loomplane-conn_...","issuer":"https://loomplane.example.com","subject":"org:aorg_...:connection:conn_...","audiences":["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]}'
```

Its name is `loomplane-` followed by the connection ID. Entra wants each credential's name to be unique in its app, so a second connection can use the same app with a credential of its own. Entra allows 20 federated credentials per app.

Then make the app a Contributor on the resource group Loomplane deploys to. The group has to exist first:

```bash
az group create --name <resource-group> --location <region>
az role assignment create --assignee <client-id> --role Contributor \
  --scope /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<resource-group>
```

Back in the dialog, fill in the directory (tenant) ID, the app's client ID, the subscription ID and the resource group, which defaults to `loomplane`. Loomplane hands Entra its token as the app's client assertion, then checks the app's role assignments the same way it checks a service principal's. The tenant, subscription and resource group are the connection's account. What [How apps pull images](/docs/clouds/azure#how-apps-pull-images) says about Contributor and Owner applies to the app as well.

## Signing keys

There's nothing for you to do here. Loomplane signs with 2048-bit RSA keys and makes a new one every 30 days. A new key goes into the JWKS a day before it starts signing, and the key it replaces stays there for a day after it stops. Clouds cache the keys, and Entra holds on to them for up to a day, so that overlap is what keeps a cloud from ever seeing a token signed with a key it hasn't fetched yet. Discovery and the JWKS go out with a five-minute cache header.

The keys turn over when Loomplane starts and with the background job that runs every 6 hours. The private halves live in Vault under an app of their own, encrypted with a key derived from `secret_key`, and only the public halves are ever published. [Security model](/docs/operations/security-model#keyless-signing-keys) has more.

## When the cloud refuses the trust

Say someone deletes the role, the identity provider, the pool or the federated credential, or edits its condition. From then on the cloud won't take Loomplane's tokens for that connection. Loomplane asks the cloud once a day whether it still trusts each keyless connection (the background job runs every 6 hours, and each connection is asked at most once a day), and a deployment that runs before the next check fails with the cloud's own error.

Once the daily check gets a refusal, the connection shows as failed with the cloud's message, starting `Daily check:`, and nothing deploys through it. The person who made the connection and the organization's owners and admins hear about it in the inbox, and by email if mail is set up, as "*name* lost its keyless access to *cloud*". Every webhook endpoint gets a `connection.keyless_refused` event. You get one notice per refusal, not one a day.

Fix the trust in the cloud, then open the connection and choose **Check again**. It asks the cloud right away, and a connection whose trust works is ready again with the same ID. If you don't, the daily check asks again a day later, and once the cloud takes the token the connection goes back to ready on its own, with no notice. That's only for a connection the daily check failed. One that failed when you chose **Check again** stays failed until you check it again yourself.

A refusal isn't always the trust's fault. If Loomplane's own issuer is down, or its public URL stops serving the keys, every cloud turns every token away. So before the daily check marks anything failed, Loomplane fetches its own discovery document and JWKS from the public URL, the way a cloud does, and looks for the key it signs with. If that fails, nothing is marked, nobody is told, and the server log has a warning. The same goes when every keyless connection to one cloud is refused in the same run and there are at least two of them: that looks like Loomplane's problem too. A server that can't reach its own public URL from inside your network never marks a keyless connection failed, so check that it can.

On AWS, STS failing to reach the issuer or to fetch its keys, and a token it calls expired, count as Loomplane's problem rather than a refusal, and so do a 5xx answer and a token Loomplane couldn't sign.

## Switch to keyless

An AWS, Google Cloud or Azure connection that uses a key, a secret or a sign-in can move to keyless. Open the connection and choose **Switch to keyless**. The dialog shows the same steps with the connection's own ID in the subject, so nothing is reserved and there's no time limit. Set up the trust and choose **Check and switch**. Loomplane checks the trust first, and if the cloud refuses it the connection stays as it was. Once it switches, Loomplane deletes the key, secret or sign-in grant it held for the connection. Settings you had, such as an AWS certificate or a Google billing export, carry over unless you empty them in the dialog.

The ID stays, and the account has to be the one the connection already uses: the AWS account and region, the Google project, or the Azure tenant, subscription and resource group. Nothing that refers to the connection breaks. To go back, choose **Replace credential** and paste a key.

## What's stored

For a keyless connection, Loomplane keeps the settings you typed, such as the role ARN or the provider's name, and nothing secret. It doesn't keep a token either. Each one is signed when a check or a deployment needs it, and the cloud's temporary credentials stay in memory for as long as that work runs.

pages.title: Nodes
pages.description: Join a machine to Loomplane as a node, deploy and build on its Docker, route domains to it, and update, drain or remove it when you're done.
pages.text:
A node is a machine that joins your organization and keeps one connection open to Loomplane. It dials out and opens no port, so a laptop behind a router and a server behind a firewall join the same way.

  A node can join, report on itself, update and be revoked. With `docker` allowed it also takes deploys and builds, and it can serve a domain directly if it has a public address. Relaying traffic for nodes behind NAT, and Kubernetes through a node, come later.

## Join a machine

Linux is supported. macOS works for development, and Windows is refused. On Linux the join installs a systemd service, so it needs root.

If you already ran `loomctl login`, run this on the machine:

```bash
sudo loomctl node join
```

`node join` uses your saved login (or `LOOMPLANE_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY`) to mint a single-use join token, then spends it. Only an owner's or admin's write key, or a signed-in session, can mint one. Your API key goes to Loomplane to make the token and nowhere else, and the machine never stores it.

Root usually has no login of its own, and `sudo` drops `LOOMPLANE_*` from the environment. So when root has nothing saved, `sudo loomctl node join` reads the login of the user who ran `sudo`. It only does that if the file belongs to that user and nobody else can write to it. On a Mac, run `loomctl node join` without `sudo`.

The machine may not have `loomctl` yet. Add a node in the dashboard (Nodes, Add node), or mint a token somewhere you are logged in, and run the command it gives you on the new machine:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://loomplane.example.com/install/node.sh | LOOMPLANE_JOIN_TOKEN=lpj_... sh -s -- --allow probe,docker
```

Use your own instance's address. The script downloads the `loomctl` release your Loomplane runs, checks it, installs it into `/usr/local/bin` and runs `loomctl node join` with the flags you gave it. The token rides in `LOOMPLANE_JOIN_TOKEN` and not on the command line, so other users on the machine can't read it from the process list while the script runs. On Linux the script asks `sudo` to keep that variable with `--preserve-env`. If your sudoers rules won't allow it, run the script as root. The `--allow` list is what you chose when you made the token.

`loomplane node join` is the same command from the server binary. It needs either `--token`, or `--url` plus `--key`.

### What you can pass

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--url` | Where Loomplane is. Taken from your login if you leave it out |
| `--token` | A join token. `LOOMPLANE_JOIN_TOKEN` works too and keeps it out of the process list. Without either, `join` mints one for you |
| `--key` | An API key to mint a token with. `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY` works too |
| `--name` | The node's name. Loomplane uses the hostname if you don't |
| `--label key=value` | A label. Repeat it for each |
| `--allow` | What Loomplane may use here, such as `docker,probe`. See below |
| `--cloud` | The Cloud this node will join. Once it connects, its Docker becomes a server in that Cloud. Can't be combined with `--token` |
| `--builder dedicated` | Marks the node as a dedicated build worker, a machine that only builds. Untrusted source builds on a node like this. Can't be combined with `--token` |
| `--edge` | Marks the node as an edge, which will serve traffic. Recorded now; edges start working once domain routing to nodes arrives. Can't be combined with `--token` |
| `--foreground` | Runs in your terminal and installs no service |
| `--state-dir` | Where the node keeps its files |

If you pass a token, mint it with `--cloud`, `--builder` or `--edge` already set, because the token carries them. The dashboard's Add node panel has a Cloud picker and a Dedicated builder checkbox for the same thing.

Check the result with `sudo loomctl node status`. It shows the node ID, the key fingerprint, the allowed endpoints and whether the service is running.

### Tokens nobody used

A token you made and never ran still works until it expires, an hour at most. You'll find the open ones at the bottom of the Nodes page, under Unused join tokens, with who made each one, the API key they used if they used one, what it's for and how long it has left. Cancel one there and no machine can join with it.

The API has the same two calls: `GET /api/v1/nodes/join-tokens` lists them and `DELETE /api/v1/nodes/join-tokens/{id}` cancels one. Neither ever returns the token itself. You can list and cancel tokens if you can make them, so an owner or an admin, from a session or a write key. An instance edge token takes a signed-in platform admin to cancel, the same as it takes one to make. Both calls land in the audit log, as `node.join_token.listed` and `node.join_token.cancelled`.

## The node's key and its state

The node creates its own Ed25519 key when it joins and keeps it in its state directory, `/var/lib/loomplane-node` on Linux. Loomplane learns the public half. The private half stays on the machine, in a directory owned by the service user, which is why `status`, `allow` and `leave` want `sudo`.

The join request is signed with the new key, over the token, the node's name and the public key. Loomplane checks that signature before it even looks at the token, and refuses the join without spending it if the signature is wrong. That's what stops someone who holds a token from joining with another machine's public key and keeping the real machine out.

Every join makes a fresh key. If the state directory still holds one from an earlier node, after a `leave` or a revoke, `join` moves it aside to `identity.key.revoked-<time>` and starts over. Loomplane refuses a key it has seen before, revoked nodes included, so a key that may have been stolen can't come back as a new node.

The state directory holds three files that matter:

| File | Owner on a Linux service | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `identity.key` | the service user, mode 0600 | The node's private key |
| `node.json` | the service user | Where Loomplane is, the node ID, and what Loomplane has narrowed the allowlist to |
| `allow.json` | root, mode 0640, group `loomplane-node` | The most the node may serve, as you set it on the machine |

The service runs `/usr/local/lib/loomplane-node/loomctl`, a copy that belongs to root. The service user can read `allow.json` and run that binary, and it can't change either. On macOS all of it belongs to you and the binary sits in the state directory, since the node runs as you there anyway.

Join refuses a directory that already holds files that aren't a node's own, so it can't take over `/var/lib`. Pass `--state-dir` an empty absolute path to keep a second node somewhere else.

## What Loomplane may use

Each node has an allowlist of endpoints. There are five names:

| Endpoint | Meant for |
|---|---|
| `probe` | Reporting what the machine has |
| `docker` | The local Docker or Podman socket |
| `dial` | Connections from the node to addresses it can reach |
| `kube` | A local Kubernetes API |
| `firecracker` | Firecracker microVMs |

`probe` and `docker` do the work today, and `dial` lets Loomplane reach the node's own loopback and the containers it runs on Loomplane's networks, nothing else. `kube` and `firecracker` are accepted and stored, so you won't have to answer again when they arrive.

An interactive `node join` shows what it found and asks whether to allow it. Say anything but yes and it allows nothing. Without a terminal, such as a script, a cloud-init run or the `curl | sh` line, it allows nothing unless you pass `--allow`. The command the dashboard gives you passes it for you:

```bash
sudo loomctl node join --token lpj_... --allow probe,docker
```

Loomplane can only narrow the list. If you remove `docker` in the dashboard, the node drops it. No message from the control plane can add an endpoint. Widening happens on the machine, as root on Linux:

```bash
sudo loomctl node allow docker
```

That writes `allow.json` first and then tells the running node. The node serves only what both `allow.json` and `node.json` allow, so code running as the service user can't widen it. The exception is `docker`, which is covered below. If `allow.json` is missing, belongs to anyone else, or can be written by other users, the node serves nothing and logs why. Run `node allow` again to fix it.

The ingress mode is the one setting that comes from the dashboard and could open something up. It decides whether public traffic reaches the node. Today the only mode that does is `direct`, covered under [Domains on a node](#domains-on-a-node).

  Access to the Docker socket is root access on that host. Anything that can start a container can mount `/` into it. Allow `docker` only on a machine you'd let Loomplane administer.

  `node allow docker` also adds the `loomplane-node` user to the `docker` group and restarts the service to pick that up. From then on, the service user is effectively root on that machine, and the ceiling in `allow.json` no longer holds it back. Removing `docker` in the dashboard stops the node using Docker, so deploys to it stop too. It doesn't take the group back: the `loomplane-node` user stays in `docker`, and the node isn't root, so it can't remove itself. To take the access back, run `sudo gpasswd -d loomplane-node docker` on the machine and restart the service. Loomplane doesn't do this for you.

## Deploy to a node

Join the node with `docker` allowed and a Cloud, and Loomplane connects its Docker as a server in that Cloud. Most nodes adopt on their own. One that needs a look first shows up on the Cloud's Changes tab with the reason and an Adopt button. The reasons are ports 80 and 443 already in use on the machine, an architecture that doesn't match the Cloud's pools, a server with that name already in the Cloud, or a token whose minter can no longer manage Clouds (or whose API key was revoked or expired). Adopt goes through the same reviewed steps as any server you connect, so you see what changes before it does.

After that the node is an ordinary server target. A pool can use it, a service can place on it, and the dashboard marks it with a Node badge and says it was connected by its owner. You can disconnect it from the Cloud, but you can't delete it, because Loomplane didn't create the machine.

The same Docker daemon can't be connected twice. If it is already in a Cloud over SSH, the node's connection is refused until you disconnect the SSH one, and the other way round. Two connections would mean two fence journals for one daemon, and fencing would stop meaning anything.

Podman works through its Docker-compatible socket. If its API leaves out something Loomplane needs to identify the daemon, the check names what's missing instead of passing. Hosts on cgroup v1 don't report their CPU and memory limits, so their capacity shows as unknown.

A deploy to a node that is offline waits for it for about two minutes. If the node hasn't come back by then, the deploy fails with `node NAME is offline since TIME`, and you can run it again once the node is back.

## Builds on a node

Join a node with `--builder dedicated` and it builds source for the Cloud it joined:

```bash
sudo loomctl node join --cloud cloud_... --builder dedicated --allow docker,probe
```

Use a machine that only builds. Untrusted source builds on a dedicated builder, so keep your services somewhere else.

## Domains on a node

A node serves a domain directly when it has a public address that answers on port 80. Loomplane confirms that from the outside before DNS points at the address, by fetching a one-time token through the node's own proxy. Until the check passes, the route keeps serving where it was. The node's page shows the address, when it was confirmed, and why not if it wasn't. A check that found nothing runs again every five minutes or so, and straight away when you set the node's ingress mode to `direct`.

If the node's address changes, Loomplane notices and checks the new one. In a zone Loomplane manages, the record moves once the new address answers. In an external zone, the route shows you the record to set, and you set it. Either way DNS never points at an address that hasn't answered.

A node behind NAT has no address to confirm, so it can't take a direct domain. Relaying traffic to it is the next piece.

## Drain a node

Draining stops new placements on the node's server. What already runs there keeps running until you move it, each with its own reviewed move.

```bash
loomctl node drain NAME
```

It lists what runs on the node first, and warns about any database with no backup policy: if the machine is lost, so is that data. It then asks. Pass `--yes` to skip the question. The Drain button on the node's page does the same, with the same review. A draining node shows as Draining.

## Commands

`loomctl node` and `loomplane node` have the same subcommands.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `join` | Joins this machine and installs the service |
| `run` | Runs the node in the foreground. The service uses this |
| `status` | Shows the node's config, key fingerprint, endpoints and whether it runs. `--json` is for scripts |
| `allow ENDPOINT...` | Widens `allow.json` and tells the node. Needs root on Linux |
| `leave [--purge] [--purge-volumes]` | Tells Loomplane to revoke the node, stops the service and removes its config. The key stays in the state directory, and the next join makes a fresh one. See [Leaving a node](#leaving-a-node) |
| `drain NAME-OR-ID [--yes]` | Stops new placements on a node's server, after showing what runs there. Uses your login or `--url` and `--key` |
| `list` | Lists the organization's nodes. Uses your login or `--url` and `--key` |
| `revoke NAME-OR-ID` | Stops Loomplane trusting a node. Use the ID if two nodes share a name |
| `update --release TAG` | Replaces the node's binary with a signed release |
| `verify-release` | Checks a downloaded release against its signature |

A node that Loomplane revoked stops itself and exits with code 77. That holds whether it was connected at the time or finds out at its next connect, so a machine that was off when you revoked it stops when it comes back. A service manager that restarts on failure should treat 77 as final. The systemd unit does.

## Leaving a node

`sudo loomctl node leave` removes the node and leaves Docker alone. The containers Loomplane started keep running. To clean up as you go:

```bash
sudo loomctl node leave --purge
```

`--purge` also removes the containers and networks Loomplane made on the machine's Docker. Volumes stay, because they hold data, and the command prints their names so you can delete them yourself with `docker volume rm`.

```bash
sudo loomctl node leave --purge-volumes
```

`--purge-volumes` deletes the volumes too, and everything in them. It asks you to type the node's name first. In a script, pass `--yes-delete-volumes=NAME` with the name instead. A wrong name changes nothing.

## If a deploy says the fence couldn't be established

Docker requests from Loomplane run under a fence, so two attempts can't act on one daemon at once. The node keeps the fence's journal in its state directory, under `fence/<hash>/state`. If the node drops in the middle of a change, the journal stays marked dirty, and the next deploy reports that the runtime effect fence couldn't establish quiescence.

When the mark names an exec, a database readiness check for instance, the next deploy asks Docker about that exec and clears the mark itself once it has finished. A mark that doesn't say what was in flight waits for you. Review it with the node's connection ID:

```bash
loomctl fence-repair conn_...
```

You get the dirty mark, a `review` digest and every exec still running in a Loomplane container. Nothing changes yet. To clear the mark, pass the digest back:

```bash
loomctl fence-repair conn_... --yes --review <digest>
```

The repair keeps the fence's epochs, so an older attempt still can't write. It's refused while another Loomplane request holds the journal's lock, while an exec in a Loomplane container is still running, or when the journal has changed since you reviewed it. Wait for whatever is running, then review again. A node older than this release can't be reviewed at all, so update it first.

If the node dropped in the middle of a container change, look at the containers on the machine before you repair, because the change may be half done. Never delete the `state` file: that resets the epochs, and the fence stops protecting you.

## Releases and updates

Releases are signed with cosign keyless, by the Release workflow of `github.com/xraph/loomplane`. `node.sh` checks them one of two ways:

- With cosign 2.4 or newer installed, it verifies the signature on the release checksums itself and then checks the archive against them. This doesn't trust your Loomplane at all.
- Without cosign, it checks the archive against a checksum your Loomplane already verified against the same signature. In that case Loomplane is vouching for the sum, and the script says so. Install cosign if you want to take Loomplane out of the chain.

With neither, the script stops. Set `LOOMPLANE_SKIP_SIGNATURE=1` to install anyway. The install goes ahead unverified and prints a warning saying so.

To move a running node to another release:

```bash
sudo loomctl node update --release v1.9.0
```

The update downloads the release, verifies it, and only then replaces the binary. It restarts the service and watches it for five seconds. If the service won't start on the new binary, or stops within those five seconds, the update puts the old one back and starts that. A binary that fails later than that isn't caught, so check `node status` after an update.

`node verify-release` runs the same check by hand, when you've downloaded the archive, `binaries-checksums.txt` and its `.sigstore.json` bundle yourself.

## Limits

Loomplane counts what reaches the node endpoints, so a script gone wrong on one address, or one misbehaving node, can't flood it.

| What | Limit | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| Joins from one address | 10 a minute | `nodes.join_rate_limit` |
| Connect challenges from one address | 120 a minute | `nodes.challenge_rate_limit` |
| Control messages from one connected node | 64 at once, then 2 a second | None |

An address over its limit gets a `429` and can try again after a minute. The count lives in the database, so every replica shares it. Each node asks for a challenge every time it reconnects, and all the machines behind one NAT share one address, so if you run more than about a hundred nodes behind a single address, raise `nodes.challenge_rate_limit` or they'll take a few minutes to all come back after a restart. Set either one to `0` to turn it off.

A connected node only sends a heartbeat every 15 seconds and a few messages when it connects, so it never gets near its limit. One that goes over is disconnected, with a warning in the Loomplane log naming the node, and nothing it sent past the limit is stored. It reconnects on its own.

## Several replicas

If you run more than one Loomplane replica, a node is connected to only one of them. A request for that node reaches the right replica over a hop between replicas. Set `nodes.advertise_url` on each replica to the address the others use to reach it. A single replica needs nothing.

Leave it out with several replicas and nothing fails loudly. Each replica only sees the nodes connected to it and reports the rest offline, and a revoke reaches a node on another replica through its next heartbeat, up to 15 seconds later, not at once. A replica with no advertise URL logs this at startup, and warns the first time it meets a node it can't reach.

Hops need `https`. On a private network you can allow plain `http` with `nodes.hop_insecure`. If your replicas use certificates from a private CA, point `nodes.hop_ca_file` at its PEM file. [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration#nodes) has the variables.

## Cutting a node off

There are three ways, and each cuts the node off the same way:

- Revoke it in the dashboard.
- Run `loomctl node revoke NAME` from anywhere you're logged in.
- Run `sudo loomctl node leave` on the machine.

The node can't reconnect afterwards. A node that was off at the time learns it was revoked at its next connect and stops. If you revoke an API key as compromised, Loomplane lists the nodes that joined with a token that key made and offers to revoke them too. Take the offer unless you're sure those machines are fine.

[Security model](/docs/operations/security-model#nodes) covers what a node can and can't do.

pages.title: Render
pages.description: Connect a Render workspace and run web services, workers and static sites with Postgres and Key Value.
pages.text:
Render builds each service itself, from your repository through its own GitHub connection. Loomplane creates the service with automatic deploys off, cancels the deploy Render starts on its own when a service is made, and deploys the commit the plan approved.

## Connect Render


In Render, create an API key.


Give Render access to the repositories you'll deploy, in Render's own dashboard, before the first deployment. Loomplane can't hand Render a connection.


Under **Integrations** in Loomplane, choose Render and paste the key. If the key reaches more than one workspace, enter the workspace ID (`tea-...` for a team or `usr-...` for a person). With exactly one it's used for you. With several and no workspace ID, the check fails and lists them.


## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
defaults:
  provider: render
  region: oregon
services:
  api:
    source: services/api
    needs: [db]
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    version: "17"
  cache:
    kind: redis
```

Regions are `oregon`, `ohio`, `virginia`, `frankfurt` and `singapore`. Render provisions Postgres 17, 16 and 15, and Key Value as its Redis.

## What it builds

A service with a Dockerfile builds from it. Otherwise Render's native runtime builds it, which it has for Go, Node and Python. A Node service starts with `npm start`, so it needs a start script. A Rust or JVM service needs a Dockerfile.

## Networking

A private service is reached on Render's private network by the other services on Render, at `http://` plus its name and port. Postgres and Key Value are reachable from services on Render only.

## Build logs

Render's build-log API can't isolate one deployment among concurrent ones, so Loomplane shows progress only. Read full logs in Render.

pages.title: Spend, latency and traffic
pages.description: What each connected cloud reports about what it costs and how your services are doing, and the permission it needs.
pages.text:
The overview shows what your connected accounts have cost this month, how many requests your services served, and which services are slowest. Each cloud account's page shows its own spend, and **Infrastructure** breaks the month down by account.

None of it passes through Loomplane. Your traffic goes straight to your services, so Loomplane reads these numbers from each cloud's own billing and monitoring, with the credential you connected. When a cloud can't answer, the card names the connection and says what to grant it.

## What each cloud reports

| Cloud | Spend | Requests | Latency | Grant |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google Cloud | From a billing export to BigQuery | Cloud Monitoring | p95 | Monitoring Viewer on the project. For spend, BigQuery Job User on the project and BigQuery Data Viewer on the export's dataset |
| AWS | Cost Explorer, for the whole account | CloudWatch, from the load balancer in front of each ECS service | p95 | `cloudwatch:GetMetricData` and `ce:GetCostAndUsage` |
| Azure | Cost Management, for the resource group Loomplane deploys into | Azure Monitor | Average | Monitoring Reader and Cost Management Reader on the resource group. Contributor already covers both |
| Render | Not available | Render's metrics API | p95 | Nothing more: the API key does it |
| DigitalOcean | The team's balance, month to date | Not available | Not available | `billing:read`, on a token made by a team owner, admin or biller |
| Vercel | Not available | Not available | Not available | |
| Your own servers and clusters | Not available | Not available | Not available | |

Azure Container Apps only reports a mean response time, so Azure services show `avg` beside their latency, never `p95`. Loomplane doesn't combine percentiles across services either, because averaging two services' p95s doesn't give you a p95 for both. The latency card lists each service with its own number.

A token has the role of the person who made it, so a DigitalOcean token with every scope is still refused the balance when its maker can't see billing. The card shows what DigitalOcean said.

Vercel and Render don't report what an account costs through their APIs, so the card mentions them once and moves on. Services on your own servers and clusters report to whatever monitoring you run there, and Loomplane doesn't read it.

## Turn on Google Cloud spend

Google Cloud only reports cost through a billing export, so there's one extra step.

1. In the Google Cloud console, open **Billing**, then **Billing export**, and turn on **Standard usage cost** to a BigQuery dataset.
2. Give the connection's service account BigQuery Job User on its project and BigQuery Data Viewer on that dataset.
3. In Loomplane, replace the connection's key and fill in **Billing export table** with the table's full name, such as `my-project.billing.gcp_billing_export_v1_0A1B2C`.

The export takes a few hours to start filling. Until it does, the month reads as zero.

## Turn on AWS spend

Cost Explorer has to be turned on once per account, in the Billing console. It can take a day before it answers. AWS charges a cent for each Cost Explorer request, so Loomplane keeps each account's bill for an hour before it asks again.

## How fresh it is

Loomplane reads each account's spend at most once an hour, and requests and latency at most every five minutes. It asks a cloud that didn't answer again after a minute, so a permission you've just granted shows up quickly.

The traffic card covers 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or 90 days, and compares the total with the same stretch before it. Requests are added up across services, which works because they're counts. The cloud readers behind these charts also collect 5xx counts, which release checks use.

## Read it from the API

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOOMPLANE_TOKEN" "$URL/api/v1/usage/spend"
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOOMPLANE_TOKEN" "$URL/api/v1/usage/traffic?range=7d"
```

Spend needs `cloud_account:read`. Traffic needs `infrastructure:read`, and only covers services in projects you can read. Each report has a `sources` list with every connection's status, `reporting`, `unavailable` or `failed`, and the reason when it isn't reporting.

pages.title: Vercel
pages.description: Connect a Vercel account or team and deploy web apps and static sites.
pages.text:
Loomplane uploads the approved commit to Vercel, which builds it into an immutable deployment served from its network, with server rendering in functions. Vercel runs web apps and static sites. It doesn't run workers, and it doesn't provision databases, so a worker needs a target such as ECS on Fargate or Render.

## Connect Vercel

Under **Integrations**, choose Vercel and paste an access token. If you deploy to a team, add its team ID (it looks like `team_` followed by letters and digits). Without one, the token deploys to your own account.

Loomplane asks Vercel whose token it is before keeping it. A token that has expired, been revoked or has no access to the team is refused.

## Sign in instead of a token

If a platform owner or admin has set up a Vercel Integration for Loomplane, the connect dialog offers **Sign in with Vercel** first and **Use a token instead** underneath. You install the Integration on Vercel and pick the team or your own account there, so you don't need a team ID. Install it in the same browser you started from. The Integration's token doesn't expire, and Loomplane asks Vercel once a day whether it still works, so an uninstalled Integration asks for a new sign-in. [Connect a cloud by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in) covers making the Integration and what happens when Vercel stops accepting it.

## Use it in a manifest

```yaml
version: 1
services:
  web:
    source: apps/web
    provider: vercel
    needs: [api]
```

A managed resource is only reachable from services on its own cloud, so a Vercel app that needs a Cloud SQL database is a problem on the plan.

## Build logs

Vercel streams its build events, and Loomplane shows them live in the deployment.

## Verified

We ran the full dashboard flow on 18 October 2026 against a real Vercel account with a pinned public Astro static site: saved placements, plan review, approval, build logs, navigating the HTTPS site, a client-side counter and cleanup. After cleanup the account showed no bindings and the old URL returned `DEPLOYMENT_NOT_FOUND`. That qualifies the static-site path. Custom domains still need their own verification.

pages.title: Your own servers
pages.description: Run services on SSH/Docker servers and Kubernetes clusters you already have, group servers into pools, and route domains to them.
pages.text:
Loomplane can deploy to a Linux server over SSH, to a Kubernetes namespace, or to a pool of servers it manages for you. You connect them under **Integrations**, and each service can pick its own connection. The plan pins that destination, its trust settings and the source commit before you approve it.

## SSH and Docker

You need a Linux host with a Docker daemon, an existing private key and the server's verified public host key. The SSH user needs access to the Docker Unix socket and TCP forwarding for readiness checks. Loomplane doesn't install Docker and doesn't use sudo.

If the server has NVIDIA GPUs, Loomplane finds them with `nvidia-smi` on every check. It needs the driver and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit in place first. [GPUs](/docs/clouds/gpus) has the steps.

Choose a published host port for a public HTTP service. Private services use the environment's Docker network. A readiness path checks the application over SSH before its binding changes.

```yaml
services:
  worker:
    source: go:cmd/worker
    provider: server
    target: conn_server
    public: false
    build: { context: . }
```

`target` is the ID of the checked connection. Replace `conn_server` with yours.

## Kubernetes

Use a self-contained HTTPS kubeconfig with an embedded CA and a token or client certificate. File references, exec authentication, insecure TLS and impersonation are rejected. Select an existing namespace. Loomplane pins its UID and checks permissions for workloads, services and secrets.

Public HTTP services need your ingress controller, a hostname and an existing TLS secret. CPU autoscaling also needs the metrics API.

```yaml
version: 1
services:
  api:
    source: go:cmd/api
    provider: kubernetes
    target: conn_cluster
    port: 8080
    health_path: /_/health
    public: false
    scale: { min: 2, max: 2 }
    build:
      context: .
      builder: conn_builder
      registry: conn_registry
```

A source build can use the SSH/Docker builder and registry shown above, or you can let the cluster build and store its images.

### Managed cluster builds

In the Kubernetes connection, set `registry_hostname` to a hostname you control, such as `images.example.com`, and save. You can leave the architecture, storage class, ingress class and ingress address empty. With cluster-admin permissions, Loomplane installs missing Traefik and cert-manager components in `loomplane-system`, detects a schedulable Linux architecture, and creates a retained copy of your default storage class. You don't need Helm on the Loomplane server.

Existing controllers are reused. Setup checks resource ownership and permissions before writing, and a repeated save resumes a partial installation. It does not replace or upgrade someone else's installation. The namespace you connect must already exist, and you still need a working dynamic storage provisioner. If there are several defaults or no default, choose the storage or ingress class explicitly. A retained class keeps the original driver parameters, topology and binding mode without changing your cluster's default class. Retention is not a backup.

The installed ingress requests a load balancer, which can incur cloud charges. While controllers or the load balancer are starting, the connection reports what it is waiting for. Recheck to refresh its state and discover the address. Point your hostname's DNS at that address. DNS is not changed by this setup. Clusters without a load-balancer controller need an `ingress_address` override and a working route to ports 80 and 443. A local cluster's private address does not establish public ACME reachability.

Set `registry_setup: existing` to manage prerequisites yourself. Connections that already provide storage class, architecture and ingress address keep that behavior unless you select `registry_setup: automatic`. Ordinary health checks never install resources. Saving an automatic connection can repair missing owned resources; deleting a connection retains its shared controllers and storage class. Controller upgrades and final removal remain operator tasks.

Leave the builder and registry empty on each service:

```yaml
version: 1
services:
  api:
    source: go:cmd/api
    provider: kubernetes
    target: conn_cluster
    port: 8080
    public: false
    build: { context: . }
```

Your first approved deployment creates a persistent registry with 20 GiB of retained storage, generated authentication, an Ingress and a cert-manager certificate.
