Loomplane uploads the approved source to a rootless BuildKit Job, publishes its image, and deploys by digest. It creates the image pull Secret for each workload. Failed rollouts restore the previous pull Secret along with the workload.

Build Jobs have a 30-minute deadline and a one-hour finished-job TTL if normal cleanup is interrupted. They receive no application secrets, service account token or host Docker socket. The nodes need user namespaces, and the namespace must allow BuildKit's unconfined seccomp and AppArmor profiles. Restricted Pod Security policies require a dedicated namespace with an appropriate policy.

The hostname must resolve and its certificate must be trusted from both pods and nodes. HTTP-01 certificate issuance needs the DNS record in place before deployment. The installed Traefik accepts streamed uploads and redirects HTTP to HTTPS, with HTTP-01 challenge routes taking priority. Loomplane also sets large-upload annotations for ingress-nginx. If you supply another controller, configure equivalent upload limits and HTTPS enforcement.

The connection shares one registry and its generated Basic credentials. Use separate namespaces and connections for workloads that must not share image access. Workload pull credentials refresh on deployment; they do not expire automatically. Removing a service retains the registry and its images. You manage image retention, backups, garbage collection and final registry removal. Its single replica depends on your storage driver for recovery.

### External images and builders

Keep an explicit `build.builder` and `build.registry` to use your existing build infrastructure. To skip source builds, give `build.image` an existing image pinned as `registry/repository@sha256:...`.

For private images from an external registry, enter the name of an existing namespace Secret in the connection's `image_pull_secret` setting. You manage its credentials and rotation. Rollback and removal leave that Secret alone, and names starting with `lp-` are reserved for Loomplane's own objects.

Forge HTTP apps without a Dockerfile can use a generated Go build, and a repository Dockerfile takes precedence over it. A private dependency needs a supported network path between its targets. Picking destinations doesn't create a cross-cluster network.

### Registry credentials

Docker publishing and server pulls accept a registry bearer token, or a repository token from your reviewed token service. Username and password connections need a bearer token exchange for authenticated Docker operations. Basic-only credentials can check registry API access but can't be delegated to Docker. Loomplane sends registry credentials only to the selected registry or its approved token endpoint. If you use a private CA, install its trust on the builder daemon, the target daemon and the Kubernetes nodes that contact the registry.

### The cluster Loomplane runs in

If Loomplane runs in Kubernetes and your operator [turned it on](/docs/operations/production-on-kubernetes#deploying-into-the-same-cluster), the Kubernetes dialog opens on that cluster. There's no kubeconfig to paste: Loomplane connects as its own service account. Name the connection, pick one of the namespaces your operator set aside, and connect. From there it works like any other Kubernetes connection, and plans pin the namespace's UID the same way.

You can't pick the namespace Loomplane runs in, or `kube-system` and its neighbours. If you'd rather use your own credentials, choose **Use a kubeconfig instead**.

## Persistent storage

Docker databases keep a named volume that survives container replacement and removal. Kubernetes uses a StatefulSet and a retained PVC. [Storage inventory](/docs/services/storage-inventory) shows what's retained.

## Servers and pools

You can provision and adopt servers inside an organization Cloud. Your installed provider adapter declares each operation separately: discovery, provisioning, resize, deletion, DNS and domain attachment. An unsupported capability is a failure you resolve with a supported account or operation. Having a provider name doesn't mean it supports a runtime.

```bash
loomctl cloud-servers cloud_...
loomctl cloud-servers options cloud_... conn_...
loomctl cloud-servers preview cloud_... --file server.json
loomctl cloud-servers apply cloud_... infraop_... --review REVIEW_TOKEN --yes \
  --wait --timeout 20m
loomctl cloud-servers show cloud_... infraop_...
loomctl cloud-servers operations cloud_...
loomctl cloud-servers retry cloud_... infraop_... --wait --timeout 20m
loomctl cloud-servers cancel cloud_... infraop_...
```

For a managed server creation, `server.json` looks like this. Get supported region, size and bootstrap image IDs from `options` for your connection.

```json title="server.json"
{
  "kind": "create",
  "name": "host-a",
  "connection_id": "conn_...",
  "region": "nyc3",
  "size": "s-1vcpu-1gb",
  "image": "ubuntu-24-04-x64",
  "cloud_revision": 1
}
```

To adopt an existing host, use `{"kind":"adopt","name":"existing-host","connection_id":"ssh_conn_...","cloud_revision":1,"confirm_adoption":true}`. You keep provider ownership of an adopted host. Loomplane can disconnect it but can't resize or delete it. Disconnecting or deleting a host is blocked while workloads, reservations or pool membership still reference it.

To review a resize, disconnect or deletion, supply `kind`, `server_id`, `cloud_revision` and `server_revision` (and `size` for a resize). The preview returns an operation ID, an exact review token, an expiry, an estimated cost and the provider actions. Reviews last 15 minutes, and `apply` prints the saved operation before it accepts your token.

Provider acceptance doesn't mean the runtime is ready. Follow the operation's provider actions and bootstrap expiry, then refresh the pinned SSH and Docker health:

```bash
loomctl cloud-servers check cloud_... server_...
```

`--wait` stops at success, failure, cancellation or a waiting checkpoint. A waiting checkpoint still needs your attention.

### Capacity and pools

```bash
loomctl cloud-servers usage cloud_... server_...
loomctl cloud-servers drain cloud_... server_...
loomctl cloud-servers drain cloud_... server_... --review DRAIN_DIGEST --yes
loomctl cloud-pools cloud_...
loomctl cloud-pools save cloud_... --file pool.json
loomctl cloud-pools save cloud_... pool_... --file pool-update.json
```

Draining disables new admission after you review current usage. It doesn't move workloads. Usage includes capacity reservations, serving workloads, execution phases and retained storage markers (which don't prove a volume exists). A pool input gives `name`, `revision` (0 for creation) and `members`, each with `server_id`, `cpu_millis`, `memory_bytes` and `draining`. Budgets must fit verified runtime capacity. A pool groups compatible Docker hosts and doesn't create a private network.

Point a target at a pool instead of an infrastructure account:

```bash
loomctl cloud-targets create cloud_... --organization --name workers \
  --provider server --runtime server --pool pool_... --tags workers
loomctl cloud-targets switch cloud_... target_... --organization \
  --provider server --runtime server --pool pool_new --revision 2
```

A pool service has one bounded replica and one active placement, and ordinary deployments keep the chosen host when they can. To pick another host for a stateless service, review a move:

```json title="move.json"
{
  "project_id": "project_...",
  "environment_id": "env_...",
  "service": "web",
  "pool_id": "pool_...",
  "destination_server_id": "server_next"
}
```

```bash
loomctl cloud-pools move cloud_... --file move.json
# Copy the returned review digest into move.json as "review", then accept.
loomctl cloud-pools move cloud_... --file move.json --yes
```

Accepting saves a 15-minute intent and starts no deployment. The response includes a conservative `local_review_and_approve_by` deadline and the exact `loomctl plan` command to run next. Review that plan, then `loomctl approve` it before the intent expires. If the source, pool, capacity or grant changes, plan again. Local data needs a separate, explicit migration.

To recover an unfinished accepted reservation, run `loomctl cloud-pools recover cloud_... --file recovery.json` with `{"plan_id":"plan_...","service":"web"}`. Read its execution revision, active or started state and digest, copy the digest into `review`, and repeat with `--yes`. Recovery fences new attempts, checks exact owned compute cleanup and releases capacity. It retains local storage and reports `storage_retained`, which isn't evidence of a backup or a data migration. A serving workload needs a reviewed delete or move. Don't clear a reservation by editing database rows. Pending mixed managed and server attempts without proof that provider work stopped stay blocked until you reconcile or finish the original operation.

## Domains and routes

DNS zones belong to the organization, apart from any Cloud or compute connection. Grant them to projects explicitly. Managed mode uses a supported DNS account. External mode returns a TXT ownership proof you publish yourself. This doesn't register domains or change registrar nameservers.

```bash
loomctl dns-zones
loomctl dns-zones create --file zone.json
loomctl dns-zones verify zone_...
loomctl dns-zones project my-project
loomctl dns-zones update zone_... --file zone-update.json
loomctl dns-zones remove zone_... --revision 3 --yes
```

Use `{"name":"example.com","mode":"external","project_ids":["project_..."]}` for an external zone, or `"mode": "managed"` with a `connection_id` for a DNS adapter. A zone update carries `revision`, `project_ids` and `renew_proof`. Renew an expired, unverified proof with `renew_proof: true` and publish the replacement TXT value. Referenced zones can't be removed.

```json title="route.json"
{
  "zone_id": "zone_...",
  "cloud_id": "cloud_...",
  "environment_id": "env_...",
  "service": "web",
  "hostname": "app.example.com",
  "port": 8080,
  "external_ttl_seconds": 7200
}
```

```bash
loomctl domain-routes preview my-project --file route.json
loomctl domain-routes apply my-project routeop_... --review REVIEW_DIGEST --yes \
  --wait --timeout 15m
loomctl domain-routes my-project
loomctl domain-routes show my-project routeop_...
loomctl domain-routes verify my-project route_... --wait --timeout 10m
loomctl domain-routes retry my-project routeop_... --wait --timeout 10m
loomctl domain-routes history my-project route_...
loomctl domain-routes ttl my-project route_... --revision 3 --external-ttl-seconds 7200
loomctl domain-routes remove my-project route_... --revision 4 --yes
```

DNS, TLS and backend verification are reported separately. A route operation prints its desired record, applied receipt, message and `not_before` drain gate. For external DNS, publish the exact record and verify again. A server route needs the public hostname to reach its ingress and the HTTP-01 challenge before a public certificate can be issued.

`external_ttl_seconds` is the maximum TTL your external DNS records previously served, including any cached value, between 60 and 86400 seconds. You have to establish that bound yourself. A successful resolver lookup and the new TTL you ask for don't establish it.

During a routed release, old and new compute coexist while DNS changes and cached traffic drain. If a legacy runtime lacks a trusted current container receipt, redeploy it through the reviewed flow before you attach a route. DNS-only retries can't repair a missing runtime identity.

  Fixture certificates and local ACME checks don't qualify your domain for public ACME, and fixture-backed provider checks don't qualify your account or DNS propagation. Stop every older app and worker binary before running migrations that touch these tables. Mixed versions with unfenced writers aren't supported.

pages.title: Canary releases
pages.description: Loomplane shifts traffic to a new version in steps, using each cloud's own weighting, and reads health from that cloud's own monitoring.
pages.text:
Loomplane shifts traffic to a new version with each cloud's own traffic weighting, so it never sits in the path of your application's requests. It reads health from the cloud's own monitoring, so what it judges is what the cloud already reports.

## Where canaries run

| Provider | Canary | Weighting | Requests | 5xx | Latency | Per revision | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cloud-run` | Yes | Revision traffic | Yes | Yes | p95 | Yes | Traffic is split with revision traffic percentages on the service. |
| `ecs-fargate` | Yes | ALB target groups | Yes | Yes | p95 | Yes | Traffic is split with weighted target groups on the ALB listener, for services behind the public or internal ALB. Service Connect calls stay on the baseline. |
| `azure-container-apps` | Yes | Revision traffic | Yes | Yes | Average | Yes | Traffic is split with revision traffic weights, in multiple revisions mode, for apps with ingress. |
| `kubernetes` | No | None | No | No | None | No | Services use a plain Ingress with no Gateway API, so there is no traffic weighting to drive. |
| `server` | No | None | No | No | None | No | Route releases are a DNS cutover, so traffic moves all at once. |
| `render` | No | None | Yes | Yes | p95 | No | Render has no traffic weighting. Its metrics are per service, not per revision. |
| `vercel` | No | None | No | No | None | No | Vercel has no traffic weighting Loomplane drives. |
| `digitalocean` | No | None | No | No | None | No | DigitalOcean has no traffic weighting. |

Services on any other target deploy all at once, and the plan says so.

## Turn one on

Set a `release` block on the environment in `loomplane.yaml`, then plan as usual:

```yaml
environments:
  production:
    release:
      strategy: canary
      steps: [5, 25, 50, 100]
      hold: 10m
```

Approving the plan starts the canary. You approve once per release, and nobody approves individual steps. The approval card on the deployment page says "Approving starts a canary" and repeats the steps and the hold, so you can see what you're agreeing to. The [manifest reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml) lists every setting and its default.

## How a ramp runs

Loomplane starts the new version beside the current one, with no traffic on it. Then it moves the first step's share of traffic to the new version, waits, reads health, and decides. A pass moves on to the next step. The last step is 100%, and passing it promotes the new version for good.

Each step holds for the `hold` you set (10 minutes by default). Cloud monitoring reports a few minutes late, so the first reading of a step also waits three more minutes after the hold ends. A 10 minute hold means about 13 minutes before the first verdict of that step. A four step ramp with the defaults takes close to an hour in total.

The decision is made by Loomplane's own controller. It doesn't use the agent and works with the agent switched off.

## What counts as healthy

For each service, Loomplane reads the new version's requests, 5xx responses and latency from the cloud's own monitoring, along with the same figures for the version it replaces. A step fails when the new version:

- has a failure share above `thresholds.error_rate`
- has a failure share more than `thresholds.error_rate_delta` above the current version's
- is slower than `thresholds.p95_latency_ratio` times the current version's latency

The error share and latency comparisons only count when the current version also served at least `min_requests` requests. Latency is p95 on Cloud Run and ECS. Azure Container Apps only reports an average, so the dashboard marks those readings "avg".

## Verdicts

Every reading ends in one of three verdicts.

`pass` means the step is healthy and the ramp moves on. `fail` means a threshold was crossed, and the canary rolls back right away.

`inconclusive` means Loomplane couldn't tell. Either the new version served fewer than `min_requests` requests in the window, or the cloud had no metrics for it. An inconclusive step doesn't pass and doesn't fail. It holds for another window and is read again, up to three extra times. If it's still inconclusive after that, Loomplane fails safe: it rolls back rather than promote a version it couldn't check. A quiet service with little traffic will hit this, so lower `min_requests` for services that are quiet by nature.

## What rolls back

A failed step sends all traffic back to the current version, removes the new one, and ends the deployment as failed. The error says which step failed and why, for example "The canary failed at 25%". Services that deploy all at once aren't part of the ramp, and the canary leaves them alone.

You can retry the deployment. The dashboard and the API then show only the verdicts of the latest retry.

## When traffic may still be split

Rollback calls the cloud's API, so it can fail too. Loomplane retries once a minute for up to an hour, so a stuck rollback can sit at "Rolling back" for a while. If it still can't move traffic back, the canary ends as `revert_failed`. If a failure hits while the new version is being promoted, it ends as `promote_failed`. In both cases the reason starts with "Traffic may still be split".

You have to act here. Open the service in the cloud, check how it splits traffic between versions, and fix it before you retry. The deployment page shows this as a red "Needs you" notice, and `loomctl deployment` prints it as `NEEDS YOU:`.

## Where a canary can't run

Only an update of something already running can ramp. A service gets no canary when:

- it's new, so there's nothing to compare it with, or it's moving to another target
- it's a worker, so it takes no HTTP traffic
- its domain routes switch over by DNS
- it runs on a Cloud target
- it's on ECS and takes no HTTP traffic or isn't behind the load balancer, or it's on Azure Container Apps and has no ingress
- it reaches Cloud SQL through a Private Service Connect route, because a candidate wouldn't carry the route
- it's the environment's database gateway, because its keys and routes follow each release in one go
- its target has no native weighting (see the table above)

The plan still goes ahead. Those services deploy all at once while the rest of the release ramps. The approval card lists a warning for each one that says why, and it doesn't say "Approving starts a canary" for them.

Some refusals block the plan instead, and the plan shows them as problems you have to fix before anyone can approve:

- On ECS, Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps, the connection's credential may lack the permissions to split the service's traffic.
- On Azure Container Apps, a release that changes app-wide ingress settings can't ramp, because those apply to every revision at once. Release that change with `direct` or `blue_green` first.
- On Cloud Run, a release that changes `public` can't ramp either. Who may call a Cloud Run service belongs to the service, not to a revision, so access only switches at Promote, for all of the traffic at once, and no step judges it. Release that change with `direct` or `blue_green` first.

Two more only show up when the canary starts, and the deployment fails with a message that says which:

- An earlier canary couldn't roll back and left the traffic split on a Cloud Run service or an Azure container app. The new canary can't tell which revision is the real one to compare against. Retry that deployment, or release once with `direct`, which gives the latest revision all of the traffic. A rollback plan is refused while a canary's revert or promotion has failed, so fix the split first.
- On Azure Container Apps, the release changes the registry the app pulls from or the identity it pulls as. Those are app-wide like ingress, but Loomplane only knows them once it has set the release up. Release that change with `direct` or `blue_green` first.

## After the canary

A canary judges a release while it ramps. A service it ramped isn't judged again afterward. The services it didn't ramp, and the environments that don't use canaries at all, can get a [post-deploy watch](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback#watch-a-release-after-it-deploys) that reads the same cloud monitoring. It needs the Requests and 5xx columns of the table at the top of this page, so Cloud Run, ECS, Azure Container Apps and Render can be watched, including Render, which has no canary. A canary that fails reverts by itself. A rollback never ramps as a canary.

## One canary per environment

While a canary ramps, the environment is busy. A new plan for it is blocked with a `canary-in-progress` problem, and an older plan that was already waiting goes stale when you approve it. Plan again once the canary settles.

## Read the verdicts

In the dashboard, open the deployment. The Canary panel sits under the steps. It shows each step as passed, holding, failed or couldn't be judged, the reason for a rollback, and a table with one row per service, step and check: errors, latency, and the figures for the current version beside them.

From a terminal:

```bash
loomctl deployment <deployment-id> --watch
```

This prints the canary block and a verdict table, and in watch mode each new verdict once.

Over the API, `GET /api/v1/deployments/{id}` returns the `canary` block, and `GET /api/v1/deployments/{id}/canary` returns it with every verdict of the current retry. A plan's `release` field carries the steps, the hold and the thresholds it was planned with. Each verdict is also sent as a `canary_verdict.updated` realtime event.

pages.title: Deployments and recovery
pages.description: What happens after you approve a plan, how to follow it, how to cancel it, and how to retry from the step that failed.
pages.text:
Approval starts a deployment, a durable Dispatch workflow that runs beside the API. Each step is an activity with retries, and a crash resumes from the last completed step. Long steps checkpoint the cloud's operation ID, so a retry waits on the build or database already under way instead of starting another.

## The steps

| Step | Where it runs |
|---|---|
| Plan again and check the revision still matches what was approved | Loomplane. A mismatch ends the deployment as stale |
| Store one tarball for each source the plan moves, at its pinned commit | Trove, so every builder gets the same bytes |
| Provision resources | Loomplane's executors, such as Cloud SQL and RDS, or a provider plugin |
| Build each service from its own source's tarball | Cloud Build, CodeBuild, Vercel, Render, App Platform or ACR Tasks, in your accounts |
| Deploy each service, with its secrets in the cloud's secret store | Ctrl Plane for Cloud Run and ECS, Loomplane's adapters for the rest, a plugin for its own targets |
| Check each public service answers, and record what runs it | Loomplane |
| Finish, recording the commit now deployed for each source that moved | Loomplane |

Steps run in order, each after everything it needs, so a service gets the address of its database when it deploys.

## Follow it

```bash
loomctl deployments my-project
loomctl deployment <deployment-id> --watch
loomctl status my-project
```

In the dashboard, a Live badge on the page confirms a recent status heartbeat. Events and build output are committed in PostgreSQL before they're delivered, so restarting the API or the worker doesn't lose status. Build output is kept for seven days, with 16 KiB per line and 10 MiB per action attempt.

Build logs depend on the target. Vercel streams them. Cloud Run and ECS poll them from Cloud Logging and CloudWatch. Render, App Platform and Azure show progress only, and the full build logs stay in each provider's own console.

## Retry from where it stopped

```bash
loomctl retry <deployment-id>
```

A failed deployment retries from the step that failed, with the plan that was approved. Earlier attempts stay visible. An interrupted Docker build may need rebuilding, and its first attempt stays visible as incomplete.

If a step fails because a connection lost a permission, fix the permission, check the connection again, then retry.

## Cancel a running deployment

```bash
loomctl cancel <deployment-id>
```

You can also cancel from the deployment's page. The step that's running finishes first, because stopping a provider halfway through a change would leave you cleaning it up by hand. The deployment is cancelled as its next step would start, and nothing after that runs. So you can only cancel while a step is still waiting: once every step has started, the deployment finishes on its own. Steps that already finished stay as they are, and so does what they deployed, since a cancel doesn't roll anything back. Capacity the deployment had reserved but not started using is released, as it is when you cancel a wait for capacity.

A deployment paused for capacity has nothing running, so it's cancelled at once. Add `--revision` and `loomctl cancel` cancels only the capacity wait you read, refusing one that changed since.

If the deployment has a canary, its candidates are reverted when it stops. You can't retry a cancelled deployment, so plan again to finish what it started.

## When a canary rolls back

In an environment with a [canary](/docs/concepts/canary-releases), each service that ramps deploys a candidate that takes no traffic. Once every action has run, the deployment moves traffic to the candidates in the release's steps, holds each step, and judges it against the baseline from the cloud's own metrics. Nobody approves the steps, since you already approved the plan. If every step passes, the candidates become what runs and the deployment finishes.

When a step fails, or the deployment can't go on, the canary rolls itself back. Loomplane moves all traffic back to the baseline and removes each candidate, and the deployment fails with one of these errors:

| The error starts with | Why |
|---|---|
| `The canary failed at 25%:` | A service's health at that step was outside the release's thresholds. The rest of the error names the service and the number. |
| `The canary couldn't be judged at 5% after 4 holds:` | The cloud didn't report enough to judge, such as too few requests or no metrics at all. An inconclusive step holds again up to three more times before it gives up. |
| `Traffic couldn't move to 50%:` | Moving traffic at that step failed, for example because the cloud refused the change. |
| An action's own error | Something failed before the ramp started. Candidates already up, still taking no traffic, are removed too. |

The bindings never changed, so the environment runs exactly what it ran before, and `loomctl deployment <deployment-id>` shows each step's verdict. A retry ramps from the first step again and judges fresh traffic.

Sometimes the revert itself fails. Loomplane tries it again every minute for an hour, and then the error ends with `Traffic may still be split:` and the cloud's last error. The canary shows `revert_failed`. Check the service's traffic in the cloud's console before you retry, because part of it may still reach the candidate.

Cancelling a deployment's wait for capacity, or stopping its workflow, reverts the candidates too, and a revert that keeps failing there ends as `revert_failed` the same way. If every step had already passed, stopping the workflow finishes the promotion instead. Either way the canary stops holding the environment, so you can plan again.

## When something moves

Replaced services and resources leave an old copy behind until the new one is up. Loomplane records what's still to remove on the binding, not the deployment, so a failed removal isn't lost if you plan again instead of retrying. Every plan warns about what's on that list. Any later deployment of the same service or resource tries again after its own work, and a failure there adds a warning without blocking the deployment.

Deleting a service or resource removes everything on that list first, then the thing itself. Each goes through the connection that deployed it, so you can move an environment to a different account and still clean up what the old one left. If that connection has been deleted, the plan tells you where the leftover runs and that it's yours to remove.

Keep a connection for as long as a plan, build, binding or deployment references it.

pages.title: Drift
pages.description: Loomplane checks on a schedule that what runs in your clouds is what it deployed, and records differences without changing anything.
pages.text:
Drift is the difference between what Loomplane deployed and what a cloud has live. Someone deletes a Cloud Run service by hand, a tunnel goes down, or a console edit changes a setting.

## How the check works

Every 30 minutes by default, Loomplane asks each target's executor what's live and compares it with the binding it recorded at deploy time. It writes down the result and touches nothing. Ctrl Plane's own drift correction isn't used, because two controllers changing one resource fight each other.

Set the interval with `LOOMPLANE_DRIFT_INTERVAL`. A value of `0` turns the check off.

## Where you see it

```bash
loomctl status my-project
```

The `DRIFT` column reads "in sync" or says what changed. The dashboard shows the same on each environment, and the `drift_findings_total` metric counts bindings found missing or changed, labelled by provider and state.

When the [built-in agent](/docs/agents/built-in-agent) is on, drift on a production environment also opens an agent report, one per drifted service or resource. The agent investigates it, and the project's people hear about it. The report resolves by itself once the binding matches what Loomplane deployed again. Drift on other environments doesn't open a report. See [Watching and reports](/docs/agents/watching-and-reports).

## Putting it back

The next plan notices what's missing or changed, and proposes the actions to fix it. You review and approve that plan like any other. A cross-cloud link with a tunnel down also shows as drift, and the next plan brings back what's missing.

  Drift only reads. If a check finds something unexpected, nothing happens to your cloud until a person approves a plan.

pages.title: Gateways and networking
pages.description: How services find and reach each other, how a gateway fronts them, and how to join Google Cloud and AWS networks.
pages.text:
How one service reaches another depends on where both run. The planner checks every `needs` relationship against the placements, so a path that can't work shows up as a problem on the plan, before you approve anything.

## Reaching other services

| Where the target runs | How it's reached |
|---|---|
| ECS on Fargate | Services in the same environment reach each other inside the VPC, at `http://name:port`, whether or not the one they need is public |
| Cloud Run, private | Only calls from the project's own services, which must send a Google ID token |
| Render, private | On Render's private network, by other services on Render, at `http://` plus its name and port |
| Azure Container Apps, private | Only from apps in the same Container Apps environment (same connection, same region) |
| DigitalOcean App Platform, private | Nothing can call one, because each service is its own app. Make it public |

A private service needed from another cloud is a problem on the plan, unless a [link](#links) joins the two networks and the caller is on Google Cloud.

A managed resource is only reachable from services on its own cloud. Postgres and Key Value on Render are reachable from services on Render only, and RDS and ElastiCache from the environment's ECS tasks.

## Gateways

A gateway is one public address in front of several services, routing each request by path. Loomplane builds each one on Bastion and runs it on Cloud Run or ECS, like a service. Your traffic never passes through Loomplane.

```yaml
gateways:
  edge:
    provider: cloud-run
    routes:
      - { path: /api, to: api, strip_prefix: true }
      - { path: /, to: web }
```

A path prefix like `/api` matches `/api` and anything under `/api/`. The longest matching path wins, so `/` catches the rest. With `strip_prefix: true`, `/api/users` reaches the service as `/users`.

A gateway gets the addresses it routes to and none of the project's variables. On ECS it can reach private services inside the environment. Anywhere else, a route to a private service is a problem on the plan, since a gateway can't present Cloud Run's ID token.

## Links

A link joins an environment's Google Cloud network to its AWS VPC, so a Cloud Run service can need a private ECS service, an RDS database or an ElastiCache cache.

```yaml
links:
  vpn:
    between: [gcp, aws]
    region: us-central1
```

Each environment gets its own link: an HA VPN gateway and a Cloud Router on the project's default network, a virtual private gateway on the account's default VPC, and four IPsec tunnels with a BGP session each. Losing an endpoint on either side keeps the link up.

Both clouds bill a VPN by the hour, whether or not anything uses it, so turn the link off in environments that don't need it. It works one way: a service on ECS can't call a private Cloud Run service, which checks Google identity tokens and not addresses. Make that service public or move the caller.

Links need more than a connection check asks for. The Google Cloud key needs Compute Network Admin (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`). The AWS key needs the VPN and route actions listed in the [manifest reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml#links). Removing a link takes it down on both clouds, Google's side first.

## Custom domains and routes

DNS zones belong to the organization, apart from any Cloud. You grant them to projects, then preview and apply a domain route for a service. Managed mode uses a supported DNS account. External mode gives you a TXT ownership proof to publish yourself. This configures DNS for a domain you already own, and doesn't buy domains or change registrar nameservers. The commands are in [Your own servers](/docs/clouds/your-own-servers#domains-and-routes).

pages.title: Organizations and roles
pages.description: Everything belongs to an organization, and four roles decide who can plan, approve and manage.
pages.text:
Every project, plan, connection, variable and API key belongs to one organization, and every request acts in exactly one. That organization comes from your signed-in session or your API key, and nothing in the request can change it. A dashboard tab that drifted to another organization gets a 409 instead of acting in the wrong place. Another organization's things aren't found, which is the same answer as something that doesn't exist, so an ID never confirms anything.

## Roles

| Role | Can |
|---|---|
| Viewer | Read everything but secret values. Changes nothing |
| Developer | Create projects and environments, analyze, edit manifests and variables, plan |
| Admin | Approve plans, retry deployments, manage cloud connections, secrets, members and backups |
| Owner | Everything, including the organization itself, and retiring backups |

Each role includes everything the one below it can do. The line that matters is approval: a developer can plan anything, and only an admin's approval of the exact revision they reviewed changes a cloud. [Roles and permissions](/docs/reference/roles-and-permissions) lists every permission.

Roles are Warden roles, checked in the service layer on every action. The dashboard hides what your role can't do, but the API checks anyway. They're mapped from your organization membership: owner to owner, admin to admin, member to developer, and anything else to viewer, so an unexpected role never grants more than reading.

## Members and invitations

Owners and admins invite people from the dashboard. With SMTP configured, Loomplane emails the invitation and reports whether it was sent, disabled or failed. Either way you get a manual link that works once, for a week, and only for an account with that address. Owners and admins change roles and remove people, never above their own role.

A role can also come from a team. If the people who ship one service shouldn't be admins everywhere, put them in a [team](/docs/concepts/teams) and give it a role on that project. Your effective role is the highest of your own and your teams'.

## API keys

Make a key under **Settings, API keys**. It acts as you, with your role, in your organization, and never more. Pick read-only and it fails every permission that isn't a read.

- The secret appears once. Loomplane stores a hash.
- A key lives 90 days unless you say otherwise, and at most 366.
- Keys can't manage keys, so a key can't outlive its own revocation.
- When you leave the organization or lose a role, your keys lose the same rights on the next request.
- Owners and admins can see and revoke anyone's keys. Everyone else sees their own.

Name a key after the machine or pipeline it's for.

## The audit trail

Chronicle records authentication, membership and project changes, plus what agents and keys change, under the person who made the key. The record keeps names and the last four characters of a key, never a value.

pages.title: Plans and approvals
pages.description: A plan lists exactly what a deployment would do, and only an admin's approval of that exact revision changes a cloud.
pages.text:
A plan is Loomplane's answer to "what would happen if I deployed this?" Making one never touches a cloud. Approving one starts the deployment.

## Make a plan

```bash
loomctl plan my-project --env production
loomctl plan my-project --env production --scope web
loomctl show <plan-id>
```

`--scope` names the repositories the plan moves, by alias. The rest stay at the commits that are already deployed, and their services are kept as they run. Without it, every source moves.

A plan pins a lockset: one analysis and commit for each source. It composes its graph from those, so it always sees the graph it was made from, even if you push or re-analyze afterward.

## Kinds of plan

Most plans are releases: the current manifest and a commit of each repository you move. Two other kinds exist, and `loomctl show` says which one you're looking at.

A promotion is made with `loomctl promote` (or `plan --from staging`). It pins the commits and manifest revision another environment runs, and reuses that environment's images where it can. A rollback is made with `loomctl rollback`. It restores the previous successful release's commits and manifest revision, and lists as left in place anything it won't touch, such as a resource that holds data. Both wait for approval like a release does. [Promotion and rollback](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback) has the details.

There's one exception to "a person approves". When a [post-deploy watch](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback#watch-a-release-after-it-deploys) sees a release breach its thresholds, Loomplane plans the rollback and approves it itself, as Loomplane automation. It's marked automatic in the audit trail, and it can approve only a rollback that a watch started. Every other plan still needs a person.

## What a plan shows

Every action, step by step, with its operation, name, provider and the reason it's there. Beside the actions you get two lists.

Problems block the plan. A Vercel app that needs a Cloud SQL database is a problem, because a managed resource is only reachable from services on its own cloud. So is a private service needed from another cloud. A plan with problems can't be approved.

Warnings don't block, but you should read them. Expect them for a service that falls back to port 8080 because it didn't declare one, for a service still using a legacy variable name, and for old resources a move left behind that you'll need to delete yourself.

Some plans are for review only: something in them has no adapter yet, or they use a [paused target](/docs/operations/monitoring#pausing-a-target). You can approve those, but approving deploys nothing.

## Releases

When the environment declares a `release` block in `loomplane.yaml`, the plan shows the release it pinned: the strategy, the canary's steps and hold, the thresholds it's judged against, and which services ramp. All of that is part of the revision you approve. Change the hold from 10 minutes to 15 and you get a new revision, so you never approve one release and get another.

A release with a canary is still one decision. You approve the plan once, and the [canary](/docs/concepts/canary-releases) ramps, holds and judges each step by itself. Nobody approves individual steps.

Only an update of something already running can ramp: an HTTP service on Cloud Run, a service behind the load balancer on ECS, or an app with ingress or a static site on Azure Container Apps. Every other service in a canary environment gets a `canary-unavailable` warning that says why (it's new, it's moving, it's a worker, its target has no traffic weighting Loomplane can drive) and deploys all at once. In a `blue_green` environment, a service with no route release to switch over gets a `blue-green-unavailable` warning and deploys the way it does today.

While a canary ramps in an environment, a new plan for it is blocked with a `canary-in-progress` problem that names the deployment. Plan again once it finishes. A plan that was ready before the ramp started comes back stale if you approve it during the ramp, so two deployments never fight over one service's traffic.

An environment without a `release` block plans exactly as it did before, with no release on the plan.

## Approve, reject or let it expire

```bash
loomctl approve <plan-id>            # asks first; --yes skips the question
loomctl approve <plan-id> --note "Release 14" --no-wait
loomctl reject <plan-id> --note "Wrong environment"
```

An approval names the revision of the plan you reviewed. If what's deployed changed since the plan was made, it comes back stale and nothing happens: you plan again. A plan that nobody decides expires after the approval window, 168 hours by default. You can set it between one minute and 90 days with `LOOMPLANE_PLANNING_APPROVAL_WINDOW`.

Developers plan and admins approve. See [Organizations and roles](/docs/concepts/organizations-and-roles).

## Moves and replacements

A service or resource that moves to another provider, region or connection is replaced. The new one starts first, and the old one goes once the new one is up and answering. A resource never moves between connections, because its data would stay behind. A plan that would provision one through another connection than the one that provisioned it has a problem until you choose the old connection again.

Turning an existing service off can produce a deletion in the next plan, so read that one carefully.

## Standalone resources

A project can hold only resources, with no repository. `loomctl plan PROJECT --catalog --env production` plans those. [Database services](/docs/services/database-services) shows how it fits together.

pages.title: Projects and environments
pages.description: A project groups the repositories you deploy together, and each environment is a separate target for plans and variables.
pages.text:
A project is the thing you deploy. It belongs to one organization, it builds from one or more repositories, and it has environments that each get their own plans, variables and deployed state.

## Create a project

In the dashboard choose **New project** and pick a repository the GitHub App can read, or paste a URL for a public one. From the terminal:

```bash
loomctl projects create "Acme shop" --repo acme/web --repo billing=acme/billing
```

Repeat `--repo` for each repository. Write `alias=repository` to name one yourself. Without one, Loomplane takes it from the repository's name.

## Sources

Each repository in a project is a source: a repository, an optional directory inside it, a tracked branch and an alias. Pick the alias carefully. It becomes part of every service ID (`svc:api:go:cmd/server`), so it never changes, and it never moves to another repository, even after you remove the source. Add the same repository again and it can take the alias back.

An analysis reads one source at one commit. To read a different branch, tag or commit for a single source, use `--ref`:

```bash
loomctl analyze acme-shop --source web --ref feature/checkout
```

Loomplane never stores a project-wide graph. It composes one on demand from the newest successful analysis of each source: IDs are qualified by alias, a source's directory filters what it contributes, resources of the same kind merge, and a dependency one repository declares on a package another provides becomes an edge between them. See [Repository discovery](/docs/concepts/repository-discovery).

## Environments

Every project starts with `production` and `preview`, and you can add more through the dashboard or the API. A plan is for one environment, and each manifest field's `environments` override applies only there.

```yaml
services:
  web:
    source: apps/web
    environments:
      preview:
        enabled: false
```

Setting `enabled: false` in an environment leaves that service, resource or gateway out, and removes it if it was deployed. Deleting an environment deletes its variables with it.

Each environment uses one connection per cloud, shared by its services and resources. With one ready account, Loomplane picks it for you. With several, you choose, and the choice is saved on the server so the dashboard, the CLI and the API all plan with it. If you want an environment's services somewhere else, see [Adopting and moving services](/docs/clouds/adopting-and-moving).

## What an environment remembers

Loomplane records the commit of each source that's deployed to each environment. That is how a scoped plan works: if you plan with `--scope web`, only the `web` repository moves, and every other source stays at the commit that's already deployed.

```bash
loomctl plan acme-shop --env production --scope web
```

pages.title: Promotion and rollback
pages.description: Promote what staging runs to production, roll an environment back to its previous release, and let Loomplane watch a release after it deploys.
pages.text:
Three things sit on top of an ordinary release. A promotion deploys to one environment exactly what another environment already runs. A rollback plans an environment back to the release before its current one. And a post-deploy watch keeps judging a release for a while after it goes live, so a bad one can be rolled back without anybody staring at a graph.

All three are plans. Nothing deploys until someone approves, with one exception that's covered under [automatic rollback](#automatic-rollback).

## Promote staging to production

```bash
loomctl promote my-project
loomctl promote my-project --from staging --to production --scope web
loomctl approve <plan-id>
```

`--from` defaults to `staging` and `--to` to `production`. `loomctl plan my-project --env production --from staging` does the same thing. In the dashboard, open Deployments and choose Promote.

The plan pins what the source environment runs, read in one snapshot. Each repository moves to the commit and analysis its last successful deployment there recorded, with the root and branch that deployment used. Repositories you leave out with `--scope` stay at what the target already runs, and a repository the source doesn't run is held the same way. If a held repository has never been deployed to the target, the plan is refused and tells you to add it to the scope.

A promotion also uses the manifest revision the source environment last deployed with, not the latest one. If you've saved a newer manifest since, the plan carries a `newer-manifest` warning that names both revisions: deploy the new one to staging first if you want it in production. When the source never recorded a revision, the plan uses the latest and warns about that instead.

A repository whose commit nothing has analyzed (the source runs it, but the deployment didn't record an analysis) gets an analysis queued when you ask for the promotion. The plan stays in planning until that finishes, and gives up with the analysis error after about six minutes. When the source recorded no release of a repository and its services run it at more than one commit, the plan is refused and names the commits: deploy one commit of it there first.

You approve a promotion like any plan. If staging releases again before you approve, what the plan would reuse can change, and the approval comes back stale.

### Which images a promotion reuses

Where it can, a promotion deploys the image staging already built, named by its digest, so production runs the bytes you tested and nothing builds twice. The plan lists a choice for every service it builds, reused or not, with the reason.

| Target | Reuses the image | Builds again when |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Run, ECS Fargate | Yes | The conditions below don't hold, or the image sits in another Google Cloud project or region, or another AWS account or region |
| Azure Container Apps | Yes | The conditions below don't hold, or the image is in another Azure container registry (the region doesn't matter) |
| Your own servers, Kubernetes | Yes | The conditions below don't hold, or the target pushes to a different registry, or staging built on its server without one |
| Render, Vercel | No | Always. They build each deployment from the commit themselves |
| DigitalOcean App Platform | No | Always. App Platform builds the newest commit of its branch, and the reason says a promotion only works while that's still the commit you're promoting |

The conditions, for the first three rows: staging ran the same commit of the service on the same kind of target, built for the same architecture, from the same build inputs (source, Dockerfile, build context, ecosystem, build command and start command), and recorded the image by digest. A release that predates digest-pinned images, or one whose connection can't read digests, has only a tag, so it builds again.

A gateway, a catalog service and a service pinned to an existing image have nothing built from a repository, so there's nothing to reuse. If the target environment's release strategy is `canary`, a reused image is what the canary ramps.

### The staging soak

A promotion plan shows how long the source environment has run exactly the commits you're about to ship, and whether it ran them healthily. The Plan tab in the dashboard has it under Source environment, and `loomctl promote` prints it before the approve line:

```text
Soak: staging has run these commits for 2h30m, healthy
```

The clock starts when the last of the commits was deployed to the source. Every service built from those commits is judged over that stretch, up to the last 24 hours, with the target environment's thresholds. A soak has no baseline to compare against, so only two of them count: the error ceiling (`error_rate`) and `min_requests`. The soak is healthy when every one of those services passes.

Unverified means missing evidence. A soak is unverified when the source runs the commits but a service had too little traffic to judge, its cloud reports no metrics to Loomplane, or they've been running for less than a few minutes. A service that exceeded the error ceiling is evidence, so that's reported as not healthy and isn't unverified. If the source doesn't run the commits at all, the line says so and why.

The soak informs your decision and nothing else. It never blocks an approval.

## Roll back an environment

```bash
loomctl rollback my-project --env production --reason "checkout 500s after release"
loomctl approve <plan-id>
```

The reason is required, up to 2,000 characters, and goes in the audit trail and in front of whoever approves. Before it plans, `loomctl rollback` prints which deployment it undoes and which it restores, with each repository's commits. In the dashboard, open the environment's newest deployment and choose Roll back.

A rollback is a normal plan. A developer creates it, an admin approves it, it expires if nobody decides, and it shows up in `loomctl plans` beside everything else. What's different is what it contains.

### What it restores

The previous release is the newest successful deployment of that environment that finished before the one you're undoing started. A rollback's own deployment counts, because it restored a state somebody approved. Cloud syncs and standalone catalog plans don't count, since they change where infrastructure runs and not the application.

A release that an earlier rollback undid is skipped, and so is one whose rollback failed. Say production ran R1, then R2, then R3. Rolling back R3 restores R2. If R2's rollback had failed before R3 shipped, rolling back R3 skips R2 and restores R1. To go to a release that was skipped, promote or deploy it explicitly.

The rollback pins every repository to the commits that release deployed, all of them moving, and uses the manifest revision it deployed with. Services return to that release's image under the same rules as a promotion (the table above), except on DigitalOcean App Platform, where a rollback goes back to the App Platform deployment Loomplane recorded for that release. If there is no such deployment, it predates the record, it ran another commit, or the release you're undoing moved the service off App Platform, the plan has a problem and can't be approved.

### What it leaves alone

A rollback only reverts services' code and settings. It never deletes, replaces or reverts a data-bearing resource, so a database keeps the rows and the schema the bad release left it with.

In practice: an update or replacement of a service that holds no data goes back. Anything else the restore would have done stays as the bad release left it, and the plan lists it under Left in place with the reason. That covers every resource (a bucket, a cache, a database), a service the release created, a service it removed, and any service that runs a catalog recipe or a component with storage.

If a service you're restoring links to a resource the release you're undoing removed, the plan has a problem called `rollback-needs-resource`. A rollback never recreates a resource, so it can't bring that service back. Release a version that creates the resource instead.

A rollback goes back all at once. It never ramps as a canary, even in an environment whose strategy is `canary`, and it arms no watch.

### When it's refused

| Situation | What you do |
|---|---|
| A deployment is running or paused in the environment | Wait for it, or cancel it |
| The environment has no earlier successful release | Nothing to restore. Deploy or promote |
| The current release is a rollback | Deploy or promote to move forward. Rolling a rollback back would only bring back the release it undid |
| The current release is a rollback that failed | Retry that rollback deployment, which finishes the move it was approved for |
| The newest deployment's canary already returned to the baseline | Nothing to roll back |
| A canary's revert or promotion failed | Fix the traffic split from the deployment, then roll back |
| You named a deployment that isn't the newest | Roll back the newest first. Naming an older one would undo every release after it |
| A release still holds a route handoff | Finish the handoff. The rollback waits for it like any other plan |

## Watch a release after it deploys

A canary judges a release while it ramps. The post-deploy watch judges it afterward, from the same cloud monitoring and with the same thresholds, and rolls it back if a service breaches them.

### Turn it on

The watch is a setting of the environment's `release` block in `loomplane.yaml`:

```yaml
environments:
  production:
    release:
      strategy: direct
      watch: 30m
      thresholds:
        error_rate: 1%
```

`watch` is a duration in whole minutes, up to `24h`. Leave it out and a `canary` or `blue_green` environment is watched for 15 minutes while a `direct` one isn't watched at all. `watch: "0"` turns it off. The plan pins the watch with the rest of the release block, so changing it gives you a new revision to approve. An environment with no `release` block deploys exactly as it always has: no watch is armed.

### What gets watched

The watch starts when a deployment finishes successfully, and covers the services that release created, updated or replaced. It skips the services a canary ramped, because the canary already judged them. It isn't armed for a rollback, a Cloud sync, a standalone catalog plan, a failed deployment, a canary that didn't promote, or a release that changed no service.

A service can be watched when its cloud reports both requests and errors to Loomplane, which today means Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Azure Container Apps and Render (the Requests and 5xx columns in the [canary table](/docs/concepts/canary-releases#where-canaries-run)). Services on your own servers and clusters report to your own monitoring, which Loomplane doesn't read. Vercel and DigitalOcean report nothing it can use. Each service the watch can't judge is listed with the reason, and it leaves the release unverified. If none of the changed services can be watched, the watch settles as inconclusive straight away.

The first reading comes about four minutes after the release finishes, because cloud monitoring reports a few minutes late. After that the watch checks every minute. It reads the service's health since the release finished and compares it with the same length of time before the deployment started. A service the release created or moved has no history, so it's judged on the thresholds alone.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `watching` | The window is still open or the readings aren't decisive yet |
| `passed` | Every watched service passed through the whole window |
| `inconclusive` | The watch couldn't decide by 15 minutes after its window ended, usually from too little traffic. The release is unverified and nothing is rolled back |
| `superseded` | A newer release replaced this one before the watch finished |
| `rolling_back` | A service breached, and the rollback is being planned, approved or deployed |
| `rolled_back` | The rollback deployment succeeded |
| `rollback_blocked` | The rollback couldn't go ahead on its own, and the watch says why |
| `rollback_failed` | The rollback deployment failed, was cancelled or never started |

A breach doesn't wait for the window to end. One failing service is enough.

Unverified means missing evidence, and it never goes back to false. A release is unverified when a changed service wasn't watched, when the watch settled inconclusive, or when a newer release superseded the watch before it could judge. The release may well be fine, but nobody has the readings to say so, and that's worth a look from you.

A newer release supersedes the watch if it starts while the watch is open, or if it changes a service the watch is judging. The watch stops and settles `superseded`. It doesn't roll back, because rolling back the older release would undo the newer one too. The same holds once a rollback is planned: if you plan the environment again before it deploys, or a newer release deploys while the rollback waits behind a Cloud sync, the rollback deploys nothing and the watch settles `superseded`.

### Automatic rollback

When a service breaches, Loomplane plans the rollback of that release, using the same rules as a manual one, and approves it itself. The plan's reason names the service and what it measured. The plan says it was started by Loomplane automation, and so does every audit entry it makes: the breach (`release_watch.breach`), the approval (`plan.approve`, marked automatic) and the settled watch (`release_watch.settle`).

This is the one place a plan is approved without a person, and the rules around it are narrow. Loomplane automation holds a role that can read a project, create deployments and approve them, but the planning service lets it create and approve only a rollback that a watch started. Every other plan, and every promotion or manual rollback, refuses it, and no session or API key ever acts as it. If Loomplane automation can't create or approve the rollback, for example because its role assignment failed, the watch settles `rollback_blocked`, and the rollback plan, if there is one, stays ready for a person to approve.

To turn automatic rollback off, turn the watch off for that environment in the manifest: set `release.watch: "0"`, use the `direct` strategy without a `watch`, or leave out the `release` block. Nothing is watched there, so nothing rolls back on its own, and every release there is unverified. The change goes through a plan like any other, so it's reviewed. Removing the `loomplane-automation` assignment in Warden doesn't last: Loomplane writes it back the next time it starts.

Planning can also refuse for good, for the reasons in [When it's refused](#when-its-refused), and then the watch settles `rollback_blocked` with the reason. If the rollback plan never finishes planning, or its deployment never starts within an hour, the watch gives up and settles `rollback_failed`. You can find the plan from the watch, and from there you decide.

## Where to see it

On a deployment's page, a Release watch panel shows the status, each watched service's verdict, the services it couldn't watch and why, and the rollback plan if it breached. Roll back sits beside Retry on a deployment that has finished, is the newest in its environment and isn't a rollback itself. The dialog shows what the rollback restores and asks for a reason, and a refusal from the server appears there in plain text.

From a terminal, `loomctl deployment <id>` prints a `Watch:` section, and `loomctl promote` prints the `Soak:` line. An agent reads the watch with `get_release_watch`, and can plan a rollback with `create_rollback` when you start the MCP server with `--allow-deploy`. A person still approves it. See [loomctl](/docs/reference/loomctl), [MCP server](/docs/agents/mcp-server) and the [HTTP API](/docs/reference/http-api).

pages.title: Repository discovery
pages.description: How Loomplane reads a repository to find services and backends without running anything from it.
pages.text:
Analyze a repository and you get its application graph: services, the packages they share, and the databases and caches they need. Loomplane reads manifests and source code without running a build, downloading dependencies or executing anything from the checkout. Every service and backend it reports comes with the file and line it was read from.

Analysis runs in `loomplane-worker`, a separate process. A checkout is one repository's tarball at one commit, extracted under hard limits on size and file count. Only regular files are written, nothing lands outside the checkout, and dependency and build output directories are skipped. The worker deletes the directory afterward.

## What it detects

| Ecosystem | What Loomplane reads |
|---|---|
| Go | `go.work`, every `go.mod`, each main package, and the frameworks and drivers it reaches by following imports through the workspace |
| Rust | Cargo workspaces and member globs, binaries the way Cargo finds them, path and workspace dependencies, and features (which database `sqlx` speaks) |
| Node | npm, Yarn, pnpm and Bun workspaces, Turborepo, Nx and Lerna. A framework counts only when the package is an app built on it, so a library that imports Next.js stays a library. Prisma's provider comes from its schema |
| Python | `pyproject.toml`, `requirements.txt`, Pipfile and uv workspaces. Each Procfile process is a service, and so is a Celery app beside a web app |
| JVM | Maven, and Gradle (with version catalogs, subprojects, `allprojects` blocks and convention plugins in `buildSrc` or `build-logic`) |
| Containers | Dockerfiles (ports, base image, which binary a build step builds) and Compose files (backing services, build contexts) |

A Gradle script that works out its dependencies in a loop or a condition can't be read without running it, and analysis never does that. Declare those dependencies plainly, or confirm them in the manifest.

Resources found only from a driver in a dependency list are marked to confirm before anything provisions them. A Go command that shares a server's packages can read as a tool, flagged for you to confirm.

## Examples and development helpers

The default graph excludes executables under `example`, `examples`, `sample`, `samples`, `fixture`, `fixtures`, `testdata`, `tests` and `__tests__` directories. It also excludes `scripts`, `tools`, `tooling`, `generators`, `codegen` and `generated`. The check applies to each path segment, across languages and container images.

You can still deploy an example. Set the source's root to that directory, or declare the executable as a Forge app or build target. Selecting `examples/polyglot` includes that application, though nested test-data directories stay excluded until you select them too.

Loomplane keeps the full analysis and applies selection when it composes the project graph. A selected app keeps the shared libraries outside its root, along with their backend requirements, and excluded services contribute nothing. The graph's analysis notes explain what was left out.

A Dockerfile whose missing source inputs exist only as `.txt`, `.tmpl`, `.tpl` or `.template` files is a generator template. It produces a note instead of an application image.

## Forge applications

Loomplane reads `.forge.yaml` and `.forge.yml` project layouts, workspace globs, custom application paths and `build.apps` targets. An app manifest supplies the name and role:

```yaml
app:
  name: analysis-worker
  type: worker
```

Use `web`, `server` or `api` for an HTTP service, `worker` for background work and `cli` for a command-line tool. A declared worker stays a worker even when it exposes health HTTP. CLI entries show up for inspection but aren't deployable.

Go discovery follows referenced local functions, callbacks, constructors and types, so separate app constructors in one package can have different framework and backend findings. Imports alone are weaker evidence than an explicit driver option or configuration.

## Backend evidence

Registered extension constructors and literal driver options, such as `grove.WithDSN("postgres", ...)`, contribute backend evidence to the app that reaches them. Scoped configuration covers Grove databases and KV stores, cache, queue, Trove stores, events and search backends.

Configuration is read in this order: `config/<app>.yaml` (or `.yml`), then the app's own `config.yaml`, then shared project defaults for registered extensions. An app-specific embedded backend or disabled extension overrides the shared default. In-memory and local-file backends don't ask for managed infrastructure.

Driver evidence records the backend and the source line, never the credentials or connection string. Malformed configuration and unsupported drivers produce notes. Dynamic factories, interface dispatch, environment-dependent selection and runtime plugins may need an explicit declaration, because analysis never evaluates them to guess.

## Re-analysis on push

With the GitHub App's webhook on, a push to a repository's default branch re-analyzes every source tracking it, so your next plan has the new commit without anyone pressing Analyze. [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories) covers the setup.

## Vite React Server Components

Loomplane recognizes `@vitejs/plugin-rsc` apps as `vite-rsc` web apps when the package has a Vite config or runs Vite in its scripts. You do not need an `index.html`. A dependency without app configuration or scripts stays library evidence.

For dynamic RSC, provide a production `start` script or a Dockerfile. Your server must serve the client assets and the RSC/SSR output from the same build, listen on `0.0.0.0`, and respect the configured port. Use `NODE_ENV=production` for production builds. The plugin's `vite preview` command is for previewing a build; define your production server explicitly.

The existing Node build paths and container targets handle these applications. Remote SSH and Kubernetes source builds require a Dockerfile, as they do for other Node apps. Dynamic deployment to Vercel is blocked until an adapter can package the server correctly. If your app generates all its pages at build time, explicitly select `kind: static-site` and verify the target's publish-directory convention.

The repository includes a complete Node server and Dockerfile under `examples/vite-rsc`. Detection reads files without executing your Vite config.

pages.title: Teams
pages.description: Give a group of people one role on a project or the whole workspace, and name the team that hears about a project's requests.
pages.text:
A team is a named group of workspace members. It carries a role on one project or on the whole workspace, and a project can name it as the team responsible for that project. Use one when the people who ship a service aren't the people who should be admins everywhere.

## Set one up

Admins and owners manage teams. That means anyone holding `member:manage`. Everyone else in the workspace can open **Settings, Teams** and read every team, its members and its roles, but can't change any of it.

1. Open **Settings, Teams** and choose **Create team**. Give it a name and a short description. The description matters if you run the [AI agent](/docs/ai), because the agent reads it to pick a team for a request.
2. Add members. The picker lists people already in the workspace, so invite someone first if they aren't.
3. Give the team a role. Pick viewer, developer or admin, then pick **Whole workspace** or one project.

From a terminal, the same steps look like this:

```bash
loomctl teams create Payments --description "Owns checkout and billing"
loomctl teams add payments grace@example.com
loomctl teams grant payments developer --project checkout-api
```

See [loomctl](/docs/reference/loomctl#teams) for every command.

## Roles a team can give

A team gives viewer, developer or admin. It never gives owner. A team has at most one role per scope, so setting a second role on the same project replaces the first.

You can only give a role at or below your own. If your effective role is admin, you can't give a team owner, and you can't change a team whose role is above yours.

## How a team's role reaches a person

Loomplane copies a team's role onto each member as an ordinary role of their own. Nothing is checked at the team level when someone acts. That's why a team's role behaves exactly like a direct one, for the dashboard, for API keys and for an agent acting on someone's behalf.

A person's effective role is the highest of their own and their teams'. Say Grace is a viewer in the workspace, and Payments gives her developer on `checkout-api`. On that project she's a developer. Everywhere else she's still a viewer.

A role on a project only counts on that project. It doesn't open workspace settings, other projects, members or clouds. One project role does carry more weight than you might expect, though: an **admin** role on a project lets its members delete that project, manage its secrets and choose its cloud connection.

The Members page shows each person's own role, the teams they're in, and a line for every team role above their own, such as "Admin on checkout-api through Payments".

Project pages ask the API what you can do on that project, so a button appears when a team gives you the right even though your workspace role doesn't. `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/permissions` returns the answer.

## Leaving the workspace

When someone leaves or is removed, their team memberships go and so do their team roles. If they're invited back, they start from their invitation role, with no teams.

## A project's responsible team

Open a project's **Settings** tab and use the **Responsible team** field, or run `loomctl projects team checkout-api payments`. Anyone with `project:update` on that project can set it, which includes a developer and anyone a team grants that right on the project. Clear it with **None** or `loomctl projects team checkout-api --none`. Deleting the team clears it too.

The responsible team only decides who is told. It gives its members no rights on the project. Give the team a role as well if you want them to act.

### Where the agent sends requests

If you turn the AI agent on, the agent has to ask a person for things now and then: a secret, an answer, a connection. It picks who to ask in this order.

1. A team it names itself, with a reason that the request shows. The team must exist and have at least one member.
2. The project's responsible team, if it has members.
3. Workspace admins.

If a team it names, or the project's team, is empty or doesn't exist, the request falls through to the next choice and says why. A request always reaches someone. Every member of the team gets the notice under their own notification preferences, and any member who has the permission can act on it. The first to act settles it.

A request to approve a plan always goes to the project's team and never to a team the agent picked. Teams work the same whether the agent is on or off. Only the routing needs it.

## Things to know

**Loomplane is the only writer of a person's Warden roles.** If you change someone's roles in Warden's console, Loomplane puts them back on the next sync, which runs when a team or member changes and at least once a minute. Make the change in Loomplane.

**authsome's own team routes are switched off.** Requests to `/authsome/v1/orgs/{id}/teams` answer 404, so there's only one kind of team. Use `/api/v1/teams`.

**The sync lock uses extra database connections.** Each replica keeps a separate pool of up to 4 connections for the lock that keeps one person's sync from running twice at once. Leave `max_connections` headroom for 4 per replica, on top of `database.pool_size`.

## API

| Method and path | What it does | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/teams`, `GET /api/v1/teams/{id}` | Read teams, with members and roles | `member:read` |
| `POST /api/v1/teams` | Create a team | `member:manage` |
| `PATCH /api/v1/teams/{id}` | Rename a team or change its description | `member:manage` |
| `DELETE /api/v1/teams/{id}` | Delete a team | `member:manage` |
| `PUT` or `DELETE /api/v1/teams/{id}/members/{user_id}` | Add or remove a member | `member:manage` |
| `PUT /api/v1/teams/{id}/grants` | Set the team's role on a project, or the workspace if `project_id` is empty | `member:manage`, at or below your own role |
| `DELETE /api/v1/teams/{id}/grants/{grant_id}` | Remove a role | `member:manage` |
| `PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/team` | Set the responsible team, or clear it with `{"team_id": null}` | `project:update` on the project |
| `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/permissions` | What you may do on one project | `project:read` on the project |

Every change is in the [audit trail](/docs/concepts/organizations-and-roles#the-audit-trail).

pages.title: The manifest
pages.description: loomplane.yaml says what your application deploys, where, and what it needs.
pages.text:
`loomplane.yaml` is the file a plan is made from. Loomplane drafts one from your analysis, you review it, and each save becomes a new revision. A plan always names the revision it was made from.

```bash
loomctl manifest my-project --draft     # print a draft from the latest analysis
loomctl manifest save my-project -f loomplane.yaml
loomctl manifest my-project             # print the saved one
```

Nothing in the manifest is Forge, or Go. Point a YAML language server at `pkg/manifest/schema.json` (its `$id` is `https://loomplane.dev/schemas/loomplane.json`) and you get completion and checks as you type. A manifest that doesn't parse is refused with every problem and its line.

## A complete example

```yaml title="loomplane.yaml"
version: 1

defaults:
  provider: cloud-run
  region: us-central1

services:
  api:
    source: go:services/api
    needs: [db, cache]
    scale: { min: 1, max: 5 }
    size: { cpu: 1, memory: 512 }
  worker:
    source: services/worker/cmd/worker
    provider: ecs-fargate
    needs: [api]
  web:
    source: apps/web
    provider: vercel
    needs: [api]
    environments:
      preview:
        enabled: false

resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    provider: cloud-sql
    version: "17"
  cache:
    kind: redis
    provider: memorystore

gateways:
  edge:
    routes:
      - { path: /api, to: api, strip_prefix: true }
      - { path: /, to: web }

ignore:
  resources: [kafka]
```

The five top-level sections are `services`, `resources`, `gateways`, `links` and `ignore`, with `defaults` and `held` for settings that apply across them. [The reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml) lists every field.

## Services, resources and gateways

A service is something you run. A resource is a backing service such as Postgres or Redis. A gateway puts one public address in front of several services. Names are lower case letters, digits and hyphens, start with a letter, and run to 40 characters at most. They're how everything refers to everything else, so a resource can't share a service's name.

`needs` is how you wire things together. A service that lists a resource or another service gets an address for it in a variable, and it deploys after it. A Postgres resource arrives as `DATABASE_URL`, a Redis as `REDIS_URL`, and another service as its name in capitals plus `_URL` (`API_URL`). A variable you set yourself wins, so you can point a service somewhere else.

## Choosing where things run

You can name a `provider` and `region` on any service, resource or gateway, or set `defaults` for all of them. A default region only comes with the default provider: a service that names another provider doesn't take it along.

In the dashboard, the Deployment targets panel on the Deploy tab sets provider, region and enabled status for each entry in the selected environment. It only offers providers that support the workload, which is why Vercel isn't offered for a worker. Saving a placement creates a manifest revision and preserves your comments, source paths and dependencies. It doesn't provision anything, because approval is what starts a deployment.

For larger setups, give your targets names or tags in an organization Cloud and refer to them from the manifest with `cloud_target` or `cloud_tags`. See [Cloud targets](/docs/clouds/cloud-targets).

## Environments and overrides

Services, resources and gateways accept an `environments` map that overrides `provider`, `region` or `enabled` for one environment. A service also takes the other settings (scale, size, port and so on) there. It can't override `source`, `kind`, `build`, `needs` or `need_options`.

An `environments.<name>.release` block sets how that environment's releases go live: all at once, blue/green or as a canary with its steps, hold and health thresholds. See [Canary releases](/docs/concepts/canary-releases) and the [loomplane.yaml reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml#environments).

## Version 2

Existing workflows use `version: 1`, and generated manifests do too. Version 2 adds an optional `federation` section that records federation proposals. Its plans stay blocked until the destination agents, network drivers and policy enforcement pass qualification.

  Federation is being built and isn't ready for production. Writing a version 2 manifest doesn't make private traffic between clouds available, and the editor never upgrades a file for you.

pages.title: Variables and secrets
pages.description: How variables layer from organization to service, how secrets are stored, and how they reach a running service.
pages.text:
