Variables are the environment a service runs with. You set them in layers, and each key takes its value from the most specific layer that sets it.

## Layers

From least to most specific:

1. Organization, every environment
2. Organization, one environment
3. Project, every environment
4. Project, one environment
5. Service, every environment
6. Service, one environment

So a service-level `LOG_LEVEL` for `production` beats a project-wide one, which beats the organization's. Setting a key that a layer already has for that environment is an error, so edit the existing one instead.

Keys start with a letter or underscore and hold letters, digits and underscores. Organization-wide variables need the admin role. Project and service variables need developer or above.

## Set them

```bash
loomctl vars my-project
loomctl vars set my-project LOG_LEVEL=debug --env preview
loomctl vars set my-project STRIPE_KEY=- --secret --env production
loomctl vars set my-project FEATURE_X=on --service svc:api:go:cmd/server
```

`KEY=-` reads the value from standard input, which keeps a secret out of your shell history. `--env` limits a variable to one environment, and `--service` limits it to one service by its graph ID. In the dashboard, the project's Variables tab does the same, and the organization's settings hold the organization-wide layer.

## Secrets

Mark a variable secret and its value is write-only. Loomplane encrypts it in Vault (AES-256-GCM, versioned) and the API never returns it, to anyone, whatever their role. A database constraint keeps secret values out of the variables table entirely.

When a service deploys, its secrets go to the cloud's own secret store and reach the service by reference, readable by that service's runtime identity only:

| Target | Where secrets go |
|---|---|
| Cloud Run | Secret Manager |
| ECS on Fargate | Secrets Manager |
| Vercel | Sensitive environment variables |
| DigitalOcean App Platform | App Platform secrets |
| Azure Container Apps | App secrets |

They never pass through Ctrl Plane, which stores what it's given as plain JSON. A secret never appears in a task definition, a list response or the CLI's output, and the integration tests check that.

## Addresses Loomplane adds

A service gets a variable for each thing it `needs`. Resource addresses hold credentials, so they're secrets and arrive through the secret store.

| Needs | Variable |
|---|---|
| Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB | `DATABASE_URL` |
| Redis, Valkey | `REDIS_URL` |
| Memcached | `MEMCACHED_SERVERS` |
| MongoDB | `MONGODB_URI` |
| AMQP brokers | `AMQP_URL` |
| Kafka | `KAFKA_BROKERS` |
| NATS | `NATS_URL` |
| Object storage | `STORAGE_URL` |
| Search | `SEARCH_URL` |
| ClickHouse | `CLICKHOUSE_URL` |
| Another service | Its name in capitals plus `_URL`, such as `API_URL` |

When two needs would share a name, each gets its own name's instead, such as `ANALYTICS_URL`. A variable you set yourself wins over a generated one.

MariaDB and Valkey resources used to get their name in capitals plus `_URL` (`DB_URL`). A service deployed that way keeps the old variable beside the new one, and the plan warns you to move off it.

## The secret key

Every key Loomplane needs is derived from `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` with HKDF under a label of its own. That includes Vault's encryption, authsome's tokens and the GitHub install state's signature. Keep the secret key out of your repository and out of your backups. Losing it loses every credential and secret; leaking it along with a database copy exposes them. [The security model](/docs/operations/security-model) has the whole picture.

pages.title: Instance fleets
pages.description: Validate a synthetic Fleet workload and understand the current qualification limits.
pages.text:
Use the Fleet acceptance harness to check your qualification inputs before you
connect a deployment target. You can validate resource limits and run the
synthetic workload locally. Live provisioning through the harness is blocked.

## Run the dry check

From the repository root, run:

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/acceptance/fleets -p 'test_*.py'
python3 tests/acceptance/fleets/run.py \
  --config tests/acceptance/fleets/config.example.json \
  --dry-run
```

The example contains synthetic identifiers and a loopback API address. The runner
doesn't contact that address. You can also supply the configuration path through
`LOOMPLANE_FLEET_ACCEPTANCE_CONFIG`.

Set an explicit organization, fleet, stage, Cloud, region and runtime. Your
configuration must include a positive budget in currency minor units, a duration
limit, and limits for instances, replicas, CPU, memory, storage and buckets. The
runner rejects missing limits, mixed organizations, duplicate instances and
unsupported capabilities. Unknown fields fail validation, which helps catch a
misspelled limit.

The workload contains a shared control service and two independent instances.
Each instance has an API, sidecar, worker, bootstrap job, database adapter and
bucket adapter. Resource demand includes every component, including bootstrap
jobs and the shared control service. The example requests 2,000 CPU millicores,
640 MiB of memory, 2 GiB of database storage and two buckets.

A valid report records `dry_run_validated`. Cost estimates and observed cost stay
`unknown`, and each live check stays `not_run`. The declared budget is a required
input; this offline harness cannot enforce a provider billing cap or establish
that the target has the capabilities you declared.

## Run the synthetic workload

The fixture uses Python's standard library. SQLite stands in for the database and
bucket adapters, with a separate file for each instance. These adapters let you
exercise bootstrap, per-instance reads and writes, queue limits and retries
without connecting a managed data service.

Create a local state directory, print its path, then bootstrap both instances:

```sh
FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
printf '%s\n' "$FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR"
python3 tests/acceptance/fleets/fixture.py --role bootstrap \
  --instance instance-a --state-dir "$FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR"
python3 tests/acceptance/fleets/fixture.py --role bootstrap \
  --instance instance-b --state-dir "$FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR"
```

Supply a distinct synthetic token for each instance through
`LOOMPLANE_FLEET_FIXTURE_TOKEN`. Start the API for one instance in a separate
terminal. Set `FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR` in that terminal to the exact path printed
above. Shell variables do not carry into an independently opened terminal:

```sh
printf 'Fixture directory printed earlier: '
read -r FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR
LOOMPLANE_FLEET_FIXTURE_TOKEN=synthetic-instance-a \
python3 tests/acceptance/fleets/fixture.py --role api \
  --instance instance-a --state-dir "$FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR" --port 8081
```

The server binds to loopback, allows at most eight concurrent handlers, and
closes connections after two seconds without socket activity. You can read `GET /health`, write JSON
`{"value":"sample"}` to `PUT /data/sample` or `PUT /bucket/sample`, and read each
value back with `GET`. Every request requires `Authorization: Bearer` followed by
that instance's token.

Submit work with `PUT /jobs/job-001` and the same JSON body. Run the worker once
to process queued work from the original terminal, where `FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR`
is already set:

```sh
python3 tests/acceptance/fleets/fixture.py --role worker \
  --instance instance-a --state-dir "$FLEET_FIXTURE_DIR"
```

A repeated job ID with the same value replays safely. A changed value fails.
The fixture retains at most 32 jobs and hashes each payload 1,000 times to produce
a bounded CPU signal. Each value is limited to 4,096 bytes, and the data and bucket
adapters together retain at most 64 values per instance.

The `sidecar` role exposes `/health` and `/metrics` using the same instance state.
The `control` role exposes `/health` and a synthetic `/instances` inventory. Both
require a token and reject data writes. Choose a separate port for each process.
These are workload fixture endpoints, not Loomplane's Fleet API.

## Cleanup and evidence

Dry runs create no provider resources. You can inspect a recorded resource list
with `--cleanup-receipt PATH` alongside `--dry-run`. The receipt must match the
configuration's run ID and complete target identity. Every resource must have an
exact ID, matching organization and run ID, and recorded creation ownership.
The runner refuses an unrecorded cleanup ID or a changed target.

Cleanup inspection deletes nothing. Its report lists all residual resource IDs,
identifies retained databases, buckets and volumes, and records
`live_cleanup_adapter_unavailable`. Keep attached data until you have a separately
reviewed retention and recovery decision. Local fixture files remain in your
chosen state directory after the processes stop.

| Check                                          | Evidence available here           |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Configuration and resource bounds              | Offline validation and unit tests |
| Bootstrap and job replay                       | Local SQLite fixture tests        |
| Neighbor credential denial                     | Local HTTP fixture tests          |
| Namespace and managed data isolation           | No live evidence                  |
| Fleet lifecycle, scaling and release execution | No live harness adapter           |
| Metadata scale at 10, 100 and 1,000 instances  | Not measured                      |

The runner returns exit code `0` for a valid dry run, `1` for rejected inputs, and
`2` when valid inputs request unavailable live execution. You still need separate
live qualification before using these results to make a rollout decision.

pages.title: Provider plugins
pages.description: Add a deployment target to Loomplane by writing a small HTTP service in Go, or in any language that speaks the protocol.
pages.text:
A provider is a deployment target: somewhere Loomplane can run a service or provision a resource. Loomplane ships with many (see the [Clouds overview](/docs/clouds)), and you can add your own without changing Loomplane.

A plugin is a small HTTP service. Loomplane reads its description at startup and puts it in the catalog next to the built-in targets, so manifests can name it, plans check against what it says it runs, and deployments, retries and drift checks drive it like any other. It runs on your infrastructure, so the credential it deploys with never leaves it, apart from the copy Loomplane keeps in Vault.

## A provider in Go

`pkg/provider/sdk` is the Go side of the protocol. You implement five methods and hand the result to `sdk.Handler`:

```go
type Provider interface {
	Describe() provider.Provider
	Check(ctx context.Context, c sdk.Credential) (*sdk.Account, error)
	Apply(ctx context.Context, job *sdk.Job) (*sdk.Outcome, error)
	Remove(ctx context.Context, job *sdk.Job) error
	Observe(ctx context.Context, t *sdk.Target) (*sdk.Observation, error)
}
```

```go
http.ListenAndServe(":9100", sdk.Handler(myProvider, os.Getenv("PLUGIN_TOKEN")))
```

`examples/provider-plugin` is a working one, a static site host in about 270 lines. Read it first, since it's the shortest way to a provider that works.

`Describe` returns the catalog entry: a name manifests use (`provider: static-host`), what it runs (`Runs`, by workload: `http-service`, `web-app`, `static-site`, `worker`), what it provisions (`Provisions`, by resource kind such as `postgres` or `redis`), its regions, and the `Cloud` its connections are for. Implement `sdk.Connector` too and the dashboard asks for a credential in your words, with the settings you list.

`Check` decides whether a credential works. You get what someone pasted under Integrations and the settings they chose. Return the account it acts as, details safe to show, and anything it's missing. A credential the cloud refused is an error wrapping `sdk.ErrRejected`, and Loomplane tells the person and never stores it. Any other error means the cloud couldn't be asked, and they can try again.

`Apply` makes a service or resource exist as the job describes. A service's job has its source (`job.Source()`, a tarball of the repository at its commit with one top-level directory, and that commit as `job.Commit`), the path of its entrypoint, its Dockerfile and build directory if it has one (`Context`, from the repository root), its port, whether it's public, its size and scale, and its variables, with the secret ones listed so you can put them in your cloud's secret store. A resource's job has its kind and version and no commit. A gateway's has no commit either, and its source is the program Loomplane generates for its routes.

Return an `ExternalID` you'll recognize later, a `URL` for a public service, a `Revision` that drift checks compare with, and for a resource an `Address` (a database URL, say). Loomplane keeps the address in Vault and hands it, as a secret, to the services that need the resource.

`Remove` deletes what a binding names, with the credential of the connection that deployed it, even when the environment deploys with another one now. Something already gone isn't an error. You also get a `Remove` for what a service or resource ran as before it moved to another provider, region or connection, once the new one is up. If that fails, later deployments of the action send it again, so it can arrive long after the move.

`Observe` reads what's live without changing anything. Return `Exists: false` when it's gone, and the live `Revision`. The drift check calls it on a schedule.

## Run it

Add the plugin to Loomplane's configuration:

```yaml title="config.local.yaml"
providers:
  plugins:
    - url: http://static-host:9100
      token: "${STATIC_HOST_PLUGIN_TOKEN}"
```

The token is a shared secret between Loomplane and the plugin, and `sdk.Handler` refuses any request without it. Loomplane describes every plugin when it starts and won't start if one doesn't answer or speaks another protocol version, because it would otherwise accept plans it can't carry out. A plugin that stops answering later makes `/_/health` unhealthy within one check interval.

Then connect the plugin's cloud under Integrations and use it in `loomplane.yaml`:

```yaml
services:
  docs:
    source: apps/docs
    provider: static-host
```

## Rules a provider has to follow

`Apply`, `Remove` and `Observe` must be idempotent. A failed deployment can be retried from the step that failed, Loomplane can restart in the middle of one, and a plugin that restarts loses its operations, so the same job can arrive more than once. `job.Key` is the same for every attempt at the same action. Use it, or names derived from the job, so a second attempt finds what the first made and converges on it.

Long work should checkpoint. `job.Checkpoint(data)` saves something a retry gets back as `job.Resume`, such as a build's ID or an operation name. `job.Progress(message)` shows on the deployment's page what the step is doing.

Never run the repository's code on the plugin's machine unless that machine is meant for it. Build on your cloud's builder, the way the built-in targets use Cloud Build and CodeBuild.

Provider plugins are trusted with the credentials of the cloud they deploy to, so only configure ones you run or trust.

## Build logs

To opt a Go plugin into build logs, implement `sdk.OperationLogger` with `OperationLogs() bool` returning true and call `job.Log(stream, message)`. The handler serves bounded pages at `/v1/operations/{id}/logs`. Older plugins can keep using progress callbacks. A plugin restart or retention loss produces a gap, and Loomplane doesn't pretend the older lines are complete.

## The protocol

You don't need Go. A plugin in any language that answers these requests as JSON, with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every request, is a provider.

| Request | Answer |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/describe` | `{"protocol": "loomplane.provider/v1", "provider": {...}, "connection": {...}}` |
| `POST /v1/check` with `{"secret": base64, "settings": {...}}` | `{"account", "details", "missing"}`, or 422 `{"error", "rejected": true}` |
| `HEAD /v1/sources/{id}` | 200 if you have that source, 404 if not |
| `PUT /v1/sources/{id}` with the gzipped tarball | 204 |
| `POST /v1/operations` with `{"kind": "apply" or "remove", "job": {...}, "source": id}` | 202 and the operation |
| `GET /v1/operations/{id}` | `{"id", "status": "running", "succeeded" or "failed", "progress", "checkpoint", "outcome", "error"}` |
| `POST /v1/observe` with a target | `{"exists", "revision"}` |

Apply and Remove run as operations because builds and databases take minutes. Loomplane starts one, then reads it until it's done. Starting the same job while it's still running should return the running operation. An operation you no longer have is a 404, and Loomplane starts it again from the last checkpoint. `pkg/provider/sdk/protocol.go` has every type.

## Test it

`internal/plugins` has the client Loomplane uses, and its tests run it against `sdk.Handler` with a fake provider, which is the quickest check that a provider speaks the protocol. `tests/integration/plugin_test.go` goes further: it connects the example's cloud, then plans, deploys, re-plans and removes a site through a running Loomplane.

pages.title: Bitbucket repositories
pages.description: Create a Bitbucket OAuth consumer once, connect workspaces to your organization, and see what a Bitbucket token can read.
pages.text:
Loomplane reads public Bitbucket Cloud repositories with no setup. A source is written `bitbucket.org/<workspace>/<repo>`, and you can paste the repository's URL wherever Loomplane asks for one. To read private repositories you create an OAuth consumer once for the whole instance, and your organization's owners and admins connect their workspaces to it. Bitbucket Data Center and Server aren't supported.

## Create the OAuth consumer

In Bitbucket, open a workspace's **Settings**, choose **OAuth consumers**, then **Add consumer**. It can live under any workspace, including one your organization will never connect.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Anything, such as Loomplane |
| Callback URL | `<public_url>/integrations/bitbucket/callback` |
| Permissions: Account | Read |
| Permissions: Repositories | Read |
| Permissions: Webhooks | Read and write |
| Everything else | No access |

Save it, then open the consumer to copy its Key and Secret.

Account Read is how Loomplane learns who signed in and checks they belong to the workspace. Repositories Read is the only access to code. Webhooks is for push events, which the Webhooks section covers. Loomplane never asks for write access to your code.

## Configure Loomplane

Set both variables for `loomplane` and `loomplane-worker`, and keep the secret out of any file you commit:

```bash
LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_ID=<the consumer's key>
LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_SECRET=<the consumer's secret>
```

Set both or neither. Loomplane refuses to start with only one. With neither, Bitbucket keeps working for public repositories, and connecting a workspace is refused with a message saying there's no consumer. Values Bitbucket turns down don't stop Loomplane starting. You still get public repositories, but not private ones until you fix them, as [Revoking access](#revoking-access) explains. The [configuration reference](/docs/reference/configuration) lists `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_API_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_WEB_URL` too, which you'd change only to point at a test double.

## Connect a workspace

An owner or admin opens **Integrations**, finds the Bitbucket card, types the workspace's slug (the `acme` in `bitbucket.org/acme`) and chooses **Connect workspace**. Bitbucket asks them to approve the consumer and sends them back to Loomplane. If they've approved it before, Bitbucket skips the question.

Each workspace is its own connection, so a second workspace means repeating the steps. Several organizations can connect the same workspace, and each gets a sign-in of its own. Once it's connected, any project in the organization whose repository sits in that workspace is analyzed with access to it.

## What a Bitbucket token can read

This is the one place Bitbucket is looser than GitHub. A GitHub installation token reads one repository. A Bitbucket OAuth token reads every repository the connecting person can read, in every workspace they belong to, because the consumer's permissions say what kind of access the token has and not which repositories it covers.

We narrow it on our side:

- A token is only used for a repository in the workspace its connection names. A connection to `acme` is never used for `other/repo`, even if the person who connected it can read that too.
- Only the organization's own connections are used, so one organization can't read code through another's.
- A connection that needs connecting again is never used. The repository is read anonymously instead, which works for a public one and fails for a private one.
- When someone connects, Loomplane checks that their Bitbucket account belongs to the workspace they typed. If it doesn't, the sign-in is dropped and nothing is kept.
- Tokens never appear in an API response, a log line, an audit record or an error message.

Access tokens live in memory only and expire within a couple of hours. The one long-lived secret is the refresh token, which is encrypted in Vault under a key derived from your `secret_key`, and disconnecting deletes it. If you want a tighter boundary, connect a workspace with a Bitbucket account that can read only the repositories you want Loomplane to see.

## When a workspace needs connecting again

The card shows Reconnect needed, with the reason, when Bitbucket stops accepting the stored sign-in, when the member who connected the workspace has left your Loomplane organization, when the Bitbucket account that connected it is no longer in the workspace, or when Loomplane can't read the stored sign-in from Vault. Anyone who may connect workspaces fixes it by connecting the same workspace again. It keeps its place, and the new sign-in replaces the old one.

When the member who connected a workspace leaves your organization, Loomplane stops reading as them at the next token renewal, which is within about two hours.

## Webhooks

When you attach a Bitbucket repository to a project, Loomplane adds a webhook to it, so a push to the default branch re-analyzes the project without anyone pressing Analyze. Your organization gets one webhook per repository. A second project on the same repository shares it, and it's removed when the organization's last source on that repository goes.

The webhook only goes in when three things are true:

- Your organization has connected the workspace the repository is in, and the connection is ready.
- The person who connected the workspace is an admin of the repository. Bitbucket only lets a repository admin add a webhook, which is also why the consumer asks for Webhooks Read and write.
- Your `public_url` is https. Loomplane only adds a webhook when it is, so a local instance on `http://localhost:8780` never gets one.

If any of them isn't, the source still attaches and Analyze works as it always has. The Sources list shows **Push re-analysis is off** beside the source, with the reason. Fix what the reason names (connect the workspace, have a repository admin connect it again, or move to an https address), then choose **Turn on**. Loomplane tries to add the webhook again and keeps it if Bitbucket agrees. You need the same role to turn it on as to connect a workspace.

Only pushes to the repository's default branch re-analyze, the same as with GitHub. A source with no branch set follows the default, and a source that names a branch is re-analyzed only while that branch is the default. A push to any other branch, a tag or a deleted branch starts nothing. Loomplane asks Bitbucket which branch is the default each time a push arrives, so if you rename it, the next push already uses the new name.

Each webhook has a secret of its own, derived from your `secret_key` and never stored, and Loomplane checks the signature on every delivery. A delivery only re-analyzes projects in the organization that owns the webhook, even when another organization has projects on the same repository.

Disconnecting a workspace removes every webhook it added, on Bitbucket and in Loomplane. If Bitbucket refuses to remove one (say the account lost admin on the repository), Loomplane stops listening to it anyway and its deliveries get a 404. You can delete it yourself on Bitbucket, under the repository's settings.

## Revoking access

You revoke a workspace one of two ways. In Loomplane, disconnect it on the Integrations card: that removes it from the organization, deletes its refresh token and takes its webhooks off. On Bitbucket, the person who connected it opens their **Personal settings**, finds Loomplane among the apps they've authorized, and revokes it there. The next renewal then fails and the card shows Reconnect needed. Disconnecting doesn't un-approve the consumer on Bitbucket, so if you want it gone on both sides, do both.

Changing the consumer's secret doesn't revoke anyone, but until you give Loomplane the new one, Bitbucket turns down every renewal. A mistyped key or secret does the same. While that lasts, Loomplane can't read private repositories, and an analysis of one fails with "the repository or ref doesn't exist, or it's private and Loomplane can't read it". Public repositories are still read, including the ones in workspaces you've connected. Push re-analysis pauses too. Loomplane renews the workspace's sign-in before it asks Bitbucket for the default branch, so it answers each push with an error, and Bitbucket's retries fail the same way until the consumer is fixed.

Analyses run in `loomplane-worker`, so its log is usually where the warning to check `bitbucket.client_id` and `bitbucket.client_secret` shows up first. The Bitbucket card on Integrations comes from `loomplane`, which only finds out once it renews a sign-in itself: when you list a workspace's repositories, attach a source, try to connect a workspace, or a push arrives. From then on the card says the consumer was turned down. No workspace is marked Reconnect needed. Each keeps its sign-in and its status, so once `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_ID` and `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_SECRET` hold values Bitbucket accepts, the next renewal works and you can read private repositories again without connecting anything.

pages.title: CI with loomctl
pages.description: Use API keys and loomctl in a pipeline to analyze, plan and, if you choose, approve deployments.
pages.text:
Anything the dashboard does, a pipeline can do with `loomctl` or the HTTP API. This page covers the pieces that matter in CI: keys, environment variables, output you can parse and exit codes.

## Make a key for the pipeline

Under **Settings, API keys**, create a key named after the pipeline, such as `github-actions-plan`. Pick the narrowest access that works.

- Read-only is enough to list, read and follow deployments, and to run `loomctl status`. The API refuses anything else.
- A write key acts as you, with your role, and can do whatever that role can. If your role is admin it can approve plans.
- Keys last 90 days by default and at most 366, so put the expiry on your calendar.
- Keys can't make keys.

Treat a key like any credential. Loomplane shows it once and stores only a hash.

## Point loomctl at Loomplane

`loomctl` reads `LOOMPLANE_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY` first. They win over a saved login, which suits CI because nothing is written to disk.

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_URL=https://loomplane.example.com
export LOOMPLANE_API_KEY=lp_live_...
loomctl whoami
```

On a machine you use by hand you don't need a key at all: `loomctl login --url https://loomplane.example.com` signs you in through the browser. If you'd rather save a key there anyway, `loomctl login --url https://loomplane.example.com --key -` reads it from standard input and saves it, readable only by you, in your user config directory. `loomctl logout` removes it. The key keeps working until you revoke it under Settings.

## A plan on every pull request

A good default is to let CI analyze and plan, and leave approval to a person. A developer key is enough.

```yaml title=".github/workflows/plan.yml"
name: loomplane-plan
on:
  pull_request:
jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      LOOMPLANE_URL: ${{ secrets.LOOMPLANE_URL }}
      LOOMPLANE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.LOOMPLANE_API_KEY }}
      LOOMCTL_VERSION: 0.1.0 # the release you run, without the v
    steps:
      - name: Install loomctl
        run: |
          curl -fsSL "https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/releases/download/v${LOOMCTL_VERSION}/loomctl_${LOOMCTL_VERSION}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" | tar -xz loomctl
          sudo mv loomctl /usr/local/bin/
      - name: Analyze and plan
        run: |
          loomctl analyze mono
          loomctl plan mono --env production --json > plan.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: plan
          path: plan.json
```

Check the release page for the exact archive names for your version and platform. On macOS or Linux workstations, `brew install xraph/tap/loomctl` is simpler.

Notes on this:

- `analyze` waits for each analysis to finish and exits nonzero if one fails. Add `--no-wait` to start it and return.
- `plan` waits until the plan is made. `--json` prints the whole plan, including `status`, `actions`, `problems` and `warnings`, which you can feed to a comment bot.
- Don't assume the exit code tells you whether the plan is approvable. Read the plan's `status` and `problems` in the JSON if you want the job to fail on a blocked plan.
- Planning doesn't touch a cloud. It's safe to run on every push.

## Approving from CI

You can approve from a pipeline with an admin's write key, but think twice. The point of an approval is that a person reviewed the exact plan, and the approval names the plan's revision to enforce that.

```bash
loomctl approve <plan-id> --yes --note "Release 14 from CI"
```

`--yes` skips the confirmation. Without a terminal, `approve` fails and tells you to pass `--yes`. The command follows the deployment and exits nonzero if it fails, with a hint to run `loomctl retry <deployment-id>`. Pass `--no-wait` to approve and return.

If what's deployed changed since the plan was made, the plan comes back stale and the command fails with "plan again". Plan again and look at the new plan before you approve it.

A common middle path: CI plans on merge to `main`, posts the plan to chat, and a human runs `loomctl approve` or clicks Approve in the dashboard.

## Useful commands in scripts

```bash
loomctl projects --json
loomctl plans mono --json
loomctl show <plan-id> --json
loomctl deployments mono --json
loomctl deployment <deployment-id> --json
loomctl status mono --json
loomctl reject <plan-id> --note "Superseded"
loomctl vars set mono API_TOKEN=- --secret --env production < token.txt
```

`status --json` is a good post-deploy gate: it lists every binding with its address, commit and drift. Not every command takes `--json`, so run `loomctl <command> --help` to see its flags. [The loomctl reference](/docs/reference/loomctl) lists them all.

## The HTTP API

`loomctl` is a thin client over the API, and `pkg/client` is a typed Go client for it. Every `/api/v1` route takes a session or an API key as a bearer token. See [HTTP API](/docs/reference/http-api).

pages.title: Deploy a monorepo end to end
pages.description: Take a monorepo with a web app, an API and a database from a GitHub URL to running services on Vercel and Google Cloud.
pages.text:
This walk-through deploys a typical monorepo: a Next.js app, a Go API behind it, and a Postgres database the API uses. The web app goes to Vercel, and the API and database go to Google Cloud. Swap in any targets from the [Clouds overview](/docs/clouds). The repository can be your own, or `examples/polyglot` in the Loomplane source, which has the same shape.

You'll need a Loomplane you can sign in to ([Quick start](/docs/quick-start)), a Vercel token, and a Google Cloud service account key with the permissions listed in [Google Cloud](/docs/clouds/google-cloud).


### Create the project and analyze it

Choose **New project** and paste the GitHub URL. Or from the terminal:

```bash
loomctl projects create "Acme shop" --repo acme/shop
loomctl analyze acme-shop
```

When it finishes you get a line like "found 4 services (3 deployable), 2 packages and 1 resources at 3f2c1a9" (your numbers will differ). In the dashboard, open the graph and check each service and database against the files it points at. A resource found only from a driver in a dependency list is marked to confirm.

If Loomplane found something you don't deploy (a demo app, say), leave it out of the manifest. If it found a resource you don't use, list its kind under `ignore.resources` so plans stop asking.


### Draft and edit the manifest

```bash
loomctl manifest acme-shop --draft > loomplane.yaml
```

Edit it so the web app runs on Vercel and the API and database run on Google Cloud:

```yaml title="loomplane.yaml"
version: 1

defaults:
  provider: cloud-run
  region: us-central1

services:
  api:
    source: go:services/api
    needs: [db]
    scale: { min: 1, max: 5 }
    size: { cpu: 1, memory: 512 }
  web:
    source: apps/web
    provider: vercel
    needs: [api]
    environments:
      preview:
        enabled: false

resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
    provider: cloud-sql
    version: "17"
```

`web` needs `api`, so it gets `API_URL`. The API is public here, which a Vercel app on another cloud needs, because a private Cloud Run service only takes calls from the project's own services. `api` needs `db`, so it gets `DATABASE_URL` through Secret Manager. If the Dockerfile copies files from across the repository, add `build: { context: . }` to the service.

Save it:

```bash
loomctl manifest save acme-shop -f loomplane.yaml
```


### Connect the clouds

Under **Integrations**, add the Vercel token and the Google Cloud key. If a check says permissions are missing, grant them and check again. Then confirm each environment uses the account you meant. With one ready account per cloud, Loomplane picks it for you.


### Add variables

Set anything your services read that Loomplane doesn't generate:

```bash
loomctl vars set acme-shop LOG_LEVEL=info --env production
loomctl vars set acme-shop STRIPE_KEY=- --secret --env production --service svc:api:go:services/api
```

The service ID comes from the graph. See [Variables and secrets](/docs/concepts/variables-and-secrets).


### Plan the environment

```bash
loomctl plan acme-shop --env production
```

Read it from the top. Check the actions are only the ones you expect (a database, an API, a web app), that each sits on the provider you chose, and that no problems are listed. Read the warnings too. A service without a `port` falls back to 8080 with a warning, and you can fix that in the manifest.


### Approve and watch

An admin approves:

```bash
loomctl approve <plan-id>
```

`approve` follows the deployment step by step and exits nonzero if it fails. Cloud SQL can take several minutes. If a step fails, fix the cause (often a missing permission) and run `loomctl retry <deployment-id>`. It resumes from the failed step.

```bash
loomctl status acme-shop
```

shows what runs where, with addresses, and flags any drift.


### Change and redeploy

Push to the repository. If you've set up the [GitHub App's webhook](/docs/guides/private-repositories#re-analyze-on-push), Loomplane re-analyzes on its own. Otherwise run `loomctl analyze`. Then plan and approve again. To move only one repository in a multi-repository project, plan with `--scope web`.


## If you don't want a database to move

Resources never move between connections, because their data would stay behind. If you change an environment's connection, choose the old one again for the resource, or plan a fresh one deliberately. See [Adopting and moving services](/docs/clouds/adopting-and-moving).

pages.title: GitLab repositories
pages.description: Register a GitLab OAuth application once, sign in from Integrations, and re-analyze projects when their default branch moves.
pages.text:
Loomplane reads public projects on gitlab.com with no setup. A source is written `gitlab.com/<group>/<project>`, and you can paste the project's URL wherever Loomplane asks for one. Nested groups work, and so does a self-managed GitLab on version 17.0 or newer. An older version connects too, with a warning on its card.

To read private projects you register an OAuth application once for the whole Loomplane instance, and your organization's owners and admins sign in to it from Integrations.

## Register the application on gitlab.com

In GitLab, open **Preferences**, then **Applications**, then **Add new application**.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Name | Anything, such as Loomplane |
| Redirect URI | `<public_url>/integrations/gitlab/callback` |
| Confidential | On |
| Scopes | `read_api`, and nothing else |

Save it and copy the Application ID and the Secret. GitLab shows the secret once. `config.yaml` already has a `gitlab:` block wired to environment variables, so set these for both `loomplane` and `loomplane-worker`, and keep the secret out of any file you commit:

```sh
LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_ID="<the Application ID>"
LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_SECRET="<the Secret>"
```

On Helm, set `gitlab.clientID` in your values and `secrets.gitlabClientSecret`, or put `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_SECRET` in the Secret named by `secrets.existingSecret`. You can also put a `gitlab:` block with `client_id` and `client_secret` in `config.local.yaml`. Set both or neither. Loomplane refuses to start with only one. With neither, public projects still work and private ones can't be read.

## A self-managed GitLab

The operator can list it under `gitlab.hosts`, with an application registered on that GitLab the same way as above:

```yaml
gitlab:
  hosts:
    - web_url: https://git.example.com
      client_id: "<the Application ID>"
      client_secret: "<the Secret>"
```

A list can't come from one environment variable, so `gitlab.hosts` has none. Put it in a `gitlab:` block in `config.local.yaml`. `web_url` has no path and may be http or https. Loomplane trusts these hosts, so a GitLab on your private network works. Links Loomplane builds to a repository, such as **Open on git.example.com**, always use https, so a GitLab served over plain http gets https links that only open if the host answers https too.

An organization can add its own instead. Someone who may connect repositories opens **Integrations**, chooses **Add a self-managed GitLab**, and enters the address, an Application ID and a Secret. The dialog shows the callback URL to use. Loomplane is stricter about these:

- The address has to be https and a host name of its own. A GitLab served under a path is refused.
- Loomplane won't call private, loopback or link-local addresses for it, and it won't follow a redirect to http or to another host.

An operator who doesn't want organizations adding their own sets `gitlab.allow_organization_hosts: false`. It defaults to true. The full list of settings, with their environment variables, is:

| Setting | Variable |
|---|---|
| `gitlab.api_url` (gitlab.com's API, `https://gitlab.com` by default) | `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_API_URL` |
| `gitlab.client_id` | `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_ID` |
| `gitlab.client_secret` | `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_SECRET` |
| `gitlab.allow_organization_hosts` | `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_ALLOW_ORGANIZATION_HOSTS` |
| `gitlab.webhook_url` | `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_URL` |
| `gitlab.hosts` | None. Use `config.local.yaml` |

## Sign in

An owner or admin opens **Integrations**, finds the GitLab card and signs in to gitlab.com or to a self-managed GitLab. GitLab asks them to approve the application and sends them back.

Loomplane acts as the GitLab user who signed in, so it can read whatever that user can. Create a dedicated GitLab user with Reporter access on the groups Loomplane should read, and sign in as that user. Once it's connected, any project in the organization whose repository that user can read is analyzed with access to it.

Loomplane seals the tokens in its vault, and GitLab rotates them every two hours. If GitLab refuses to renew one, the card shows **Sign in again**, and signing in again replaces the old sign-in. Disconnecting removes the connection and revokes the sign-in at GitLab.

## Re-analyze on push

Each connection gets a webhook URL and a secret that proves a delivery came from your GitLab. The URL is `<webhook_url>/api/v1/gitlab/webhook/<connection id>`, where `gitlab.webhook_url` (`LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_URL`) defaults to your `public_url`. Set it only when GitLab reaches Loomplane at a different address than people do.


In GitLab, open **Settings**, then **Webhooks**, on the project or on its group. Paste the URL from the connection's **Webhook** panel on Integrations and tick **Push events**. Group webhooks need GitLab Premium on gitlab.com.


Set the secret. Which way it goes depends on your GitLab version.

On GitLab 19 and newer, GitLab makes the signing token. Choose **Generate signing token** in GitLab and copy it, because GitLab shows it once. Paste it into **Paste GitLab's signing token** on the panel and choose **Save signing token**. Loomplane keeps it and checks every delivery's signature with it.

On older versions, choose **Create secret** on the panel. Copy the secret token it shows, once, and paste it into GitLab's **Secret token** field.


Push a change to the default branch. The project's Analyses tab should show another analysis finishing at the new commit, with `created_by` set to `gitlab-push`.


Only pushes to a project's default branch re-analyze, and only in the organization that owns the connection. A push to any other branch, a tag or a deleted branch does nothing.

## Deploying

Every deployment target but two builds from the archive Loomplane fetched. Render and DigitalOcean App Platform build from the repository themselves, through their own GitLab connection, so connect GitLab in Render's or DigitalOcean's dashboard first. They build gitlab.com sources only. A source on a self-managed GitLab can't deploy to either, and the plan reports it.

pages.title: Notifications and webhooks
pages.description: Get deployment results and the agent's reports by email, and send signed webhooks to your own systems.
pages.text:
Open **Notifications** to read deployment results, change your deployment email preference and, as an owner or admin, manage signed webhooks.

## Email

Deployment mail goes to the person who started the deployment. Loomplane checks their current organization membership and project access before delivery. Account recovery and verification mail don't follow the deployment preference.

An empty SMTP host disables email. Invitations then show a manual link and say that email is disabled. Production requires implicit SMTP TLS (commonly port 465) and a valid sender address. If the server needs authentication, set the username and password together, and keep the password outside committed configuration.

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_PORT=465
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_TLS=true
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_USERNAME=loomplane
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_PASSWORD=...
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_FROM=accounts@example.com
```

Set `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL` to the address people use, because recovery and invitation links are built from it.

### Read mail from a folder

On your own machine you don't need a mail server at all. Point Loomplane at a folder and each email lands there as an `.eml` file you can open in any mail client:

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_MAIL_DIR=.forge/mail
```

A relative path is resolved from where the API starts, and `.forge/` is already gitignored. The files hold whole messages, reset and invitation links included, so they're readable by you only. Set this or an SMTP host or a Resend key, not more than one. Production refuses it.

### Test with Mailpit

```bash
docker run --rm --name loomplane-mailpit \
  -p 127.0.0.1:1025:1025 -p 127.0.0.1:8025:8025 \
  axllent/mailpit:v1.30.0
```

Then, before you start the API:

```bash
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_PORT=1025
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_FROM=accounts@example.com
export LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_TLS=false
```

Open Mailpit at `http://127.0.0.1:8025`.

### What's stored

Herald keeps encrypted SMTP credentials and sanitized delivery outcomes. It doesn't keep recipient addresses, rendered security mail, reset tokens or invitation links in its history. Invitations report `sent`, `disabled` or `failed` on their own, so a delivery failure doesn't discard a valid invitation. Password reset always returns the same public response for known and unknown addresses, so look at sanitized server diagnostics when delivery fails.

## Delivery and retries

A database trigger captures each terminal deployment attempt in the same transaction that writes it. Notification processing retries up to ten times, then marks its health check unhealthy. After you fix the cause, retry processing from the Notifications page. A replay keeps completed channels and Relay's durable acceptance identity, so it doesn't create a second webhook event.

SMTP delivery is at-least-once. A crash after the mail server accepts a message but before Loomplane records success can produce a duplicate.

## Signed webhooks

Owners and admins add endpoints on the Notifications page. An endpoint must be public HTTPS on port 443. Loomplane blocks private and reserved addresses, resolves again when it connects and refuses redirects.

The signing secret appears once, after you create the endpoint or rotate its secret. Store it in your receiver's secret manager. Verify the `X-Relay-Signature` header against the exact request body and `X-Relay-Timestamp`, and apply a tolerance on the timestamp on your side.

Relay owns HTTP retries and the delivery history. The page shows each attempt, its HTTP status and the next retry, and the public API doesn't keep response bodies. A receiver that returns 410 gets its endpoint disabled.

Deployment payloads hold allowlisted IDs, status, attempt and an application link. They leave out build logs, variables and raw provider errors.

## The agent's notices

When the [built-in agent](/docs/agents/built-in-agent) is on, it sends four kinds of notice of its own. Each one lands in the inbox, goes by email and fires one webhook for the workspace, however many people it reaches.

| Webhook type | When | Who gets it |
|---|---|---|
| `agent.request.created` | The agent needs a decision from someone | The people it asks. See [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#who-is-asked) |
| `agent.report.created` | The agent opened a report, or one came back or happened again | The members of the project's responsible team (owners and admins when it has none), and the person who started the deployment it's about |
| `agent.budget.created` | The agent stopped investigating because the month's AI budget is spent, and again when it starts | Owners and admins |
| `agent.release.created` | A [release preparation](/docs/agents/release-preparation) ended: promoted by the agent, stale, stopped, blocked or failed | The person who asked, and the members of the project's responsible team (owners and admins when it has none) |

A report or release notice reaches a person only while they have `deployment:read` on its project, and a budget notice only while they have `ai:manage`. The project's team counts only when the project names one. When it doesn't, owners and admins already have it. Repeats of one report send at most one notice an hour. [Watching and reports](/docs/agents/watching-and-reports#notices) has the whole story.

The webhook's body is the notice: `project_id` (empty for a budget notice), `subject_id`, `title`, `body`, `path`, `url` and `need`, the permission a person needs to read it. A release notice's `metadata` carries `release_report_id`, `plan_id` and `state`. A report's `metadata` carries `report_id`, `signal`, `severity` and `environment`, and its title and body have already had the project's known secrets redacted and been through the agent's outbound scan.

### Turn off the agent's email

The agent's mail has a switch of its own, apart from deployment mail. Both are on until you change them, and each person sets their own:

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"agent_email": false}' "$URL/api/v1/notifications/preferences"
```

The body changes only the fields it carries, so this leaves `deployment_email` as it was. `GET /api/v1/notifications/preferences` returns both. With `agent_email` off you still get the agent's notices in the inbox.

## Loomplane Cloud notices

When Loomplane Cloud work for your workspace is stopped, restored or held back, owners and admins get an inbox notice and the workspace gets one webhook. Add these types to an endpoint to hear them.

| Webhook type | When |
|---|---|
| `platform_cloud.suspended.created` | Loomplane Cloud work for the workspace was stopped |
| `platform_cloud.restored.created` | Loomplane Cloud work for the workspace was restored and is starting again |
| `platform_cloud.waiting_capacity.created` | Loomplane Cloud work is waiting for room on a host |

The body is the notice, with the same fields as the agent's notices.

pages.title: Private repositories
pages.description: Create a GitHub App once, connect it to your organization, and re-analyze projects when their default branch moves.
pages.text:
Loomplane reads public GitHub repositories with no setup. To read private ones it needs a GitHub App, which your organization's admins install on their GitHub accounts. You create the App once for the whole Loomplane instance.

## Create the App

From a checkout of Loomplane, GitHub's App Manifest flow does most of it:

```bash
go run ./scripts/github-app -org your-org
```

Open the local address it prints and review the permissions on GitHub. After you create the App, the command writes its settings to the ignored `config.local.yaml` and its private key to `.loomplane/github-app.pem`, both readable only by you. It refuses to overwrite an existing key or add a second GitHub configuration. Restart Loomplane, then connect the account under Integrations.

For an instance that's publicly reachable, add `-url https://your-loomplane.example -webhook` to turn on push events. The local flow leaves webhooks off because GitHub can't reach localhost.

### Or create it by hand

On GitHub go to **Settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps, New GitHub App**. Use the organization's settings if the App should belong to it.

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| GitHub App name | Anything. Its slug goes in `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_APP_SLUG` |
| Homepage URL | Your Loomplane's public URL |
| Callback URL | `<public_url>/integrations/github/setup` |
| Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation | On |
| Expire user authorization tokens | On |
| Webhook | Active, URL `<public_url>/api/v1/github/webhook`, with a secret you generate (`openssl rand -hex 32`). Or off, if you'd rather press Analyze yourself |
| Subscribe to events | Push |
| Repository permissions: Contents | Read-only |
| Repository permissions: Metadata | Read-only (GitHub requires it) |
| Repository permissions: Issues | Read and write (only Loomplane's agent uses it, to open an issue per report. Leave it at No access if you don't run the agent) |
| Everything else | No access |
| Where can this GitHub App be installed? | Any account, unless only your own organization uses this Loomplane |

Create it, then on its page note the App ID and the Client ID, generate a client secret, and generate a private key (GitHub downloads a `.pem`).

## Configure Loomplane

Set these for both `loomplane` and `loomplane-worker`, and keep the secret and key out of any file you commit:

```bash
LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_APP_ID=123456
LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_APP_SLUG=your-app-slug
LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=Iv23li...
LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=...
LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/github-app.pem
```

`LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY` takes the PEM itself instead of a path, which suits a secret store that only does variables, and newlines written as `\n` work. Loomplane refuses to start with only some of these set, or with a key it can't parse.

For GitHub Enterprise Server, also set `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_API_URL` to `https://<host>/api/v3` and `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_WEB_URL` to `https://<host>`.

## Connect an account

An owner or admin opens **Integrations** and chooses **Install on GitHub**. GitHub asks which account to install on and which repositories to allow, then sends them back. From then on, any project in the organization whose repository that installation can see is analyzed with access to it. Choose repositories later in the App's settings on GitHub.

What happens underneath:

- Connecting. GitHub's redirect carries the installation's number and a one-time code. Loomplane exchanges the code for the installer's own token and checks that their account can see that installation, because the number alone proves nothing. The state in the link is signed, lasts 15 minutes and names the organization and person who started it. The installer's token is used for that one check, then dropped.
- Analyzing. For each analysis the worker mints an installation token limited to that one repository and to reading its contents, and GitHub expires it within the hour. Loomplane stores no token, and uses an organization's own installations only, so one organization can't read another's code.
- Disconnecting removes the installation from the organization in Loomplane. The App stays installed on GitHub until someone uninstalls it there.

## Issues for agent reports

Loomplane's agent opens one issue per report on the repository the report is about. For that, the App needs the Issues permission, and every account it's installed on has to accept it. If your App was created before it asked for Issues, add the permission in the App's settings on GitHub. GitHub then asks the owner of each installation to review and accept it. Existing installations keep working while they wait: until an owner of that account accepts, reports for its repositories go to Herald only, and AI settings names the installation that's waiting, with a link to its page on GitHub. You don't reconnect anything. Loomplane trusts what it last read of an installation's permissions for five minutes, so the first report after an owner accepts can still go to Herald only for up to five minutes. After that, open reports for the account's repositories get their issues.

The token Loomplane mints for a report can write issues on that one repository and nothing else, and GitHub expires it within the hour. If you don't run the agent, leave Issues at No access, or pass `-no-issues` to `scripts/github-app`.

## Re-analyze on push

With the webhook on, set its secret in `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` for `loomplane`. When a repository's default branch moves, every source tracking it (one that names no branch, or names the default) is analyzed again, in whichever projects have it. Only organizations that connected the installation the push came through hear about it. Pushes to other branches and deliveries without a matching signature do nothing.

A public repository doesn't need an App for this. Add a webhook to the repository itself with the same URL and secret and the push event.

## Verify the connection


Connect the account from Integrations and confirm it appears after GitHub sends you back. Reload to check it persists.


Open New project, choose a private repository from the account's group and analyze it. The graph should name the repository and its exact commit.


On the App's **Permissions & events** page, check that Push is selected. A working webhook URL alone doesn't subscribe the App to pushes.


Push a change to the default branch, or redeliver an existing push from GitHub's Recent Deliveries. Confirm GitHub receives HTTP 202 with `analyses_started` above zero, and that the project's Analyses tab shows another analysis finishing at the new commit.


The analysis worker has to be running too. If Loomplane accepts a push but the analysis stays queued, check the worker's health at `http://localhost:8781/_/health` (or wherever you serve it) and its database connection.

For local development you can point the App's webhook at a Smee channel and run its client in another terminal:

```bash
npx smee-client --url https://smee.io/YOUR_CHANNEL --target http://localhost:8780/api/v1/github/webhook
```

Set the same webhook secret in GitHub and Loomplane. Smee's HTTP 200 only means it accepted the delivery, so check the client's terminal for Loomplane's 202. If the API was restarting when Smee forwarded the event, wait for it to become healthy and redeliver from GitHub. Smee channels receive push metadata for the repositories your App can access, including commit messages and authors.

A redelivered older push analyzes the source's current tracked branch. To check a fresh push, compare the finished analysis's `commit_sha` with the push's commit and confirm `created_by` is `github-push`. Keep private keys and webhook secrets out of shell arguments and diagnostic output.

pages.title: How it works
pages.description: The path from a repository to a running service, and what Loomplane checks along the way.
pages.text:
Every deployment follows the same seven steps. Once you know them the rest of these docs are easier to read, since each page takes one step and goes deep.

## 1. Analyze

You add one or more repositories to a project. A worker downloads a tarball of each at one commit and reads it. Nothing from the repository runs: no build scripts, no package managers. The worker finds services, the packages they share, and the databases and caches they need, and it records the file and line behind every finding. See [Repository discovery](/docs/concepts/repository-discovery).

## 2. Draft the manifest

From that analysis Loomplane drafts a `loomplane.yaml`. You edit it in the dashboard or with `loomctl manifest save`, and every save is a new revision. This file says what deploys, where, and what each service needs. See [The manifest](/docs/concepts/the-manifest).

## 3. Connect clouds

Under Integrations you add credentials for the clouds your manifest names. Loomplane checks each with its cloud first and tells you which permissions are missing. Credentials live in Vault, encrypted with a key derived from your secret key. See [Clouds](/docs/clouds).

## 4. Plan

A plan is for one environment. It lists every action a deployment would take, in order, with the problems that would block it and the warnings worth reading. Planning never touches a cloud. A plan names the manifest revision and the exact commit of every repository it moves.

## 5. Approve

A developer can plan anything. Only an admin's approval changes a cloud, and the approval names the plan's revision. If the world changed since you looked, the plan comes back stale and nothing happens. See [Plans and approvals](/docs/concepts/plans-and-approvals).

## 6. Deploy

Approval starts a durable workflow. It stores one source tarball per repository, provisions resources, builds each service on its cloud's own builder (Cloud Build, CodeBuild, Vercel, Render, App Platform or ACR Tasks), deploys it, and checks that public services answer. If a step fails, you retry from that step. See [Deployments and recovery](/docs/concepts/deployments-and-recovery).

## 7. Watch for drift

On a schedule (every 30 minutes by default), Loomplane compares everything it deployed with what each cloud has live. It records differences and changes nothing. The next plan, approved like any other, puts things back. See [Drift](/docs/concepts/drift).

## Where each piece runs

Loomplane is two processes over one PostgreSQL database. `loomplane` serves the API and dashboard, runs the deployment workflows and records everything. `loomplane-worker` analyzes repositories, in a separate process that holds no sessions and serves nothing but health checks.

Your builds run on your clouds' builders, in your accounts. Gateways and provider plugins run on your infrastructure. Application traffic goes straight to your services.

pages.title: Backing up Loomplane
pages.description: Back up and restore Loomplane's own database with one command, and know what a backup does and doesn't contain.
pages.text:
This page is about Loomplane's own data. For the databases it deploys for you, see [Backups and test restores](/docs/services/backups-and-test-restores). The commands here are `loomplane` commands, run with the same configuration the server runs with.

## Back up

```bash
loomplane backup --out loomplane-backup.tar.gz
```

A backup is one file. It holds every table in Loomplane's database, Loomplane's own and every library's (authsome, Warden, Chronicle, Dispatch, Ctrl Plane, Vault, Keysmith), copied in one snapshot so the tables agree with each other however long the copy takes. You can run it while Loomplane is serving. The file is written beside its final name and renamed once it's complete, and only you can read it.

```bash
loomplane backup inspect loomplane-backup.tar.gz
```

shows which Loomplane made a backup, when, and how many rows each table has, without restoring anything.

A backup holds secrets the way the database does: cloud credentials and variables as Vault ciphertext, API keys as hashes. Reading them needs the `secret_key` Loomplane ran with. Keep that key somewhere other than beside the backups, or a restored Loomplane will start without being able to deploy.

Not in a backup: the source tarballs in `storage.url`, which Loomplane fetches again from GitHub when it needs them, and anything in your clouds. A restore brings back Loomplane's record of what runs where, and the next drift check compares it with what's live. If you use local recovery objects, back up the `artifact-data` volume too. They can't be recreated by fetching source code.

Schedule it however you schedule things. With cron, one a night kept for two weeks:

```bash
0 3 * * * cd /srv/loomplane && loomplane backup --out backups/loomplane-$(date +\%F).tar.gz && find backups -name 'loomplane-*.tar.gz' -mtime +14 -delete
```

In the Docker stack, run it through Compose as shown in [Upgrades and releases](/docs/operations/upgrades-and-releases#with-the-docker-stack). Store backups off the host.

## Restore

Stop Loomplane, then run this against an empty database:

```bash
loomplane restore loomplane-backup.tar.gz
```

Restore makes the tables the backup's schema had, loads every row in one transaction, then migrates the database up to this Loomplane's schema. It refuses a database a Loomplane has already run on. Pass `--force` to replace what's there. If loading the rows fails, the load rolls back, but the tables restore made stay, so the database no longer counts as empty: fix what the error names and run the restore again with `--force`. Start Loomplane again with the `secret_key` it ran with before.

A backup made by a newer Loomplane can't be restored by an older one, because its rows fit a schema the older one lacks. Restore with the same version or a later one. A backup from before a released schema change still restores: restore loads a backup at the schema it was taken at and migrates it up from there.

### Knowledge and backups

If the agent's [knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge) was on when you backed up, the backup includes its vector table, and that needs somewhere to go. Restore into a Loomplane that has `ai.enabled` on, `ai.knowledge` configured with the same `dimensions` as the one that made the backup, and the pgvector extension available in its Postgres.

Restore checks all of that before it touches the database. If AI or knowledge isn't configured, it says what to set. If the sizes differ, it gives you the backup's size and yours. If the database can't have pgvector, it says why, for example that the extension isn't installed or that the role isn't allowed to create it. When it refuses, the target is left as it was, so you can fix the config or the database and run the same command again, without `--force`.

A backup taken with knowledge off carries no vector tables and restores anywhere.

After a restore, test sign-in, open a project, and run a plan to see that connections still decrypt.

pages.title: DigitalOcean
pages.description: Host Loomplane itself on DigitalOcean with App Platform, a Droplet and cloud-init, or the Marketplace 1-Click.
pages.text:
This page is about hosting Loomplane itself on DigitalOcean. If you want Loomplane to deploy your own services to DigitalOcean, that's a different job, and [DigitalOcean as a cloud](/docs/clouds/digitalocean) covers it.

There are three ways to do it. Pick one from the table, then jump to its section.

| | App Platform | Droplet with cloud-init | Marketplace 1-Click |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost per month | About $42 ($37 for the app, $5 for Spaces) | About $48 for 8 GB, $24 for the 4 GB minimum | The Droplet size you choose |
| Analysis disk | Capped at 2 to 4 GiB | Whatever the Droplet has | Whatever the Droplet has |
| Who looks after the server | DigitalOcean | You | You |
| Upgrades | Redeploy the app | Re-run the install script with a new version | Same as a Droplet |

App Platform is the least work. A Droplet gives you the most room, and the worker isn't squeezed by a small scratch disk. The 1-Click is a Droplet with the install already done.

## App Platform

You need two Spaces buckets before you deploy, one for artifacts and one for backups. Loomplane checks that they exist and doesn't create them. Bucket names are unique per region across all DigitalOcean customers, so use a prefix of your own, like `acme-loomplane-artifacts` and `acme-loomplane-backups`. Create a Spaces access key too.

Then build the storage URL. Keep `us-east-1` exactly as written, because it's the signing region. Put your real region (`nyc3`, `ams3`, `sfo3` and so on) in the endpoint only:

```text
s3://ACCESS_KEY:SECRET_KEY@us-east-1/BUCKET?endpoint=https://REGION.digitaloceanspaces.com&path_style=true
```

`BUCKET` should be your artifact bucket.

Now deploy:

[![Deploy to DigitalOcean](https://www.deploytodo.com/do-btn-blue.svg)](https://cloud.digitalocean.com/apps/new?repo=https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/tree/main)

DigitalOcean asks for four values:

- `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY`: the output of `openssl rand -base64 32`. Keep it in your secret manager.
- `LOOMPLANE_STORAGE_URL`: the Spaces URL above.
- `LOOMPLANE_ARTIFACT_BUCKET`: the artifact bucket name.
- `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_BUCKET`: the backup bucket name.

DigitalOcean's button officially supports one service, and this template has two (the API and the worker). If the button refuses it, use `doctl` instead. Fetch the template and pull the app spec out of it:

```bash
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xraph/loomplane/main/.do/deploy.template.yaml
sed -n '/^spec:/,$p' deploy.template.yaml | sed '1d; s/^  //' > app.yaml
```

Add a `value:` line to each of the four entries in `app.yaml` that don't have one, then create the app:

```bash
doctl apps create --spec app.yaml
```

When the first deploy finishes, open the `loomplane` component's Runtime Logs and find the `setup is waiting` line. Its `url` field opens `/setup` with the one-time token filled in. You can also open the component's Console and run `loomplane setup-token` to get the link again. Then create your account and organization.

The template uses App Platform's dev database, which is fine for a trial and not for real work. For real use, create a DigitalOcean Managed PostgreSQL cluster and point `LOOMPLANE_DATABASE_URL` at it.

App Platform can't follow an image tag, so the template uses `:latest`. To upgrade, redeploy the app. To stay on one version, change the tag to a release such as `v1.2.3`. The template redirects `/_/metrics` and `/debug` to `/`, so neither is reachable from outside.

Scratch space on App Platform is small, so the worker runs one analysis at a time. Very large repositories can fail there. If yours do, move to a Droplet.

## Droplet with cloud-init

Copy the raw contents of [`cloud-init.yaml`](https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/blob/main/deployments/digitalocean/cloud-init.yaml) from GitHub. The three values sit in the `install.env` block near the top, and they're the only thing you edit:

- `LOOMPLANE_DOMAIN`: the hostname you'll serve Loomplane on.
- `ACME_EMAIL`: where Let's Encrypt can reach you.
- `LOOMPLANE_VERSION`: optional. Leave it empty for the newest stable release.

Create an Ubuntu 24.04 Droplet and paste the whole file into the **User data** box under Advanced options. We recommend 8 GB (`s-4vcpu-8gb`, about $48 a month). You can go down to 4 GB (`s-2vcpu-4gb`, about $24), but then set `LOOMPLANE_ANALYSIS_CONCURRENCY=1` (the bundle defaults to 2). The easy way is to uncomment that line in the cloud-init file before you create the Droplet. On a running Droplet, change the value in `/srv/loomplane/.env` and apply it with `cd /srv/loomplane && docker compose up -d`.

Point an A record for your domain at the Droplet's IP. Caddy fetches the certificate once DNS resolves.

The install takes several minutes. Follow it with `tail -f /var/log/cloud-init-output.log`. When it's done, the setup link is printed at the end of that log, and it shows in the SSH login message until setup is complete. To get it again:

```bash
cd /srv/loomplane && docker compose exec loomplane loomplane setup-token
```

The install generates the secret key and the Postgres password on the box and writes them to `/srv/loomplane/.env` (mode 600). Copy that file somewhere safe now. Without the key, Loomplane can't decrypt the credentials it has stored.

To upgrade, prepare the new version and then start it:

```bash
LOOMPLANE_VERSION=vX.Y.Z /usr/local/lib/loomplane/install.sh prepare
/usr/local/lib/loomplane/install.sh start
```

Preparing the new version also points your `.env` at the matching image and leaves your secrets and domain alone. The stack itself is the one [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker) describes.

## Marketplace 1-Click

Once the Loomplane listing is published in the DigitalOcean Marketplace, create a Droplet from it, point your DNS at the Droplet and SSH in as root. The `loomplane-setup` wizard asks for your domain and ACME email, starts the stack and prints the setup link.

If you log in before the first boot finishes, the login message says Loomplane is still installing. Log in again in a minute or two. Secrets are generated on each Droplet at first boot, and none are baked into the image.

Upgrades and the `.env` file work as they do for a plain Droplet.

## Optional push gateway

Droplets and Marketplace installs use the production Docker bundle, so you
can run the gateway beside Loomplane and its workers on the same host.
After the initial setup, follow [the Docker gateway setup](https://loomplane.dev/docs/operations/production-on-docker#optional-push-gateway)
from `/srv/loomplane`. Set `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.push-gateway.yaml`
in `.env`, provide the gateway image, hostname and key files, then run
`docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240`.

Point the gateway's separate hostname at the Droplet too. Caddy serves both
hostnames through ports 80 and 443, so you don't open another port in the
Droplet firewall. Keep gateway credentials in the mounted key files, outside
cloud-init user data. Back up those files alongside `.env`.

An installer upgrade keeps the gateway opt-in, hostname and existing keys.
It updates the Loomplane image from the new bundle. Pin the gateway image
separately in `PUSH_GATEWAY_IMAGE`, and choose a published gateway version
when you upgrade it. After starting an upgraded bundle, restart Caddy to
reload its configuration: `docker compose restart caddy`.

On DigitalOcean Kubernetes (DOKS), use the Helm option with
`push.gateway.enabled=true`. Set `push.gatewayUrl` to the gateway's public
HTTPS hostname, create its Secret in the release namespace, and configure
its Ingress or HTTPRoute as shown in the
[push notifications guide](https://loomplane.dev/docs/operations/push-notifications#alongside-loomplane).
Your ingress controller provides the public entry point; provision its load
balancer, DNS and TLS certificate through your usual cluster setup. The
same chart option works with other Kubernetes providers that support those
standard resources.

| Where you host Loomplane | Gateway option |
|---|---|
| DigitalOcean Droplet with cloud-init | Production Compose overlay in `/srv/loomplane` |
| DigitalOcean Marketplace Droplet | The same overlay after the first-login setup |
| DOKS or another Kubernetes cluster | Helm Deployment and Service, with an Ingress or HTTPRoute |
| Other Linux Docker hosts | The production Compose overlay |
| App Platform and Miget templates | Continue to use the hosted gateway |

You need push credentials for the mobile app you ship. The store app uses
XRaph's gateway.

To exercise these paths locally, run `make test-digitalocean` for the Ubuntu
installer, upgrade and installed Compose bundle, or `make test-push-kubernetes`
for the Helm chart. Both build images and use disposable local resources.
The Kubernetes test sends an encrypted notification to a local provider
fixture and checks HTTPS routing, restarts and key rotation. It does not
create DigitalOcean resources or send a notification to a real phone.

## Backups

On App Platform the dev database has no managed backups. A Managed PostgreSQL cluster does, and DigitalOcean takes them daily. Artifacts and recovery objects live in Spaces.

On a Droplet or a 1-Click, follow [Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) and keep a copy of `.env` somewhere off the box. DigitalOcean's own Droplet backups are worth turning on as well.

pages.title: Install on Linux
pages.description: Install loomctl and the Loomplane server on Linux from a .deb, an .rpm or a release archive, run the server under systemd, then upgrade or remove both.
pages.text:
Every [GitHub release](https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/releases) carries Linux builds of both programs for amd64 and arm64. `loomctl` is the command-line client, and you can put it on any machine. The server is `loomplane` (the API and dashboard) plus `loomplane-worker` (repository analysis), and it wants a host of its own with PostgreSQL. This page runs the server straight on the host under systemd. If you'd rather keep it in containers, [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker) covers that setup.

## What a release ships for Linux

For a release tagged `v1.2.3`:

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `loomctl_1.2.3_amd64.deb`, `loomctl_1.2.3_arm64.deb` | `loomctl` in `/usr/bin`, for Debian and Ubuntu |
| `loomctl-1.2.3-1.x86_64.rpm`, `loomctl-1.2.3-1.aarch64.rpm` | The same for Fedora, RHEL and their relatives |
| `loomctl_1.2.3_linux_amd64.tar.gz`, `loomctl_1.2.3_linux_arm64.tar.gz` | The bare binary, for any distribution |
| `loomplane_1.2.3_amd64.deb`, `loomplane_1.2.3_arm64.deb` | The server: both binaries, the dashboard, `config.yaml`, a settings file and two systemd units |
| `loomplane-1.2.3-1.x86_64.rpm`, `loomplane-1.2.3-1.aarch64.rpm` | The same server package for dnf |
| `loomplane_1.2.3_linux_amd64.tar.gz`, `loomplane_1.2.3_linux_arm64.tar.gz` | The server as an archive, with the same units under `systemd/` |
| `binaries-checksums.txt` | SHA-256 of every file above |
| `binaries-checksums.txt.sigstore.json` | A Sigstore signature over that checksum file, made by the Release workflow |

There's also a `loomctl` container image, `ghcr.io/xraph/loomctl`, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

## Download and verify

Pick the release and your architecture first. Every command below reuses these two variables:

```bash
VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/xraph/loomplane/releases/latest \
  | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"v\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
case "$(uname -m)" in
  x86_64) ARCH=amd64 ;;
  aarch64 | arm64) ARCH=arm64 ;;
  *) echo "Loomplane ships Linux builds for amd64 and arm64 only" >&2 ;;
esac
echo "$VERSION $ARCH"
```

That asks GitHub for the newest stable release. For a host you'll keep, set `VERSION=1.2.3` yourself so you know what you installed. Then fetch the checksums and their signature next to whatever you download:

```bash
BASE=https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/releases/download/v$VERSION
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/binaries-checksums.txt"
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/binaries-checksums.txt.sigstore.json"
```

Once the files you want are in the same directory, check them. `--ignore-missing` skips everything in the list you didn't download:

```bash
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
```

The checksum file proves the download wasn't damaged. To prove the Release workflow in `xraph/loomplane` made it, verify its signature with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/system_config/installation/):

```bash
cosign verify-blob \
  --bundle binaries-checksums.txt.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/xraph/loomplane/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/(tags/v.+|heads/main)$' \
  binaries-checksums.txt
```

It should print `Verified OK`. A release cut from the Actions tab is signed from `main` and one cut from a tag push from that tag, which is why the identity allows both. Once you have `loomctl`, `loomctl node verify-release` runs the same check without cosign.

## Install loomctl


```bash
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomctl_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
sudo apt install "./loomctl_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
```


The rpm names use the kernel's architecture names, `x86_64` and `aarch64`:

```bash
RPM_ARCH=$(uname -m)
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomctl-${VERSION}-1.${RPM_ARCH}.rpm"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
sudo dnf install "./loomctl-${VERSION}-1.${RPM_ARCH}.rpm"
```


This works on any distribution, Alpine included, since the binary is static.

```bash
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomctl_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
tar -xzf "loomctl_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz" loomctl
sudo install -m 0755 loomctl /usr/local/bin/loomctl
```

Without root, put it in `~/.local/bin` instead and make sure that's on your `PATH`.


```bash
docker run --rm ghcr.io/xraph/loomctl:v$VERSION --version
```

The image runs `loomctl` as its entrypoint. Its main job is joining a machine as a [node](/docs/clouds/nodes) when that machine has no service manager.


Check it, then sign in. `--no-browser` prints the sign-in address instead of opening it, which is what you want over SSH:

```bash
loomctl --version
loomctl login --url https://loomplane.example.com --no-browser
```

Open that address on your laptop or phone, check the code matches, and approve it. CI signs in with an API key instead, which [CI with loomctl](/docs/guides/ci-with-loomctl) covers, and [the loomctl reference](/docs/reference/loomctl) lists every command.

## Install the server

### What you need
