- A Linux host on amd64 or arm64 with systemd 239 or newer. Ubuntu 20.04, Debian 11, RHEL 8 and anything newer qualify.
- PostgreSQL 17, on this host or reachable from it. A managed database works fine.
- A hostname pointed at the host, with TCP ports 80 and 443 open for HTTPS.
- 2 CPU cores and 8 GB of RAM to start, plus disk for the database, deployment sources and checkouts the worker unpacks (up to 2 GiB per analysis). Measure your own workload before you go smaller.

Loomplane never runs your code, so the host needs no Docker, no Git and no build tools.


### Set up PostgreSQL

Skip this if you already have a database. On Debian or Ubuntu, the PostgreSQL project's own repository has version 17 for every supported release:

```bash
sudo apt install -y postgresql-common
sudo /usr/share/postgresql-common/pgdg/apt.postgresql.org.sh -y
sudo apt install -y postgresql-17
```

On Fedora or RHEL, follow the [PostgreSQL download page](https://www.postgresql.org/download/linux/redhat/) for your release. Then make a role and a database for Loomplane. A hex password needs no escaping in a URL:

```bash
DB_PASSWORD=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
sudo -u postgres psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  -c "CREATE ROLE loomplane LOGIN PASSWORD '$DB_PASSWORD'" \
  -c "CREATE DATABASE loomplane OWNER loomplane"
echo "postgres://loomplane:$DB_PASSWORD@127.0.0.1:5432/loomplane?sslmode=disable"
```

Keep that last line. It's your `LOOMPLANE_DATABASE_URL`. Use `sslmode=require` or stricter for a database on another machine.


### Install the package


```bash
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomplane_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
sudo apt install "./loomplane_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
```


```bash
RPM_ARCH=$(uname -m)
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomplane-${VERSION}-1.${RPM_ARCH}.rpm"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
sudo dnf install "./loomplane-${VERSION}-1.${RPM_ARCH}.rpm"
```


The archive holds what the package installs, so you put each piece in place yourself. Binaries go in `/usr/local/bin`, where the units look first.

```bash
curl -fsSLO "$BASE/loomplane_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz"
sha256sum --check --ignore-missing binaries-checksums.txt
mkdir loomplane && tar -xzf "loomplane_${VERSION}_linux_${ARCH}.tar.gz" -C loomplane
cd loomplane

sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /var/lib/loomplane \
  --shell /usr/sbin/nologin loomplane
sudo install -m 0755 loomplane loomplane-worker /usr/local/bin/
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/share/loomplane /etc/loomplane
sudo rm -rf /usr/local/share/loomplane/dashboard
sudo cp -r dashboard /usr/local/share/loomplane/dashboard
sudo install -m 0644 config.yaml /etc/loomplane/config.yaml
sudo install -m 0640 -g loomplane systemd/loomplane.env /etc/loomplane/loomplane.env
sudo sed -i 's|^LOOMPLANE_DASHBOARD_DIR=.*|LOOMPLANE_DASHBOARD_DIR=/usr/local/share/loomplane/dashboard|' \
  /etc/loomplane/loomplane.env
sudo install -m 0644 systemd/loomplane.service systemd/loomplane-worker.service /etc/systemd/system/
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
```


Either way, the files land here:

| Path | |
|---|---|
| `/usr/bin/loomplane`, `/usr/bin/loomplane-worker` | The binaries (`/usr/local/bin` from the archive) |
| `/usr/share/loomplane/dashboard` | The built dashboard the API serves |
| `/etc/loomplane/config.yaml` | Defaults. Leave it alone, since an upgrade replaces it |
| `/etc/loomplane/loomplane.env` | Your settings and secrets, readable by root and the `loomplane` group only |
| `loomplane.service`, `loomplane-worker.service` | The systemd units, both running as the `loomplane` user |
| `/var/lib/loomplane` | Deployment sources. systemd creates it on first start |
| `/var/lib/loomplane-work` | The worker's checkouts |

Installing starts nothing. You fill in the settings first.


### Fill in the settings

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
sudoedit /etc/loomplane/loomplane.env
```

Four values are required:

| Variable | |
|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_ENVIRONMENT` | Already `production`. Leave it |
| `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL` | `https://` and your hostname, no path |
| `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` | The value `openssl rand -base64 32` printed |
| `LOOMPLANE_DATABASE_URL` | The URL from the PostgreSQL step |

The rest of the file has optional settings (email, off-host backups, the AI section) with a comment on each. Any `LOOMPLANE_` variable from [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration) can go here, and both services read the same file.

  `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` encrypts every cloud credential and secret Loomplane stores. Generate it once, keep a copy in your secret manager, and keep it out of your backups. If you lose it, you lose every stored credential.


### Start it

Start the API first. It applies the database migrations before it serves, and the worker waits for them.

```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now loomplane
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8780/_/health/live && echo
sudo systemctl enable --now loomplane-worker
systemctl status loomplane loomplane-worker --no-pager
```

The first start migrates an empty database, so give it a minute. If `curl` fails, `journalctl -u loomplane -e` says why, and a missing setting is named there.


### Put HTTPS in front

Both services listen on `127.0.0.1` only. A reverse proxy serves your hostname over HTTPS and passes traffic in. With [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com/docs/install), which gets and renews the certificate for you, `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile` is:

```text
loomplane.example.com {
	# Health and metrics stay on the host.
	@internal path /_/health /_/health/* /_/metrics /_/metrics/* /debug/*
	respond @internal 404

	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8780 {
		# Send events as they happen. WebSocket upgrades work as is.
		flush_interval -1
	}
}
```

```bash
sudo systemctl reload caddy
```

nginx works too, as long as it passes WebSocket upgrades and turns off buffering for the API's event streams (`proxy_buffering off`).


### Finish setup

Setup needs a one-time link. The API logs it as a `setup is waiting` warning (`journalctl -u loomplane | grep setup`), and `loomplane setup-token` prints it again.

Operator commands like that one need the service's settings and the service's user. They also read a `.env` from the directory you run them in, so start them from `/var/lib/loomplane`. This shell function does all three, and the rest of this page uses it:

```bash
lp() {
  sudo -u loomplane sh -c 'cd /var/lib/loomplane && set -a && . /etc/loomplane/loomplane.env && set +a && exec loomplane "$@"' loomplane "$@"
}
lp setup-token
# Finish setup at https://loomplane.example.com/setup?token=...
```

Open that link, create your account and your organization, and connect a repository. The first account owns the instance. [Quick start](/docs/quick-start#deploy-your-first-project) picks up from there.


## Run it as a service

The two units behave like any other systemd service:

```bash
systemctl status loomplane loomplane-worker
journalctl -u loomplane -u loomplane-worker -f
sudo systemctl restart loomplane
```

Change a setting by editing `/etc/loomplane/loomplane.env` and restarting both. systemd restarts either service if it exits with an error, and starts both at boot once you've enabled them.

The units lock things down. Each runs as `loomplane` with no capabilities, can't gain privileges, sees a read-only filesystem apart from its own directory under `/var/lib` and a private `/tmp`, and can't see `/home`. To change one, use a drop-in instead of editing the unit, so an upgrade doesn't overwrite it:

```bash
sudo systemctl edit loomplane
```

The `loomplane` binary has operator commands too: `migrations`, `migrate`, `backup`, `restore` and `setup-token`. Run them through the `lp` function from the setup step. Put it in root's shell profile if you'll use it often:

```bash
lp migrations
# N applied, 0 pending.
```

[Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) covers backups. With this layout, the files to keep besides the database are `/var/lib/loomplane` and `/etc/loomplane/loomplane.env`, and the secret key belongs somewhere other than those backups.

## Upgrade

### loomctl

Install the newer package over the old one (`sudo apt install ./loomctl_...deb` or `sudo dnf install ./loomctl-...rpm`), or replace the binary in `/usr/local/bin`. Your sign-in stays.

### The server

The order matters: back up, stop both services, install, start the API so it migrates, then start the worker. [Upgrades and releases](/docs/operations/upgrades-and-releases) explains why, and how to roll back.

```bash
VERSION=1.2.4   # the release you're moving to

# Back up with the version you have now, while nothing writes.
sudo systemctl stop loomplane-worker loomplane
lp backup --out /var/lib/loomplane/pre-upgrade.tar.gz
sudo cp /var/lib/loomplane/pre-upgrade.tar.gz /root/

# Download and verify the new release as above, then install it.
sudo apt install "./loomplane_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"   # or dnf install ./loomplane-...rpm

lp migrations   # shows what the new version will apply
sudo systemctl start loomplane
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8780/_/health/live && echo
sudo systemctl start loomplane-worker
```

Copy that backup off the host too. The package keeps your `loomplane.env`, and it never starts or restarts the services by itself, so nothing runs the new version until you start it.

From the archive, it's the same order. Stop both, copy the new binaries into `/usr/local/bin` and the new `dashboard` into `/usr/local/share/loomplane/`, replace `/etc/loomplane/config.yaml`, then start the API and the worker. Compare the new `systemd/` files with yours too, since a release can change them.

Loomplane won't start against a database a newer version migrated. Going back means restoring the backup you made before upgrading.

## Uninstall

### loomctl

```bash
loomctl logout
sudo apt remove loomctl        # or: sudo dnf remove loomctl
```

From the archive, `sudo rm /usr/local/bin/loomctl`. `loomctl logout` ends your session on the server and deletes the saved login under `~/.config/loomplane`.

### The server

Removing the package stops and disables both services. It leaves your data, your settings and the `loomplane` user, in case you meant to reinstall:

```bash
sudo apt remove loomplane      # or: sudo dnf remove loomplane
```

`apt purge loomplane` removes `/etc/loomplane` as well. To remove everything else, once you're sure you have the backup you want:

```bash
sudo rm -rf /var/lib/loomplane /var/lib/loomplane-work /etc/loomplane
sudo userdel loomplane
sudo -u postgres psql -c "DROP DATABASE loomplane" -c "DROP ROLE loomplane"
```

From the archive, stop and disable both services, then delete the two unit files from `/etc/systemd/system`, the binaries from `/usr/local/bin` and `/usr/local/share/loomplane`, and run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` before the commands above.

pages.title: Miget
pages.description: Run Loomplane on Miget as a Compose Stack built from this repository, with a managed PostgreSQL database.
pages.text:
You can run Loomplane on [Miget](https://miget.com) as a Compose Stack built from `deployments/miget`. Miget builds the image from the repository, so you don't need a published release. You get the API and dashboard, the analysis worker and a managed PostgreSQL database.

## Deploy

Generate a secret key first and keep it in your secret manager:

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
```

Then create the stack in Miget:

1. Choose **Compose Stack**, pick the repository and the branch you want to track, and set the compose path to `deployments/miget`.
2. On the review step Miget asks for `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` and fills in a random value. Replace it with your key. Loomplane only accepts 32 bytes encoded as base64 and won't start with anything else.
3. Pick a Resource with room for the stack. It asks for 1.5 GB of RAM (512 MB each for the API, the worker and the database), a 2 GB artifact volume and 2 GB of database storage. If analysis of a big repository runs out of memory, raise the worker's `ram` in `compose.miget.yaml` first.
4. Deploy, wait for both builds, and open the `loomplane` app's URL.

Setup needs a one-time token. The `loomplane` app logs it as a `setup is waiting` warning with a `url` field, a link that opens `/setup` with the token filled in. If the log has scrolled away, run `loomplane setup-token` in a shell on that app and it prints the link again. Then create your account and organization, and connect a repository.

Loomplane's encryption keys come from that secret, and stored credentials can't be decrypted without it, so set it once and leave it alone on later deploys.

## What Miget runs

| Service | On Miget | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `loomplane` | Public app on port 5000 | API and dashboard, with the artifact volume |
| `loomplane-worker` | Private app | Repository analysis |
| `db` | Managed PostgreSQL | Backed up daily by Miget |

`compose.miget.yaml` switches both apps to production and wires them up. The public URL comes from Miget's `${{loomplane.public_url}}` and the database URL from `${{db.url}}`, so you never type either one. If you move to a custom domain, check that both apps see it in `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL`, because sign-in redirects are built from that address.

Miget runs every Compose service as its own app and drops `entrypoint:` and `command:`, which is why the image picks its process from `LOOMPLANE_PROCESS`. It's `api` unless you set `worker`. Any other value stops the container with an error, so a typo can't quietly start a second API.

## Optional settings

The stack leaves out the GitHub App, email and recovery storage. Add them as environment variables on the Miget apps once the stack is up:

- The six `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_*` credentials go on both apps. Set them together. See [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories).
- The `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_*` SMTP settings go on `loomplane`. Production uses implicit TLS, usually on port 465.
- `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_BUCKET` go on `loomplane` if you want recovery objects off the artifact volume.

[Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker) explains each one.

## Try it locally

Plain `docker compose` ignores `compose.miget.yaml`, so you can run the same stack on your laptop in development mode, with a Postgres container standing in for the managed database:

```bash
cd deployments/miget
cp .env.example .env
# put the output of `openssl rand -base64 32` in LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY
docker compose up --build --wait
```

Open [http://localhost:5000](http://localhost:5000).

## Things to know

Miget builds the image twice, once per app, and each build compiles the dashboard and the Go binaries. Expect the first deploy to take a while.

On the first deploy the worker can start before the API has finished migrating the database. It restarts until the migrations are in, then settles.

Miget picks the PostgreSQL version for the managed database, while the production Docker stack pins PostgreSQL 17. Check which major version you got before you restore a backup from elsewhere.

Miget backs up the database every day and keeps those backups for at least seven days. It doesn't back up the artifact volume. Point `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_URL` at independent object storage if you need recovery objects to survive losing that volume.

pages.title: Monitoring
pages.description: Health checks, Prometheus metrics, live deployment state, and how to pause a target during an incident.
pages.text:
## Health

`/_/health` reports each part of Loomplane, provider plugins included. A plugin that stops answering makes it unhealthy within one check interval. `/_/health/live` and `/_/health/ready` are for your orchestrator's probes. The worker serves the same checks on its own port (`:8781` by default). Public proxies shouldn't expose these routes, and the Docker stack's Caddy blocks them.

If a database timeout stops Dispatch's durable worker, the API starts a replacement on its own: one second later at first, doubling up to thirty seconds while the database stays down. Until a replacement is polling, `/_/health` reports the dispatch extension as unhealthy and the log has a `durable workflow worker stopped` warning for each attempt. A replacement only claims tasks whose lease has run out, so a plan the failed worker had claimed picks up again once that lease expires. If the extension stays unhealthy after the database is back, restart the API.

Watch this health result in your process supervisor. A running HTTP listener doesn't tell you deployment work is moving.

## Metrics

`/_/metrics` serves Prometheus metrics: the Go runtime's, Dispatch's jobs and workflows, and Loomplane's own, prefixed `forge_loomplane_`.

| Metric | Labels | What it counts |
|---|---|---|
| `deployments_total`, `deployment_duration_seconds` | `status` | Deployments that finished, and how long they took |
| `deployment_steps_total` | `provider`, `op`, `status` | Each action of a deployment |
| `deployment_step_duration_seconds` | `provider`, `status` | How long each provider takes |
| `plans_total` | `status` | Plans worked out: ready, blocked or failed |
| `plan_decisions_total` | `decision` | Approved, rejected, stale or expired |
| `drift_findings_total` | `provider`, `state` | Bindings found missing or changed |
| `analyses_total`, `analysis_duration_seconds` | `status` | Repository analyses, from `loomplane-worker` |
| `api_key_authentications_total` | `result` | Requests with an API key, accepted or rejected |
| `connection_checks_total` | `cloud`, `result` | Credential checks: ready, incomplete, rejected or unavailable |

Alerts worth having:

- `deployment_steps_total{status="failed"}` rising for one provider, which usually means its connection lost a permission.
- `api_key_authentications_total{result="rejected"}` climbing, which is a revoked key still in a pipeline, or someone guessing.
- `drift_findings_total`, which means something changed in a cloud outside Loomplane.

## Live deployment state

Proxy `/api/v1/realtime/ws` with WebSocket upgrades and leave `/api/v1/realtime/events` unbuffered for SSE. Both use the same authenticated contracts and an organization-scoped cursor. The dashboard falls back to SSE after a WebSocket failure, then to REST recovery when the stream is stale. A **Live** badge confirms a recent status heartbeat. A page that's disconnected must not be treated as current.

Events and build output are committed in PostgreSQL before delivery. Conduit notifications wake other API replicas, which read the durable sequence. You can restart an API or deployment worker without relying on its memory for status or checkpoints. An interrupted Docker build may need rebuilding, and its earlier attempt stays visible as incomplete.

Build output is retained for seven days, with 16 KiB per line and 10 MiB per action attempt. The deployment log endpoint pages retained output. A cursor older than the retention produces a gap and a current snapshot. Collector checkpoints and cloud credentials are excluded from public events, and runtime variables stay out of Docker build arguments.

Keep a connection while a plan, build, binding or deployment references it. Changing a host key, namespace UID, CA or reviewed registry endpoint needs another connection check and plan. Rotating a credential can keep the same destination. Removal uses each binding's recorded connection and ownership labels, including resources left pending cleanup after a replacement.

## Pausing a target

To stop Loomplane deploying to a target, during an incident on a cloud for instance, name it in `providers.paused`:

```yaml
providers:
  paused: [render, cloud-run]
```

or set `LOOMPLANE_PAUSED_PROVIDERS=render,cloud-run`. Plans that use a paused target are still made, and can be reviewed and approved, but they say they're for review only, and approving one deploys nothing. What already runs there keeps running, and drift checks still read it. A name that isn't a target stops Loomplane from starting, so a typo can't leave a target running that you meant to pause. Restart Loomplane to pause or unpause one.

pages.title: Production on Docker
pages.description: Run Loomplane on one Linux host with Docker Compose, Postgres 17 and Caddy for HTTPS.
pages.text:
This stack runs one API and dashboard, one analysis worker, Postgres 17 and Caddy. It tolerates container restarts. A host failure still takes it offline, so keep backups off the host. It isn't a high-availability setup. For that, use [Production on Kubernetes](/docs/operations/production-on-kubernetes).

## Requirements

A Linux host with Docker Engine, Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer, and a hostname pointed at that host. Open TCP ports 80 and 443 for Caddy's HTTPS certificates and browser traffic. Start with 2 CPU cores, 8 GB of RAM and enough disk for your repositories, database and recovery objects, and measure your workload before you pick something smaller.

## Install

Download the Docker bundle from the GitHub release you want to run, verify its checksum against the release's `SHA256SUMS`, and extract it into `/srv/loomplane`. The bundle holds `compose.yaml`, the `Caddyfile`, `.env.example`, `image.txt` and a README. It pins `.env.example` to the image digest in `image.txt`.

You can also use `deployments/production` from a source checkout. Then choose a published image tag or digest yourself. The example version is a placeholder, not a promise that a release exists.

Run these in the directory that holds `compose.yaml`:

```bash
umask 077
cp .env.example .env
openssl rand -base64 32
openssl rand -hex 32
```

Edit `.env`. Set `LOOMPLANE_IMAGE`, `LOOMPLANE_DOMAIN` (a hostname without `https://` or a path) and `ACME_EMAIL`. Put the first generated value in `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` and the second in `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`.

The stack sets the public URL to `https://` and your domain. That URL is also the OpenID Connect issuer AWS, Google Cloud and Azure trust for [keyless connections](/docs/clouds/keyless), and they fetch `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and `/.well-known/jwks.json` from it themselves. Caddy passes both through to the API. If the hostname only resolves inside your network, everything else still works, but keyless stays off.

Keep that secret key in your secret manager. Loomplane derives encryption keys from it, and your database backup needs the original key to recover stored credentials. Generate it once, not on each deployment.

The stack passes secrets to containers through environment variables. Protect `.env` with mode 600, restrict Docker access to administrators, and don't paste `docker compose config` or `docker inspect` output into tickets, since both can reveal those values. Validate with `config --quiet`.

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240
docker compose ps
```

Open `https://YOUR_HOSTNAME`. Setup needs a one-time token, so get the link first. The API logs it as a `setup is waiting` warning with a `url` field, and `loomplane setup-token` prints the same link:

```bash
docker compose exec loomplane loomplane setup-token
# Finish setup at https://YOUR_HOSTNAME/setup?token=...
```

Open that link, create your account and organization, then connect a repository. Once setup is done the command prints `Setup is complete.` The token comes from `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY`, so it stays the same across restarts. Caddy gets and renews the certificate and forwards WebSocket and SSE traffic to the API. Health and metrics routes are blocked at the public proxy.

If GHCR requires authentication, run `docker login ghcr.io` with a token that can read the package. A newly published package may need its visibility set to public in GitHub before anonymous pulls work.

## Optional push gateway

You can run the push gateway in this stack, behind the same Caddy instance.
Use this if you operate XRaph's gateway or ship your own mobile app build.
The store app needs XRaph's push credentials, so running a gateway with your
own Firebase project or Apple key won't enable push for that app.

Point a second hostname, such as `push.example.com`, at this host. It must
be different from `LOOMPLANE_DOMAIN`. In `.env`, uncomment and set:

```dotenv
COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.push-gateway.yaml
PUSH_GATEWAY_IMAGE=ghcr.io/xraph/loomplane-push-gateway:VERSION
PUSH_GATEWAY_DOMAIN=push.example.com
PUSH_GATEWAY_SEALING_KEY_ID=k202611
```

Choose a published gateway version, preferably pinned by digest. The Docker
bundle includes `compose.push-gateway.yaml` and `Caddyfile.push-gateway`.
`COMPOSE_FILE` keeps the gateway enabled for subsequent `docker compose`
commands, including upgrades on a DigitalOcean install.

Prepare its secret files from the directory containing `compose.yaml`:

```bash
umask 077
mkdir -p secrets
openssl rand -base64 32 > secrets/sealing-key
touch secrets/previous-sealing-key secrets/apns-key.p8
cp /path/to/firebase-service-account.json secrets/fcm-service-account.json
sudo chown 10001:10001 secrets/*
sudo chmod 0400 secrets/*
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240
```

These commands start an Android gateway. For iOS, copy your Apple `.p8` key
to `secrets/apns-key.p8`, give it the same owner and permissions, and set
both `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_ID` and `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_TEAM_ID` in `.env`.
Set `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_BUNDLE_ID` when your app uses a different bundle ID.
The Compose option requires a Firebase service-account file even if you
also enable iOS. Keep the empty previous-key and Apple files when unused.

The option sets the API and workers' gateway URL to
`https://PUSH_GATEWAY_DOMAIN` and enables push. Only Caddy publishes ports
80 and 443. On the gateway hostname it exposes `/v1/registrations` and
`/v1/send`, limits request bodies to 64 KB and keeps health checks private.
Your phones and server both need to reach that hostname over HTTPS.

Back up `secrets/` securely alongside `.env`. Never regenerate the sealing
key on restart. Gateway key rotation follows the push notifications guide;
keep `COMPOSE_FILE` enabled for those commands too. After an upgrade,
restart Caddy to reload the mounted configuration. To return to the hosted
gateway, run `docker compose stop push-gateway`, remove `COMPOSE_FILE` from
`.env`, then run `docker compose up -d --remove-orphans` and
`docker compose restart caddy`. The base stack uses
`LOOMPLANE_PUSH_GATEWAY_URL`, which defaults to XRaph's gateway.

## Configuration and storage

The API runs migrations before it becomes healthy, and Compose starts the worker after that check passes. Both run as UID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, a PID limit and a temporary `/tmp`. The API gets a writable artifact volume, and the worker gets its own scratch volume for repository checkouts. Neither container gets the host's Docker socket. Connections to deployment targets use Loomplane's normal credential and approval flow.

| Volume | Contents |
|---|---|
| `postgres-data` | Accounts, credentials, jobs, deployment state and audit records |
| `artifact-data` | Deployment source artifacts and local recovery objects |
| `analysis-work` | The worker's scratch space for repository checkouts |
| `caddy-data` | TLS certificates and Caddy's certificate authority state |
| `caddy-config` | Caddy's saved runtime configuration |

One analysis can unpack up to 2 GiB of source, which is more than the 1 GiB RAM-backed `/tmp`, so checkouts go to `analysis-work` on disk. Keep a few GiB free on the host for it. The worker runs two analyses at once by default. Set `LOOMPLANE_ANALYSIS_CONCURRENCY` in `.env` to change that (the minimum is 1). Each extra analysis needs more disk and more memory, so raise the worker's `mem_limit` in `compose.yaml` along with it. The volume is only scratch space, so you don't need to back it up.

Volume names carry the Compose project prefix `loomplane-production`, so keep that project name stable across upgrades. `docker compose down` keeps the data, and `docker compose down --volumes` deletes it.

Only Caddy publishes host ports. Postgres sits on an internal Docker network. The API and worker also have outbound access for GitHub and cloud APIs. Database traffic stays on this host's Docker network with TLS disabled. If you move Postgres off the host, supply a separate Compose override with a certificate-verified database URL and remove the bundled database dependency.

Set the optional GitHub App variables together when you need private repositories ([Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories)). You can put a multiline PEM in a single-quoted `.env` value, and the webhook secret must match in Loomplane and GitHub.

Email is off until you configure SMTP. Production uses implicit TLS, usually on port 465. Verify delivery with your mail provider before you rely on account recovery.

`LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_URL` can point recovery objects at independent storage. Without it they share the local artifact volume. It doesn't schedule backups of Loomplane's own database.

## Knowledge needs pgvector

The agent's [knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge) keeps its vectors in Loomplane's own Postgres, so that Postgres needs the pgvector extension. The default `postgres:17-alpine` doesn't have it. To use knowledge, set `POSTGRES_IMAGE` in `.env` to an image that does, such as `pgvector/pgvector:pg17`, and take a [backup](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) first, because that image is Debian-based and an existing data volume can sort text differently. Loomplane creates the extension itself when `ai.enabled` and `ai.knowledge` are both set and the image has it.

Nothing changes without it. With the stock image, Loomplane starts as always and the knowledge switch stays off with a reason.

Backups follow knowledge. A backup taken with knowledge on includes its vector tables, so a restore needs a target with `ai.enabled`, `ai.knowledge` configured, pgvector available and the same `dimensions`. Otherwise the restore refuses, or fails on the dimensions. See [Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane#knowledge-and-backups).

## Check health

```bash
docker compose ps
docker compose logs --tail=100 loomplane loomplane-worker
docker compose exec -T loomplane wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8780/_/health
docker compose exec -T loomplane-worker wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8781/_/health
```

The probes include extension health, so a stalled durable worker can make a container unhealthy even while its HTTP listener answers. The API replaces a durable worker that a database timeout stopped, and turns healthy again once the replacement is polling. Docker's restart policy restarts exited processes but not a running unhealthy container. Alert on unhealthy state, find the cause, and restart the affected service after database or provider access recovers.

Logs rotate at 10 MB per file with five files per container. Send logs and metrics to your monitoring system before you need longer retention, and keep metrics access inside a trusted Docker network. See [Monitoring](/docs/operations/monitoring).

## Next

[Upgrades and releases](/docs/operations/upgrades-and-releases) covers upgrading and rolling back. [Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) covers the database backup and the artifact volume.

pages.title: Production on Kubernetes
pages.description: Run Loomplane highly available with its Helm chart, on your PostgreSQL and S3-compatible storage.
pages.text:
The Helm chart runs Loomplane with no single pod you can't lose: two API replicas and two analysis workers, spread across nodes and zones, with disruption budgets and rolling updates that never drop below the replicas you asked for. Migrations run once, before any new pod serves. You bring PostgreSQL and object storage.

## Requirements

- Kubernetes 1.27 or newer, with nodes in two zones if you want to survive losing one.
- Helm 3.8 or newer, or Helm 4.
- PostgreSQL 17 that the cluster can reach. The chart doesn't make the database highly available, so a managed or replicated one (CloudNativePG, for example) decides how available Loomplane is.
- S3-compatible storage with two buckets you create first: `loomplane-artifacts` and `loomplane-backups`. AWS S3, GCS interoperability, R2, Spaces and MinIO all work. A ReadWriteMany volume works too.
- An ingress controller or a Gateway API implementation, and a hostname.

## Install

Put the credentials in a Secret, so none of them sits in a values file or Helm's history:

```bash
kubectl create namespace loomplane
kubectl -n loomplane create secret generic loomplane \
  --from-literal=LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)" \
  --from-literal=LOOMPLANE_DATABASE_URL='postgres://loomplane:PASSWORD@db.internal:5432/loomplane?sslmode=verify-full' \
  --from-literal=LOOMPLANE_STORAGE_URL='s3://us-east-1/loomplane-artifacts'
```

Keep that secret key in your secret manager. Loomplane derives the keys that encrypt stored credentials from it, and a database backup can't recover them without it.

Write a `values.yaml`:

```yaml
publicURL: https://loomplane.example.com
secrets:
  existingSecret: loomplane
serviceAccount:
  # An S3 URL without keys uses the pod's cloud identity.
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/loomplane
ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-send-timeout: "3600"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 64m
  tls:
    - secretName: loomplane-tls
      hosts: [loomplane.example.com]
```

Install the chart from the release you want, then check it:

```bash
helm install loomplane oci://ghcr.io/xraph/charts/loomplane --version 1.2.3 \
  --namespace loomplane -f values.yaml
kubectl -n loomplane rollout status deploy/loomplane
helm test loomplane -n loomplane
```

Setup needs a one-time token. The first API pod logs it as a `setup is waiting` warning with a `url` field, and you can print the link again from any API pod:

```bash
kubectl -n loomplane exec deploy/loomplane -- loomplane setup-token
# Finish setup at https://loomplane.example.com/setup?token=...
```

Open that link and create the first account. It owns the instance.

The proxy buffering and timeout annotations matter: the dashboard streams live events over server-sent events and a WebSocket. The chart also sends `/_/health`, `/_/metrics` and `/debug` to a Service with no pods, so the public ingress refuses them. Prefer the Gateway API? Set `httpRoute.enabled` and `httpRoute.parentRefs` instead of `ingress`.

`publicURL` is also the OpenID Connect issuer that AWS, Google Cloud and Azure trust for [keyless connections](/docs/clouds/keyless). They fetch `/.well-known/openid-configuration` and `/.well-known/jwks.json` from it over the internet, so keep it HTTPS on a hostname they can reach, and let `/.well-known/` through to the API if you put anything in front of the ingress. Every replica serves the same keys from the database.

## What survives what

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| An API pod crashes | The other replica serves while it's replaced. |
| A worker dies mid-analysis | Its job goes back on the queue after 30 seconds and another worker takes it, without using a retry. |
| A node drains | Disruption budgets let one API pod and one worker go at a time. |
| A zone fails | Spread constraints keep a replica in each zone you have. |
| An upgrade | New pods migrate under a lock, then replace old ones one at a time. A failed migration stops the rollout and the old pods keep serving. |
| PostgreSQL goes down | Loomplane goes down with it. |

Replicas share everything through PostgreSQL. Jobs are leased to one worker at a time, Ctrl Plane's scheduler runs on one elected API pod, sessions and rate limits live in the database, and live events reach every pod through `pg_notify`. You don't need sticky sessions.

## Upgrades

Take a [backup](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane) first, then upgrade:

```bash
helm upgrade loomplane oci://ghcr.io/xraph/charts/loomplane --version 1.2.4 \
  -n loomplane -f values.yaml
```

Migrations only go forward, and an older Loomplane refuses a database a newer one migrated. After an upgrade that migrated, `helm rollback` won't start the old version: restore your backup instead. When a release's notes ask for downtime, set `api.strategy.type` and `worker.strategy.type` to `Recreate` for that upgrade.

## Knowledge needs pgvector

The agent's [knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge) keeps its vectors in Loomplane's own Postgres, so that database needs the pgvector extension. Use an image that ships it, such as `pgvector/pgvector:pg17` (or the same for CloudNativePG), or run `CREATE EXTENSION vector` on a managed Postgres that offers it. Set `ai.enabled` and `ai.knowledge` and Loomplane creates its vector table at start. Nothing changes without pgvector: Loomplane starts as always and the knowledge switch stays off with a reason.

A backup taken with knowledge on includes its vector tables. Restoring it needs a target with `ai.enabled`, `ai.knowledge` configured, pgvector available and the same `dimensions`, or the restore refuses or fails on the dimensions. See [Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane#knowledge-and-backups).

## Sizing

Each API pod opens a little over 20 database connections and each worker about 16, so set PostgreSQL's `max_connections` for your replicas plus one extra of each during a rollout. Workers unpack repositories into an 8 GiB scratch volume by default (`worker.tmpSize`), because one analysis can take 2 GiB and a worker runs two at once. Turn on `api.autoscaling` and `worker.autoscaling` to scale on CPU.

Set `metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` to have the Prometheus Operator scrape `/_/metrics` on both processes.

## Deploying into the same cluster

You can let people deploy to the cluster Loomplane runs in, with no kubeconfig to paste. List the namespaces it may use:

```yaml
inCluster:
  enabled: true
  namespaces: [apps, preview]
  createNamespaces: true
```

The chart mounts the service account token in the API pods only, and binds a Role in each namespace with what a [Kubernetes connection](/docs/clouds/your-own-servers#the-cluster-loomplane-runs-in) checks for. The Kubernetes dialog under **Integrations** then opens on this cluster.

Every organization on your instance shares that service account, so any of them can deploy into any namespace you list. That's right for a single-team install. On a shared one, leave it off and hand out kubeconfigs scoped per team. Loomplane always refuses its own namespace, where its database password and secret key live, and `kube-system`, `kube-public` and `kube-node-lease` too.

`inCluster.clusterPermissions` (on by default) adds the cluster-wide reads that GPU inventory and retained storage need, plus updating persistent volumes so a database's volume survives recovery. Without it, those show as unavailable and plain deployments still work.

## Without Helm

Each release attaches `loomplane-VERSION-kubernetes.yaml`, the chart rendered for `kubectl apply` with an ingress-nginx Ingress. Create the Secret above, replace `loomplane.example.com`, and apply it.

## Optional push gateway

Set `push.gateway.enabled=true` to deploy a gateway alongside the API and
workers. Supply its own Secret, a published gateway image version and a
public HTTPS hostname in `push.gatewayUrl`. The chart can create an Ingress
or HTTPRoute that publishes only the two push routes. See the
[push notifications guide](https://loomplane.dev/docs/operations/push-notifications#alongside-loomplane)
for a configuration example, TLS and key rotation. Hosting a gateway requires
push credentials for the mobile app you ship.

pages.title: Push notifications
pages.description: How the Loomplane app gets alerts and approvals from a self-hosted server through XRaph's push gateway, and how to run a gateway of your own.
pages.text:
The Loomplane app gets alerts and approvals from any self-hosted server through XRaph's push gateway at `push.loomplane.com`. You have nothing to install on your side. Turn push on, make sure the server can reach the gateway, and pair the app as usual.

## What the gateway sees

The gateway is a relay. A Loomplane server sends it a message, it hands that to Apple or Google, and they deliver it to the phone. For each send it sees:

- the sending server's public key fingerprint,
- the platform (`android` or `ios`) and the kind of send (`show` or `withdraw`),
- the phone's push token, inside the gateway's own sealed handle,
- the urgency,
- an opaque collapse ID,
- the TTL,
- an encrypted payload it can't open (HPKE to a key only the phone holds).

It never sees your workspace, project, titles, bodies or actions. On iOS the phone first shows a generic placeholder (title "Loomplane", body "New notification") and swaps in the real text after it decrypts the payload. Android gets a data-only message, and the app builds the notification itself once it decrypts.

The gateway stores nothing. It has no database and no volume. Its logs carry the server key fingerprint, the platform, the urgency, the kind of send, the outcome and the latency, and no handle, token or payload. The source is open under [`cmd/loomplane-push-gateway`](https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/tree/main/cmd/loomplane-push-gateway) in the Loomplane repository.

## On your server

Two settings control push:

| Setting | Environment variable | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `push.enabled` | `LOOMPLANE_PUSH_ENABLED` | `true` |
| `push.gateway_url` | `LOOMPLANE_PUSH_GATEWAY_URL` | `https://push.loomplane.com` |

The gateway URL must be `https`. The one exception is a gateway on your own machine (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `::1`), where plain `http` is accepted only when the server runs in development. Anywhere else the server rejects an `http` URL.

The server needs outbound HTTPS to the gateway's host, and nothing inbound. With push off, the app says so and hides its push settings. The inbox and email keep working.

A gateway outage loses nothing. The server's outbox retries, and the inbox has every item whether or not a push got through. Here is what the server hears back from a send:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `202` | Accepted and handed to Apple or Google. |
| `400` | The request is malformed. |
| `401` | The signature is missing or wrong, it is more than 300 seconds off the gateway's clock, or the handle was issued to a different server key. |
| `410` | The handle is retired or the platform says the token is dead. The server deletes that device, and the app registers again on its next launch. |
| `429` | You're over a limit. `Retry-After` says when to try again. |
| `502` | Apple or Google refused the push, or the platform isn't one this gateway serves. |

Two limits apply. Each server key gets 50 sends per second. Each device (platform plus token) gets 30 sends per minute, so a phone that registers again doesn't start with a fresh budget.

You can't point the store version of the app at your own gateway. Apple and Google tie push to the app's signing identity, and only XRaph holds the keys for the store build.

## Running the gateway

You only need this if you work for XRaph or you ship your own build of the app, with your own Firebase project and APNs key. If you run a server, you can stop reading here.

The gateway reads `PUSH_GATEWAY_*` environment variables. Secrets come in only as files named by `*_FILE` variables, mounted as Docker secrets. There's no way to pass a secret as a value.

### Configuration

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_ADDR` | `:8790` | Listen address inside the container. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_SEALING_KEY_ID` | none, required | Name of the current sealing key, 1 to 32 letters, digits, `-` or `_`. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_SEALING_KEY_FILE` | none, required | File holding 32 random bytes in base64 (`openssl rand -base64 32`). |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_PREVIOUS_SEALING_KEY_ID` | unset | ID of the key you rotated away from. Set it with its file, never alone. Must differ from the current ID. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_PREVIOUS_SEALING_KEY_FILE` | unset | File holding the previous key. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_FCM_CREDENTIALS_FILE` | unset | Firebase service-account JSON. Turns Android on. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_FCM_BASE_URL` | Google's endpoint | Tests only. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_FILE` | unset | Apple `.p8` key. Turns iOS on. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_ID` | none | The 10-character key ID from Apple. Needed with the key file. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_TEAM_ID` | none | The 10-character team ID from Apple. Needed with the key file. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_BUNDLE_ID` | `com.loomplane.app` | The app's bundle ID. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_BASE_URL` | Apple's endpoint | Tests only. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_SERVER_RATE` | `50` | Sends per second per server key. |
| `PUSH_GATEWAY_HANDLE_RATE` | `30` | Sends per minute per device (platform and token). The name is older than the behavior. |

The gateway needs at least one of the two platform key files. It refuses to start when a platform's variable is set without that platform's key file: `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_ID`, `_TEAM_ID`, `_BUNDLE_ID` or `_BASE_URL` without `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_FILE`, or `PUSH_GATEWAY_FCM_BASE_URL` without `PUSH_GATEWAY_FCM_CREDENTIALS_FILE`. That's on purpose, so a typo in a file variable fails at start instead of quietly turning a platform off. To turn a platform off, unset all of its variables.

The two `*_BASE_URL` variables exist for tests. The gateway logs a warning at start when one is set.

### Alongside Loomplane

For a single host, [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker#optional-push-gateway)
includes an opt-in gateway in the same Compose project as Loomplane and its
workers. You set `COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.push-gateway.yaml`, supply
the gateway hostname and key files, and Caddy serves both hostnames on the
same ports. Normal installs continue to use XRaph's hosted gateway.

With Helm, enable `push.gateway.enabled`. The chart deploys a separate
workload and ClusterIP Service, and optionally an Ingress or HTTPRoute.
Set `push.gatewayUrl` to its public HTTPS address. A gateway needs a
hostname different from the dashboard because its public proxy serves
only the two push routes.

Create a Secret in the release namespace. Keep these files outside git:

```bash
kubectl -n loomplane create secret generic loomplane-push \
  --from-file=sealing-key=./secrets/sealing-key \
  --from-file=fcm-service-account.json=./secrets/fcm-service-account.json
```

Add these values to your existing Helm configuration:

```yaml
push:
  gatewayUrl: https://push.example.com
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    image:
      tag: VERSION # Use a published gateway tag, or set digest instead.
    existingSecret: loomplane-push
    sealingKeyId: k202611
    ingress:
      enabled: true
      className: nginx
      annotations:
        nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: 64k
      tls:
        - secretName: push-tls
          hosts: [push.example.com]
```

Provision the TLS certificate through your ingress controller or certificate
manager. You can use `push.gateway.httpRoute.enabled` with `parentRefs`
instead, attached to a Gateway with an HTTPS listener and a certificate for
the push hostname. If you manage the proxy separately, leave both route
options off and forward only `/v1/registrations` and `/v1/send` to the
`<release>-push-gateway` Service on port 8790. Keep `/_/health` private and
configure a 64 KB request limit at your proxy.

For Traefik, enable TLS on the HTTPS entry point (or set the ingress
`traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.tls` annotation to `"true"`). When you
also use the chart's dashboard ingress with `blockInternalPaths=true`, set
Traefik's `providers.kubernetesIngress.allowEmptyServices=true`. That keeps
the blocked health and metrics routes active even though their target
Service has no endpoints. The gateway itself uses exact route matches for
its two public paths.

The gateway mounts only its own Secret. API and worker pods do not mount
it, and the gateway does not receive their database or encryption settings.
For iOS, add `apns-key.p8` to the Secret, enable `push.gateway.apns.enabled`
and set its `keyId`, `teamId` and `bundleId`. You can turn off FCM with
`push.gateway.fcm.enabled=false` for an iOS-only Kubernetes gateway.

The gateway reads keys at startup. After changing the Secret, restart its
Deployment with `kubectl -n loomplane rollout restart deploy/loomplane-push-gateway`
(use your release's name). During rotation, include `previous-sealing-key`
and set `push.gateway.previousSealingKeyId` in the same upgrade. Every
replica must use the same keys and IDs. Rate limits apply per replica, so
keep the default single replica unless you account for the larger total.

Hosting the gateway requires credentials for the mobile app you ship. Verify
registration and a real notification on each enabled phone platform after
you configure DNS, TLS and those credentials.

### Setup

The stack lives in `deployments/push-gateway`: the gateway, and Caddy in front of it for TLS. Only Caddy keeps state (its certificates). Run this from that directory:

```bash
umask 077
mkdir secrets
openssl rand -base64 32 > secrets/sealing-key
touch secrets/previous-sealing-key secrets/apns-key.p8
cp /path/to/firebase-service-account.json secrets/fcm-service-account.json
cp /path/to/AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 secrets/apns-key.p8
sudo chown 10001:10001 secrets/*
sudo chmod 0400 secrets/*
cp .env.example .env
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose up -d --wait
```

Compose wants every secret file to exist, so the `touch` creates empty ones for what you don't use. An empty file stays unused until its ID is set in `.env`. Skip the `.p8` copy if you're running Android only.

The container runs as uid 10001, and Compose bind-mounts each secret with the host's ownership. A file that user can't read stops the gateway from starting. The `chown` and `chmod` above handle it, and they need `sudo` because only root can hand a file to another user. `chmod 0444` works too if you can't `chown`.

Edit `.env` before you start. Set `PUSH_GATEWAY_IMAGE` to the gateway image pinned by the digest from the release summary (`ghcr.io/xraph/loomplane-push-gateway@sha256:...`), not a bare tag, `PUSH_GATEWAY_DOMAIN` to your hostname, `ACME_EMAIL` to an address for certificate notices, and `PUSH_GATEWAY_SEALING_KEY_ID` to a name for your key. The Compose file turns iOS on only once `PUSH_GATEWAY_APNS_KEY_ID` is set, so keep that and the team ID together.

Caddy serves only `/v1/registrations` and `/v1/send`, and answers 404 for everything else. The gateway's health check stays inside the Docker network.

Keep the host's clock synced. The gateway refuses signatures more than 300 seconds off its own time.

### Rotating the sealing key

Every device handle is sealed under a key the gateway holds. To rotate it:

1. Pick a new key ID you have never used, such as `k202702`. Don't reuse an old one: the gateway answers `410` only for an ID it doesn't know, and a known ID with different key bytes gets `400` forever, so those devices never re-register.
2. Stop the gateway: `docker compose stop push-gateway`.
3. Move the current key file aside: `mv -f secrets/sealing-key secrets/previous-sealing-key`. The old file is owned by uid 10001 with mode 0400, so `-f` is what lets it replace the empty one. Put the old ID in `PUSH_GATEWAY_PREVIOUS_SEALING_KEY_ID`.
4. Write the new key: `(umask 077; openssl rand -base64 32 > secrets/sealing-key)`.
5. Give the new file the same owner and mode as in Setup: `sudo chown 10001:10001 secrets/sealing-key` and `sudo chmod 0400 secrets/sealing-key`. Without that, uid 10001 can't read it and the gateway won't start.
6. Set the new ID in `PUSH_GATEWAY_SEALING_KEY_ID` in `.env`.
7. Run `docker compose up -d`.

If you rotate again inside the 90 days, the older key drops out early, because only one previous key is kept. Devices sealed under it get `410` and register again.

Keep the previous key for 90 days. That gives apps time to register again. After that, empty it with `sudo truncate -s 0 secrets/previous-sealing-key` (keep the file, Compose wants it), clear its ID, and run `docker compose up -d` again. Phones that registered during the window carry on. A phone whose handle was sealed under a key the gateway no longer holds gets `410`, its server drops the device, and the app registers again on its next launch.

## Local deployment checks

Run `make test-push-kubernetes` to build both images and install the chart
in a disposable kind cluster. The test covers API and worker startup,
HTTPS through both Ingress and Gateway API, registration and an encrypted
notification sent from Loomplane to a local provider fixture. It also
checks key mounts, gateway pod replacement, sealing-key rotation and
turning the bundled gateway off. It creates its own kubeconfig and deletes
its cluster when it finishes.

`make test-digitalocean` exercises the Ubuntu installer and upgrade with
the gateway enabled, checks that key permissions and configuration survive,
and runs the installed release bundle locally. You need Docker, Python 3,
OpenSSL, curl and jq; the Kubernetes check also needs kind, kubectl and Helm.
These checks use generated test keys. Verify actual phone delivery after
you configure your own DNS, TLS and Apple or Firebase credentials.

pages.title: Security model
pages.description: Who can do what, where every secret lives, what runs where, and how Loomplane is tested.
pages.text:
Loomplane holds credentials to your clouds and deploys code to them, so it's worth knowing exactly what it protects, how, and what it leaves to you. To report a vulnerability, see `SECURITY.md` in the repository.

## Who can do what

Everything belongs to an organization, and every request acts in one. The organization comes from the signed-in session or the API key, and nothing in the request can change it. Another organization's projects, plans, deployments, connections, variables and keys aren't found, the same answer as something that doesn't exist, so an ID never confirms anything.

Roles are checked on every action. Approving is the line that matters: a developer can plan anything, and only an admin's approval of the exact revision they reviewed changes a cloud. An approval of a plan whose world changed since comes back stale. [Roles and permissions](/docs/reference/roles-and-permissions) has the full list.

An API key acts as the member who made it, with their role, and never more. A read-only key fails every permission that isn't a read, keys can't manage keys, and they lose rights when a member loses a role. Every key expires within a year. Keysmith stores a hash, and the key shows once.

## Where secrets live

| What | Where | Who can read it back |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud credentials | Vault, encrypted with a key derived from `secret_key` | Deployments, in memory, to call the cloud |
| Secret variables | Vault, likewise | Deployments, to hand to the cloud's secret store |
| Database passwords Loomplane generates | Vault, under a key of their own | Deployments, to build the address services get |
| API keys | Keysmith, as hashes | Nobody |
| Passwords | authsome, as bcrypt hashes | Nobody |
| SMTP credentials | Herald, encrypted with a purpose-specific key derived from `secret_key` | The delivery engine only |
| Webhook signing secrets | Relay store wrapper, encrypted with a separate derived key | The signer. One-time response on create or rotation |
| Keyless signing keys | Vault, under an app of their own, encrypted with a key derived from `secret_key` | The issuer, to sign tokens. Only the public halves are published |
| The Hugging Face token | Vault, under `loomplane-ai-credentials`, encrypted with a key of its own derived from `secret_key` | Loomplane, to call Hugging Face, and the engine of a gated model, through a file only it reads |
| Model API keys | Vault, like generated database passwords | Deployments, to hand to the model's guard, its engine and the services that link to it |

Read APIs never return stored credential values. New API keys and webhook signing secrets appear once, when you create or rotate them. The audit trail records key names and the last four characters of an API key, never a value.

Secrets reach a service through the cloud's own secret store: Secret Manager on Cloud Run, Secrets Manager on ECS, sensitive variables on Vercel. Each is readable by that service's runtime identity only. They never pass through Ctrl Plane, which stores what it's given as plain JSON.

Everything depends on `secret_key`. Keep it out of the repository and away from your backups. Losing it loses every credential and secret, and leaking it together with a copy of the database exposes them.

## Keyless signing keys

For a [keyless connection](/docs/clouds/keyless), Loomplane is an OpenID Connect issuer at your public URL, and AWS, Google Cloud or Azure trust the tokens it signs. Nothing about such a connection is a secret you'd store, but the signing keys are, because whoever holds one can act as every keyless connection.

The keys are 2048-bit RSA and sign with RS256. A new one is made every 30 days and published a day before it signs, and the old one stays published for a day after it retires, so a cloud's cached copy always has the key in use. The private halves stay in Vault. Discovery and the JWKS at `/.well-known/` carry public keys only and need no session.

A token lasts 10 minutes and names one connection in its subject, `org:{organization ID}:connection:{connection ID}`, which the cloud's trust has to match exactly. Loomplane signs only when it's handed a ticket the issuer made for that subject and audience, and a credential you paste that's shaped like a keyless handout is refused before it gets that far. Neither a token nor a ticket ever reaches an API response, a log or the audit trail.

## Models

Each model Loomplane deploys runs as two containers: an inference engine and a guard in front of it. The engine listens only on the environment's private network, and its port is never routed. The guard is a Caddy server whose port is the only one that can be. It answers `/health` to anyone, so probes need no key, and refuses every other request with a 401 unless it carries `Authorization: Bearer` and the model's key. Its admin API is off and it has no log directive, so nothing writes a request's `Authorization` header anywhere.

The key is 32 random bytes, base64url, starting `lpm_`, generated per model. Linked services get it as `MODEL_API_KEY`, the guard reads it from its environment, and vLLM and llama.cpp get it too, so they refuse a request without it even from inside the network. The Text Embeddings Inference engine isn't given the key, so for those models the guard is the only check. No API response, page or log shows the key.

The workspace's Hugging Face token is write-only. Saving it checks it with Hugging Face first. Its value goes to Vault, under the `loomplane-ai-credentials` app with a key label (`loomplane/vault ai credentials v1`) no other Vault app shares, and the database keeps only `hf_…` with its last four characters, the account it belongs to and when it was set. It never appears in an API response, a plan, a log, an error or the audit trail, which records the account and the token's revision. Only admins (`ai:manage`) can set or remove it, and removing it is refused while a deployed gated model still downloads with it.

Loomplane sends the token only to the Hugging Face host in `ai.models.huggingface_url`, which must be https unless it's a loopback address. Every redirect off that host is refused, except a file download to Hugging Face's own CDNs, which goes without the token. A pasted repo is read anonymously first. When a gated model deploys, the token goes into the engine's `/etc/loomplane/hf/token` (mode 0400) and nowhere else: not an argument, not a variable a plan records. The engine exports it as `HF_TOKEN` to its own process and downloads from the same host, `huggingface.co` or the mirror in `ai.models.huggingface_url`. A plan records only the token's revision, so a new token shows as an update. Anyone with Docker access to that server, or who can read Secrets in that namespace on Kubernetes, can read the file.

Models pasted from Hugging Face never run their repository's own code. A registry entry may, but only code reviewed at the commit the entry pins, and nothing a manifest sets can turn it on.

## What runs where

Nothing from a repository runs on a Loomplane machine. Analysis only reads files, in pure Go parsers behind size and file-count limits, in a worker that holds no sessions. Builds run on the clouds' own builders (Cloud Build, CodeBuild, Vercel and so on), in your accounts. Gateways and provider plugins run on your infrastructure, and application traffic never passes through Loomplane.

Provider plugins are trusted with the credentials of the cloud they deploy to, so only configure ones you run or trust. Each needs its own token, and a plugin refuses any request without it.

## Nodes

A node is a machine you joined with `loomctl node join`. It dials out to Loomplane over one WebSocket and opens no inbound port. It proves who it is with its own Ed25519 key, which stays in its state directory (`/var/lib/loomplane-node` on Linux). Every join makes a fresh key and signs the join request with it, so nobody holding a token can claim another machine's public key. Loomplane refuses a key it has seen before, revoked nodes included. Your API key is used once to mint a single-use join token, and the machine never stores it. Only an owner's or admin's write key, or a session, can mint one. The install command carries the token in an environment variable, so it never shows in the process list.

What a node can do is whatever its allowlist says, and the allowlist can only get smaller from Loomplane's side. Widening it takes `sudo loomctl node allow` on the machine itself. On a Linux service the most the node may serve lives in `allow.json`, which belongs to root, and the binary the service runs belongs to root too. The service runs as its own user, which can read both and change neither, so a bug in the node can't widen its own allowlist or replace itself. That holds until you allow `docker`: the Docker socket is root's, so `node allow docker` puts the service user in the `docker` group and it is then effectively root on that machine. Narrowing `docker` from Loomplane stops the node using it but doesn't take the group back. Run `sudo gpasswd -d loomplane-node docker` on the machine for that. Today only `probe` does anything, which reports what the machine has. No message from Loomplane can add an endpoint to the list.

The ingress mode is the exception: you set it in the dashboard, and it will decide whether public traffic reaches the node once domain routing to nodes arrives. Nothing serves `public` on a node yet.

Access to the Docker socket is root access on that host, so allow `docker` only on machines you'd let Loomplane administer.

Revoking a node, from the dashboard, with `loomctl node revoke`, or with `node leave` on the machine, ends its trust. A node that was off at the time is told at its next connect, once its signature checks out, and stops. Revoking an API key as compromised lists the nodes that joined with a token it made and offers to revoke them. Releases are signed with cosign keyless, and `node update` verifies one before replacing the binary. [Nodes](/docs/clouds/nodes) has the steps.

## Private repositories

For a private repository the worker mints a GitHub App installation token limited to that one repository and to reading its contents, and stores it nowhere. An organization's analyses only use installations that organization connected, and connecting one needs GitHub to confirm the person connecting can see it. See [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories).

## Recovery email and outgoing notifications

Authsome creates, expires and consumes recovery tokens and revokes existing sessions after a password reset. Loomplane fences redemption with a PostgreSQL advisory lock, because the pinned Authsome otherwise allows simultaneous redemption. Each API admits one reset operation at a time on a dedicated, bounded database connection, so waiting reset requests can't use up the application pool. Conflicting requests return 429.

Recovery links use the configured public URL. Browser pages set `no-referrer`, and reset tokens never enter notification history or audit metadata. Provider error details become a fixed delivery failure message.

Deployment payloads contain allowlisted IDs, status, attempt and an application link, and exclude build logs, variables and raw provider errors. Delayed mail and inbox reads check current project access and organization membership. The outbound HTTP transport blocks private and reserved DNS results, dials only validated addresses, verifies TLS and refuses redirects. [Notifications and webhooks](/docs/guides/notifications-and-webhooks) covers the details.

## How it's tested

- Every route's authorization: an integration test asks for each of an organization's things from another organization, as a developer, as a viewer and with a member's key, and fails on anything that isn't refused.
- Fuzzing for what reads input anyone can send: the manifest parser, repository analysis, the credential parsers and the code that repacks a repository's tarball, which mustn't write a file outside its directory. `make fuzz` runs each for 30 seconds.
- Known vulnerabilities: `make vuln`, and CI on every push, run govulncheck against Loomplane's code and everything it imports. The Go toolchain is pinned in `go.mod` to a release with every standard library fix.
- Static analysis: golangci-lint with gosec, on every push.
- Secrets in tests: integration tests check that secrets reach the cloud's secret store and never a task definition, a list response or the CLI's output.

pages.title: Upgrades and releases
pages.description: Upgrade a running Loomplane safely, roll back with a backup, and build and publish versioned releases.
pages.text:
## Upgrade

The order matters: back up, stop both writers, swap the image, start the API, then the worker.

1. Back up ([Backing up Loomplane](/docs/operations/backing-up-loomplane)).
2. Stop `loomplane` and `loomplane-worker`.
3. Replace the binaries, the package or the image. [Install on Linux](/docs/operations/linux#upgrade) has the commands for a `.deb`, an `.rpm` or an archive.
4. Start `loomplane`. It applies new migrations before it starts serving.
5. Start `loomplane-worker`.

```bash
loomplane migrations
```

shows how many migrations the database has and which are pending, before you start. `loomplane migrate` applies them without starting the server, if you'd rather do that step alone.

Loomplane won't start against a database a newer Loomplane migrated, because it would read and write a schema it doesn't know. Going back a version means restoring the backup you made before upgrading. In development it only warns, since branches share a local database. Migrations only move forward. Each is written to be safe to run again, and none is edited after release. A fix is a new migration.

### With the Docker stack

Before an upgrade, stop both writers, take a backup with the currently installed image and copy it off the host:

```bash
umask 077
mkdir -p backups
docker compose stop loomplane-worker loomplane
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -v "$PWD/backups:/backups" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  loomplane backup --out /backups/pre-upgrade.tar.gz
```

Back up `artifact-data` while the API is stopped, using your volume backup tool. Record the current image digest and keep the old Compose files and `.env`. Replace the deployment files with the next release bundle, change only `LOOMPLANE_IMAGE` in your existing `.env`, then:

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240
docker compose exec -T loomplane loomplane migrations
```

Check sign-in, a repository analysis and a deployment's live status. Take a fresh backup before you retry an upgrade that partly ran.

### Rolling back

Changing the image back is safe only when the schema is compatible. To recover from an incompatible upgrade, stop both application services, use the previous image with a new empty database volume, and restore your pre-upgrade backup:

```bash
# Point compose.yaml at the recovery database volume before running this.
docker compose up -d --wait postgres
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -v "$PWD/backups:/backups:ro" --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  loomplane restore /backups/pre-upgrade.tar.gz
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240
```

Restore the matching artifact data and the original secret key too. Keep the failed database volume until you've verified the restore, and test this on a separate host before your first upgrade.

### Cloud and server migrations

When an upgrade touches routing or server tables, stop every older app and worker binary before you run migrations and start only upgraded binaries afterward. Mixed versions with unfenced writers aren't supported.

Migration `native_point_creation_identity` keeps native cloud snapshot points at full nanosecond precision. Allow time for the table rewrite and its exclusive lock, and stop older processes first, since their writes use the previous uniqueness constraint. Downgrade refuses while any native point history remains.

## Versions

When building from source, use `make build VERSION=your-version`, or `make build-cli VERSION=your-version` for `loomctl` alone. The API, worker and CLI share `internal/buildinfo.Version`. For custom build scripts, pass `-ldflags "-X github.com/xraph/loomplane/internal/buildinfo.Version=your-version"`.

## Build and test your own image

From the repository root:

```bash
make image VERSION=v0.1.0
bash scripts/test-production.sh loomplane:v0.1.0
```

The test creates a unique Compose project with random credentials, a local TLS certificate and a random loopback port. It checks the dashboard, authentication, blocked public health routes, extension probes, database backup and persistence across container recreation, then removes only that project's containers and volumes. Public certificate issuance, mail delivery, GitHub App installation and real cloud deployment need separate live checks.

## Publish a release

Push a `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tag that's on `main`, or run the Release workflow from the Actions tab with the version you want. A manual run tags the commit you started it from, so start it from `main`:

```bash
gh workflow run release.yml --ref main -f version=v1.2.3
```

Prerelease suffixes such as `-rc.1` are accepted. The workflow runs lint, unit and integration tests, creates the GitHub release, then builds and smoke-tests native AMD64 and ARM64 images. Both must pass before the multi-platform tag is published to `ghcr.io/xraph/loomplane` with provenance and SBOM attestations.

The workflow attaches a Docker deployment bundle, its checksum, manifest details and the immutable image reference to the release. A release of `v1.2.3` publishes `v1.2.3` and `1.2.3`, and moves `1.2`, `1` and `latest` only while it's the newest release in each of those lines. Rerunning or patching an older release can't drag `latest` backwards, and a prerelease moves nothing. A `0.x` release skips the major tag. To see what a tag would publish:

```bash
bash scripts/release-image-tags.sh v1.2.3
```

Pin the exact version or the digest from `image.txt` in production. The moving tags are for trying things out. Wait for the workflow to finish before you announce an image. Your repository needs Actions enabled, Linux ARM64 runner access and permission to write GHCR packages. With the `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` secrets, every tag is mirrored to Docker Hub as well.

GoReleaser attaches binaries to the same release. `loomctl` ships for macOS, Linux and Windows and installs with `brew install xraph/tap/loomctl` or from the `xraph` Scoop bucket. The `loomplane_*` archives carry the API, the worker, `config.yaml` and the built dashboard for Linux and macOS, and the Linux ones add the systemd units. Unpack one, set `LOOMPLANE_DASHBOARD_DIR=./dashboard` and run `./loomplane` from that directory. For Linux on amd64 and arm64 it also builds a `.deb` and an `.rpm` of each, `loomctl` and `loomplane`, which [Install on Linux](/docs/operations/linux) uses. `binaries-checksums.txt` lists every one of these files, and the release workflow signs it.

The units and the package scripts live in `deployments/linux`. To build the archives and packages without publishing anything:

```bash
goreleaser release --snapshot --clean --skip=docker,homebrew,scoop,publish
```

They land in `dist/`. Homebrew and Scoop update only when the repository has a `HOMEBREW_TAP_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret that can push to `xraph/homebrew-tap` and `xraph/scoop-bucket`. Without it, the archives still publish.

When one part of a release fails you don't need a new version. Run the workflow again with the same version and set `target` to `cli` or `docker`. Only that part publishes, from the existing tag, into the existing release. Tick `skip-tests` if the tag already passed them:

```bash
gh workflow run release.yml -f version=v1.2.3 -f target=docker -f skip-tests=true
```

You don't need a release to run the latest code. Once CI passes on `main`, the Docker workflow publishes AMD64 and ARM64 images as `ghcr.io/xraph/loomplane:main`, which moves with `main`, and `ghcr.io/xraph/loomplane:sha-<commit>`, which never moves. Pin the `sha-` tag in `LOOMPLANE_IMAGE` so a restart doesn't pull a build you haven't read. Those images skip the release checks and the ARM64 smoke test, so keep them for staging and early trials.

pages.title: Quick start
pages.description: Install Loomplane on a Linux host with Docker, install loomctl, and deploy your first project.
pages.text:
This page gets a production Loomplane running and a first project deployed. If you only want to try it on your laptop, jump to [Develop Loomplane locally](#develop-loomplane-locally). To run it under systemd from a `.deb` or `.rpm` without Docker, follow [Install on Linux](/docs/operations/linux).

## Install with Docker

You need a Linux host with Docker Engine, Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer, and a hostname pointed at that host. Open TCP ports 80 and 443, because Caddy uses them for HTTPS certificates and browser traffic. Start with 2 CPU cores and 8 GB of RAM, plus enough disk for your repositories, database and recovery objects. Measure your own workload before you pick something smaller.


### Download the release bundle

Download the Docker bundle (`loomplane-<tag>-docker.tar.gz`) from the [GitHub release](https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/releases) you want to run. Check it against the release's `SHA256SUMS`, then extract it into `/srv/loomplane`. The bundle pins `.env.example` to an image digest, which `image.txt` also records.


### Fill in `.env`

Run these from the directory that holds `compose.yaml`:

```bash
umask 077
cp .env.example .env
openssl rand -base64 32
openssl rand -hex 32
```

Edit `.env`. Set `LOOMPLANE_DOMAIN` to a bare hostname (no `https://`, no path) and `ACME_EMAIL` to an address Let's Encrypt can reach. Put the first generated value in `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` and the second in `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`. `LOOMPLANE_IMAGE` is already pinned by the bundle.


### Start it

```bash
docker compose config --quiet
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d --wait --wait-timeout 240
docker compose ps
```

Open `https://YOUR_HOSTNAME`, create an account and name your organization. Caddy gets and renews the certificate for you.


  `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` encrypts every cloud credential and secret you store. Generate it once, keep it in your secret manager, and keep it away from your backups. Lose it and you lose every credential. [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker) covers the rest of this stack.

## Install loomctl

`loomctl` is the command-line client. It also serves the MCP server for AI agents.


```bash
brew install xraph/tap/loomctl
```


Each release has a `.deb` and an `.rpm` for amd64 and arm64. On Debian or Ubuntu, with `VERSION` set to the release you want (`1.2.3`, no `v`):

```bash
ARCH=$(dpkg --print-architecture)
curl -fsSLO "https://github.com/xraph/loomplane/releases/download/v$VERSION/loomctl_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
sudo apt install "./loomctl_${VERSION}_${ARCH}.deb"
```

[Install on Linux](/docs/operations/linux#install-loomctl) has the rpm, the plain archive and how to verify the download.


Install it from the `xraph` Scoop bucket.


Each GitHub release carries `loomctl_<version>_<os>_<arch>` archives for macOS, Linux and Windows.


## Deploy your first project


### Create a project

In the dashboard choose **New project** and give it a GitHub or GitLab URL. Any public monorepo works as is. Private ones need a GitHub App or a GitLab sign-in, which [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories) and [GitLab repositories](/docs/guides/gitlab-repositories) set up.


### Analyze it

Choose **Analyze**. You get the services it builds, the packages they share and the databases they need, each one linked to the line it came from.


### Save a manifest

Open **Deploy**. Loomplane drafts a `loomplane.yaml`. Edit it if you want to, and save it. Every field is in the [manifest reference](/docs/reference/loomplane-yaml).


### Connect your clouds

Under **Integrations**, connect the clouds the manifest names. Each credential is checked with its cloud before Loomplane keeps it, and you're told which permissions are missing. The per-cloud pages walk through each one, starting with the [overview](/docs/clouds).


### Plan, approve, watch

Plan an environment. You see every action in order, anything in the way, and anything worth knowing. An admin approves the plan, and you watch each step build, deploy and answer. The environment then shows what runs where.


The same flow works from a terminal. Sign in, approve the code in the browser tab it opens, then:

```bash
loomctl login --url https://loomplane.example.com
loomctl analyze mono
loomctl manifest save mono -f loomplane.yaml
loomctl plan mono --env production
loomctl approve <plan-id>
```

CI has nobody to approve a code, so it uses an API key from **Settings, API keys** instead. See [CI with loomctl](/docs/guides/ci-with-loomctl) for pipelines.

## Join a machine as a node

Got a machine you'd rather use than a cloud, even one behind a router? Join it as a node. With `loomctl` logged in, run this on the machine:

```bash
sudo loomctl node join --allow probe
```

The machine may not have `loomctl` yet. Then add a node in the dashboard (**Nodes**, **Add node**), tick what Loomplane may use, and paste the one line it gives you. Either way the node dials out, so there's no port to open, and it shows under **Nodes** once it connects.

Today a node reports what the machine has and takes signed updates. Deploying to it comes next. [Nodes](/docs/clouds/nodes) covers the rest, including why allowing `docker` hands over root on that machine.

## Develop Loomplane locally

This is for working on Loomplane itself, or kicking its tires. You'll need Go 1.26 (the right patch release downloads itself), Node.js 24 with pnpm, and Docker with Compose for the local PostgreSQL.

```bash
make up                                       # PostgreSQL on localhost:55532
```
