```bash
cp config.local.yaml.example config.local.yaml
make setup
make run
```

`make run` builds everything and starts the API and the analysis worker. Open [localhost:8780](http://localhost:8780), create an account and name your organization.

For hot reload while you change Loomplane, run `make dev` instead. It serves the dashboard on [localhost:5173](http://localhost:5173) and reloads the API as you edit.

No Go or Node on your machine? `make stack` builds the image and runs everything in Docker on the same port. It runs in development mode with the development secret key, which is fine on a laptop and nowhere else. Production refuses to start unless you set `LOOMPLANE_ENVIRONMENT=production`, `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` and an https `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL`.

pages.title: Configuration
pages.description: Every LOOMPLANE_ environment variable and config.yaml setting, with its default and the rules Loomplane enforces at startup.
pages.text:
Loomplane reads `config.yaml` from its config directory, then `config.local.yaml` beside it, with `LOOMPLANE_` environment variables wired into the YAML as `"${LOOMPLANE_SOMETHING:-}"`. A key in `config.local.yaml` wins over `config.yaml`. When a variable is unset, the built-in default applies. `loomplane` also loads a `.env` file from its working directory, if there is one.

The config directory is the current directory, or `LOOMPLANE_CONFIG_DIR`. The Docker image sets that to `/etc/loomplane`. `config.local.yaml` is ignored by Git, so it's the place for your own overrides. Keep secrets in the environment, not in either file.

## Core

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_ENVIRONMENT` | `development` | `development`, `staging` or `production`. Production refuses the development secret key and an `http://` public URL |
| `LOOMPLANE_HTTP_ADDR` | `:8780` | Where the API listens |
| `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL` | `http://localhost:8780` | The address browsers and the CLI reach Loomplane at. Recovery and invitation links are built from it, and it's the issuer [keyless connections](/docs/clouds/keyless) trust, which needs https on a host the internet reaches. Must be an absolute URL, and https in production |
| `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY` | A development key | 32 random bytes, base64 (`openssl rand -base64 32`). Every credential and secret is encrypted with keys derived from it. Keep it safe and away from your backups |
| `LOOMPLANE_DATABASE_URL` | Required | PostgreSQL DSN. Falls back to `DATABASE_URL`, which platforms like App Platform, Render, Heroku and Miget set for you |
| `LOOMPLANE_DASHBOARD_DIR` | `apps/dashboard/dist` | The built dashboard. Without one the API still runs and serves no dashboard |
| `LOOMPLANE_STORAGE_URL` | `.loomplane/storage` | Where deployment sources are kept, as `file:///path` |
| `LOOMPLANE_ARTIFACT_BUCKET` | `loomplane-artifacts` | The artifact bucket name |
| `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_URL` | Unset | An independent backend for recovery objects, such as an S3-compatible URL. Empty uses the artifact backend |
| `LOOMPLANE_BACKUP_BUCKET` | `loomplane-backups` | The bucket for recovery objects |
| `LOOMPLANE_REQUIRE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION` | On when email is set up | Whether an account must verify its email before it can sign in or use the API. Unset, it's on wherever Loomplane can send mail (SMTP, Resend or a mail directory) and off where it can't, since nobody could get a code. `true` or `false` forces it; production refuses `true` with no mail. The account that runs first-time setup is verified by setup itself |
| `LOOMPLANE_SESSION_COOKIE` | `loomplane_session` | The HttpOnly session cookie's name. Cookies are shared by every port on a host, so another authsome app on the same host needs a different name |
| `LOOMPLANE_PASSKEY_RP_ID` | `public_url`'s host | The domain passkeys are bound to, such as `example.com`. A browser only offers a passkey on that domain or its subdomains. Changing it strands every passkey already registered, so set it before people add any |
| `LOOMPLANE_PASSKEY_ORIGINS` | `public_url`'s origin | Comma-separated origins people sign in from with a passkey, each on the RP ID or a subdomain of it. On `localhost` the page's own origin also works, so the Vite dev server needs nothing set |
| `LOOMPLANE_AUTHSOME_APP_ID` | Built in | The authsome app (`aapp_...`) that holds Loomplane's users |
| `LOOMPLANE_AUTHSOME_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` | Built in | That app's public key |

## Planning, drift and providers

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_PLANNING_APPROVAL_WINDOW` | `168h` | How long a plan waits for a decision, from `1m` to `2160h` (90 days) |
| `LOOMPLANE_PLANNING_ENDPOINT_DENIED_CIDRS` | Unset | Ranges an endpoint check from a Kubernetes target never connects to, as a comma-separated list such as `10.20.0.0/16,192.0.2.7`. A bare address is one host |
| `LOOMPLANE_DRIFT_INTERVAL` | `30m` | How often deployments are compared with what's live. `0` turns it off. Otherwise at least `1s` |
| `LOOMPLANE_PAUSED_PROVIDERS` | Unset | Comma-separated target names whose plans are review only. A name that isn't a target stops startup |
| `LOOMPLANE_WORKER_HTTP_ADDR` | `:8781` | Where `loomplane-worker` serves its health checks |
| `LOOMPLANE_ANALYSIS_WORK_DIR` | System temp directory | Where checkouts are extracted during analysis |
| `LOOMPLANE_ANALYSIS_CONCURRENCY` | `2` | Analyses one worker runs at once. At least 1. Each can unpack up to 2 GiB |

Loomplane's own host, its database, its API and its provider plugins are always refused by endpoint checks, as are loopback, link-local and `0.0.0.0/8` addresses, AWS's IPv6 metadata service, and the NAT64 forms of all of these. Other private ranges are dialable, since real endpoints live there.

## GitHub

Set the five App settings together, or none. Loomplane refuses to start with some of them set. See [Private repositories](/docs/guides/private-repositories).

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_API_URL` | `https://api.github.com` | GitHub's REST API, or your GitHub Enterprise Server's `/api/v3` |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_WEB_URL` | `https://github.com` | Where people install the App and sign in |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_APP_ID` | Unset | The App ID |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_APP_SLUG` | Unset | The App's slug |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY` | Unset | The PEM itself. Newlines written as `\n` work |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE` | Unset | The path to the PEM, instead of the key itself |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The App's OAuth client ID |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The App's OAuth client secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` | Unset | The secret GitHub signs deliveries with. Empty turns webhooks off |

## Bitbucket

Public Bitbucket Cloud repositories need none of this. To read private ones, set the client ID and secret together, or neither. Loomplane refuses to start with only one of them set.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_API_URL` | `https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0` | Bitbucket Cloud's REST API |
| `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_WEB_URL` | `https://bitbucket.org` | Where repository archives are served |
| `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The OAuth consumer's key |
| `LOOMPLANE_BITBUCKET_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The OAuth consumer's secret |

## GitLab

Public projects on gitlab.com need none of this. Set the client ID and client secret together, or neither. Loomplane refuses to start with only one. See [GitLab repositories](/docs/guides/gitlab-repositories).

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_API_URL` | `https://gitlab.com` | Where Loomplane reads gitlab.com from. Change it only to point at a test double |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The Application ID of the OAuth application registered on gitlab.com |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | That application's Secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_ALLOW_ORGANIZATION_HOSTS` | `true` | Whether organizations may add a self-managed GitLab of their own. `true` or `false` |
| `LOOMPLANE_GITLAB_WEBHOOK_URL` | Unset | Where GitLab reaches the webhook, when the public URL isn't an address GitLab can reach. Empty uses `LOOMPLANE_PUBLIC_URL` |

Self-managed GitLabs that you trust are a list, so they have no variable. Put them under `gitlab.hosts` in `config.local.yaml`.

## Email

An empty host, with no Resend key or mail directory, disables email. Setting a username, password or sender without a host is an error.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_MAIL_DIR` | Unset | Writes each email to this folder as an `.eml` file instead of sending it. Development only; production refuses it |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_HOST` | Unset | The SMTP server |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_PORT` | `1025` | Its port, 1 to 65535 |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_USERNAME` | Unset | Set with the password |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_PASSWORD` | Unset | Set with the username |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_FROM` | Unset | A single sender address |
| `LOOMPLANE_NOTIFICATIONS_SMTP_TLS` | `false` | Implicit TLS, commonly on port 465. Production requires it |

## Push notifications

Loomplane can send phone notifications through a gateway that hands them to Apple and Google. A gateway address must use `https`, with no user info, query or fragment. In development, `http` works for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1` only.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_PUSH_ENABLED` | `true` | Turn it off and the app hides push settings for this server |
| `LOOMPLANE_PUSH_GATEWAY_URL` | `https://push.loomplane.com` | The gateway that hands notifications to Apple and Google. Only XRaph's gateway can reach the store app |

## Nodes

Machines that join an organization hold one connection to a replica. When you run several replicas, a request for a node reaches the replica that holds it over a hop on `/_/nodes/hop`, signed with a secret every replica derives from `LOOMPLANE_SECRET_KEY`. With one replica you set nothing here.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_NODES_ADVERTISE_URL` (`nodes.advertise_url`) | Unset | Where the other replicas reach this one, such as `https://replica-a.internal:8780`. It must be an absolute http or https URL with no user, query or fragment, or startup stops. Set each replica's own address. Use `https`, or a private network with the setting below. With several replicas on one database and no advertise URL, each replica only reaches the nodes connected to it, and logs a warning when it meets one it can't |
| `LOOMPLANE_NODES_HOP_INSECURE` (`nodes.hop_insecure`) | `false` | Allow the hop over plain `http`. The hop carries stream bytes, so turn it on only on a private network |
| `LOOMPLANE_NODES_HOP_CA_FILE` (`nodes.hop_ca_file`) | Unset | A PEM file of the roots that verify the other replicas' certificates. Unset uses the system roots |
| `LOOMPLANE_NODES_JOIN_RATE_LIMIT` (`nodes.join_rate_limit`) | `10` | How many joins one address may send a minute. Past it the address gets a 429 until the minute is up. `0` turns the limit off |
| `LOOMPLANE_NODES_CHALLENGE_RATE_LIMIT` (`nodes.challenge_rate_limit`) | `120` | How many connect challenges one address may ask for a minute. Every node reconnects after a restart, and nodes behind one NAT share this budget, so raise it if you run more than about a hundred machines behind one address. `0` turns it off |

## Cloud sign-in

| Variable | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_DIGITALOCEAN_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The client ID of the DigitalOcean OAuth app (`clouds.oauth.digitalocean.client_id`). Set it with the secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_DIGITALOCEAN_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The app's client secret. When both are set they apply to every organization and lock that cloud on the Cloud sign-in page |
| `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The client ID of the Vercel Integration (`clouds.oauth.vercel.client_id`). Set it with the secret and the slug |
| `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The Integration's client secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_OAUTH_SLUG` | Unset | The Integration's slug, the last part of its address on Vercel (`clouds.oauth.vercel.slug`). Required once the ID and secret are set |
| `LOOMPLANE_GCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The client ID of the Google OAuth client (`clouds.oauth.gcp.client_id`). Set it with the secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_GCP_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The OAuth client's secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_AZURE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | Unset | The Application (client) ID of the Azure app registration (`clouds.oauth.azure.client_id`). Set it with the secret |
| `LOOMPLANE_AZURE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | Unset | The app registration's client secret |

Each cloud's values lock only that cloud's row on the Cloud sign-in page, and they win over an app registered there. [Connect a cloud by signing in](/docs/clouds/cloud-sign-in) explains how to register each app, and every one of them uses `{public_url}/integrations/oauth/callback` as its callback.

## Cloud API endpoints

These exist so tests can stand fakes in for real clouds. Leave them empty in a live deployment.

`LOOMPLANE_GOOGLE_ENDPOINT`, `LOOMPLANE_VERCEL_ENDPOINT`, `LOOMPLANE_AWS_ENDPOINT`, `LOOMPLANE_RENDER_ENDPOINT`, `LOOMPLANE_DIGITALOCEAN_ENDPOINT` and `LOOMPLANE_AZURE_ENDPOINT` replace the matching cloud's API host.

The setting `clouds.enrollment_url` (set it in `config.local.yaml`) is the reachable HTTPS callback base that managed servers use to enroll. Empty uses the public URL, and a local address can't provision remote servers.

## Cloud capacity

  Automatic capacity is off by default and still being qualified. Turn it on only where you're ready for Loomplane to buy servers at your clouds on its own.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_AUTOMATIC_CAPACITY_ENABLED` | `false` | Lets pools add servers on their own, within each Cloud's capacity policy (`clouds.automatic_capacity.enabled`). Off, you can still save a policy on the Cloud's **Capacity** tab, but nothing grows and nothing waits for approval: a deployment that doesn't fit waits for a server you add. Pools never shrink on their own either way |

## YAML-only settings

These have no variable wired in `config.yaml`. Set them in `config.local.yaml`.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `database.pool_size` | `16` | Open connections. `0` keeps the driver's default |
| `orchestration.concurrency` | `4` | Jobs one process runs at once. At least 1 |
| `orchestration.poll_interval` | `1s` | How often idle workers look for jobs |
| `identity.base_path` | `/authsome` | Where authsome's API is mounted |
| `providers.plugins` | `[]` | A list of `{url, token}`. See [Provider plugins](/docs/extending/provider-plugins) |

`providers.paused` also accepts a YAML list, in place of the variable.

## AI

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_ENABLED` | `false` | Turns on the [AI section](/docs/ai) (`ai.enabled`): the Models and AI settings pages, their API and the model kinds. Off, a plan with a model resource gets a `catalog-feature-off` problem, and models already running keep running |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_MODELS_HUGGINGFACE_URL` | `https://huggingface.co` | The Hugging Face Hub, or a mirror of it, that Loomplane reads repos, model cards and gated checks from, and that model engines download weights from (`ai.models.huggingface_url`). The workspace's Hugging Face token is sent there, so it must be https, with plain http allowed only for `localhost` or a loopback address. A user, query or fragment stops startup. vLLM and Text Embeddings Inference get a mirror as `HF_ENDPOINT`, and llama.cpp fetches its GGUF from it |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_PROVIDER` | `anthropic` | The provider the infra agent uses by default (`ai.provider`): `anthropic`, `openai` or `openai-compatible`. Only read when `ai.enabled` is on |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_API_KEY` | empty | The server's API key for that provider (`ai.api_key`). It's optional even with the agent on, because a workspace can bring its own key. Loomplane never logs it or serves it to the dashboard |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_BASE_URL` | empty | The provider's endpoint (`ai.base_url`). You need it for `openai-compatible`, and it overrides the default endpoint for the others. It must be http(s) without a user or password, and https in production unless it's `localhost` |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_MODEL` | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | The agent's default model (`ai.model`). It isn't the `ai.models` registry block below, which only says where model weights come from. The agent uses `claude-haiku-5-5` for cheap summarising steps |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` | empty | The provider for retrieval embeddings (`ai.knowledge.embedding_provider`): `openai` or `openai-compatible`. Anthropic has no embeddings API, so it can't be used. Empty turns retrieval off |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_EMBEDDING_API_KEY` | empty | The key for the embedding provider (`ai.knowledge.embedding_api_key`). Never logged or served |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_EMBEDDING_BASE_URL` | empty | The embedding endpoint (`ai.knowledge.embedding_base_url`). Required for `openai-compatible` |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_EMBEDDING_MODEL` | empty | The embedding model (`ai.knowledge.embedding_model`). Required once a provider is set. Pick one whose native size is at most 2000 dimensions, such as `text-embedding-3-small` |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS` | `1536` | The vector size (`ai.knowledge.dimensions`), from 1 to 2000. It must match the embedding model, and every workspace shares it, because the vector column has one fixed size. `text-embedding-3-small` at 1536 is the default |
| `LOOMPLANE_AI_DOCS_BUDGET_USD` | `5.00` | The most indexing the docs may spend, in USD (`ai.knowledge.docs_budget_usd`). A decimal above 0 and at most 1000. Checked only when an embedding provider is set |

Knowledge also needs pgvector in Postgres, and the embedding model needs a price: an OpenAI model nexus lists, or an `ai.prices` entry for an `openai-compatible` one. Without either, nothing else changes. Knowledge stays off and the settings page says why. [Knowledge](/docs/agents/knowledge) has each reason and its fix. The docs are indexed once per release, billed to a `loomplane-system` tenant and capped by `LOOMPLANE_AI_DOCS_BUDGET_USD`.

With `ai.enabled` on, Loomplane checks these at startup and names the key that's wrong. With it off, none of them are checked, so a stray variable can't stop a server that doesn't run the agent.

`ai.prices` has no variable. Set it in `config.local.yaml` as a list of `{provider, model, input_per_million, output_per_million}`, in decimal USD such as `"3"` or `"0.80"`. The agent uses server prices only: nexus's own catalog, plus the models you list here. A price a workspace sets on its own provider key doesn't apply to the agent, so a model nexus doesn't know needs an entry here. Each provider and model pair can appear once.

Embeddings are priced the same way. For `openai`, Loomplane uses nexus's own price for the embedding model, so `text-embedding-3-small` needs no entry. For `openai-compatible`, the embedding model needs an `ai.prices` entry with provider `openai-compatible` and the model name, and its `input_per_million` is the embedding price. Without one, the server refuses every embedding. Set both amounts to `"0"` for a local model that costs nothing.

## Process and container

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_CONFIG_DIR` | The directory that holds `config.yaml` |
| `LOOMPLANE_PROCESS` | `api` (default) or `worker`. The Docker image's entrypoint starts `loomplane` or `loomplane-worker` from it, for platforms such as Miget that drop `command:` overrides. Any other value stops the container |
| `LOOMPLANE_PORT` | The host port `make stack` publishes. Defaults to 8780 |
| `LOOMPLANE_URL`, `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY` | Used by `loomctl`, not the server |

The production Compose bundle also reads `LOOMPLANE_IMAGE`, `LOOMPLANE_DOMAIN`, `ACME_EMAIL`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `POSTGRES_IMAGE` and `CADDY_IMAGE`. See [Production on Docker](/docs/operations/production-on-docker).

## Federation

  Federation is still being built. Leave every switch below at `false` unless you're working on it. Enabling the listener doesn't qualify a cloud provider or make a service reachable across clouds.

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_ENABLED` | `false` | Authorized in-process destination management. Doesn't enable traffic or public routes |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_IDENTITY_ENABLED` | `false` | Local SPIRE administration and enrollment cleanup. Needs the switch above |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_IDENTITY_ORGANIZATION_ID`, `..._TRUST_DOMAIN`, `..._ADMIN_SOCKET` | Unset | Its scope and canonical Unix socket address |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_RUNTIME_ENABLED` | `false` | A separate mTLS agent listener. Needs `ENABLED` |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_RUNTIME_LISTEN_ADDRESS` | Unset | An explicit IP and port |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_RUNTIME_ORGANIZATION_ID`, `..._TRUST_DOMAIN`, `..._WORKLOAD_API`, `..._SIGNING_KEYS_FILE` | Unset | Scope, SPIRE Workload API socket and scoped signing keys. Must match the identity scope when both are on |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_LAUNCH_ENABLED` | `false` | Needs runtime and identity |
| `LOOMPLANE_FEDERATION_LAUNCH_CONTROL_ENDPOINT`, `..._AGENT_IMAGE`, `..._TRUST_GENERATION` | Unset, unset, `0` | Launch settings |

pages.title: HTTP API
pages.description: How to authenticate to Loomplane's API, where its OpenAPI document lives, and what each route group does.
pages.text:
Everything the dashboard and `loomctl` do goes through one HTTP API. The OpenAPI document is served at `/openapi.json`, and `/swagger` in development. `pkg/client` is a typed Go client for it.

## Authentication

Every route under `/api/v1` except `/api/v1/public-config` sits behind a guard. It accepts an authsome session or a Loomplane API key as a bearer token:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOOMPLANE_API_KEY" \
  https://loomplane.example.com/api/v1/projects
```

Session cookies also work (authsome sets an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax cookie), and that's what the dashboard uses. The organization comes from the session or key. The dashboard sends `X-Loomplane-Org` with the organization it believes it's in, and a mismatch returns 409. Make an API key under **Settings, API keys**. API keys can only be created and revoked from a signed-in session, and not with another key.

`GET /api/v1/session` returns who you are, your organization and your permissions.

## Route groups

All paths are under `/api/v1`.

| Group | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `/projects` | Projects and their sources, environments, analyses, manifest (get, put, draft, edits, revisions), plans, rollbacks, release watches, deployments, bindings, graph, variables, backup policies and recovery |
| `/projects/{id}/clouds`, `/cloud-changes`, `/cloud-syncs` | Project views of Clouds, targets, placement previews and syncs |
| `/projects/{id}/domain-routes`, `/route-operations` | Domain routes and their operations |
| `/analyses` | One analysis and its graph |
| `/plans` | Get a plan, approve it, reject it, read its deployment, read a promotion's soak |
| `/deployments` | Get a deployment, read its logs, its canary and its release watch, retry it |
| `/variables` | Organization-wide variables |
| `/connections` | Cloud connections: create, check, replace a credential, delete, read storage |
| `/connection-clouds`, `/providers` | The cloud types you can connect, and the provider catalog |
| `/clouds` | Organization Clouds: targets, grants, servers, pools, changes and syncs |
| `/dns-zones` | Organization DNS zones |
| `/catalog` | Catalog endpoints and kinds |
| `/github` | GitHub installations and the repositories they can read, plus the webhook |
| `/api-keys` | List, create and revoke API keys |
| `/members`, `/invitations` | People |
| `/teams` | Teams |
| `/notifications` | Notifications, preferences, retry and signed webhooks |
| `/agent/reports`, `/agent/watcher` | The built-in agent's reports and its watcher, while the agent is on. See [Agent reports](#agent-reports) |
| `/service-backups`, `/service-restores`, `/service-backup-retirements` | Database recovery |
| `/native-recovery-sources`, `/native-recovery-copies` | Native cloud snapshots and copies |
| `/infrastructure` | Ctrl Plane's status, and the server enrollment callback |
| `/activity` | The audit trail |
| `/usage` | Spend this month, and requests and latency, read from each connected cloud ([what each reports](/docs/clouds/spend-and-traffic)) |
| `/realtime` | Live events |
| `/session`, `/public-config` | Who you are, and what the sign-in page needs |

The document at `/openapi.json` has every operation, its parameters and its schemas. It's the source for the dashboard's generated clients (`make gen-client`).

## Key flows

Analyze, plan and approve with `curl`:

```bash
# Analyze
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}' "$URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT/analyses"

# Plan an environment
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"environment":"production"}' "$URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT/plans"

# Approve the revision you read
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"revision":"..."}' "$URL/api/v1/plans/$PLAN/approve"
```

Planning runs in the background. The create call returns the plan at once, so read `GET /api/v1/plans/{id}` until it's done planning. An approval carries the plan's `revision` (and an optional `note`). If the plan's world changed, it comes back stale and nothing happens. The OpenAPI document has the full shapes.

## Promote, roll back and watch

A promotion is a plan with `from`:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"environment":"production","from":"staging","scope":["web"]}' "$URL/api/v1/projects/$PROJECT/plans"
```

`from` pins the commits and manifest revision that environment runs. `scope` still names the repositories that move. The plan comes back with `kind` set to `promotion`, and its `artifacts` say which images it reuses.

| Route | What it does | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /projects/{id}/environments/{environment}/rollback-target` | What a rollback would undo and restore, and each repository's commits. Takes an optional `deployment_id`, which has to be the newest. Changes nothing | `deployment:read` |
| `POST /projects/{id}/rollbacks` | Plans the environment back to its previous successful release. The body is `{"environment", "reason", "deployment_id"}`, and `reason` is required. Returns the plan with `kind` set to `rollback`, and a person approves it | `deployment:create` |
| `GET /deployments/{id}/watch` | The deployment's post-deploy watch: its status and verdict, the services it judges and those it can't, and any rollback plan. 404 when it has none | `deployment:read` |
| `GET /projects/{id}/environments/{environment}/watch-coverage` | How long a release there would be watched, which services a canary would ramp, and whether each other service can be watched | `deployment:read` |
| `GET /projects/{id}/environments/{environment}/release-evidence` | What the watch says about the environment's current release. `unverified` means missing evidence | `deployment:read` |
| `GET /plans/{id}/soak` | How long a promotion's source has run exactly the commits the plan moves, and whether healthily. A plan that isn't a promotion returns 422 | `deployment:read` |

A rollback that can't go ahead returns 409 (a deployment is running, there's no earlier release, or the canary already dealt with the release) or 422 (the newest deployment isn't the one you named, or the current release is a rollback), with a message that says what to do. A promotion from an environment that runs nothing returns 409, and one that holds back a repository never deployed to the target returns 412. Watch updates arrive on the realtime stream as `release_watch.updated` events. See [Promotion and rollback](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback).

## Agent reports

These routes exist only on a server with `ai.enabled` on, and answer 409 while the agent is off in your workspace. [Watching and reports](/docs/agents/watching-and-reports) explains what a report is.

| Route | What it does | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /agent/reports` | Lists reports, newest first, as `{"reports": [...]}`. Takes `status` (`open` by default, `resolved`, `closed` or `all`), `project_id` and `limit` (1 to 100, 50 by default). You only get the reports of projects whose deployments you can read | `agent:use`, and `deployment:read` on each project |
| `GET /agent/reports/{id}` | One report: its facts, evidence, findings, investigation and issue | `agent:use`, and `deployment:read` on its project |
| `POST /agent/reports/{id}/close` | Closes an open report. The body is optional: `{"reason": "..."}`, at most 500 characters. If the report has a GitHub issue, Loomplane comments there and closes it | `deployment:create` on its project |
| `GET /agent/watcher` | Whether the watcher is paused, why (`budget`) and since when, when it last ran, and `issues`: whether the server has a GitHub App, and for each installation whether it has accepted the Issues permission, with its `manage_url` | `agent:use` |

A report in a project you can't read returns 404, as one that doesn't exist does. Closing a report that isn't open returns 409, and a bad `status`, `limit` or reason returns 422.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"reason":"Fixed in the config"}' "$URL/api/v1/agent/reports/$REPORT/close"
```

A report's `issue.state` is `none`, `open`, `closed`, `waiting_for_permission` (its installation hasn't accepted Issues), `no_repository` (no repository Loomplane can open an issue on) or `failed` (the last attempt failed and is retried). `issue.error` says why when there's no issue or the last attempt failed. Its `investigation` is `none`, `queued`, `running`, `done`, `failed` or `skipped`, and `investigation_note` says why when one failed or was skipped. Changes arrive on the realtime stream as `agent_report.updated` events.

## Release reports

These routes exist only on a server with `ai.enabled` on. [Release preparation](/docs/agents/release-preparation) explains what a report holds and what the gates are.

| Route | What it does | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /projects/{id}/release-reports` | Starts a release preparation and returns 202 with the report. The body is optional: `{"from", "to", "scope", "replace"}`. `from` and `to` are environment names and default to the project's only staging and production ones. `scope` is a list of source aliases. `replace` supersedes a production plan someone else has open | `agent:use` and `deployment:create` on the project |
| `GET /projects/{id}/release-reports` | Lists the project's reports, newest first, as `{"reports": [...]}`. Takes `limit`, 1 to 50, 20 by default | `deployment:read` |
| `GET /release-reports/{id}` | One report: state, gates, evidence, concerns, and the plan and request it's about | `deployment:read` on its project |
| `POST /release-reports/{id}/cancel` | Stops a preparation that's still going | The person who asked, while they hold `agent:use`, or `deployment:approve` |

Every route needs a person acting as themselves, which includes an API key made by one. A report in another workspace returns 404. A request with a plan already open on production, a preparation already running there, or a report that has finished returns 409 with the reason. A project without a staging or production environment, or with more than one and no `from` or `to`, returns 422. Changes arrive on the realtime stream as `release_report.updated` and `release_report.deleted` events, which leave out the evidence and the concerns. Read the report again for those.

## Live events

`/api/v1/realtime/ws` upgrades to a WebSocket, `/api/v1/realtime/events` serves server-sent events, and `/api/v1/realtime/snapshot` returns the current state for REST recovery. All three use the same authenticated contract and an organization-scoped cursor.

`GET /api/v1/deployments/{id}/canary` returns where a canary release has put traffic and the verdict of every step it judged: the weights, the error rate and latency it read, the verdict and the reason. It needs `deployment:read`. A deployment that deployed everything at once returns `canary: null` and no verdicts. A retry ramps again and judges afresh, so the verdicts are the current retry's; each carries its `retry`. The same verdicts arrive on the stream as `canary_verdict.updated` events, to a subscription that names the deployment (like build output), and in the snapshot for the deployments it names. The dashboard falls back from WebSocket to SSE, then to REST recovery when the stream goes stale.

Proxy the WebSocket route with upgrades and keep the SSE route unbuffered. See [Monitoring](/docs/operations/monitoring).

## Status codes

Stale, busy and referenced-resource conflicts return 409, and invalid or blocked changes return 422. Placement reviews and syncs accept work with 202 and a persisted ID, and they take an idempotency key, so a lost response can be recovered by repeating the same request. Another organization's resources return 404.

## Go client

`pkg/client` wraps the API with the same transport `loomctl` uses:

```go
c := client.New("https://loomplane.example.com", apiKey)
who, err := c.Session(ctx)
```

pages.title: loomctl
pages.description: Every loomctl command, grouped by what it does, with its main flags.
pages.text:
`loomctl` is Loomplane's command-line client and MCP server. It calls the API through `pkg/client`, signed in as you or with an API key, so anything it does, a script can do the same way. Run `loomctl --help`, or `loomctl <command> --help`, for the flags on your version.

## Install

```bash
brew install xraph/tap/loomctl
```

On Linux, each release has a `.deb` and an `.rpm` for amd64 and arm64, and [Install on Linux](/docs/operations/linux#install-loomctl) walks through them. You can also install it from the `xraph` Scoop bucket, or unpack a release archive. To build from source, `make build-cli` writes `bin/loomctl`.

## Connect to Loomplane

On your own machine, sign in as yourself:

```bash
loomctl login --url https://loomplane.example.com
```

It prints a short code and opens the dashboard's **/device** page with the code filled in. Sign in there if you aren't already, check the code matches the one in your terminal, and approve it. `loomctl` picks up the sign-in a few seconds later. If you belong to more than one organization it asks which one to act in, or you can name it up front with `--org`. On a machine with no browser, add `--no-browser` and open the address it prints on your phone or laptop instead.

The sign-in is your own account, with your role in each organization, so you don't make or paste a key for it. loomctl renews it while you use it, and `loomctl logout` ends the session on the server as well as forgetting it here.

CI wants an API key instead, since nobody is there to approve a code. `loomctl` finds the server and key in `LOOMPLANE_URL` and `LOOMPLANE_API_KEY`, or in the file `loomctl login` writes (`loomctl.json` under `loomplane` in your user config directory, readable only by you). The environment wins over the saved login.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `login --url URL [--org ORG] [--no-browser]` | Signs you in through the browser and saves the sign-in |
| `login --url URL --key KEY` | Checks an API key and saves it in place of a sign-in. `--key -` reads the key from standard input |
| `organizations [--json]` | Lists the organizations your sign-in can act in, with a `*` by the current one |
| `organizations use ORG` | Acts in another of your organizations, by slug, name or ID. An API key stays in its own |
| `logout` | Forgets the saved login. A sign-in's session ends with it; a key still works until you revoke it |
| `whoami [--json]` | Who loomctl acts as and what it may do |

## Projects and analysis

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `projects [--json]` | Lists the organization's projects |
| `projects create NAME --repo REPO` | Creates a project. Repeat `--repo` for each repository, and write `alias=repository` to name one |
| `analyze PROJECT [--source ALIAS] [--ref REF] [--no-wait]` | Reads a project's repositories. `--source` is repeatable. `--ref` is a branch, tag or commit for one repository |
| `manifest PROJECT [--draft]` | Prints the saved `loomplane.yaml`, or a draft from the latest analysis |
| `manifest save PROJECT [-f FILE]` | Saves a new revision. The file defaults to `loomplane.yaml`, and `-` reads standard input |
| `vars PROJECT [--json]` | Lists variables. Secrets show no value |
| `vars set PROJECT KEY=VALUE [--env E] [--service S] [--secret]` | Sets a variable. `KEY=-` reads the value from standard input |

## Teams

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `teams [--json]` | Lists teams with their member counts and roles, such as `developer on checkout-api` or `admin on the workspace` |
| `teams show TEAM [--json]` | Shows a team's description, roles and members. `TEAM` is a slug, name or ID |
| `teams create NAME [--description TEXT]` | Creates a team |
| `teams delete TEAM --yes` | Deletes a team. Without `--yes` nothing is sent |
| `teams add TEAM EMAIL` | Adds a workspace member, found by email |
| `teams remove TEAM EMAIL` | Takes a person out of a team |
| `teams grant TEAM viewer\|developer\|admin [--project P]` | Gives the team a role on a project, or on the whole workspace without `--project` |
| `teams revoke TEAM [--project P]` | Removes the team's role on that project, or on the workspace |
| `projects team PROJECT TEAM` | Names the team responsible for a project |
| `projects team PROJECT --none` | Clears it |

Managing teams needs `member:manage`. Setting a project's team needs `project:update` on it. See [Teams](/docs/concepts/teams).

## The built-in agent

These need the agent on. On a server with `ai.enabled` off they print "This Loomplane doesn't run the agent (ai.enabled is off)." and exit 1.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `agent [--project REF] [--conversation ID]` | Opens a chat at a `you> ` prompt. Each line is a message, and the answer streams in as the agent writes it. When the agent asks a question you can answer, it asks it right there (`agent asks: ...`, options numbered): type the text or an option's number, or press Enter to leave it pending. Other requests print how to answer them. `/new` starts a new conversation, `/stop` stops the agent's task, `/follow` watches a task you left pending, and `/quit` or the end of input leaves. Ctrl-C while the agent answers stops its task and takes you back to the prompt. At the prompt it leaves. `--conversation` carries on one you started, picking up the agent where it waits |
| `agent ask PROMPT [--project REF] [--conversation ID] [--json] [--no-wait]` | Asks one thing and prints the answer. Text goes to standard output as it comes. Each tool the agent uses goes to standard error as `· name (risk)`, then `  ok`, `  failed: why` or `  refused: why`. A question for a person prints with how to answer it. `--json` prints each event as one JSON line on standard output and nothing else. With `--no-wait`, a task that waits for a person exits 3 and tells you the `loomctl agent --conversation ID` to carry on with. Ctrl-C stops the task and exits 130 |
| `agent conversations [--project REF] [--json]` | Lists your conversations: ID, project, title, status and when they were last updated |
| `agent conversations rename ID TITLE` | Renames one of your conversations (up to 120 characters) |
| `agent conversations delete ID` | Deletes one of your conversations, and stops the agent if it's still on it |
| `agent requests [--all] [--mine] [--json]` | Lists what the agent is asking people for: ID, kind, project, question, who it was sent to, who it's asked for, and its age. `--all` includes settled requests. `--mine` keeps what's asked of you, your teams or, for admins, the workspace. A plan to approve adds the line `approve with: loomctl approve PLAN --revision REV` |
| `agent requests answer ID TEXT...` | Answers a question |
| `agent requests provide ID` | Sets the secret the agent asked for. The value comes from standard input, hidden on a terminal, and a value given as an argument is refused. It's never printed |
| `agent requests done ID` | Says you connected GitHub or a cloud account |
| `agent requests decline ID [--reason TEXT]` | Turns a request down. The agent sees the reason |
| `agent reports [--all \| --status resolved\|closed] [--project REF] [--json]` | Lists what the watcher found: ID, severity, project, environment, title, how often and how long ago it was seen, and its GitHub issue. You get the open reports unless you pass `--all` or a `--status` |
| `agent reports show ID [--json]` | Shows one report: its facts, what the agent's investigation found (summary, likely cause, suggestions and how sure it is) and the issue link |
| `agent reports close ID [--reason TEXT]` | Closes a report. The reason is kept with it |
| `agent watcher [--json]` | Says whether the watcher is watching or paused, and why if it's paused. It also lists each GitHub installation and whether it has accepted the Issues permission, so you can see why an issue hasn't been opened |

`agent ask` exits 0 when the agent finishes, 1 when it fails, is stopped, or refuses the message (a 409: it's still on your last one, it's off for your workspace, or the budget is spent), 3 when `--no-wait` met a request, and 130 after Ctrl-C. A run Loomplane's safety checks stopped prints "Loomplane's safety checks stopped this answer." and exits 1.

See [What needs a person](/docs/agents/what-needs-a-person#requests) for who is asked and who can answer.

### Releases

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `release prepare PROJECT [--from ENV] [--to ENV] [--scope ALIAS] [--replace] [--wait] [--json]` | Asks for a release. Loomplane plans the promotion, collects evidence and has the agent review it. It prints the report's ID and path. Without `--from` and `--to` it uses the project's only staging and production environments. `--scope` takes aliases and is repeatable or comma separated. `--replace` replaces a production plan someone else has open. With `--wait` it follows the report every 3 seconds until it finishes or waits for a person, then prints it |
| `release report ID [--json]` | Shows a release report: its state and reason, the seven gates as `pass` or `FAIL` with their details, each source's direction, commits and migrations, the soak, canaries, coverage, images and budget, and the agent's concerns under "From the agent". Text from outside Loomplane is printed in quotation marks. A report waiting for a person ends with `approve with: loomctl approve PLAN --revision REV` |
| `release list PROJECT [--json]` | Lists a project's release reports: ID, environments, state, how many gates passed and its age |
| `release cancel ID` | Stops a preparation that's still going |

Preparing needs `deployment:create` and `agent:use` on the project. `loomctl mcp` has no tool that prepares a release, so a model can't start one through it. See [Release preparation](/docs/agents/release-preparation).

## Plans and deployments

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `plan PROJECT [--env production] [--from ENV] [--scope ALIAS] [--catalog] [--no-wait] [--json]` | Plans a manifest for an environment. `--from` pins the commits another environment runs, which makes it a promotion. `--scope` is repeatable. `--catalog` plans standalone resources |
| `promote PROJECT [--from staging] [--to production] [--scope ALIAS] [--no-wait] [--json]` | Plans `--to` to run what `--from` runs, reusing its images where it can. Prints a `Soak:` line with how long `--from` has run those commits and whether it was healthy |
| `rollback PROJECT --reason TEXT [--env production] [--deployment ID] [--no-wait] [--json]` | Plans an environment back to its previous successful release. `--reason` is required. It prints which deployment it undoes and which it restores, and the plan lists what it leaves in place. `--deployment` has to name the environment's newest |
| `plans PROJECT [--json]` | Lists a project's plans |
| `show PLAN_ID [--json]` | Shows what a plan would do and anything in the way, with a `Release:` line when the environment sets a release strategy. A promotion or rollback adds a line saying what it moves, which images it reuses and, for a rollback, what it leaves in place |
| `approve PLAN_ID [--revision REV] [--yes] [--note TEXT] [--no-wait]` | Approves a plan, which deploys it, and follows the deployment. `--revision` approves only if the plan is still at that revision |
| `reject PLAN_ID [--note TEXT]` | Rejects a plan |
| `deployments PROJECT [--json]` | Lists a project's deployments |
| `deployment ID [--watch] [--json]` | Shows a deployment step by step. A canary adds a `Canary:` line and a table of the current retry's verdicts (step, weight, service, verdict, errors, latency and reason). When a revert or promotion failed it adds a `NEEDS YOU` line, because traffic may still be split. `--watch` follows it and prints each verdict once as it arrives. A deployment with a post-deploy watch adds a `Watch:` section with the status, each service's verdict and the services it can't watch. The `--watch` flag follows the deployment, and the Watch section is the release watch, which is a different thing |
| `retry DEPLOYMENT_ID [--no-wait]` | Retries a failed deployment from the step that failed |
| `status PROJECT [--json]` | What runs each service and resource, with addresses and drift |

## Database services and recovery

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `services create NAME --target CONN [--kind K] [--provider P] [--region R] [--env E] [--json]` | Plans a standalone database service. `--kind` is `postgres` (default), `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis` or `valkey`. `--provider` is `server` (default), `kubernetes`, `rds` or `cloud-sql` |
| `services add PROJECT_ID --kind K --name RESOURCE --target CONN [--provider P] [--version V] [--env E]` | Plans a catalog service added to an existing project (`server` or `kubernetes`) |
| `backups PROJECT`, `backups show ID`, `backups create PROJECT --resource NAME`, `backups retry ID` | List, read, create and retry backups. `create` takes `--env` and `--request-id` |
| `backups policy PROJECT --resource NAME --every-hours N [--disable]`, `backups policies PROJECT` | Set and list backup schedules |
| `backups retention ID`, `backups retire ID`, `retirements ...` | Preview and run [retention](/docs/services/retention). `retirements`, `retirements show`, `retirements history`, `retirements retry` follow them |
| `backups retention-policy`, `retention-set`, `retention-history`, `retention-pause` | Automatic deletion policy |
| `backups native-sources`, `native-inventory`, `native-refresh` | Native cloud snapshot history |
| `backups native-copies review`, `create`, `show`, `cleanup` | Native recovery copies |
| `restores PROJECT`, `restores create BACKUP_ID`, `restores show ID`, `restores delete ID --yes` | Isolated test restores |
| `storage CONNECTION_ID [--json]` | Read-only [storage inventory](/docs/services/storage-inventory) |

Recovery commands that wait take `--wait` and `--timeout` (45 minutes by default, and it must be positive), plus `--json`.

## Clouds, targets and infrastructure

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `clouds [PROJECT] [--organization]`, `clouds create`, `show`, `update`, `delete` | Manage Clouds. With `--organization` no project argument is needed |
| `clouds assignment`, `assign`, `switch-default` | Assign a Cloud to an environment and change its default placement |
| `cloud-targets`, `show`, `create`, `update`, `delete`, `switch` | Manage targets within a Cloud |
| `cloud-grants CLOUD`, `grant CLOUD PROJECT [--targets IDS]`, `revoke CLOUD PROJECT` | Project access to a Cloud |
| `cloud-syncs`, `show`, `wait`, `retry`, `revert`, `routing`, `apply` | Follow and recover a placement change |
| `cloud-servers CLOUD`, `options`, `check`, `usage`, `preview`, `apply`, `drain`, `operations`, `show`, `retry`, `cancel` | Servers inside an organization Cloud |
| `cloud-pools CLOUD`, `save`, `move`, `recover` | Server pools |
| `dns-zones`, `create`, `update`, `verify`, `remove`, `project` | Organization DNS zones |
| `domain-routes PROJECT`, `preview`, `apply`, `show`, `retry`, `verify`, `remove`, `ttl`, `history` | Domain routes |

Most of these review before they act and apply only with `--yes`. Many take `--wait`, `--timeout` and `--request-id`. [Cloud targets](/docs/clouds/cloud-targets), [Adopting and moving services](/docs/clouds/adopting-and-moving) and [Your own servers](/docs/clouds/your-own-servers) show them in context.

## Nodes

`loomctl node` joins and manages machines that connect to Loomplane. `loomplane node` has the same subcommands. See [Nodes](/docs/clouds/nodes).

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `node join [--token TOKEN] [--name NAME] [--label K=V] [--allow ENDPOINTS] [--cloud ID] [--builder dedicated] [--edge] [--foreground] [--state-dir DIR]` | Joins this machine and installs the service. Reads the token from `LOOMPLANE_JOIN_TOKEN` too. Without a token it mints one with your login, and under `sudo` that is the login of the user who ran `sudo`. Needs root on Linux |
| `node run [--state-dir DIR] [--root-allowlist]` | Runs the node in the foreground. `--root-allowlist` trusts only a root-owned `allow.json`; the systemd unit sets it |
| `node status [--json]` | Shows this node's config, key fingerprint, endpoints and whether it runs |
| `node allow ENDPOINT...` | Widens what Loomplane may use here: `docker`, `dial`, `probe`, `kube` or `firecracker`. Writes `allow.json`, then tells the running node. Needs root on Linux |
| `node leave [--purge] [--purge-volumes [--yes-delete-volumes=NAME]]` | Revokes this node, stops its service and removes its config. The next join makes a fresh key. `--purge` also removes the containers and networks Loomplane made on this machine's Docker. `--purge-volumes` deletes its volumes and their data too, and asks you to type the node's name first; `--yes-delete-volumes=NAME` answers for you in a script |
| `node drain NAME-OR-ID [--yes]` | Stops new placements on the node's server, after listing what runs there and warning about databases with no backups. Asks first unless you pass `--yes`. Moving what runs there is a reviewed move each, in the dashboard |
| `node list [--json]` | Lists the organization's nodes |
| `node revoke NAME-OR-ID` | Stops Loomplane trusting a node |
| `node update --release TAG` | Replaces the node's binary with a signed release, and rolls back if the service won't start or stops within five seconds |
| `node verify-release --release TAG --archive FILE --checksums FILE --bundle FILE` | Checks a downloaded release against its signature |

`join`, `list`, `revoke` and `drain` take `--url` and `--key` too. `revoke NAME` only matches live nodes. A node that Loomplane revoked exits with code 77, including one that was off when you revoked it and finds out at its next connect.

## AI agents

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `mcp [--allow-deploy]` | Serves Loomplane's tools over MCP on standard input and output. `--allow-deploy` also offers `approve_plan`, `retry_deployment` and `create_rollback`. See [MCP server](/docs/agents/mcp-server) |

## Server commands

The `loomplane` binary has its own commands, run with the same configuration the server runs with:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `loomplane` (also `serve`, `start`, `run`) | Serves the API and dashboard |
| `loomplane info` | Prints name, version and environment |
| `loomplane extensions` | Lists registered extensions |
| `loomplane backup --out FILE` | Backs up the database to a file. `backup inspect FILE` reads it |
| `loomplane restore FILE [--force]` | Restores a backup into an empty database |
| `loomplane migrations` | Shows applied and pending migrations |
| `loomplane migrate` | Applies pending migrations |

`loomplane-worker` runs repository analysis. `loomplane-agent` is the federation destination agent, which isn't ready for production.

pages.title: loomplane.yaml
pages.description: Every field of the loomplane.yaml manifest, with its type, limits and meaning.
pages.text:
This is the complete field reference. For how to think about a manifest, read [The manifest](/docs/concepts/the-manifest) first. The JSON schema at `pkg/manifest/schema.json` (`$id` `https://loomplane.dev/schemas/loomplane.json`) is the machine-readable version, and it's also the MCP resource `loomplane://schema/loomplane.yaml`. Loomplane rejects unknown fields and unsupported versions. A manifest can be up to 256 KiB.

## Top level

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` or `2` | Required. `1` for all existing workflows. `2` adds the optional `federation` section |
| `defaults` | object | `provider`, `region` and `cloud_tags` for everything that doesn't set its own |
| `services` | map, up to 100 | What the application runs, by name |
| `resources` | map, up to 100 | Backing services, by name. A resource can't share a service's name |
| `gateways` | map, up to 10 | Public entry points that route by path |
| `links` | map, up to 5 | Private network links between Google Cloud and AWS |
| `environments` | map | `release`: how each environment's releases go live. Version 1 only. See [below](#environments) |
| `ignore` | object | `resources`: kinds analysis found that you don't use |
| `held` | object | `same_address`: `block` (default) or `warn` |
| `federation` | object | Version 2 only. See [below](#federation-version-2) |

Names (of services, resources, gateways, links and environments in overrides) match `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,39}$`: lower case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, 40 characters at most.

## defaults

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provider` | Provider for every service, resource and gateway that sets none |
| `region` | Region for the same. It only applies together with the default provider: a service that names another provider doesn't take the default region |
| `cloud_tags` | Up to 8 tags used to pick a Cloud target for every service with no placement of its own. Can't be combined with `provider` |

## services

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `source` | string | Required. Where the service's code is, as analysis found it: a Go main package's directory, a Rust binary's source file, a Node package's, Python project's or JVM module's directory, or a Dockerfile. A Python Procfile process other than `web` is `shop/Procfile/worker`. When two ecosystems have a service at one path, prefix the ecosystem: `go:`, `rust:`, `node:`, `python:`, `jvm:` or `container:` |
| `repo` | string | The alias of the repository the service is in. A project with one repository can leave it out |
| `kind` | enum | Corrects what analysis decided: `http-service`, `web-app`, `static-site` or `worker` |
| `build` | object | See [build](#build) |
| `provider` | string | Where it runs, by the provider's name |
| `region` | string | The provider's region |
| `target` | `conn_...` | The checked server or Kubernetes connection to run on |
| `cloud_target` | string | A named target in the environment's assigned Cloud. Can't be set with `cloud_tags` |
| `cloud_tags` | array | Up to 8 tags. Selects the one target that carries every tag. Can't be set with `cloud_target` |
| `endpoint` | object | See [endpoint](#endpoint) |
| `health_path` | string | A readiness path, such as `/_/health`. Starts with `/` |
| `port` | 1 to 65535 | The port it listens on. Without it, the one its Dockerfile exposes, or 8080 with a warning |
| `public` | boolean | Whether it gets an address on the internet. Yes for anything that serves HTTP, no for a worker, unless you say |
| `scale` | `{min, max}` | Instances. `min` is 0 or more, `max` is 1 to 100. On targets that let you choose |
| `size` | `{cpu, memory}` | `cpu` is virtual CPUs above 0 and up to 8 (such as 0.5 or 2). `memory` is MiB, 128 to 32768 |
| `needs` | array of names | Resources and services it talks to. Each gets it an address in a variable, and it deploys after them |
| `need_options` | map | Options passed to a need, by need and then by option name |
| `enabled` | boolean | `false` leaves it out |
| `environments` | map | Overrides by environment name. Takes every field above except `source`, `repo`, `kind`, `build`, `needs` and `need_options` |

`provider`, `cloud_target` and `cloud_tags` can't be mixed at the same level. An effective direct `provider` or `target` also conflicts with Cloud placement, including one inherited from `defaults`.

### build

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `context` | The directory its Dockerfile builds from, from the repository root. `.` is the root. Without it, the context a Compose file gives the Dockerfile, or the Dockerfile's own directory |
| `builder` | For Kubernetes source builds: the `conn_...` of the SSH/Docker builder |
| `registry` | The `conn_...` of the OCI registry |
| `image` | An existing image pinned as `registry/repository@sha256:...`, instead of building |

Loomplane passes the Dockerfile to the build by its path from the context, so it can sit anywhere. A service without a Dockerfile is built from its source, and `build` on it is ignored with a warning.

### endpoint

Settings for a service on your own server or cluster.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `host_port` | The published host port, 1 to 65535 |
| `hostname` | The public hostname |
| `ingress_class` | The Kubernetes ingress class |
| `tls_secret` | The name of an existing Kubernetes TLS secret |

### need_options

Options a service hands to something it needs, by need name and then option name:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    source: services/api
    needs: [fabriq]
    need_options:
      fabriq:
        tenant: acme
```

The need has to be in `needs`. Option names are lower case letters, digits and underscores, start with a letter and run to 32 characters. A value is up to 200 characters with no newline or other control character. Which options a kind accepts is checked when you plan.

The dashboard and `POST /projects/:id/manifest/edits` can change these in place without touching your comments. `link` adds a need to a service (with options if you give them, replacing old ones as a whole; with none, they stay). `unlink` removes the need and its options, and fails if the service doesn't need it. `set_use` sets one dependency on a catalog resource and leaves the rest of its `uses` alone. Send one of the three per edit.

## resources

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `kind` | Required. `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `redis`, `valkey`, `mongodb`, `kafka`, `rabbitmq`, `nats`, `object-storage`, `search`, `memcached`, `clickhouse` and so on: the names analysis uses, or a catalog kind |
| `provider`, `region` | Where it's provisioned |
| `version` | The engine's version, such as `"17"`. Without it, the provider's newest |
| `target` | The `conn_...` of the checked server or Kubernetes connection a catalog resource runs on |
| `uses` | Where a catalog resource gets each dependency |
| `settings` | Values a catalog kind takes, by setting name. Names follow the need option rule; a value is up to 1024 characters. The kind says which settings it has and what each must look like, and that's checked when you plan |
| `environments` | `provider`, `region`, `enabled`, `gpu`, `target` or `settings` by environment name |

An environment's `target` replaces the resource's, and an environment that changes the provider doesn't keep the resource's target. Each setting an environment sets replaces that one setting, and the rest come from the resource.

`POST /projects/:id/manifest/edits` can change a resource in place as well. `update_resource` sets its `provider`, `target`, `gpu` or `settings`, leaving out what you don't send. A setting sent as `""` is deleted, and `clear_gpu` drops the GPU. Send `environment` with it and the change goes under that environment instead, where `enabled` turns the resource on or off. `remove_resource` takes the resource out, but not while a service needs it or another resource uses it: unlink those first.

### uses

A catalog resource can depend on other things, such as a Postgres for its data or a Redis for its cache. By default Loomplane provisions a new one of each and wires it in. `uses` chooses something else, one dependency at a time, keyed by the dependency's name as the catalog lists it.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `resource` | Use another resource in this manifest. It must exist and can't be the resource itself |
| `external` | Connect to an endpoint you added to the catalog, by its ID (`endpoint_` and 26 characters) |
| `enabled` | Turn an optional dependency on or off. `false` can't go with `resource` or `external` |

Set `resource` or `external`, not both. Set nothing and you get a new one.

```yaml
resources:
  db:
    kind: postgres
  gateway:
    kind: sample
    target: conn_your_server
    uses:
      postgres:
        resource: db
      redis:
        external: endpoint_01jbz7q5mx8vh3k2r9t4w6y0ae
      falkordb:
        enabled: true
```

`sample` stands in for a catalog kind with those three dependencies, and `conn_your_server` for one of your checked connections. The manifest checks what it can see on its own: that `db` is in it and isn't `gateway` itself, and that the endpoint ID has the right form. The rest waits until you plan, when Loomplane finds out whether the kind has a dependency called `postgres`, whether `db` is a kind it accepts, and whether the endpoint answers from the target.

## gateways

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `provider`, `region` | Where it runs: `cloud-run` or `ecs-fargate` |
| `routes` | Required. 1 to 50 routes |
| `environments` | `provider`, `region` or `enabled` by environment name |

A route is `{path, to, strip_prefix}`. `path` is a prefix such as `/api` that matches `/api` and anything under `/api/`. `to` is the service name. `strip_prefix` removes the prefix first, so `/api/users` arrives as `/users`. The longest matching path wins.

## links

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `between` | Required. The two clouds it joins: `gcp` and `aws` |
| `region` | Where the Google Cloud side runs. Put it where the Cloud Run services that use it run |
| `environments` | `region` or `enabled` by environment name |

A link needs more than a connection check asks for. The Google Cloud key needs Compute Network Admin (`roles/compute.networkAdmin`). The AWS key needs `ec2:CreateVpnGateway`, `ec2:AttachVpnGateway`, `ec2:DetachVpnGateway`, `ec2:DeleteVpnGateway`, `ec2:DescribeVpnGateways`, `ec2:CreateCustomerGateway`, `ec2:DeleteCustomerGateway`, `ec2:CreateVpnConnection`, `ec2:DeleteVpnConnection`, `ec2:DescribeVpnConnections`, `ec2:DescribeRouteTables`, `ec2:EnableVgwRoutePropagation` and `ec2:CreateTags`. See [Gateways and networking](/docs/concepts/gateways-and-networking#links) for what a link builds and bills.

## environments

`environments.<name>.release` says how that environment's releases go live. An environment without a release block deploys the way it always has. The block is for version 1 manifests: a version 2 manifest that carries one is refused until federation and releases work together.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `strategy` | `direct`, `blue_green` or `canary` | Required. `canary` moves traffic to the new version in steps |
| `steps` | list of 1 to 10 integers | Canary only. Traffic percentages, strictly increasing, each 1 to 100, ending at 100. Default `[5, 25, 50, 100]` |
| `hold` | duration | Canary only. How long to watch each step, in whole minutes from `1m` to `24h`, such as `10m` or `1h30m`. Default `10m` |
| `thresholds.error_rate` | percentage | Highest share of failed requests a step may show. Above 0% and at most 100%. Default `1%` |
| `thresholds.error_rate_delta` | percentage | How far above the current version's failure share a step may be. Above 0% and at most 100%. Default `0.5%` |
| `thresholds.p95_latency_ratio` | number | How many times the current version's p95 latency a step may reach, from 1 to 10. Default `1.3` |
| `min_requests` | integer | The fewest requests a step needs before its health counts, 1 to 1,000,000. Default `200` |
| `watch` | duration | How long Loomplane watches a release's health after it deploys, in whole minutes up to `24h`, such as `15m` or `1h`. `0` turns it off. Default `15m` for `canary` and `blue_green`, and no watch for `direct`. A breach rolls the release back automatically |

Percentages are written with a percent sign, such as `1%` or `0.5%`. Thresholds and `min_requests` are allowed with every strategy, because a canary and the post-deploy watch both read them, and a promotion's staging soak reads the error ceiling and `min_requests`. `steps` and `hold` are refused with any strategy but `canary`. Environment names follow the same rule as other names.

```yaml
environments:
  production:
    release:
      strategy: canary
      steps: [5, 25, 50, 100]
      hold: 10m
      thresholds:
        error_rate: 1%
        error_rate_delta: 0.5%
        p95_latency_ratio: 1.3
      min_requests: 200
```

See [Canary releases](/docs/concepts/canary-releases) for what a canary does with these settings, and [Promotion and rollback](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback#watch-a-release-after-it-deploys) for the watch.

## ignore

`ignore.resources` lists resource kinds analysis found that the application doesn't use, so plans stop asking about them.

## held

`held.same_address` decides what a scoped plan does when a held service uses a service that was deleted outside Loomplane and that the plan creates again. The held service isn't redeployed, so it keeps the old address.

With `block` (the default) that's a problem until you add the held repository to the scope. With `warn` it's a warning, but only when the planner can tell the address won't change: a Cloud Run service created again with the name, region and connection it had, which gets the same URL. Anything else, including a replacement, is still a problem.

```yaml
held:
  same_address: warn
```

## Variables Loomplane adds

| Needs | Variable |
|---|---|
| Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB | `DATABASE_URL` |
| Redis, Valkey | `REDIS_URL` |
| Memcached | `MEMCACHED_SERVERS` |
| MongoDB | `MONGODB_URI` |
| AMQP brokers | `AMQP_URL` |
| Kafka | `KAFKA_BROKERS` |
| NATS | `NATS_URL` |
| Object storage | `STORAGE_URL` |
| Search | `SEARCH_URL` |
| ClickHouse | `CLICKHOUSE_URL` |
| Another service | Its name in capitals plus `_URL` (`API_URL`) |

## Provider names

`vercel`, `cloud-run`, `cloud-sql`, `memorystore`, `cloud-storage`, `ecs-fargate`, `rds`, `elasticache`, `s3`, `cross-cloud-vpn`, `render`, `digitalocean`, `azure-container-apps`, `azure-database`, `azure-managed-redis`, `server`, `kubernetes`, plus any [provider plugin](/docs/extending/provider-plugins). The [Clouds overview](/docs/clouds) says what each runs and provisions.

## Federation (version 2)

  Federation is still being built. Version 2 records federation proposals, and its plans stay blocked until destination agents, network drivers and policy enforcement pass qualification. Don't use it to try to get private traffic between clouds.

To convert a file, review its destinations and public exposure, change `version` explicitly, add the `federation` section and review the resulting blocked plan. Keep the original for rollback. The editor never upgrades it for you.

| Map | Contents |
|---|---|
| `destinations` | Name to `{id: dest_..., environments: {env: dest_...}}`. IDs must resolve in the organization, project and environment |
| `network_links` | `{from, to, transport}` where `transport` is `imported` or `ipsec` |
| `service_exports` | `{service, destination, exposure: private, port, protocol, identity}`. `protocol` is `http`, `grpc` or `tcp`, and `identity` is `workload` or `gateway` |
| `access_grants` | `{source_service, source_destination, export, methods, paths, grpc_methods, expires_at}` |
| `placements` | `{service, destination}` |

Each map allows 100 entries. A grant allows 16 HTTP methods, 32 paths of up to 1024 bytes, or 32 gRPC methods of up to 256 bytes (gRPC selectors look like `/package.Service/Method`). `expires_at` is RFC 3339, and an expired grant is rejected at execution even if the manifest still parses. Exports need `public: false` and an explicit service `port` that matches. Every export and source grant needs a matching placement. `needs` still controls configuration and startup order and grants no access.

Connections supply credentials through Vault, so manifests contain no tokens, kubeconfigs or certificate keys. Management is off by default and turned on with `federation.enabled`. See [Configuration](/docs/reference/configuration).

pages.title: Roles and permissions
pages.description: What each organization role can do, permission by permission, and how API keys and the Warden check fit in.
pages.text:
Loomplane has four roles per organization. They're Warden roles, checked in the service layer on every action, and each includes everything the role below it can do. A permission is named `resource:action`. Two more roles belong to identities that aren't people: [Loomplane automation](#loomplane-automation) and [the AI agent](#the-ai-agent). Neither is ever a person's role.

## The roles

| Role | Description |
|---|---|
| Viewer | Reads everything, changes nothing. Can't see secret values |
| Developer | Creates projects and environments, analyzes, edits manifests and variables, and requests deployments |
| Admin | Approves deployments, manages members, cloud accounts and secrets |
| Owner | Everything, including the organization itself |

Your authsome organization role maps to one of these: `owner` to Owner, `admin` to Admin, `member` to Developer, and anything else to Viewer, so an unexpected role never grants more than reading.

## Permission matrix

An X means the role holds it.

| Permission | Viewer | Developer | Admin | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `project:read`, `environment:read`, `deployment:read`, `infrastructure:read`, `cloud_account:read`, `member:read`, `variable:read` | X | X | X | X |
| `destination:read`, `network:read`, `service_backup:read` | X | X | X | X |
| `ai:read` | X | X | X | X |
| `agent:use` (talk to the AI agent, see its requests) | X | X | X | X |
| `project:create`, `project:update` | | X | X | X |
| `environment:manage` | | X | X | X |
| `deployment:create` (request a plan) | | X | X | X |
| `analysis:run` | | X | X | X |
| `variable:manage` (project and service variables) | | X | X | X |
| `access_grant:propose` | | X | X | X |
| `ai:edit`, `ai:tool_secret`, `ai:publish_nonproduction` | | X | X | X |
| `deployment:approve` | | | X | X |
| `project:delete` | | | X | X |
| `infrastructure:modify` | | | X | X |
| `organization_cloud:manage` | | | X | X |
| `cloud_account:manage` | | | X | X |
| `secret:manage` | | | X | X |
| `member:manage` | | | X | X |
| `repository:connect` (GitHub installations) | | | X | X |
| `organization_variable:manage` | | | X | X |
| `service_backup:manage`, `service_restore:manage` | | | X | X |
| `ai:manage` | | | X | X |
| `destination:manage`, `network:manage`, `service_export:manage`, `access_grant:approve`, `access_grant:revoke`, `federation_trust:manage` | | | X | X |
| `organization:administer` | | | | X |
| `service_backup:retire` | | | | X |

The `destination`, `network`, `service_export`, `access_grant` and `federation_trust` permissions belong to federation, which isn't ready for production.

The `ai` permissions belong to the [AI section](/docs/ai). Today `ai:read` lets you see its pages and the models deployed in your projects, `ai:edit` lets you deploy and change models outside production, and `ai:manage` does that in production and sets the workspace's Hugging Face token. `ai:tool_secret` and `ai:publish_nonproduction` are held already and guard nothing yet. `agent:use` is for the workspace's AI agent: every role holds it, viewers included, so anyone can ask the agent something. The agent's own settings need `ai:manage`.

A secret variable's value isn't readable by anyone, whatever their role.

## Teams

A [team](/docs/concepts/teams) can give viewer, developer or admin, on the whole workspace or on one project, and never owner. Loomplane copies the team's role onto each member as a role of their own, so a team's role is checked the same way a direct one is. Your effective role is the highest of your own and your teams'. The roles nest, so the highest one holds everything the lower ones do.

A project role only counts on that project. Workspace actions such as creating projects, managing members and managing clouds still check your workspace role. An admin role on a project lets its members delete that project, manage its secrets and choose its cloud connection.

`session.permissions` and `loomctl whoami` list your workspace-wide permissions. To see what you hold on one project, team roles included, call `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/permissions`. Project pages in the dashboard do this for you.

Loomplane's sync is the only writer of a person's Warden roles. A change made in Warden's console is undone the next time that person syncs, so make role changes in Loomplane. Each replica also opens up to 4 extra database connections for the sync lock, so leave `max_connections` headroom.

## API keys

A key acts as the member who made it, with their role, in their organization, and never more. A read-only key fails every permission that isn't a read. Keys can't manage keys. When a member leaves or loses a role, their keys lose the same rights on the next request.

Every key expires: 90 days by default, at most 366. Keysmith stores a hash, and the key shows once. `GET /api/v1/session` (or `loomctl whoami`) shows which permissions your key has.

## Loomplane automation

Every organization also has one identity that isn't a person: Loomplane automation. It's reserved for automatic rollback, which rolls back a release whose watch or canary failed, and it will do nothing else. It acts only when a [post-deploy watch](/docs/concepts/promotion-and-rollback#automatic-rollback) breaches, and you'll find each time in your audit log. It's there whether or not you turn the AI agent on, because automatic rollback doesn't use AI.

You'll see it as "Loomplane automation" in the dashboard and the audit log, and `pkg/client` names it the same way with `client.ActorName`. Its ID is `loomplane:` followed by your organization's ID, which is what a rollback it makes shows as `created_by` and `decided_by`. Its audit events carry `actor: system` and `actor_name: Loomplane automation`, so you can filter for them.

It holds one Warden role, `loomplane-automation`, as a service account. Loomplane writes that role into each organization the first time it checks anything there after starting, and resets it to the list below each time, so if someone widens it by hand it goes back at the next start. It holds:

| Permission | Why |
|---|---|
| `project:read`, `environment:read`, `deployment:read`, `infrastructure:read` | To read the release it will roll back |
| `deployment:create`, `deployment:approve` | To plan the rollback and approve it |
| `infrastructure:modify` | To deploy the rollback and restore its routes |

Warden isn't the only limit. The code refuses it everywhere a person works: it can't create, approve or reject a plan through the API, change a Cloud placement, choose a connection or draft a manifest. Automatic rollback and the deployment of a rollback it approved are the only things that act as it. To stop it rolling back an environment, turn that environment's watch off in the manifest; taking its Warden role away doesn't last past the next start. It can never retire a backup, and no session or API key can sign in as it. It isn't a member, so it doesn't appear among your members and you can't give its role to anyone.

## The AI agent

A workspace that turns the AI agent on gets a second identity that isn't a person. Its ID is `agent:` followed by your organization's ID, and that's what you'll see as `created_by` or `decided_by` on anything it does. It holds one Warden role, `agent`, as a service account.

Loomplane writes that role only when you turn the agent on, and only into your organization. Turning the agent off takes the role away from it. Each time you turn it on again, the role is reset to the list below, so a Loomplane upgrade that changes it reaches you then. The role is what a developer holds, minus `ai:tool_secret` and `ai:publish_nonproduction`, plus `deployment:approve` and `infrastructure:modify`:

| Permission | Why |
|---|---|
| Everything a viewer holds, `agent:use` included | To read what it's asked about |
| `project:create`, `project:update`, `environment:manage`, `deployment:create`, `analysis:run`, `variable:manage`, `access_grant:propose`, `ai:edit` | To do a developer's work when you ask |
| `deployment:approve` | To approve a plan |
| `infrastructure:modify`, only while running a deployment it approved | A deployment the agent approved runs as the agent, and deploying it writes to your infrastructure |

Beyond approving, it holds no admin permission you can use through it. `infrastructure:modify` is checked in code as well as in Warden: Loomplane refuses it to the agent everywhere except the deployment of a plan it approved, so a chat or any other agent work can't change your infrastructure with it. It can't set secrets, delete a project, change cloud accounts or members, or retire a backup, and no session or API key can sign in as it.

When you chat with the agent (which comes in a later version), it acts for you. Every check then asks about both of you, and the agent may do something only when you could do it yourself and its role allows it too. So a viewer's chat can read but never deploy, and an owner's chat still can't set a secret. A read-only API key can't use the agent at all, because `agent:use` isn't a read permission. That includes `loomctl agent requests`. When it works alone, outside a chat, its role is the only limit.

Its audit events carry `actor: agent` and `actor_name: Loomplane agent`. In a chat they also carry `on_behalf_of` (the person it acted for), and when they come from one of its tools, `task_id`, `run_id` and `tool`.

## Where this is enforced

The dashboard hides what your role can't do, but the API checks regardless. Another organization's projects, plans, deployments, connections, variables and keys aren't found, which is the same answer as something that doesn't exist. A request's organization comes from the session or key, and the `X-Loomplane-Org` header the dashboard sends only helps a stale tab find out (it gets a 409), since it never selects an organization.

[Organizations and roles](/docs/concepts/organizations-and-roles) covers the people side, and [the security model](/docs/operations/security-model) covers the rest.

pages.title: Backups and test restores
pages.description: Back up a database service on a schedule, prove the backup restores into an isolated copy, and read native cloud snapshot history.
pages.text:
A backup you've never restored is a guess. Loomplane backs up a database with the engine's own client, then restores it into a throwaway copy and checks that the application role can get in.

## Back up now, or on a schedule
